_childDocuments_.review: Mild story and gameplay spoilers with finer details omitted.I was very excited for this game when I saw development progress years ago. Beautiful art, a cool premise, and a lot of promise from its sources of inspiration. I didn't expect another Metroid, but I did expect a carefully crafted world with a nice mystery and some clean movement in service to it. Ghost Song opens up promising all three and ends up delivering on none of them, in some ways underdeveloped and in others overdesigned. It's still a gorgeous game clearly made with love and this version runs just fine, but I can't recommend it in its current state unless you have the fortitude to enjoy it for what it is.The level design leaves a lot to be desired. There are few shortcuts even after you've unlocked the scant few upgrades that influence the gameplay meaningfully; fast travel is possible, but only at specific save points that are still several rooms away from many important locations and junctions; and the progression of the game is tied to delivering items from the far reaches of the map back to the game's 'town', where you are explicitly denied fast travel, can only carry one at a time even if multiple are available to you, and nothing changes on the way back besides an additional littering of the same two enemy types that only serve to slow you down. When I wasn't delivering a macguffin, I was deliberately avoiding interacting with save points in order to control where my last save was, gaming save+quit's property of returning you to your last save point. To rub salt in the wound, you can only level up at those fast travel points, though thankfully that doesn't set your save location...Most areas are completely disconnected in theme outside of a specific corruptive biome that is reused multiple times (though only two are required with the third being optional). This biome is loosely explained but never sees a resolution, so any gravity from seeing it in multiple places around the map is lost without payoff.NPC dialogue is almost completely disconnected from the gameplay at large, alternating between voiced conversations where the Deadsuit mumbles and a character exposits, and silent text that ends up meatier but with rare relevance. There are only a couple of characters that have implied relevance to the player's origins and one of them is easily missed even if you've already combed the entire map despite spelling out a major plot point that's only vaguely hinted at otherwise. Many other minor NPCs have a habit of randomly travelling across the map in ways you would never realistically encounter them in time to stay up to date on their questlines - where failing to keep up with them between macguffin deliveries means being locked out for the playthrough. They even have unique equipment! In combination with the stricture described above, any nonlinearity the game retains transforms from freedom to obligation. But even if optional missables are no issue for you, it remains that you'll be running through the same literally empty rooms over and over as you progress the plot.The game teases you with the plot for two hours or so before dumping it all on you at the end; the climax suddenly looms near and what's left of the story scrounges itself together in a bid to - and it's over, where the grand finale never comes. Unless I missed a true final boss (which I hope is true, despite being very thorough with everything but NPCs), the game's ending resolves little of the overarching story and merely sends off the surviving characters you've had no reason to invest in.The gameplay is very simple - shoot gun and occasionally use subweapon, cash out on your overheated gun with melee attacks, use subweapons and equipment to manipulate overheat or ignore it as you see fit. The balance is all over the place and it quickly flattens out - in actuality, the gun's terribly weak even when upgraded and your gun stat is for specific subweapons, the subweapons are rarely worth spending the time to set up or the energy they ask for if they're not the single required subweapon, and melee starts off horribly clunky and quickly becomes gamebreaking by the end. For reference, the basic melee attack locks you in place despite requiring you to be right next to enemies to hit them, many of which won't flinch or have instant untelegraphed lunges. This is also a game with universal contact damage and extremely low iframes; standing inside enemies is usually a terrible idea until you hit critical mass and can ignore the damage you're eating. You can mitigate this by finding faster or higher-reach melee weapons, but it never eliminates the problem; one melee weapon is outright invulnerable while performing its air attack but still has issues being used offensively because it can't be cancelled into your singular defensive option. I used it for a couple of bosses it was overwhelmingly fitting against, but otherwise relied on the high-reach weapons, one of which had arcs hitting above and below. The fact that melee is so broken (to your pain and benefit) is unfortunate, since it's the only other way your movement changes outside of the couple of upgrades you receive. These sorely needed a way to swap between them quickly, if not just being additions to an ever-expanding comprehensive moveset, and the game is weaker with their implementation of mutual exclusivity.Many bosses and some normal enemies have enormous hitboxes that dissuade you from getting close at all unless you have a way to facetank them. There are three stats, and if you aren't picking Resolve and then adjusting the rest through your equipment slots, you're going to struggle with the bosses that take any build you might have concocted and flatten them out into "keep your distance and wait your turn". Many attacks are not telegraphed, have no predictive pattern, and do very high damage in a game that has limited and delayed healing; doesn't feel very great when each boss only has a couple of attacks, too. There's nothing to chance on hoping most bosses won't do that one move that will instantly catch you; you WILL frequently pay the price for doing anything interesting and it had better be worth it.There's a sprint mechanic but you're mostly spending stamina to move at normal speed for a while; horizontal speed is glacially slow without a different upgrade that basically replaces sprinting. You cannot sprint defensively because you need to build up speed, you cannot use it offensively outside of a specific melee weapon that has a dash attack, and entering and leaving sprint is extremely clunky, requiring you to be on the ground and not performing other actions. It's almost exclusively reserved for running through rooms you're already familiar with, and even then it's so strict and muted that there's not much benefit to trying to get use out of it.Visual feedback on player actions is generally poor. It's hard to tell when your iframes begin and end, whether you just took a single instance of damage or two that were independently tracked, and whether your gun is hot enough for the bonus melee damage to kick in. There's screen shake everywhere, too - for melee attacks, for taking damage, for firing some weapons - and there's no way to turn it off or at least subdue it. It can be very hard to tell what hit you in darker or more detailed rooms. Spike traps or enemy pits in your first blind visit to a room can be devastating because of this.There's too little good that came to fruition and too much bad that bogs it down, but there is definitely good, and I'm hoping for Old Moon's success moving forward - just can't recommend Ghost Song right now. Some patches and a bit more content tying up the endgame would do this game huge favors.

_childDocuments_.review: I appreciate when a lot of effort goes into creating and presenting a believably alien world in a Metroidvania. Where one is lost from the onset, piecing the world and lore bit by bit, and it's done masterfully here. - amazing use of parallax with both background and foreground utilising similar visual elements as the enemies you face, albeit appearing dormant. Sometimes they stir, other times they wake up and attack and it gives off the feeling of constant unease. This applies to exploration, with narrow pathways and jumping into the unknown, quite the unnerving experience. I do appreciate that goo, blood and tar coat your outfit as you traverse various landscapes too. - plays a huge part and ambience is used heavily. Sounds are alien and serve to create an atmosphere of foreboding and unease. The soundstage can be wide or suffocatingly small – the crackle of heat on your weapon, sound of crumbling rocks, gurgling corridors lined with infection, metal on metal footsteps reverberating across a chasm or simply incorporating the noise of silence, that loud foreboding silence. There’s a great soundtrack here too if you’re into ambient instrumental/electronic fusion. You’ll hear a sombre piano progression or a melancholic guitar strum set the scene for a desolate and abandoned world. there’s plenty of lore to unpack and discover, quite the imaginative universe. Voiced dialogue is very welcome, breathing warmth into the world and grounding the characters. There’s a fair amount of existential questions surrounding oneself and your place in the world. There’s a little too much self-doubting for my liking, though I can understand given the premise and where the story takes you. wise, you're balancing between your regular blaster, special attacks and melee. All ranged attacks overheat your arm canon, which in turn amps up the damage for your melee attacks due to the heat but slows your fire-rate. You choose your style, it's a decent mechanic allowing for varied attack patterns to be strung together. Upgrades are presented in modules (think charms), with a blend of balancing available suit power and the cost of said upgrades to equip. It’s the exploration to get them that’s rewarding, with hidden pathways and secrets aplenty. There aren’t that many movement upgrades though, which makes what’s present highly rewarding.One poorly communicated feature is that you can perform a suit shutdown (to change gear) outside of save points too, simply hold 'down' on the D-Pad. does borrow a little from souls-like, in that difficulty can be quite punishing from the onset. Rigid movement along with mechanically stiff combat forces you to make critical decisions, is landing that extra hit on an enemy worth the risk of getting hit in exchange?Enemies are odd and from the onset you don't really know if they're hostile or neutral. Named enemies crop up here and there and the feeling of having to dispatch something that appears to be fighting you against their own will is unnerving.
_childDocuments_.name: Ghost Song

_childDocuments_.review: This game took me a couple of hours to go from "I can play like 2 hours a day and it's chill, I'm enjoying this, but after a while I get a little bored so I have to take a break" to enjoying getting lost in its mazes and just overall letting myself be carried by its intriguing universe. The voice acting felt clumsy sometimes, but I found that endearing. Some boss fights were a little easy - or can be depending on whenever you encounter them #justmetroidvaniathings - but most were just the right kind of challenging to me. Easy enough not to feel punishing, and hard enough to still apprehend the encounter and not be certain you'll get it first try. This game had me very invested in most of its characters and very intrigued as to the lore of its world(s) and its history. Its got moments, emotionally - some bits mixed in funny with sad, tragedy with beauty, etc... this game made me feel things, and once your movement opens up and your upgrades make it so combat isn't as big a block, it's a lot of fun! No game is perfect, and I wouldn't call this one an S-tier but I will definitely keep a soft spot for it. This is a hidden gem.
_childDocuments_.name: Ghost Song

_childDocuments_.review: I wanted to like this game - I really love metroidvanias, and the art + atmosphere here is wonderful.  However, I found the combat tedious and difficult without being actually challenging, and the lack of movement options frustrating.  The overheat mechanic is great, but without movement options to support switching back and forth between ranged and melee, it hampers more than helps.  I probably will never go back to finish this, and the most annoying part about that is that there are almost certainly cool areas with great art that I won't get to see.
_childDocuments_.name: Ghost Song

_childDocuments_.review: Another one of those games that reminds you why video games are worth experiencing. This game is such an intriguing and engaging experience. Every inch is meticulously crafted, every sound is pitch perfect, and the world is haunting, yet inviting. I have more than once stopped to simply stare at the scenery, just drinking in the atmosphere. It's enchanting.And thankfully, the game play is a match! As mentioned, the exploration is constantly rewarding. It's a rare thing to find a game of this style grasp how the exploration cycle is supposed to work so profoundly. In a game of this type, you'll frequently run into paths you can traverse, lacking a particular skill. This is expected. But Ghost Song rewards you for finding those inaccessible paths. Each time I found a spot I had to revisit, I was rewarded with something like a module (think Charms from Hollow Knight), or possibly a new weapon. It means that exploring is encouraged, even if you find a path you can't follow all the way down just yet. The combat is also quite fun. The run and gun style works extremely well, with a nice balance between three main styles of attack: basic gun, melee, and special gun. There are some truly harrowing encounters, which only add to the game's entrancing atmosphere.This is gold standard for the genre. Do not skip this one.
_childDocuments_.name: Ghost Song

_childDocuments_.review: I had this game on my wish list for a long time and was super excited for it. Beautiful looking metroidvania in a art style really similar to a real metroid? SIGN ME UP!Unfortunately, the combat just sucks all of the fun out of this game. Enemy's are absolute health sponges, and combat revolves around switching from a nearly useless short-range pea shooter to a clunky melee attack, then dodge, dodge, dodge. The combat is so tedious and not fun, it just kills all enjoyment i could get from the game. The level design also nothing special. It's super pretty, but just a drag to play.
_childDocuments_.name: Ghost Song

_childDocuments_.review: Contains SpoilersWas close to being a good game. It was fun to play, but felt grindy at times. Fast travel options are limited, and a lot of gameplay elements felt overused. For example the red skulls with green glowy eyes that activate only when you have a ship part. Also every boss felt like the same boss, there isnt a single memorable boss fight in this game.I cannot recommend this game as it feels unfinished.For every good thing about the game, there's a bad thing holding it back:- Has good movement(other than sprint mechanic which is useless), but wonky combat- Good map design, not many points of interest- Lots of movement upgrades, not many opportunities to use them- Lots of upgrades for suit and weapons, but a handful of them are actually useful- Areas are beautiful and vibrant, but the bosses are lackluster (didnt feel like the bosses were designed to fit the style of combat, not to mention the janky hitboxes)- Story started out strong, ended up being pretty mediocreThe main quest is just a fetch quest where you have to go and find 5 ship parts that are scattered across the mapLeveling up anything other than gun power felt uselessThe world currently feels empty, and there are rooms that are mapped out a bit out of place on the minimapThere are too many breakable walls which are required for you to progress (they can be easily missed)The missile and the critter spawner are the only weapons you needNo closure for main character story (atleast with the ending i got)Story 5/10Art 8/10Gameplay 5/10Music 5/10Overall 6/10
_childDocuments_.name: Ghost Song

_childDocuments_.review: Aesthetically sublime, mechanically adequate, this game is the epitome of style over substance. Adjust your expectations: this isn't a super deep Metroidvania, it's more a surface level read of the genre with some really nice alien ambience. The vibe is what this game is all about, which is good, because it's all it really has to offer. This is not Hollow Knight, it's not even Super Metroid.  Combat's ok. Platforming/traversal is ok. Exploration is ok. Art is gorgeous; this is the Ghost Song experience.

_childDocuments_.review: Ghost Song is a metroidvania that takes inspiration from the great games we all love, but doesn't really give me a reason to love its use of these mechanics. The setting is great but the soundtrack is so quiet and subdued that everything feels empty. Maybe that was the point of it, but it gets old quickly to only be hearing the sounds of your blaster and enemies, they didn't really give me more to appreciate. What you see in the first couple minutes is the same sort of vibe you'll experience through the whole game. I also felt that finding the upgrades necessary to reach the objectives was uncomfortably confusing. I got lost a lot and not having a minimap made that a frustrating experience. The characters were interesting at the beginning, but the environment being so sad made them feel boring near the end of the playthrough. Overall, I just found this game frustrating. Frustrating exploration with no minimap, bad decision for a Metroidvania. Frustrating that I can't heal except a few times and then I need to have a rest to refill my heals. I understand this is a souls-like trope, however I find it frustrating in souls games as well, I would've felt better if enemies dropped health in small quantities like many Metroidvanias.Frustrating that statues and save spots were separate things. I don't see who would enjoy only being able repair or level up at certain spots on the map. Frustrating that boss fights were not interesting mechanically, and they deal so much damage, and then if you happen to die you'll be even more at a disadvantage because your max health is lowered and you can't repair because most likely the save point that you spawned at doesn't have a statue and going to a statue would take so long that instead you decide to just try the boss again. I really wanted to like this game, but I ended up finishing it just to check it off the list and immediately uninstalled.
_childDocuments_.name: Ghost Song

_childDocuments_.review: Ghost Song has a great atmosphere, but the combat feels more like a chore than fun, and you should only get the game if you can't get enough of metroidvanias.The atmosphere and the general theme of the game is great. Every single piece of environment gives you the feeling that you are inside a living, breathing world. The variety of build options is nice. It is great to have multiple ways to deal with enemies by changing your loadout in a metroidvania, and Ghost Song offers that as well. The combat system is so clunky. None of the weapons or fighting styles in general I tried felt great. Both melee and ranged combat styles felt frustrating. When it comes to the enemies and boss fights, they seemed uninspired. The bosses' attack patterns are not fun to play against, they are neither hard nor easy, but just plain. Another problem I had with the game is about pacing. You may unlock the fast travel option pretty late in the game depending on your journey, which is frustrating.  I had a really hard time dashing and running at the same time, and my fingers were hurting by the time I progressed a considerable amount in the game.To sum it up, I'd say that

_childDocuments_.review: An absolutely gorgeous trek through an alien moon. This is a game that fans of the metroidvania genre better not miss. I haven't explored a world this alien since Zebes itself!What I wasn't expecting was that the game seems to have a surprisingly interesting and mysterious story as well. The central mystery around your character, known simply and Deadsuit, has me wondering what's going on.Finally, I'm really enjoying the gameplay itself. The game feels a tiny bit stiff, but the world is designed around this so it's not like I'm struggling with the controls to get the games objectives accomplished. After I beat this one I'll come back and update if I have anything more to say. As of now, I can't recommend it enough!
_childDocuments_.name: Ghost Song

_childDocuments_.review: While I agree with some negative reviews, I don't think it's enough to call the game objectively bad, especially not enough to warrant a negative review. From a technical standpoint, everything works. Outside of that a lot of stuff people complain about is subjective. I ultimately did enjoy the time I spend with the game, but it is not flawless.My personal gripes are: - very few fast travel stations that force you to backtrack through areas you've been through a hundred times- save locations are usually at least 4-5 rooms away from bosses, so if you want to quickly try again, you're gonna waste your time and/or health running through rooms you've emptied but that are now repopulated because the game saved when you died- it's very easy to miss out on NPC interactions/dialogue because you either had to talk to them prior, had to go through specific area but took a different route or had to go to a specific location after delivering X ship parts, often combination of all of these (which explains why there's so much backtracking and why fast travel is so limited)
_childDocuments_.name: Ghost Song

_childDocuments_.review: I followed this game when I saw the Kickstarter campaign posted in 2015 (2014? memory is hazy) and all I can say is it lived up to everything it looked like so many years ago. To keep it short and concise: The combat and movement is a middle ground of Super Metroid and Hollow Knight with a Souls esque pacing and leveling. There are standard enemies you will struggle with and revisit later and laugh at how easily you can dispose of them with an updated and leveled arsenal. All of the bosses I've encountered have been challenging and memorable. The environments are stunningly crafted and rich in detail, while not being overwhelming. There's key pieces that will fill your screen with with color and perspective, give you glimpses into what this world might have been, juxtaposed with these inscrutable details deep in the wells of this place that are microcosms of the world above, shrouded in darkness. Characters that will talk with you and give you a human glimpse into what happened on Lorian, why things are the way they are, and if maybe things could be different. Or maybe things would have always been this way. A Metroidvania that stresses more than ever, it's the journey more so than the destination, that really matters.
_childDocuments_.name: Ghost Song

_childDocuments_.review: this is one of the times when I wish I can give ok instead of yes or no as a rating, the game is the most basic metroidvania around, it does nothing new at all! it has some good elements but for me the bad outweigh the good+ good map+ decent Variety of enemies+ decent weapon options- really really poorly designed bosses - the powers are the most basic even for a basic mertoidvania,  double jump,  wall jump and dash! it is really disappointing- poor fast travel options without any added value- after each boss you need to go back to the beginning of the map without using fast travel without any reason, just to increase the play time.+/- the game takes hollow knight charm system but doesn't do anything with it+/- the story is ok with a lot of unnecessary dialogueI think the game would have been better if it was released at the beginning of the 2010s, but now and after the leap a lot of indies did it sadly really pales in comparison
_childDocuments_.name: Ghost Song

_childDocuments_.review: CHOOSE EXPLORER MODE!! After 5 hours of playing this game I can say its definitely worth a try.  The only problem I have with this game is the inconvenience with its backtracking.  There are not nearly enough save points that you can fast travel too.  If you choose the games normal mode you will lose a bit of health upon death.  The only way to replenish it back to normal is to find specific save points.  The problem is there isnt enough of them in the game.  I feel like the devs probably thought this would increase the difficulty but all it does is increase the annoyance because it takes too long to backtrack all the way to specific save points just to level up and fix your health.  If you consider yourself to be really good at super metroid or hollow knight then this probably wont be an issue for you but if your an average player choose easy mode.
_childDocuments_.name: Ghost Song

_childDocuments_.review: Holy Toledo, this game! Metroidvanias are my favorite, and I feel like the developers hijacked my brain and created a game that was entirely tailored to my interests. Everything from the eerie atmosphere, the wonderful hand-drawn environments, the music and voice work, the weapon exchange, and the glorious upgrading system....it was an exciting experience for me from beginning to end. I was enthralled with Ghost Song, and when I wasn't playing it, all I could do was think about the next time I'd get to play it. I can't wait to play this game again in the future. Old Moon, you've created a unique and immersive 2D masterpiece!
_childDocuments_.name: Ghost Song

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR - A competent metroidvania even if the dialogue and plot left me cold.Moment to moment gameplay is pretty solid. The game world is quite well designed but not particularly large and the backtracking feels more like the dev trying to fill out the runtime rather than genuine exploration and mastering of the environment. It does look nice though.Boss battles are good to passable. Some are quite creative in their design and enjoyable to fight. Some arenas are a little too cramped leading to damage rushing rather than any skill based approach. Most bosses you'll be able to kill on the first try with a bit of luck and patience. A couple will require some grinding and multiple attempts. None are frustratingly difficult.The story is fine if you're into that sort of thing, but it just doesn't do it for me. I'm all for a bit of plot in my metroidvanias, but I signed up to explore dangerous alien ruins and confront cosmic horrors. I did not agree to whinging about about poetry, tap dancing and my bloody feelings. I was way more interested in the B plot about how the planet came to be the way it is, rather than the A plot of rescuing a bunch of whiny big girls blouses.In all, a decent game worth playing if you're into the genre. I personally didn't much care for the story elements, but your mileage may vary.
_childDocuments_.name: Ghost Song

_childDocuments_.review: Poorly designed metroidvania that fights you every step of the way. It forced many soulslike mechanics that don't really fit the game and make exploration and boss fights a chore. All enemies are extreme damage sponges and no amount of progression alleviates this issue. You character on the other hand is very easy to kill and there is not much you can do to increase your survivability. I noticed multiple perks/skills you equip don't really work as described. For example, I equipped one skill that was creating a decoy every time I used a dodge, however enemies almost never attacked that decoy, making this whole skill a waste of your resources.Artstyle is pretty good, but level design sucks and there will be multiple pointless rooms with no enemies, no items, no nothing. These are just filler and the transitions between rooms isn't especially quick, making crossing longer distances a chore.There are also not enough fast travel points. There are a bit more checkpoints/save points which will regenerate your healing, but even these are often way too far from the boss, making retrying a boss fight a frustrating experience. Not to mention that dying in this game reduces your max health, which accumulates and can't be repaired at checkpoints. You can only fix that damage at the before mentioned fast travel points. This leads to situations when you are struggling against a boss and each retry reduces your chances of success and requires around 5 minutes of runback to the boss. If you want to fix that permanent damage you have to waste around 15 minutes of your time to get all the way back to fast travel point and then go back to the boss. Who thought this is a good design? Even Dark Souls 2 gave you consumables to remove health reduction.If only combat or traversal felt remotely good. No luck here too, running costs stamina and you movement speed is glacial. Combat has almost no feedback, especially considering the sponginess of enemies.Pretty negative so far, so whats good? Not much. Visuals are good, I like the use of colder colors and monster designs are pretty unique. Environments however get pretty repetitive and there aren't many highlights or interesting landmarks.Story is pretty nonsensical and the way characters talk will really test your patience. They severy overused the line of dialogue that is simply: "...". What is this? An amateur hour? Overall the writing and story feel extremely amateurish and straight up depressing. Someone projecting I guess, but come on, you are selling this to people.Playing Ghost Song has been an excersize in frustration and tedium. There aren't many redeeming qualities here and there is no way I can recommend this game to anyone. No matter the price, this is a waste of time, especially in a genre filled with so many amazing experiences.
_childDocuments_.name: Ghost Song

_childDocuments_.review: Ah man, this is a real shame. It had the potential to be absolutely amazing like Hollow Knight, but they just couldn't put forward the necessary game length for a Metroidvania to be considered great.What's here is still a good bit sized offering, but as I've always said for Metroidvanias, length is key. The bigger the game world is, the more exploration there is and the bigger path there is for characterization and sense of openness.Still good, but also a real shame. It seems weird to me that almost a decade was spent developing this, and they considered making it as an answer to there never being another Metroid made again. Surely they must have known this wasn't big enough
_childDocuments_.name: Ghost Song

_childDocuments_.review: Ghostsong could have been a niche game to experience for its compelling story and excellent atmosphere. But the plot leaves you hanging so poorly at the end. The ending feels like there should be more. Even with the second ending, you won't feel satisfied or fulfilled. There are so many questions left unanswered and so much potential wasted.
_childDocuments_.name: Ghost Song

_childDocuments_.review: Ghost Song is a beautifully-crafted game with fun game mechanics, an eerie atmosphere, a mysterious premise, and interesting paths to explore. It feels like what you would get if you smashed Hollow Knight and Super Metroid together. However, unlike those two masterpieces, this game is short and sometimes feels like a prototype project. You find a cool area, only to discover that it is mostly empty, explore it in less than 5 minutes, and move on. You frequently expect a huge boss fight at the end of an area, but there isn't one. Then, just when you're finally geared up for a huge and satisfying finale... the game kind of... just... stops.For the price point and the fun it provided, I think Ghost Song is a worthy purchase. However, for all the genuinely amazing moments you get in the game's world development and artistic direction, underneath all that polish lies a fairly basic and short-lived experience.
_childDocuments_.name: Ghost Song

_childDocuments_.review: I have been waiting on this game since it was first showcased nearly a decade ago and so far it has delivered beyond expectations.    The art direction is incredibly beautiful and disturbing at the same time, any fans of the SNES hit Super Metroid will feel right at home with how the world feels so completely alien and isolated. Traversing the environment has been very enjoyable with many secrets to be found.  Combat feels fluid and engaging, you have many ranged and melee options available to defend yourself while you explore your surroundings. This game takes ideas from Dark Souls in that you have energy and stamina that you manage in order to use your abilities so expect to be trying new things to deal with new threats and situations. While the game is difficult it doesn't feel unfair, taking your time to understand new enemy attacks and patterns is necessary. As the player you can improve your character by spending a resource called Nanogel to increase various parts of your stats such as health, energy/stamina, physical defense or gun power and by finding various equipment which either you use as an equipped item or technology that you can install into your own system.  There are limitations to much you can equip but as you increase various thresholds into your character you can start using more based on how much power is available for your upgrades.  So far the story is very interesting which each interaction with an NPC leaves you wanting to know more about what is going on with the moon you are exploring.  The voice acting is on point but minimal in most interactions which is a shame because it really adds to the harrowing somber atmosphere of the game.  Overall I am very impressed with the game so far and I really hope it gets the recognition it deserves.
_childDocuments_.name: Ghost Song

_childDocuments_.review: Metroid-Vania is my favorite genre, so I like to try interesting ones when I see them. There's many positive and negatives things to say about Ghost Song, but read other reviews for that. Here is the ultra-short version.If you familiar with the genre, it's very tight to the tropes, with a bit more of a modular "build" system rather than a linear upgrade path. Leans heavily in to tropes from Dark Souls, too, with similar exp and death mechanics and the unbelievably baffling decision to utilize the health gating system on death from Dark Souls 2 that absolutely not a single person liked. The isolating and foreign atmosphere is quickly hindered by frequent NPCs and dialog.If you're not familiar with the genre and want to try one, go play like Axiom Verge or download an emulator and try Super Metroid. This one is mid as hell.
_childDocuments_.name: Ghost Song

_childDocuments_.review: Ever play a game for a good amount of time and think: Wow...I feel like I have done a lot but gotten nowhere at the same time?Yeah, that sums up Ghost Song.It s a beautiful artsy looking game....so it has that going for it. But when you boil down to the game play, much like all "art", the fun was what had to be sacrificed to make room.Combat is just dreadfully bad. You gun has too small a range and heats up fast. When it heats up your shot speed drops, but yet....you can now melee attack better. Melee attack range is too short to be exceptionally useful. Add that your shots do maybe 20 damage to begin with...and enemies start with like 300 hp. it makes a simple battle just exasperating. And the power ups that you get at the beginning really should have been something you started with out the door. I am getting that same feeling I got playing Axiom Verge: maximum effort, minimum gain.Having a game lean more to the Metriod side of the Metroidvania style is nice...but this might me a little turned up too much on everything else that it sucks the enjoyment of exploration out.
_childDocuments_.name: Ghost Song

_childDocuments_.review: If you cannot stop playing until you almost starve to death, you know it's an awesome game.I'm hooked and loving it all the way.There are many unique traits which set it apart from other metroidvanias.Give it a shot, it's very interesting and fun. The atmosphere, story, characters and music are glorious.Controls are smooth, abilities are nice and level design is amazing.BUT it's rather short, I was like WTF when it ended and there are obviously some things I must have missed
_childDocuments_.name: Ghost Song

_childDocuments_.review: It is my BGOTY (Blandest Game Of The Year). It isn't even horrible, just... bland, nothing sticks out. Everything feels lukewarm and undercooked.-The main quest is just a fetch quest with horrible padding. -Bosses and enemies are boring.-Graphics are nice, but every area looks kinda similar. Same goes for the music.-Movement upgrades are boring, nothing you have seen before in metroidvanias and also the upgrades are just... there, no special room or events before them.-Ugh, stamina meter... It seems every game has to be dark souls nowadays-Storywise everything just happens, no buildup for anything and the writing is very awkward and dull.-Leveling is a bit pointless.-Controls are ok even though movement speed is a bit too slow. (even though there is a speed booster upgrade, but it is pointless, you barely go any faster and it consumes stamina)I had a high hopes for this game, i even backed this on kickstarter. _childDocuments_.name: Ghost Song

_childDocuments_.review: Poorly designed difficulty. Unfun mechanics. After playing another Metroidvania that got it right, Frogmonster, Ghost Song's issues with difficulty are obvious.1. Losing max health on death and having to crawl back to one of only ~5 repair locations on the map is terrible. You just lost a fight - now either go do it again with disadvantage, or do a long, pointless trek back and forth across the map so you can do it again at full strength. What the hell?2. Same for dropping nanogel/souls on death. Just because a famous game series did it, doesn't mean it's good game design . Most of the time if you drop it, it's not a huge deal. But if you drop it in a boss room - you're ♥♥♥♥♥♥. You can't just pick it up and leave. If that room holds a substantial amount of nanogel, it's essentially hostage until you can beat that boss. You can't do ANYTHING else, you can't go ANYWHERE else until that's dealt with for fear of losing it.3. Most bosses/minibosses in the game are essentially a joke - with the exception of the optional ones and the . The final boss is awful unless you cheese it. It has so much damage resistance and health, you might as well be shooting a pea shooter at it. This curve just feels bizarre. 4. In general, you have very limited 'ammo' (energy) and heat to work with - and enemies have a lot of health. You'll find that even late-game you're overheating and out of energy against a couple of basic fodder. It's just bizarre. Heat   makes sense - it's encouragement to use your melee. Except here's the thing - against bosses using melee isn't something you can always do when you're hot. They may be skirting around out of range, they may be using attacks that would punish you up close. Etc. So you can't always use it. The only good thing about Ghost Song is the non-gameplay parts of it. The visuals, the sci fi, etc. Those parts are still pretty good, in spite of the gameplay.
_childDocuments_.name: Ghost Song

_childDocuments_.review: Very mixed on Ghost Song. There are some incredibly charming moments and some quality writing buried under some slightly iffy narrative presentation — too much of it is a little too easy to miss, and thus the ending can seem anticlimactic.My first play through, I very quickly ended up returning three ship parts, not realising the game scales enemies up with each part returned. Having done so, the game actually out-scaled me quite badly, and the next few bits felt like a real slog. It felt like I needed to grind to level up a bit more, but everything was hugely bullet spongy as a result of the difficulty scaling being so aggressive.My second play through was smoother, more moderately-paced having learned from play through 1, and much more completionist in its approach, so I appreciated the story and characters much better. There are still some hefty critiques I'd make in terms of combat, however:- The invincibility time after being hit is pathetically short, and because there is no knockback the contact damage can tick again almost instantly and wipe out your health in the blink of an eye. This feels awful.- The dash move sometimes dashes the wrong direction for reasons unknown.- Many boss enemies spawn in rooms with enemies already there, adding a layer of extra difficulty to proceedings that feels a little unfair at times. The Ogre boss is especially egregious, for the adds, the water than slows your movement, and the aforementioned contact damage — just touching his flail even when it is laying still is enough to wipe out your entire health bar if you don't quickly dash away.- Aiming could do with sensitivity options and some slightly more generous hit boxes. There are a lot of small flying enemies in the game and targeting them is a bit too tricky at times, especially in boss fights which spawn a lot of bullet-spongy spores.But the story is lovely, there is some profound writing and deep ideas (now I've actually found that narrative depth, as it's kinda hidden), and the map is reasonably sized and varied with some diverse biomes. I enjoyed mapping the game out, even if it involved a lot of work fixing some of the room seams and transitions from the original in-game map.
_childDocuments_.name: Ghost Song

_childDocuments_.review: As a fan of the genre, I don't mind generic metroidvanias, but this one is held back by a mix of bad ideas and poor execution. The punish mechanics upon death and the stamina bar feel so forced that not only they don't add anything to the gameplay but also makes everything feel more like a chore. The combat feels terrible, everything takes a lot of hits and can take a big portion of your health if you're not careful. The melee combat is the worst ofender, the definition of high risk low reward, not only it consumes the stamina that is needed for the mobility tools that are fundamental, there is also contact damage that damages you at the same rate that receiving a direct hit.The balance and the pacing is all over the place, some bosses are bullet sponges that can beat you in three hits and others can be easily cheesed. You will find important items after though rooms or in some random place. There are far better options for indie metroidvanias with a soulslike flavor, like Grime or Blasphemous.
