_childDocuments_.review: Very fun if you follow the Marvel Universe...it is story rich but a bit slow in spots if you aren't used to strategy style game play. I am (Dr.) strangely hooked on going deeper into the story just because it is amazing. I do however lose track of time while i'm playing this game...which I guess means it is pretty immersive. I really love the banter between which is better, Science/Technology vs. Religion/Mysticism....which is a hot topic in our time.  Grab it on sale or not but it is definitely worth a look see if you like comics or anything Marvel!
_childDocuments_.name: Marvel's Midnight Suns

_childDocuments_.review: I've played this game at length, but the more I played, the less exciting it was.The writing is good, in the sense that most characters feel like their comics' counterparts. The character specific mechanics are often interesting representations of that character as well.However, this doesn't solve the real issues with this game. The biggest issue is that unlike most deck building games, there isn't a strong loop where you get a deck that surpasses an increasing difficulty, and the excitement of failure in deck builders. The loop is also relatively long, which makes the entire process feel slow.
_childDocuments_.name: Marvel's Midnight Suns

_childDocuments_.review: Really enjoying this. Expecting Xcom3? You're gonna hate it. Expecting usual Marvel AAA attempt? You're gonna hate it.If you're somewhere in between like me the game is really good. Combat so far is fantastic and new mechanics are still being introduced at 30ish hours.I also really enjoy the abbey stuff. But if you passed the expectation barrier at the beginning this likely will be what makes or breaks this game for you.I really like having the character and relationship building as it gives more foundation when some plot happens to any character. Actions you take in the RPG convo heavy abbey content also directly tie in to combat effectiveness through a variety of mechanics. On first play through, really liking it. It's replay-ability on future play throughs is TBD.Overall pacing is a little hit or miss at the moment for me. If I could complete multiple combat missions in a single day I would have no complaints. Typical game play loop goes.... Hunter wakes in the morning>Interact with characters/upgrade/crafting stations>select main combat mission> Return to abbey at night> explore larger abbey grounds> select a character/group for friendship building cut-scene> Hunter goes to bed> repeatAnimations transitions and movement in third person are a little wonky though. Hopefully this gets a little extra polish in early patches. And please Firaxis add a walk TOGGLE option in third person and don't make my character auto switch from slow run to super sprint.

_childDocuments_.review: This is an amazing game that, for whatever reason, got a very poor reception from the community.  I haven't followed Marvel comic storylines for decades but this is a real gem which deserved better.  The VO and story were doing pretty darn well and kept me engaged and playing through missions.I have only 4 complaints.1) Only one mission a day?  BORING!  I want to grind things out and not have to go through a whole day per mission.  You should have been able to assemble teams and send each team out on their own mission per day rather than 95% of the roster sitting idle each day.2) I am not sure I like this new trend toward adding a card aspect to everything but it works well enough but I like my games to be more skill based.  Having a random card draw just adds randomness which can screw you regardless of skill.3) I think they might have been improved the DLCs by adding more story content 4) Please, for the love of god, make DLCs standalone AND integrated into the storyline (if you must).  I have too many games to replay a bunch of them so making it to where you had to basically start a new game to get the full experience every DLC was a bummer.I bought this at full price and got the Legendary Edition with all the extra costumes but I would say to wait till it's at least 25% - 50% off if you are going to purchase.  And make sure to get the DLCs so you can get the whole experience right out of the box.

_childDocuments_.review: I never write reviews but simply this is not an XCOM game. _childDocuments_.name: Marvel's Midnight Suns

_childDocuments_.review: This is a great game! Review after review it gets top ratings. It has three elements: exploration, social, and strategy card game. All three are engaging and well developed. Some of the best writing of ANY Marvel property! You really feel like you have built a personal relationship with your team of superheros. The card play was unfamiliar and not the XCOM-like strategy everyone was expecting but it turned out to be really fun. I WANT MORE!If I was to give some critiques it would be the marketing and roll out window. Honestly the ads were confusing and only gave weight to one aspect of the game from what I saw. It is really frustrating to have such an emotionally intelligent, story driven playable comic with phenomenal voice talent get sold as a XCOM clone with a Marvel stamp. And all those XCOMers that didn't get the clone they wanted, talked crap online when they found out it was a card play strategy game. Just a huge mess, and now the people who gave it a chance despite the haters and loved it are most likely not getting an extended season pass. Not because the game does not deserve it but because of poor marketing and online trolls.
_childDocuments_.name: Marvel's Midnight Suns

_childDocuments_.review: Great game. Weakest part is the abbey/social part. The combat/cards/animations are cool and fun, every hero feels unique. Fights are can be challenging and the objectives vary enough that you don't get bored. Writing is typical marvel fare, so if you hate marvel writing, then you'll hate the script of this game, if not, you'll have no problems.Also, other than being turn based strategy, the game is nothing like XCOM.

_childDocuments_.review: While Midnight Suns is not going to be everyone's cup of tea, it is a very unique blend of gaming genres,  For myself anyway as an avid fan of Deckbuilders, Turn based tactics and (more recently) with games such as Lost Ediolons or Persona type "Friendship simulators" there is a lot to love here.  Look when I first saw some previews and reviews I thought it was gonna be worse than it is I thought I wouldn't enjoy exploring the abbey and doing superhero hangouts but honestly I find that I do enjoy those aspects of this game too.Firaxis has another long running franchise hit on their hands here if they can keep expanding on all the interesting crafting and leveling up systems and keep adding in more variance and more expansions with new characters, stories and enemies to the game anyhow.I'd say give it a try as for me I've been really pleasently surprised and keep finding myself just wanting more of pretty much everything they have got going on here.The Micro transactions are not needed  but they are not over priced either in my opinion and you will unlock enough skins in the game for most folks anyhow is my gut.  But for me I find the Legendary edition to be worth the money in this case and I really did not think I would be saying that going in.Hands down the most tactical super hero and immersive moments of  RPG type fun I've had in a super hero game since the good old days of Freedom Force.
_childDocuments_.name: Marvel's Midnight Suns

_childDocuments_.review: Hey there, fellow Marvel fans! It's your favorite Merc with a Mouth, Deadpool, here to give you the lowdown on the new game, Marvel Midnight Suns. And let me tell you, it's a real doozy.First off, the graphics are great. I mean, it's no surprise - we're talking about Marvel here. These guys know how to make things look cool. And the story is pretty sweet too - you get to team up with some of the biggest names in the Marvel universe, from Captain America to Wolverine to...wait, who are these new guys again? The Midnight Suns? Sounds like a ska band.But let's talk about the real star of the show: yours truly. That's right, I'm in the game! And I gotta say, they really nailed my personality. The witty one-liners, the swordplay, the breaking the fourth wall - it's like they took me straight out of the comics and put me in the game.The gameplay itself is a lot of fun, with plenty of opportunities for team-ups and special moves. And the bad guys are suitably bad - we're talking demons, vampires, the whole shebang. But I do have to admit, it can get a bit repetitive at times. I mean, how many times can you punch a demon in the face before it gets old?All in all, Marvel Midnight Suns is a fun and entertaining game that's definitely worth a play. And if you're a fan of Deadpool, like I know you are, then it's a no-brainer. I mean, who wouldn't want to spend hours playing as the Merc with a Mouth, cracking wise and taking down baddies? It's a dream come true. Now if you'll excuse me, I have to go practice my one-liners in the mirror. Chimichangas!

_childDocuments_.review: Early impressions are extremely positive. To get the negatives out of the way first:- Apparently this game has Denuvo. Most of the negative sentiment surrounding that is due to easily disprovable misinformation spread by people who want the moral justification to pirate everything. Everyone needs to calm the heck down.- There's some minor stuttering at first (major if you have RTX on - just turn it off, it's not worth it) as the game seems to lack shader-prewarming and caches new shaders every time a new effect plays. It's pretty minor, stops quickly, and the game as a whole is turn-based. Can't quite say "I don't care", but it's really not the end of the world.- The game uses hearts to indicate when you're making characters happy and yet it doesn't have romances. 0/10, Firaxis and/or Marvel are cowards. You can't tell me I've put up with a lifetime of on-again-off-again superhero romances in comics only to have some claim as to the importance of existing relationships in canons. Valentine's Day DLC or we riot.The Good:- While animations are admittedly clunky in dialogue, there does seem to be a tremendous amount of it. Can't say it bothers me all that much. It's far above the quality of most games of this scale. The combat animations are fantastic, and the game as a whole is bright and colorful with great environmental destruction during battle.- The combat is excellent. The card system doesn't feel tacked on, and while combat as a whole does feel strange compared to other tactics games, it does feel extremely superhero-y and that's definitely the point. Your heroes constantly mix up their moves, chucking foes into each other, webbing people in place, and - when powered up - absolutely annihilate the battlefield. This is not XCOM, where individual soldiers are weak and need to work as a team. You'll be badly outnumbered, blasting even strong opponents to bits turn after turn, with the primary danger coming from strong enemies, bosses, or getting swarmed. Doesn't seem easy, just well-balanced for what comic book characters should feel like in something like this.So that's a quick run through from about 4 hours of play. I'm very much so enjoying my time with the game, even with a few reservations. You definitely need to love Marvel, and want a tactics/dating-sim-with-no-dating vibe so you can be best friends with Spider-man even if Magick will never make googly eyes at you. I do want that, so strongly recommend so far.
_childDocuments_.name: Marvel's Midnight Suns

_childDocuments_.review:
After centuries of sleep, Lilith, Mother of Demons, has been revived by Hydra through a twist of dark magic and science. Lilith stops at nothing to complete an ancient prophecy and bring back her evil master, Chthon. Pushed to the brink, the Avengers desperately look to fight fire with hellfire and enlist the help of the Midnight Suns - Nico Minoru, Blade, Magik and Ghost Rider - young heroes with powers deeply rooted in the supernatural, formed to prevent the very prophecy Lilith aims to fulfill.

In the face of fallen allies and the fate of the world at stake, it will be up to you to rise up against the darkness!

Marvel's Midnight Suns is a new tactical RPG set in the darker side of the Marvel Universe, putting you face-to-face against demonic forces of the underworld as you team up with and live among the Midnight Suns, Earth's last line of defense.

name: Infernax
detailed_description: ● Multi-endings based on player's decisions. ● Challenging castle-dungeons and lots of boss battles. ● Ruthless bloodthirsty monsters that want you super duper dead. ● Level up system to tailor your experience to your liking. ● Buy new items and unlock skills to help you in your quest of reversing the curse. ● A dangerous and unique open world with many secret areas to uncover. ● Play with friends, or by yourself with the addition of a support character, Cervul the squire. ● Pucker up buttercup because it's about to get gory. Infernax is the adventures of a great knight who returns to his homeland only to find it plagued with unholy magic. While on your quest to find and destroy the source of this corruption by any means necessary, you will face ruthless creatures, dangerous beasts, and precarious terrains. Every decision you make is crucial, would you rather: ● slay or help someone? ● use your experience gained from slashing monsters to get more life, mana or damage? Think well before deciding on what to do my friend. A single choice can change the game; remember that thing you did to that guy? Farmer Pepper remembers. Smash as many monsters as you can to get some money, spend your savings to buy better weapons and armors from the blacksmith, gear up and get stronger for this journey of smashing even more faces! Every choice you make open up different side quests to obtain powerful weapons and skills or money Storm the Castle and slay their bosses before more innocent fall to the mysterious curse that plagues your land. In the end, only you can rid the land of Upel of these monsters, whichever way you decide to do it; you do you, dude... ● DEUX OR DIE UPDATE Return to the lands of Upel as the Duke Alcedor, this time joined by your trusty squire Cervul as you attempt to regain control from the forces that plague your duchy. The new mode is playable as a standard 2-player local co-op or as one player hot-swap mode that allows a single person to control both characters by switching on the fly. Use Cervul's various tools to bring victory, or ruin, to the land and the people that inhabit it in this newly rebalanced version of the game!

_childDocuments_.review: I am writing this positive review after having beaten Infernax on Classic Mode with the "Ultimate Good" ending unlocked. It took me 11 hours to reach this point, during which I unlocked 15 out of the game's total of 30 achievements. Overall, I was deeply impressed. My playthrough saw me fighting, platforming and adventuring across tightly designed areas and dungeons in a well-realized setting with very reasonable difficulty design and a steady and satisfying sense of character progression.The biggest hurdle I faced early on in Infernax was the fact that playing on Classic Mode meant that dungeons didn't have any checkpoints. Losing all my lives would send me all the way back to the dungeon's entrance and erase any progress I had made prior to saving. At first, this punishing system made me want to switch to Casual Mode so that I could enjoy having safety nets within dungeons that would make death would less punishing. I viewed this safety net as especially important in case I died prior to a boss, because having a checkpoint within a dungeon would prevent me from suffering through any excessively long runbacks. However, I quickly realized that Infernax was one of the extremely few instances of a game where no checkpoints in dungeons was justified. Here is why:Because of all of this, Infernax has completely justified its reason for having its Classic Mode both be free of checkpoints in its dungeons and be brutal enough to take away any progress I made between the time I saved your progress and lost all my lives in a dungeon. ()Upon finishing Infernax, I immediately combed through the Infernax wiki site and various YouTube videos just to catch a quick glimpse of what else remained in the game that I had not yet seen even after reaching the Ultimate Good ending. I was extremely taken aback to learn that the game actually contained multiple playable characters that each had distinct weapons and playstyles (such as a wizard character and even a futuristic character with a machine gun inspired by the run-and-gun genre). I also did not realize just how much in the way of unique bosses there was still left for me to fight by pursuing the other morality routes in the game. For a game that only takes up 206.2 megabytes of space on my hard drive, Infernax sure has a deceptively rich amount of content and replayability contained within it that puts most modern 70 dollar Triple-A single-player titles to shame. There are even traditional cheat codes that I could type in the game to activate a variety of effects, ranging from overpowered hacks (like infinite health and magic) to goofy ways of playing the game (such as a cheat that makes my character half-sized or one that gives me a motorcycle).It's so rare to see a game that does so many things so well. I don't think I need to go into just how gorgeous the art design and sprite work is for this game. That much is evident just from looking at its screenshots and trailers. The soundtrack also has quite a number of memorable tunes. Character dialogue is also written in a manner that is appropriate for the game's fantasy medieval setting (unlike, say, God of War: Ragnarok, which has most of its characters eerily talking like modern Californian Gen-Z youths).Unfortunately, no game is perfect. I still have criticisms of Infernax. Here is a quick list:Nevertheless, despite these complaints, I wholeheartedly recommend Infernax. It's one of the best games of 2022. It deserved far more recognition than it did in the year's awards circles. The fact that Stray (a walking simulator with zero challenge and zero replayability) was the indie darling of 2022 among gaming journalists and awards ceremonies is more proof that the people and organizations who control videogame discourse deserve no such power over the industry.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a really mixed bag for me but I liked it enough to finish it.As far as the good, I love the theme and the general feeling of the combat is pretty good. I grew up on these kinds of games and I'm a huge metalhead just like these devs. Let me crack skeletons in the face, give me cool satanic ♥♥♥♥ to look at, and name all your achievements after metal songs and I'll at least check out your game. Although I thought the basic enemies were nothing special to look at the bigger enemies that give their artist some room to work with look awesome. You don't often get really grotesque things in pixel art form and that for sure was a big highlight for me. The cutscene and pre-bossfight images are incredible.Now for the bad...Your health is represented as blocks and the damage done seems to be number based or damage was just broken at times in my playthrough. There were times where I got hit by the same attack and it visible took away different amounts of visible blocks of health. This made it really hard to know when I should have been healing.This feels kinda like Castlevania 2: Simon's Quest and I incorrectly assumed this was going to be linear like 1 and 3. There's lots of backtracking through a bland overworld and some absurdly vague hints on how to progress the game that you will likely have to look up much like the infamous crouch in a corner BS from Simon's Quest. You can eventually find a teleport spell to make backtracking not as bad but it's very late in the game and easy to pass up.If you're into replaying games for both the good and evil routes, there looks to be a lot here from the little bit I looked up on youtube. I rarely replay games unless they're amazing. On a single run this felt a bit lacking with enemy variety and the good route is kinda bland. I'd highly recommend playing evil if you want something more memorable.Castles can be cleared while missing incredibly useful power-ups in them. One wrong turn means that you might fight a boss while leaving some parts of the castle undiscovered. If you beat the boss, you get warped out of the castle and have to go back through the castle again to find the power-up you missed. I really don't understand why they didn't make these impossible to miss since I think you need every last one of them to get through the game.Potions. You need to go out of your way to fill them up and they're the one thing that does not reset between deaths. If you drank a potion in a boss fight and die, you'll reset to the last room you entered with everything restored except for potions you may have drank.I hate RPG elements in games that are not designed to be a role playing game from the ground up. It's just an added layer of nonsense that could easily be replaced by scaling enemy damage and health with your player's stock attack power and health in mind.

_childDocuments_.review: is a metroidvania through and through. It has everything you would expect from challenging platforming to unlocking new paths with your freshly gained abilities. However, this game does much more than just copy paste the formula you have seen countless times over and over. Infernax is a love letter to metroidvanias as well as player-controlled narrative. differentiates itself from its competition in its approach to a story. You assume control of a duke, who after a long time returned to his homeland, only to find it swarmed with demonic creatures from the depths of Hell. Armed with your trusty mace and shield, you go on a purge to cleanse your lands once and for all. However just after the few first minutes, a choice screen pops up. A man just got possessed. Will you kill him, or will you try to help him? In the world of , your choices actually matter. They might lead to secret boss fights, different questlines or even affect how certain level screens look. On top of that, the game has 4 different main endings, based on the choices you made.  Will you rather see the world burn or become the paragon people need?In its core, gameplay is as any other run of the mill metroidvania. Platforming is accompanied by responsive controls and tight design. There never was a moment I would feel the game was at fault whenever I failed a jump or missed a platform. The combat is simplistic with one attack button, one spell button and one for potions. And that is all you need. Nevertheless, even with a simple mindset, there is depth to be achieved. As hinted at, on your journey through the hellscape you once called home, you will gain numerous spells to make your adventure a tiny bit easier. Those range from summoning a thunderstorm to fully healing yourself. On top of the choices, it is the spells that allow you to customize your experience a tiny bit more to your liking as well as give you a bit more freedom developing your own strategies as various situations arise.To give you a bit of an edge in battle, you can also buy one time use potions, that either refill your health, mana, or both. And if you would still struggle with some parts, there is even an option to buy extra lives, that respawn you at the start of the level screen once you die. And these are permanent upgrade and that’s what I call a steal. To top of the core mechanics, you have a very simple upgrade system constituting of buying a stronger mace, better armour or spending your EXP gained from ripping and tearing to upgrade health, mana or damage dealt letting you shape your fate even more on top of all the other stuff. prides itself on pixel art visuals that manage to stay simplistic yet perfectly depict the gory and messed up nature of the world. Whether it is a boss designed with guts hanging from his body or simple death animations, that vary for each individual death you can encounter in the game. It is astonishing to see, how detailed the game is and how much care has been put into designing every single element. Not only does the game look great, it even has a day and night cycle. With that in place, it changes both the visuals of the background, but also the enemy types that spawn on individual level screens. This gorgeous package is wrapped in 8-bit soundtrack, that compliments the entire aesthetic. It does not happen often for this type of music, but I have to say that I did listen to some songs even outside of the game. With everything good, something bad must come at the hands of the devil. The experience overall feels great, however I personally had one issue with the game. The difficulty curve does not feel well designed. At the start you will struggle a lot as you will lack items, checkpoints, and overall skills necessary to clear the game. However, as the game progresses and you get your hands on the healing spell, three healing potions and a stronger weapon, you will find yourself just standing still, mashing attack button and occasionally healing, crushing any boss you come across. It feels rewarding to finally be the one on top, but it is in a stark contrast as to how the game started.

_childDocuments_.review: Is this game a masterpiece? Not sure yet, but it is one of the finest Commodore C-64 (or NES) inspired games I have played in a long time. Everything here oozes quality 8-bit game - the graphic, the sound... but maybe not the design. It is actually very playable, at least in the lower (of 2) difficulty settings. You don't die every 3 seconds, like in the also recently released Beholgar, and the game offers considerably more than just platforming and hack 'n slay. It is more like a metroidvania in 8-bit, with many at first inaccessible locations, an auto-map, NPCs to talk to, magic spells to learn, potions to drink, a journal with your open quests (yes, there is more to do than just "save the land"), weapons and armor to equip, skills to learn, power/health/mana stats to upgrade. In the main menu you can read a Demonology book with pictures of all types of monsters you encountered so far (and how many you already killed). During some fights, NPCs fight side by side with you, quite immersive. There is a day/night cycle with different monsters, monsters get pushed back when you hit them (and don't simply overrun you while you hit them multiple times - I look at you, Beholgar!). Everything is quite simple and presented like on the C-64 (or NES, or Master System if you insist) - there are no long stats and texts, only a few spells, NPCs mostly just have a sentence or two to say and monsters just run along their (programmed) path. Ok, some attack you when they notice you. Monsters respawn when you re-enter a location, so you can kill them again for XP and gold. There are often decisions to make - and they lead to different, drastic outcomes. Often unexpected.The core gameplay is a classic 2D action game - walk, duck, jump and kill every enemy with your mace (or other weapon/spell), but the presentation is interesting and the controls are tight. When you leave a location the screen takes a second to refresh - I am sure they could have switched instantly, but this is just like in the old days. And it gives you time to take a sip of your coke. Despite all the bells and whistles around, and the lower difficulty compared to many of the old classic games, the game is still not easy. Monsters kill you, when you fall into water or lava you die, traps squash you. The game can be saved in shrines (which also heal you and replenish your mana), but it will cost you XP and gold to reload. Death is always only a step away if you are not careful. Technically it looks and sounds like an 8-bit game, but of course I do play on 4K with VSYNC enabled and with my wireless XBox controller. And there are no loading times nor do I have to switch floppy discs.Retro styled gaming at its finest for today's audience. It just gives you the impression that you play an old classic, but in reality you play a modern, highly playable 2D sidescrolling hack 'n slay/platformer.

_childDocuments_.review: I had fun with Infernax. It takes the rotten, discarded heart of the oldest Castlevania games and builds a brand new experience around it. In a sense, it is what Castlevania 2 should've been; or perhaps it is what people who played these games as kids  them like.It’s fun bashing things, the music is dope more often than not, and the punishing but fair difficulty adds a lot of weight to pretty much everything you do. Also, there’s a lot of game in here. Not only your quests, your powers and even the final section of the game are highly variable depending on your choices thorough the game - but also there are lots of little modifiers to the game, such as playing it in Contra mode (BLAST those zombies with a MACHINE GUN!) and alternative characters. And coop! It transforms the experience so much that the devs suggest you first play it alone, and only bring a friend later for a second playthrough.Still, I have some complaints. My playthrough was Ultimate Good, and I played on classic mode, which makes you restart from a save statue when you run out of lives, losing all progress (no worries - you can always turn that off!). First off, the difficulty. This is a “hard dungeons, easy bosses” kind of game. Okay, not quite; the bosses aren’t “easy”, but they expect you to be out of resources after a hard gauntlet and if you pay attention and use your head, you should be able to beat them on the first try, maybe second. That is not a complaint - I actually love that about Infernax.What I don't love is that most of my deaths in dungeons were caused by falling to my death. Either by being knocked back and falling into lava, or missing a difficult jump later on. I felt like those deaths clashed with pretty much everything else - you fight carefully, avoid damage, only use healing when you absolutely need to... but then you die just the same by falling. Truly, Castlevania's heart lives on.Also, the game's morality is a bit... weird. Almost every decision you make affects your morality score, which in turn affects other things (also including your loadout! That’s always a cool thing). But the moral code boils down to this: Humans always good (unless cultist!), and demons always bad. Kill cultists and demons, no exceptions, help everyone else - unless you want to be a Bad Dude (TM), and Infernax makes being evil just as viable as being good.To sum things up: do you want to smash undead things with 8-bit style but some more modern sensibilities? This is what Infernax is. Annoying at times, but when it's fun, it's very fun. At least it was for me!

_childDocuments_.review: Infernax is a metroidvania with RPG elements. It took me 20 hours to complete all achievements;That being said, I loved every minute I spent playing this game. They determine which quests will be available, how the NPCs will view you, etc. Taking that into account, there are more than 5 endings! Replayability is here folks!There are different versions of the main character that you can use to play the game. Also, the game has a built-in "cheat" system, in case you finish the story but want to see the other stuff the game has to offer.You can't go wrong with this title, I more than recommend it!

_childDocuments_.review: What we have here is an exceptional  successor that follows the proto-metroidvania design of 1987's , but discards all the (potentially translation-based) obfuscation of the source material.  There is no  here, either.  Full of cheeky cut scenes and 8-bit gore effects, the selling point it pushes the most is .  Will you be good?  Will you be bad?  Just how bad?  Exactly how good?  And that's  nifty, I think -- but if you're the kind of guy so fed up with real-world evil you don't want to pretend to be a brigand, Satanist, or globalist stooge even in a video game, your replayability with this one will be quite limited.Is that a bad thing, though?  The Ultimate Good campaign is robust enough.  The platforming really is pixel-precise enough to sell a linear experience.  The cenobite-like bosses look great and are fun to fight, and the final level pushes you to the brink, as it should.  So I think I'll just see this as a one and done, but in another way, that's too darned bad:  imagine if the choices you made in-game had all the same potential for cheekiness, but weren't so starkly black or white -- i.e., to break the dam or not to break the dam, to kill the monster or to abet the monster, to burn the village or not to burn.  And imagine you couldn't just load the game after a hard choice!  A bit of a Telltale-ism would go a long way toward improving the sequel.

_childDocuments_.review: Let me preface this by saying that I didn't really play these types of games growing up as much as some others that have left reviews. Sure, I had Symphony of the Night, but I was so afraid of losing progress that I didn't ever progress. I never beat the game. Dark Souls was similar - you die and die and lose what you gained... So I tried this on a whim. It looked cool, sort of like Doom mixed with Castlevania - and then the dying started happening. At first I was frustrated, tempted to return it, even, but I kept on picking it up. In that is where I learned the satisfaction of playing games styled in an older, less forgiving time. Achieving something actually feels like an accomplishment. Beating a boss after you died 20 times just trying to get to it... and it doesn't give you cool armor or anything, you just get to progress. But that, in itself, feels amazing - seeing the "Castle Cleared!" words at the top, after a nail biting and close fight (where one false step means you start over at the start of the dungeon)... hell, it's hard to put into words. Even if I were to fail, though (and I did, a LOT), you still walk away with something... knowledge you didn't have before, or a better understanding of a specific enemy. Death in this game only means you wasted your time if you didn't learn anything or improve from it.I keep seeing nostalgia thrown in some reviews here. Nostalgia has taken a negative connotation recently, showing that a game is merely playing off memories of bygone days, but this game isn't just that. Sure, I'll admit my bias in that completing this game, to me, represents overcoming something I never could when I was younger, but from the most objective standpoint I can provide, this is marvelous game that I urge newer players to enjoy as well. There is challenge and reward in each fight, stylized in 8-bit retro sword and sorcery, with puzzles and moral choices that require attention to dialogue and detail.  The latter point - moral choices - increase replayability, nipping at you with possibilities of what could've been if you hadn't decided to do your playthrough as a paragon of righteousness. Using the $1:1hr rule, if this is something your interested in, you'll definitely get your money's worth at multiple playthroughs. Those going for a one-and-done will probably land around the 12 to 15hr mark, and in that case may be best waiting for a sale. All together, Infernax is a well packaged game full of fun and tension that will have you thinking of ways to get out of work early just to get back to it.

_childDocuments_.review: After having completed my first playthrough with the ultimate good path, I feel I am in a good place to state my opinion of the game.It's great!Basically, the Zelda II: The Advenutre of Link removes the overworld gameplay and replaces it with classic metroidvania navigation in a fantasy medieval crusades setting in the stylings of what Shovel Knight has normalised as a form of retro-fidelity. And it's pretty good.Designwise, there were a couple of things I didn't like very much, like the slippery part of the charge attack or ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ such as my completionist self in pain from watching those small map corners not getting tagged as explored without going into some awkward or possibly lethal-likely jumping manouvre. I did like how it stuck to its guns in how it embraced Zelda's approach to upgrades and progression, giving it a very satisfying appreciation of how some things used to be in an age where save slots were still a recent adopted concept (technology permitting). Fast travel and checkpointing is decent and anything more generous would likely be overkill, but I do dislike how dungeons are filled with instant death pits that can set you back a handful or two of minutes if you're not careful; on the other hand, you can optionally disable instant-death stuff in the accessibility options, so make of my comment whatever you want.Music and sound were pretty good, really fit the game. Sprites are absolutely amazing. Cutscenes, while rare, are also very clean and crisp. Overall an amazing art style. Has accessibility options for highlighting yourself, enemies and things you can interact with, as well as stuff for photosensitive people, so that's definitely a plus.The moral decisions are one of the best gimmicks in the game, in my opinion. It really seems to make for the spice that incentivises replayability with the alternate characters you can play with (one unlocked out of the bat for new players, but I recommend only playing him after having gone once through the normal game unless you really want to), as well as tying some achievements to this moral system. Some of them are also hilarious in how they play out by subverting your expectation slightly.As a fan of the better Castlevania titles and retro games, as well as some of the retro Castlevania games, I am very glad I made this purchase. Now all I have to do is get the 100%, but it won't feel like a chore: it will feel like a good time.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a great game in the genre. They captured the retro feel of a Castlevania experience while upgrading a lot of elements for modern sensibilities.It's unfortunate that you don't get more upgrades in the way of move sets for the main character, the spells and some techniques you get help make that better. You can also play different characters and variations of characters but for your whole playthrough.The best thing that really makes this an easy recommend is the coop play. If you've got someone to remote play together with, the game is a really fun time. A little RPG-lite couch coop enjoyment.The game also isn't super long so you could blow through different playthroughs in 5ish hours after your first playthrough that would take closer to 8 ~ 9 hours.
_childDocuments_.name: Infernax

_childDocuments_.review: Here's another game that looks and plays the way we remember the NES games of our youth (in reality they were much uglier and way less playable :)A classic-style metroidvania, with about 8 hours of gameplay, and a nice potential for replayability: there are at least 4 endings, plus a bunch of secrets scattered all over the world. Gameplay is on the easier side: fairly challenging, at times tricky, but never overly punishing: this game is not a cakewalk, but not Blasphemous either.Recommended for both modern players and nostalgic old 8/16 bit fans.
_childDocuments_.name: Infernax

_childDocuments_.review: Its a love letter and call back to Castlevania 2 and Zelda 2 but done better in those games. Though it doesn't have as many spell like Zelda 2 I think it controls much better.  The music is amazing and the demons, blood and guts the enemies produce when you hit them and the large amount of player death scenes also add weight to your failures too.  Overall, I really like this game.
_childDocuments_.name: Infernax

_childDocuments_.review: it is exceedingly rare I feel compelled to 100% a game, but this time I did it, and still had some steam to spare. Brilliant retro title. The platforming and combat are just challenging enough to make you pay attention, but rarely frustrating, and once you know what you're doing, a run is reasonably snappy.  The different routes based on your choices and combinations of choices are interesting and satisfying, the different character classes feel like entirely different experiences, The controls are snappy and responsive.Main complaints revolve around the way specific powers work. It is WAY too easy to launch yourself off a cliff with the forward thrust, and there's no way to cancel out of it once you have the move charged. Allowing the player to jump-cancel or crouch-cancel out of the dash would be helpful. A few spelling and grammar mistakes here and there "Light shown down" for example. Certainly nothing unforgivable. Recommendation for new players if you care about getting all the achievements without having to do as many runs as I did : Do the evil route first, and regardless of route, always finish Urzon Citadel before going to Robert's hideout. This lets you get five endings from just two runs, instead of five runs the way I did it. The remaining two endings will require dedicated playthroughs. One is easy. The other is not. So yes, I did seven playthroughs. I like this game that much.
_childDocuments_.name: Infernax

_childDocuments_.review: 29 hours of game time, 30 of 30 achievements, 4 different save files for different runs. Yes, I believe I can recommend it.From the screenshots and extra visuals on the Steam page, it's probably easy for someone to tell if this game is for them. It's very much styled after and inspired by the old NES era. It does have the usual Metroidvania additions of having a map, unlocking progression through pickups, eventual fast travel, and items and leveling up. There are no standard difficulty levels but more rather a regular mode and an assisted difficulty mode that has extra save points. Without spoiling too much, there are unlockable things for new save files that can make the game harder or even easier. Otherwise, the difficulty of the standard run is the same. It's only easier or harder depending on how much you grind to level up and buy items; typical for the Metroidvania genre. The first run through the game was the most frustrating as the dungeon platforming can be a bit punishing. After getting the hang of how the game wants you to jump, it's not as bad but it might be frustrating for some.The game is definitely for mature audiences with the themes being discussed in the game and the graphical pixel art gore. The game plays very smoothly for the style and the music is very well done! Aside from looking up how to accomplish some of the endings, I kept myself blind to the events of the game and how the extras play out. I'm very glad I did! Experiencing the surprises for myself made for some great moments. If not for the unlocks, I wouldn't have done a 100% completion of the game. They did help for the last couple of runs and was pretty cathartic going through the last time as a completely overpowered character to just wreck the game's challenges to get the last couple of achievements.I had my frustrations with the game and I've had some fun playing it. I definitely don't regret the purchase. The game does a pretty good job with the pixel art elements and the retro soundtrack is well done with a few tracks that like to get stuck in my head. If the game looks appealing to you and you like classic Metroidvania mechanics, then you'll probably like this game as well.
_childDocuments_.name: Infernax

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a freaking masterpiece.Everything about it has tons of thought. Dialogue, when and what music, the artstyle, gameplay and platforming. Seriously reminds me of the days when games had polish and thought put into it's design. Like, not just "and then the player does this/needs to do this to get past this part" like a lot of even major party games are guilty of today. But stuff like when to stop playing music, the right sound effects for the right scene. Weighty consequences for decisions (seriously, the last time I enjoyed a game with as drastically a changing good/evil path, this much; was KotoR 1), enemy placement. It's all ~perfect~If you like Castlevania, Zelda 2, Hey Ice King wytog, Metroid, Wario World. You absolutely owe it to yourself to give this game a shot. You will not be disappointed. In fact, the only criticism I could possibly think of for this game; is that it might be a little too easy for some Castlevania/other Metroidvania (looking at you, Rondo of Blood/Blasphemous crew) fans. Even then, I think the story is fun enough to warrant a playthrough or two for them. I enjoyed those games, and there's some cheap shot enemy placement to tickle that itch. Which is a good, as any fan of those games knows, it's super rewarding knowing just where and when to jump to fly through them in no time flat.It's a shame this game released right before elden ring and everyone's all preoccupied with that, because this is easily one of the most polished independently developed I've seen in the past 15 years.11/10 game.
_childDocuments_.name: Infernax

_childDocuments_.review: Infernax takes ideas from Castlevania 2 and Zelda 2 on the NES, and mixes in some of its own unique inspiration for what makes a very satisfying, fairly replayable experience. Like Castlevania, the entire game world takes place in a single, inter-connected side scrolling game space. There are a few villages spread about, which in fashion of both games sell you upgrades and give you side quests. There are also dungeons with keys and bosses, though none of them are terribly complex and are more about combat and platforming challenges.Where Infernax separates itself from its inspirations though, is its morality system. At several points in the game, your supposedly holy knight will be challenged with choices that change which side quests he can accept, which NPCs will be receptive to him, and ultimately alter your playstyle in some way or another. Stay good, and you keep your trusty shield. Go evil, and you'll toss it aside for a large sword with superior reach. Your spells will also change too.The only major criticism I have is the game's difficulty plateaus around the mid-way point, and once your endgame levels are reached and best gear obtained you absolutely clean the floor with everything, especially the bosses with the exception of the Ultimate Good Path final boss.
_childDocuments_.name: Infernax

_childDocuments_.review: So if you have seen some of my other reviews, you may know that I like to compare new games I play to old ones I have played in the past, particularly if they are retro style games.  You might be expecting me to say something like "this game is Simon's Quest meets Dark Souls, blah blah blah..." Yeah, that is a little too on-the-nose for me right now...The game I really want to highlight as a strong influence to this one is The Adventure of Link.  Consider the hero's weaponry: the mace and shield combo he starts out with, while refreshingly original, is much more akin to the sword and shield combination that Link uses then the Belmont whip (yes, I know Simon gets a shield too, but you have to equip a relic for that, whereas Alcedor has the shield from the beginning).  Consider the way the character levels up: in both games, you apply XP to one of three stats (Attack Power, Life, and Magic) which increases the relative level therefore; there is no analog to this in Simon’s Quest.  Consider the magic system: the Shield, Thunderstorm, Heal, and Hellfire spells are blatant rip-offs of the Shield, Thunder, Life, and Fire spells from Adventure of Link; I was almost expecting our knight to transform into a fairy at some point.  Consider how each castle is self-contained with keys, a special treasure and boss: this much more like the Palaces from Zelda II as opposed to the Mansions from Castlevania II; the only thing missing is the overworld map.  When you take into account some of the other Zelda-inspired elements--potions, bottles, and even the way some enemies move and attack--you begin to see that there is more to this game than just another Castlevania clone.  Since The Adventure of link is my favorite Zelda game (yes, you heard me: I know I am a blasphemer by saying this un-ironically, but there it is) I really appreciated its influence in this game.Another old game Infernax seems to be taking some cues from is Fable with its morality system.  I enjoy how the choices matter in this game, with consequences that cannot always be fully groked without alternate playthroughs.  Because of this and the myriad alternate endings and bonus characters unlocked thereby, this game has a great deal of replay value.  And to anyone who complains about how the option to be evil and the imagery makes this game “Satanic”, it should be pointed out that if you are paying attention, it is obvious that the path of ultimate good is the cannon ending.Of course, the game is not perfect, and the part of it I really hated was the skills: I cannot tell you how many times I got fracked up by trying to do the Skycall to no avail, despite hitting the buttons indicated in the description; seriously devs: a simple double-jump would have been SO much better!    Also lost a few lives accidentally doing the guided strike... since this was a retro-style game anyway, I would have gone with something more traditional.Anyway, I did like some of the other Castlevania-inspired elements of the game.  The graphics and sound are top-notch for the genre.  I saw some folks complaining about how you cannot control the jump height, but I didn’t miss it.  Not a huge fan of the gore though, and although the blood-soaking and multiple death animations are an interesting mechanic, I could take them or leave them; none of these contributed much to the game play.  I did enjoy some of the occult references: for example, Brother Alcedor is clearly a Templar... clear at least to those who know...  I should probably practice prudence about the rest of that topic, except to say the fact that I got the “Hallowed Be Thy Name” ending on classic mode in my first playthough would have made my fellow Knights Kadosh proud... if they cared about video games anyway...In the final analysis, this layered Metroidvaina is definitely GROOVY.  Just be sure send the kiddies to bed before you play it.
_childDocuments_.name: Infernax

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR: It's very fun and worth the price, but the platforming will probably piss you off.Pros:- Delicious retro aesthetic- Satisfying, yet simple combat- Substantial world to explore, but not overwhelming- Secret characters and morality choices add surprising depth- Good music and splash art throughoutCons:- Annoyingly precise platforming in places- Fixed distances for jumps and other movement exacerbates the above- Bosses can feel too easy in general (though this is often welcome after a punishing run to reach them)- Writing is fairly shallow and plotlines are contrived (though this hardly affects the fun factor)Final opinion: Buy it! it's incredibly cheap for the value it offers, and the fun generally outweighs the pain.
_childDocuments_.name: Infernax

_childDocuments_.review: A friend showed me this game 2 weeks ago. I got totally hooked. I finished every endings, found everything, got all achievements. If you like the retro-style game, and especially if you liked Castlevania 2 (however the clues are easily found in Infernax), I'd highly recommend the game. Translation is great too, as I played both english and french version.For the price, the game is a no-brainer. The only thing I'd add, was a 'boss replay', directly from the library books. Other than that, it's a gem.
_childDocuments_.name: Infernax

_childDocuments_.review: This is probably the first time I've reviewed a game on Steam, but this game deserves it. I had an absolute blast with the game, it scratched every retro itch I had. You can tell there was a lot of work put into it. I'll go over some pros and a few cons.Pros- Classic mode is definitely the way to go when playing- Game play is smooth and precise- Feels fair, every death I had felt fair and I learned from it- Bosses were fantastic in design - Quests add a lot of flavor- Morality system was great with subtle hints in game that tells you which alignment your character is heading- Multiple endings add a lot of replay value- Music was top notch with subtle hints of Castlevania in some tracks- Pixel art cutscenes were fantastic and very well done- Platforming was fair and I've never felt that anything was cheap or trial and error type game play- Nothing felt too cryptic in the game as long as you read the dialogue, except one Easter egg that I won't spoil, but that's just a nod of the cryptic nature of the game it's originally from- Unlockables galoreCons- Most bosses are on the easy side- Too many ways to heal makes the game fairly easy- Regular enemy variety felt lacking. Most of the time there are only like 3 enemy types per area, wish they could have made more for varieties sake- I wish armor uprades were a little more flashy, but that's a minor gripe- Wish enemies dropped items that restored mana. Alternatively the game could have used to breakable objects that dropped them like candles or somethingThere might be some things I'm missing from both categories but overall I'm giving the game a 9/10. Easily worth the money since I'm already 22 hours in and I'm still not done with the game. I look forward to future games from this developer if any are planned.

_childDocuments_.review: Zelda 2 and Castlevania 2 on the NES came together and had a baby. This is that baby and it's a very successful one at that!Game is incredibly fun! _childDocuments_.review: As of 4 hours in, so far a great game.It strikes a very good balance between challenge and fun, though your mileage may vary if you are not familiar with games like this. Do stick with it though, it has a more forgiving difficulty mode if you don't like how punishing it might be for the more casual crowd!The co-op really makes the game shine. There's been a lot of thought and polish put into it. It doesn't make the game too easy either as the difficulty ramps up a little if you decide to play in 2P mode, which is highly appreciated!The visuals and audio are pretty spot on for the era that the game is emulating, with the soundtrack being particularly fitting. _childDocuments_.review: It's taken a lot of the Castlevania elements and done their own spins on them. There are some good and quite a few bad. I'm leaning more towards meh. Buy this on sale if you really want to scratch that metroidvania itch The devs clearly took a LOT of inspirations from the NES era Castlevania games and a few bits from the later series, but rather than build up on those gameplay experiences they really missed the marks on some of them. Fluid movements. Unlike your NES era BelmontMultiple endings. Decent replay valueUnlockable game mode. The animators really liked their death animationsGrotesque and gory boss designs. Special attacks' executions... Richter uppercut and No new game + where stuff carries overLevel design. Death pits. Tight jumps. Stuff designed to knock you into said pits Dungeon designs are also made to intentionally waste your time with dead ends with no way to quick warp back to the start. Dungeon lacks quick warp out unless you are playing on casual mode. Unreliable health display. Powerups are intentionally placed at dead ends that require backtracking. QoL spells are mainly obtained AFTER areas I could really, REALLY use them. Multiple endings. It's not everyday that you get the choice to be irredeemably evil or be half baked about it. Endings do change to reflect this. This is absolutely this game's strongest point. Though IMO, the morality point system is rather stringent. Some NPCS be like: You have to be this good/evil to accept our awesome quests. Part of this is understandable, but at the same time... I'm controlling the duke of this domain, are these NPCS seriously giving me/the duke lips about quests? Most NPCs are also really blasé about whatever evil acts you've committed. Dialogue barely change to reflect anything. Missed opportunities really. The additional game modes you can unlock are... neat. Mileage is going to vary around this feature. Some are really great and do break the game a tad, and some just... meh. There are a lot of unique death animations. Some absolutely gross enemies and bosses for sure. It's hard not to look at this game and not think of the original Castlevania games on the NES, Castlevania 2 Simon's Quest in particular due to the exp and shopping systems. There are even a few Castlevania related easter eggs if you know where to find them. Your mace wielding character can freely control his jump like a modern video game character. He walks faster and jumps higher than a Belmont. (But he hits weaker than a Belmont...) Duke Man in some way has more tricks than a Belmont pre Igarashi days. He can use spells, and even do some budget Richter moves. Granted, not all of this is executed well. If you check out other reviews people will talk about the lack of an air jump, instead you get this budget Richter upper cut. It's a bit awkward when the bog standard air jump would've done the trick just fine. Character mobility for the most part is fine, though the Richter uppercut is questionable IMO in its application in this game. You are required to use it as a weird air jump to progress. You are far more likely to die from the stage's various instant death pitfalls than most enemies. There's already the telltale sign of abundant deathfall mechanics incoming within the first 2 hours of the game. In order to get to the second dungeon, I must time my jump precariously across THREE screens worth of a death chasm and my only platforms of choice are... falling/retracting spike chandeliers. While these makeshift platforms are bigger than than a typical block, their timing and the ceiling allowed for the jump isn't what I call generous. The developers must have realized that, yeah, that's a bit sketch so they have a life system. It's still ass. While the precision platforming isn't as unforgiving as some of the modern platformers, this is just an exercise in tedium rather than fun.  While exploring dungeon you are bound to come across branching paths. Some are locked away behind closed doors, so you must obtain keys hidden around the dungeon to unlock these doors. Problem is, these keys are always at a dead end and backtracking is a beach. And they make you do this for EVERY. SINGLE. DUNGEON. Sometimes multiple times in the later dungeons because  It's just pointless time wasters. The neat powerup is also hidden somewhere around the dungeon, but like the key, it's at the end of a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ dead end somewhere and I'll have to backtrack to an earlier branching point. I'd be less peeved if I have the power to teleport to the beginning of the dungeon. Metroid and flipping Castlevania both put their powerups AFTER a boss fight to ensure players can't possibly miss the shiny. The powerups in this game aren't optional either, you actually do need them to progress to the next dungeon. So why are they tucked away in a dead end somewhere? Even outside of the dungeon you won't gain access to the teleport spell until after dungeon 3. That's close to the half way point of the game. Remember dungeon 2 that's located after 3 screens of annoying death chasms? You have to do this ♥♥♥♥ backwards too to leave this area because you don't have teleport. In order to buy the teleport spell, you need the air attack powerup from dungeon 3. Dungeon 3 is also located after a few screens of potential death traps with annoying flying eyeballs flying above revolving safe spots. The other attack spell that would be handy against these freaks is only accessible after you finish dungeon 3. Sheesh this gets old...The health blocks make no sense. The presentation and style implies that enemies will do set damage each time, no hidden damage tax. But that's not how it is in this game. Assuming each block of health bar represents 10 health points, enemy damage feels like they are doing some weird things like -13.35 damage to you. How does that -3.35 reflect on your display? It doesn't! I don't see that extra 30% of my 1 health block gone. It's very questionable. If they are doing this weird number game, they should've stuck with a health bar/pool display. Even a butt ugly straight up number display is fine. Especially if they introduce an armor system where I'm assuming it's reducing damage taken based on percentage. If you are expecting something to fill that Castlevania/Metroidvania void, you'll have to temper your expectations. Infernax will feel a bit lacking if you've been exposed to newer Metroidvania games with a lot more pizazz and other quality of life goodies. For this price, there are other games in this genre that are longer and better. Infernax isn't bad by any means, it's just overshadowed by all the other great games. This game can definitely do better if the devs polish up on some of their weak points. That HP display really needs to be adjusted.

_childDocuments_.review: I have not played Castlevania 2 so I'll refrain from calling this "castlevania 2 but good" but either way this is an amazing non-linear 2D sidescroller.The best feature is the morality system, it's not a nuanced morality system, just righteously good actions and dastardly evil ones, but every choice has practical outcomes. Only did a good playthrough but even good actions with immediate rewards have bad outcomes later.So glad I bought this on a whim.
_childDocuments_.name: Infernax

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic game, which instantly takes the top spot of the genre.A few years ago weirdly enough the Hentai game "Midnight Castle Succubus" was game of the year for me as it was basically a really good spiritual successor to the NES sidescrolling RPGs (Adventues of Link, Faxanadu, Battle of Olympus, Simon's Quest) with some arbitrarily tagged on erotic content to market it as an adult game.Now Infernax doesn't go the hentai route (except for one picture with bare breasts), however it also does incorporate some of the hentai platformers ideas, such as every death giving you a unique death animation.The platforming in Infernax is the perfect mix of challanging and not too mean spirited, riding the perfect spot between frustration and motivation. Of course you get a bit angry if you die, but you're mostly angry on yourself for not having nailed that jump, instead of blaming the game too much. And for those who are blaming the game still, there is an easy mode and cheats.So, it's a very good Simon-esque Metroidvania-ish platformer, but I want to highlight a couple of things that usually fly under the radar of other devs.- There is a photosensitivity option, toning down flashes and such. It works very well, without ruining the immersive moments.- Dialogues are kept short and too the point. It doesn't devolve into reading a visual novel to progress through the game. Those dialogues happen with NPCs in town, your game doesn't get interrupted by misplaced "cutscenes". There is an art to the less-is-more approach and Infernax nailed it.- It's one of the rare horror games, which doesn't devolve into animal-cruelty or other offputting triggers. Now it is gory, yes. But it's a game that provides escapism rather than showcasing every mundane cruelty. The enemies are all creatively designed demons, there are no cheap shots, where you go kill the fauna, because the designers couldn't come up with an enemy design. There's the occasional crow pecking, but it flies away and is not subject to attacks.What is admittingly a bit weird of the game is that you only ever have one weapon (the mace and shield) and you only get stronger versions of it which don't do anything special. And you also can upgrade your damage with XP. This is weird for two reasons. For one, when you buy better armor, you take less damage and XP upgrades your health pool. But what the interaction between better weapons and XP damage boost is, isn't really clear.And then again, there are other weapons in the game - but these are restricted to subsequent playthroughs with other "classes" or an in-game event, which effectively change your class midgame. Contrast that with Battle of Olympus, where you had your basic club, then got a fire shooting staff, then got a sword which does not shoot, but overcomes resistances and finally you get a lightning shooting sword, which is strong, but the shot isn't as usefull as the firestaff. So, you have a reason to switch to another weapon thoughout the game. In Infernax you are stuck with better versions of one weapon, yet weirdly can switch back to less good ones.However, these other classes with their respective weaponry are very well integrated into the game. So, they do this giant efford, which is worth of a standalone game, yet is just put in as a gimmick. Imagine an icecream truck, who just sells vanilla icecream, you look in the back see all the delicious other variants and the truck driver tells you that those are secrets, you only get once you finished your vanilla icecream. That being said, it's still a damn awesome vanilla.Any complaints about the game I might have are really minor. Like "oh that animation when you get a new item is 3 seconds too long".This game is absoultely awesome, takes the top spot of the genre, gives me enough and leaves me looking forward to a sequel or even some endless rogue-dungeon dlc thing or something. Unless you are put off by the gore, this is an abusolute recommendation, even if you're not usually into the genre, this is such a good entry that you might just wanna try it anyway.
_childDocuments_.name: Infernax

_childDocuments_.review: A brilliant hybrid of Castlevania 2 and Zelda 2.  You have the world design, music, and gameplay of Simon's Quest, but with the exp and leveling system found in The Adventures of Link.  A run through the game is not terribly long, expect to spend probably 7 hours on your first time around and maybe 5 on subsequent laps through the game.  It is important to note that this game is designed to be replayed as there are choices made during the game that change not only aspects of the gameplay, but the ending and even the final boss.  Aside from this, there are a lot of extra unlockables and easter eggs along the way.  If you loved Castlevania 2, you will love this for sure.
_childDocuments_.name: Infernax

_childDocuments_.review: This game brings me back to the NES days of gaming and felt like a spiritual successor to games like Battle of Olympus, Castlevainia 2: Simon's Quest, and Faxanadu. If you enjoyed these types of games in the 80's and 90's you will not be disappointed in Infernax! Well worth the price even if it is a fairly short game.

_childDocuments_.review: while many people, myself included, have compared this game to a simons quest (castlevania) type experience, i would argue this game's flow is more like a darker Zelda 2 sort of play. the experience is pretty highly refined, and the game itself has many accessibility options for difficulty and play adjustment so its up to the player to really decide on their difficulty experience. the additional (secret) character options all give good refreshes to the game, with varying style and in some cases even new music for certain areas. this was an incredibly enjoyable experience for me, and if you enjoy games like zelda 2/castlevania simons quest then pick this up. but know that there are some metroid-esque elements, but i would argue the game itself is not actually a metroidvaniaalso as an additional note, when playing with the cheats, do NOT enable/disable the jetpack with other cheats at the same time (do jetpack first and leave the menu, then go back in and do whatever other cheats you want), as it appears to cause a softlock as of current build (hangs on black screen) observed on windows desktop and steam deck

_childDocuments_.review: An absolute treat of a game. Not only is it entertaining in terms of mechanics (like everything is very tight and polished to the point that you can totally abuse the game if pay attention to how things work), the variety of magic, skills, and the way the story unfolds makes it interesting for a number of playthroughs. I mean, there's a total of 9 endings to this game. And you get SOMETHING in return for each and every one of them: be it a new character with a unique weapon or a different set of mechanics altogether, or a secret code that adds some whacky but cool feature that you can turn on and off at will. Like in the good old days of gaming.Oh and the pixel art and music in this game are absolutely superb. Check them both on the internet if you fancy, because the screenshots don't do justice to the awesome boss screens and cut-scene elements of the game.

_childDocuments_.name: Infernax

_childDocuments_.review: I'll preface that Faxanadu was my favorite game growing up and I've played through it several times over the years when I get that itch and I've been looking for something new to scratch that itch most of my adult life. This game is that game.Overall I'd highly recommend this game. I've played through it several times now and will probably revisit this game in the future. To avoid spoilers I won't tell you why you should play through it several times but I will tell you that after playing through it you will find new ways to play that change the game and make it a different enough of an experience that I didn't get bored.The only thing I wish this game had that it didn't would be more gear and weapons. While the main character wields a mace it would have been nice to choose a sword, axe, etc as well as different types of gear that would change my combat style or appearance and offer different benefits.
_childDocuments_.name: Infernax

_childDocuments_.review: It's not bad, but has issues.First is that there should be checkpoints before the bosses, or at least a little closer to them. If we game over to them we have to slog our way through half the dungeon, which on most dungeons isn't too bad, but on later ones it is hell, literally.Second is enemies only drop gold, but with the health/magic system, they definitely should occasionally drop health and mana. The only ways to recover these as it is are limited potions and checkpoints, which only appear halfway through the dungeons and certain spots on the overworld.Last is the weird enemy balance when it comes to your arsenal vs enemies. Basically all the bosses are designed so you can reliably beat them with just your basic weapon if you're patient enough to dodge their attacks, the magic just makes them a bit easier. On the other hand many of the later non-boss enemies are next to impossible to fight without using magic, either they teleport or fly out of your reach, or they have such insane reach of their own actually dodging their attacks after smacking them is hilariously difficult.Downsides out of the way, the different endings and interactions are rad, no spoilers.Being able to just turn on godmode and fly if you're not enjoying a segment was also thoughtful, though I wish we could turn them on and off at will rather than just at overworld saves, as I wanted to fight a certain boss legit after skipping passed the annoying enemies in the way.Enemy variety is very satisfying, the many different ways enemies attack you and the different methods to counter them feels very rewarding, especially since we have a whole book to fill up. I think this is my favorite part about the game.
_childDocuments_.name: Infernax

_childDocuments_.review: Started out strong, but quickly began relying on mediocre platforming with constant instant death as a consequence.  I could have dealt with the ultra-specific and awkward enemy hitboxes and their  ever-increasing spammy attacks, but the bad platforming and ultra-sparse save points don't do this game any favors.  I won't ask for a refund but this goes onto the uninstall bonfire.The art and music were pretty great, at least.

_childDocuments_.review: Decent enough game that takes more than just some inspiration from older NES games.I'm down one playthrough so far, i'll see if the novelty of the game stays fresh after multiple playthroughs. Would i recommend it ? Sure, but do expect the game to be flawed on many aspects. Pros - Seems the studio is from Quebec, that's always a plus - Graphics work great for the game, it is very reminiscent of the NES / early SNES- Music is enjoyable and does remind me of stuff like Shovel Knight- Short enough to be done in about 2 sittings. Took me almost 9 hours, and i,d say at least an hour and a half to two hours were mostly cheap platforming deaths ( See Cons)- Many easter eggs that made me laugh out as i found them.- Multiple "paths" adds to replayability- Magic being used for some puzzles is a lovely touch. it's not just about combat- Seems there are unlockables after each playthrough, including secret characters, that might add to the lifespan of the game. Cons- Janky controls. I suppose they wanted to emulate the older castlevania games, but there's a reason they stopped making those games back then. The game seems to have problems with quick controller movements, often sending me into the sky and / or ending a jump attack abruptly by doing the ground pound attack. Add to that the fact that you never entirely know if you're gonna undershoot or overshoot a charge since you don't see far enough ahead on some maps. - Lack of "long range options". The main character is very limited combat wise, especially when tricky enemy placement  complicates jumps and such. There's a reason why the old Castlevania games gave you secondary weapons. The closest you get are a few spells that just cost too much mana to be worth it, especially since during a good portion of the game you cannot replenish your mana "on the fly". As a whole, the magic system didnt feel right to fill that spot- The armor system. Does it even work below the 4th one ? I cannot say i saw any tangible difference between the rusty, chainmail and silver armor. Same with the shield spell. I did notice a sudden increase in defence with the last armor though. - Hit boxes feel off. Hard to describe it, but often felt like attacks i did should've hit, yet i end up being damaged by some enemies that seems out of reach. - Lack of enemy variety. Sure, there's a lot of "reskinned" enemy, but it usually boils down to the same enemy with the same attack pattern, only with more HP. How many time can you fight a Giant Skeleton with a sword and not get bored ? - Bosses are mostly a joke. Final boss on my run i litterally stood there and spammed attack and it was over before i knew it. - Insta Death Pits / Hazards. At this point i feel it's a staple, and a crutch, for indie platformers. Coupled with the jank of the controls, it's just gets overly frustrating to mess up a jump because an enemy was in a slightly bad spot or because you sometimes stop dead in your track during a jump hitting sometimes, yet sometimes you slide on the "side" of the block you'd have hit.

_childDocuments_.review: this is one has a very mixed feelling for me. I have followed Berzerk Studio for years, played a lot of their games, and as a fan of the genre was really looking forward for their rendition of a metroidvania game, more Castlevania 2 than anything else. I like the setting a lot, I love the music, I love the animations, it's super fluidy, I enjoy the gore and bizarre choices thoroughly of the blood and visceras and stuff. It's really nice to hit things with a mace and the animation is very good, it feels 'heavy' when you swing.  I love the difficulty of it, the mobs and bosses patterns and tricks that you have to learn etc, but the controls are not adequate for the tasks of platforming/precision jumping they propose. The game is hard on purpose, of course, to make you die a lot and expend time repeating the same dungeons a lot, falling from places etc, but at the same time it clearly is made more difficult by poor polishing/programming. There are a lot of times that the combinations of key pressed to do some movements (air dashes, 'super' jumps, stuff like that) are simply not recognized by the game in the time window you have to execute them. I play on the keyboard and I play a lot of hard metroidvanias with precision platforming and never had a problem that couldn't be bested with a 'I'LL GIT GUD ò.ó' attitude, but this time it didn't work. Most of the times I overcome those areas in the game it feels like luck and not skill and it's not readly repeatable. I bought this game at launch, played a lot and waited for a few months before writing this review because I thought they would release a patch or new version that would address it, but they didn't. I thought it was a problem for keyboards, but reading reviews from people that played with controllers saying the same thing I cannot recommend the game, unfortunately.
