_childDocuments_.review: I would just like to start off with I am awful with reviews, but I will try my best to convey my thoughts about this game.The good:-LOOT, and LOTS OF IT.-The secondary firing on most weapons.-Unique individual worlds that have a lot of content to them instead of being mostly empty.-Skins and small cosmetic content you can unlock while playing.-Additional skins, small cosmetic content that can be bought with Eridium that you earn from killing badass enemies and melee Eridium deposits / Eridium containers.-Good ol' co-op with friends!-Did I mention TONS OF LOOT?-A lot of fresh enemies as well as ones that have returned from previous Borderlands games.-Typical Borderlands humor that I've always loved.-DLC I have never been a fan of in games, but the stuff that gets released for this game generally has quite a bit of content that can be worth it.-Weapon handling and combat makes for more diverse ways to eliminate enemies.-The sliding feature to get to cover is interesting-Similar end goal compared to the other games (open a vault / open multiple vaults)-Places will generally scale to your lvl now instead of you being insanely far ahead if you've been off doing side quests or DLC instead. I find that to be quite refreshing.-Going back to previous DLC comments, I've finally finished all DLC that has been offered to this game so far, and I would like to say I thoroughly enjoyed all of them. All of them added tons of content and significant game-play time that adds replay value. In my opinion, my favorite DLC of the group would have to be Bounty of Blood. -Ammo boxes and in-game content including enemies resets much faster compared to older games in the series. You usually had to save and then reload the game in order to reset boxes for ammo, loot, etc etc.The bad:-The Calypso Twins: Boring rotten brats compared to the villains of previous games.-What did you guys do to Cl4pTr4p? He's not himself anymore, at all.(NO longer relevant)-Incessant stuttering: Granted I am currently playing on a potato laptop because I am deployed overseas and have to have the graphics turned all the way down or off, and 50% scaling, but, ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ this is bad. My desktop at home which is still a beast suffered from some stuttering before I had to leave and then utilize my laptop.(/NO longer relevant)-incessant grinding: seems to be a bit more compared to the older Borderlands (which can also be seen as okay by someone else)-incessant nerfing of weapons on a constant basis, which in return you'll need to go grind again for a newer or older weapon that hasn't been nerfed yet. -If you aren't a constant player you can miss out on some content called "events".-Driving can be obnoxious compared to the older games-Almost too much stuff to unlock, because that can make the game feel "grindy" as mentioned before.In conclusion, I am still going to recommend the game because it has brought me entertainment and joy in some rather austere environments I've been in. The good for me also outweighs the bad I have mentioned. Thanks for taking the time to read my awful review. :)Edit 2: Kind of on the fence that they are releasing a season 2 to keep the content rolling in, but even though it has been almost a year since I played it on my desktop until now, it seems some of the stuttering bugs have been hammered out as I no longer have major FPS drops throughout playing the game. I am on my second play-through and enjoying it more than ever before because of the stability.

Amara beats bad guys into pancakes with her psychic fists. Moze’s best friend is a 10-ton walking killing machine. And Zane, the semi-retired corporate hitman... well, he’s Zane.  Hunting Alone? name: Metro Exodus
detailed_description: Owners of Metro Exodus are also entitled to the Metro Exodus PC Enhanced Edition - a stunning visual upgrade that REQUIRES a Ray-Tracing Capable GPU as part of the minimum spec. The DLC for Metro Exodus is also Enhanced – purchasing the Metro Exodus Expansion Pass, or The Two Colonels / Sam’s Story individually, entitles you to the Enhanced version of that content, accessible via the Metro Exodus PC Enhanced Edition. Metro Exodus The year is 2036. A quarter-century after nuclear war devastated the earth, a few thousand survivors still cling to existence beneath the ruins of Moscow, in the tunnels of the Metro. They have struggled against the poisoned elements, fought mutated beasts and paranormal horrors, and suffered the flames of civil war. But now, as Artyom, you must flee the Metro and lead a band of Spartan Rangers on an incredible, continent-spanning journey across post-apocalyptic Russia in search of a new life in the East. Metro Exodus is an epic, story-driven first person shooter from 4A Games that blends deadly combat and stealth with exploration and survival horror in one of the most immersive game worlds ever created. Explore the Russian wilderness across vast, non-linear levels and follow a thrilling story-line that spans an entire year through spring, summer and autumn to the depths of nuclear winter. Inspired by the novels of Dmitry Glukhovsky, Metro Exodus continues Artyom’s story in the greatest Metro adventure yet. Features Embark on an incredible journey - board the Aurora, a heavily modified steam locomotive, and join a handful of survivors as they search for a new life in the East Experience Sandbox Survival - a gripping story links together classic Metro gameplay with new huge, non-linear levels A beautiful, hostile world - discover the post-apocalyptic Russian wilderness, brought to life with stunning day / night cycles and dynamic weather Deadly combat and stealth - scavenge and craft in the field to customize your arsenal of hand-made weaponry, and engage human and mutant foes in thrilling tactical combat Your choices determine your comrades’ fate - not all your companions will survive the journey; your decisions have consequence in a gripping storyline that offers massive re-playability The ultimate in atmosphere and immersion - a flickering candle in the darkness; a ragged gasp as your gasmask frosts over; the howl of a mutant on the night wind - Metro will immerse and terrify you like no other game…
about_the_game: Owners of Metro Exodus are also entitled to the Metro Exodus PC Enhanced Edition - a stunning visual upgrade that REQUIRES a Ray-Tracing Capable GPU as part of the minimum spec. The DLC for Metro Exodus is also Enhanced – purchasing the Metro Exodus Expansion Pass, or The Two Colonels / Sam’s Story individually, entitles you to the Enhanced version of that content, accessible via the Metro Exodus PC Enhanced Edition. Metro Exodus The year is 2036. A quarter-century after nuclear war devastated the earth, a few thousand survivors still cling to existence beneath the ruins of Moscow, in the tunnels of the Metro. They have struggled against the poisoned elements, fought mutated beasts and paranormal horrors, and suffered the flames of civil war. But now, as Artyom, you must flee the Metro and lead a band of Spartan Rangers on an incredible, continent-spanning journey across post-apocalyptic Russia in search of a new life in the East. Metro Exodus is an epic, story-driven first person shooter from 4A Games that blends deadly combat and stealth with exploration and survival horror in one of the most immersive game worlds ever created. Explore the Russian wilderness across vast, non-linear levels and follow a thrilling story-line that spans an entire year through spring, summer and autumn to the depths of nuclear winter. Inspired by the novels of Dmitry Glukhovsky, Metro Exodus continues Artyom’s story in the greatest Metro adventure yet. Features Embark on an incredible journey - board the Aurora, a heavily modified steam locomotive, and join a handful of survivors as they search for a new life in the East Experience Sandbox Survival - a gripping story links together classic Metro gameplay with new huge, non-linear levels A beautiful, hostile world - discover the post-apocalyptic Russian wilderness, brought to life with stunning day / night cycles and dynamic weather Deadly combat and stealth - scavenge and craft in the field to customize your arsenal of hand-made weaponry, and engage human and mutant foes in thrilling tactical combat Your choices determine your comrades’ fate - not all your companions will survive the journey; your decisions have consequence in a gripping storyline that offers massive re-playability The ultimate in atmosphere and immersion - a flickering candle in the darkness; a ragged gasp as your gasmask frosts over; the howl of a mutant on the night wind - Metro will immerse and terrify you like no other game…
short_description: Flee the shattered ruins of the Moscow Metro and embark on an epic, continent-spanning journey across the post-apocalyptic Russian wilderness. Explore vast, non-linear levels, lose yourself in an immersive, sandbox survival experience, and follow a thrilling story-line that spans an entire year in the greatest Metro adventure yet.

_childDocuments_.review: Metro Exodus takes the journey from snowy and radioactive Moscow and its dark tunnels, to the vast, diverse and beautiful Russian far east. Enhanced version is the way to play, if you can run raytracing. While gamma correction is a bit off, causing some areas too bright or too dark, and there are occasional glitches, enhanced version has much better ambient illumination, less image noise and the ability to turn off motion blur completely and adjust FOV.Metro Exodus not only has great stealth and excellent gunplay, but also an enjoyable amount of realism, such as the need to prioritize stealth and avoid combat as resources are scarce in a post-apocalyptic world. Weapons also start to wear out with more dirt and mud covered, causing jamming and damage and accuracy loss (the game provides a hardcore realistic difficulty as well). Additionally, the ability to customize weapon parts automatically wins a score from me. However, some design choices of the game are not to my liking (they are not bad) and some are just plain bad.Metro Exodus has a unique approach to characterizing. The game often has five to ten minutes of just people talking to fully immerse players into the role of listener, from which you can learn valuable insights of the characters: their pasts, motives, traits, stands and thoughts, fully fleshing out the characters and forming a connection between them and players. Some of these stories are very entertaining with clever sarcasm about real-life social phenomena, and I totally respect this immersive way of characterizing. However, as a psychopath who always watches videos at 1.5x speed, I find these conversations too lengthy and I prefer something shorter and more condensed.The moral point system dictates a good or bad ending in the Metro series. Previous games have harsher requirements such as listening to every lengthy dialogue. Fortunately, Metro Exodus does not require it, but you still need to take a non-lethal approach in many missions, which handicaps players. It is not just me being a blood thirst maniac wanting to kill everyone, it effectively strips away lots of approaches on dealing enemies taking away many gameplay features, and you have to read walkthroughs a lot. While it can be frustrating, the good ending is so beautiful and all seem worthy.Let’s dive into the bad side. Though Metro Exodus is a good game, the pacing is far from being good, and the lack of long and consecutive levels is the root cause. With levels being relatively short, after finishing one level, the game tends to put players through long story sequences or require them to traverse a long distance in the open world, before they can have another short-lived level of action. The open world session pacing is the worst, with the much better and tighter pacing in late-game linear sessions and DLCs. It feels like the developers didn't have enough content in the middle of the game, so they stretched out what they had for far too long.Metro Exodus changes to a semi-open-world-semi-linear structure, marking the first open world title in the series. However, the open world is the weakest part of the game. It is partially to blame for the sloppy pacing as reason mentioned, and it is vast and empty. Though the emptiness fits in the post-apocalyptic setting, it doesn’t justify the emptiness itself being lackluster in terms of gameplay. In fact, I really think the open world is unnecessary. Extra exploration for upgrades in the open world can easily be rearranged as linear levels, which not only paces the game better but also addresses the lack of long and consecutive levels to some degree. That said, it is at least better than those mundane checklist open worlds created just for the sake of making the game longer.The story of Metro Exodus is based on a premise I find hard to believe (I didn’t read the novel), that there are people outside Moscow but was kept as a secret for years. From what I can recall, previous games did not foreshadow this, and it makes events in the last game look like a joke. The transition between knowing the truth and accepting it is also stiff and awkward, but it pales in comparison to the laughable silent protagonist.The last two Metro games both have a silent protagonist, which was popular in the last two decades. I never found it jarring in the last two games, due to writers taking such good care of the fact that Artyom (protagonist) doesn’t talk, hence they never put him in a position being asked for a direct response. But the writers of Metro Exodus did not have such a heart. There are numerous occasions someone on the radio asks something like “Artyom, what is going on”, and Artyom responds with nothing but awkward silence, which completely breaks the immersion. This game goes the extra mile for immersion and realism in gameplay and storytelling, but somehow, they screwed up something so prominent. In stark contrast, DLC protagonists can talk, and you can immediately tell DLCs have a much more immersive presentation than the base game.From the resource management focus combat to the bold storytelling design that might not win everyone’s favor, Metro Exodus is a slow burner compared to traditional FPS titles that are usually fast and thrilling. It suffers from poor pacing and a mediocre open world and is flawed in story and writing, but I still think it is a unique and excellent game after all. Two DLCs are also of high quality, with emotionally contagious plots, good level design and new weapons and parts (you only get the silent sniper rifle in DLC). These two DLCs are must-play as I think they even transcend the base game in many aspects.

_childDocuments_.review: Metro Exodus has a great story combined with multiple places and a lot of action. From sandstorms to snowstorms, NPCs to monsters, it's all here. This game is worth its price and isn't one you would want to miss. This whole game is based around action, love, snow, and sand but most importantly, the train you're all on. To survive you will have to do a lot of things. This could include killing monsters or NPCs but sometimes even driving vehicles.[]I don't remember any negative things about this game. The whole story stayed with me. I love this game and so should you. The game is well thought out. Did I mention there are drivable vehicles?I'd recommend this game to everyone interested in playing a game with a great storyline that is based on action. I think this game is more for people into the story than into the killing. The whole game is based on the story and action is the way you choose as a player. For me, the story sold this game.--------------------Metro Exodus is one of my favorite games. This is due to the overall impact it had on me. Metro Exodus has an amazing story that takes you through multiple environments and gives you plenty of things to discover. The game involves a lot of action from killing monsters to people. The graphics of the game are amazing but didn't really bother me that much. It was mostly the overall 'vibe' the game had. I enjoyed playing it and I am thinking of buying the DLC to have even more fun :). I try to remember some negative things about this game but I actually don't have any. I remember the game sometimes being a bit scary but this still doesn't reach the level of horror. Metro Exodus is not like many other games. It's a mix while at the same time it isn't. The game is unique and involves multiple endings, places, NPCs, and more. It feels amazing to drive on a train while trying to find someplace to continue life.  There are also a few 'pyscho' or 'trippy' events in the game. Of course, there are monsters but there is also this awful weather that freezes you to death and eventually, makes you even lose your mind a bit.

_childDocuments_.review: For a starter, this has to be the best FPS game I've played since the original S.T.A.L.K.E.R.Beautiful semi open world locations with insane level of detail and graphics that for me hold the #1 spot on PC. Well crafted and challenging (if you choose so) difficulty system, solid soundtrack and audio design, although some of the sound choices could be executed better. The atmosphere is spectacular and it leaks out of the screen. All coated with a classic, but well made story that takes us through a harsh journey through post apocalyptic Russia and shows the importance of brotherhood, sacrifice and love.I'd also recommend playing with Russian dubbing. It fits the world and I see no sense playing with ENG one, especially that it's quite worse than original.It really is a shame that the game got bombed with bad reviews because of the Epic Store choice, yes, it was poorly executed but the people who worked their hearts out on this game don't deserve the backlash at all. There are also some bugs and crashes, but nothing that can't be fixed in short term.

_childDocuments_.review: This was easily my favorite Metro game. I know some people complain that it's too much of a departure from the previous games, but that's exactly why I liked it. I never really liked fighting mutants in dark train tunnel after dark train tunnel. I dislike horror and jump scares, but I adored the world of Metro and was always fighting through it. THIS installment is far more my type of game. Most enemies are humans rather than monsters, and it's a lot more open world and in the sunshine. While some people might not like it, my claustrophobia is very appreciative. While the gampeplay and the story are great, and I am recommending this game to any fans of this genre, I still have to mention a few huge negatives. Mainly, my computer hates this game. I was excited to play an up to date Metro with all the bells and whistles, only to find that the back end of this feels like a game from ten years ago. The menu's, the settings, the way everything interacts is dated and awful. My game would freeze a lot (never while playing, only when in the settings). My monitor hates this game, getting it the right resolution was rough and I could never get it borderless. And I bet this is a PC only thing, but going through my inventory and guns was a NIGHTMARE. It took me forever to figure out you have to vaguely click somewhere to the left of what you actually want to select, and even then it didn't always work.Overall it has some technical problems but the game itself is great, and if you liked the other Metro games at all you should love this.

_childDocuments_.review: First off, i'm not going to be a baby about the whole Epic vs Steam, this is a review for the game not the company behind it:The game takes place after Glukhovsky's Metro 2035 Book (Summed up below)End of the book in relation to the start of the game:The overall story of Metro Exodus is by far one of the most gripping experiences I have had in a while. Each larger section of the game is comprised of smaller good and bad endings which overall adds up to a good or bad ending. Receiving the good ending however, is not as complicated as it was in the first game, and in this, you only need to not be an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. After reading both the 3 Books, extended lore books and played the 3 games, I will say that the developers behind Exodus have done just to Glukhovskys universe and developed a captivating plot twist of events which had me shed tears at the end.Oleksii Omelchuk has created a suspenseful and dramatic score which helps set the Exodus game in motion. From what I can tell he has inspiration for the soundtrack from orchestral score artists such as John Murphy. He also touched down on Russian roots using a Balalaika to create what I like to call the Exodus Overture rift which can be heard throughout different songs pulling everything together.The beginning of Metro Exodus plays like a large open world sandbox allowing the player to explore where they want when they want hiding upgrades and story around each map. As you continue to play through however each location becomes more and more narrow lessening the players experience to free roam and becomes more of the classic Metro experience from the first two games. The levels introduce vehicles, weapon upgrades and attachments, deep character building interaction lastly stealth and combat gameplay opportunities.The graphics are great, there are actually 5 setting options, Low, Medium, High, Ultra and Extreme allowing for maximum customization. One thing that really ticks me off is no windowed/windowed borderless mode. The enemies from the previous Metro experiences have also been overhauled to create a spooky atmosphere and diverse selection of mutants.Overall the game to me is definitely GOTY. The new Ranger update has me pulling my hair out with the Iron Man mode, which disables quick saving and checkpoints and only allows saving between levels. Some very unique experiences to the game update as well yields: Full immersion : the time in game can reflect IRL time. 1 day = 1 day IRL as opposed to 1 day = 2 hours IRL. All enemies gain +1 armour level, harder creatures, enemies use grenades more often, limited backpack option means  crafting at benches and not on the fly, and lastly different weapon modes such as 1 weapon slot, no weapon slots, previous weapon slots or start with the crossbow (which you get at the second to last level of the game).Story - 5/5Music - 5/5Gameplay - 5/5Graphics - 5/5Overall - 10/10

_childDocuments_.review: It runs kinda janky on my non-nVidia potato but it is a pretty old computer.  Even still, if you've got an ATI card you're gonna miss out on whatever wowie-zowie nVidia stuff they've put in here.  That's just what these guys do.The plot beats in the game sometimes feel like a ten year old's adventure.  "And then he tries to save the old lady, but they shoot him!  But his medal stops the bullet!  And then he beats them all up! And then he rescues his wife!  And then everybody cheers because he's so awesome!"But y'know, that's okay.  He is awesome, because I am awesome at FPS.Anyway, it's all bleak and worn-out and post-apocalyptic-ish and maybe I'm kind of tired of rummaging through everybody's lunchbox for another handful of nuts, but mercifully there's no levelled gear because if there were chinos +1 I'd refund this game so fast I wouldn't be allowed to write a review.  (I did that for another game that rhymes with "Mildlands: Drakepoint")Where was I?  Right.  Sneakin' is fun and fairly credible.  Guns are crappy and amusing for it, and most of them are just pieces of garbage hammered out of plumbing scrap and a couple nails, so you're SOL if you have strong opinions about M-whatevers.  Did I say it was bleak?  They're drinking mushroom vodka.  I mean how bleak is that?  Can't even have proper potato vodka, that's how bleak.  Russians without proper vodka.It being out in the open world means sniping gets useful and time of day matters, since there's this weird "sun" thing in the sky, instead of the endless tunnels from the previous games.  So there's that.  It's a different experience. You should get it, because it's pretty STALKER-oid (and that's good) and it's on Steam now after being in Epic-Siberia, so you can tell the devs they should sell to Steam earlier.  You know?I feel like I've been rambling.  Somebody can pay for an editor.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is like they combined Fallout 4 and Wolfenstein and kept the worst of both and added a few jump scares. The crafting is unnecessary, boring, and only there because crafting is 'in.' Metro's never had great cover mechanics or been a great FPS but in the Metro it was less of an issue. Being suddenly swarmed by zombies (yeah there's zombies now) and watchmen in an open field, it'd be nice to be able to actually take cover. And of course the open world adds nothing to the game. In fact it detracts from the charm that the first two had. The open world is pretty, but empty except for a few packs of animals, the occasional surprise demon, and the areas that are populated with people. It may as well have been a metro system with a few branching lines. Overall 6/10. There's better horror games, better fps games, and better open world post apocalypse games. Metro Exodus falls short in every category and lost the charm of the originals.Update: Beat the game. Got the 'good' ending. The last mission is the only mission I enjoyed and was the only one which stayed true to the originals. No change in rating, 6/10.

Many obstacles conquered.Before this we thought the world to be a desolate place.Wait... There's a guy who used to say that all the time.Bear something... _childDocuments_.review: As an assiduous Metro series' fan, I can say that Exodus is a good ending for a very powerful story-driven game. 10/10.     My wife is russian, and she watched the whole game beside me as I was playing. Living every moment, every dialogue, like she was there at her homeland (we don't live in Russia). She is also big fan of the series' soundtrack, and so am I.      We finished the game yesterday and we can't stop thinking of it. It makes you see life differently, makes you pay more attention to those you love, to the moments you live. When you complete the game, it feels like you have some kind of "fresh start". With a new perspective of life, because it's just that short and fragile.       If you love Metro series and russian culture, there should be a really enjoyable purchase for your account.     I have bought the golden version with soundtrack and artwork. Couldn't be any happier.     I wish I could forget everything about the series, and play them all over again.

_childDocuments_.review: Hello,This game is great. Having played a lot of other post nuclear war games this game was outstanding. The graphics are just great even on high the game looks phenomenal. It offers the player much more customization than its predecessors. You can upgrade the Revolver from being just an ordinary pistol to a sniper rifle. The game is also very realistic in the terms of damage. In Fallout when you get a better suit of armor you become a bullet sponge but, in this game, however you can die after 3-4 shots and can be killed even by the environment, for example anomalies and when you run out of filters for your gas mask. The gas mask can break and you´ll have to fix it up or tape it together for the time being. I also liked that the weapon cleaning mechanic was added to the rechargeable flashlight. The maps are open and there are many easter eggs hidden in the irradiated regions of Russia. The DLC´s were also great. I liked Sam`s Story more than The Two Colonels but in my opinion, they are both very well made and fit the Story perfectly. One problem I encountered when I played the game was the fall damage. Most of my deaths in this game are caused by me underestimating the high ground. But other than that, this is definitely worth to take a look at if you liked games like Fallout. _childDocuments_.review: Metro Exodus is an excellent entry in the post-apocalyptic series, combining a new direction of sandbox level design, with the gritty setting of the irradiated Russian countryside. The levels remind me of Far Cry 2 with the ability to spot and identify targets from afar, and choose your point of entry with each engagement. The levels also hold true to the design of the previous games, with alternate paths tucked away leading to advantageous positions for engagements, or a cache of weapons, ammo or resources.The modular nature of the weapons in Exodus offer a huge degree of adaptability, with is very refreshing for the franchise, as you are no longer confined to modifying at trader shops located exclusively within a handful of metro stations. The weapons also feel great, with awesome new improvements to classic weapons like the Tikhar and Helsing, as well as some new additions. Some fan favourites like the Duplet and (my personal favourite) the VSS are missing. Fortunately with the existing weapon list, you can modify other weapons to replicate these missing classics.The visuals and graphics are simply amazing. Considering how the series looked not too long ago, the team at 4A have made great strides in improving the look and feel of their games, and I hope this series can continue to reach an ever expanding fanbase. I understand that people are upset at the Epic Store exclusivity, and I can't blame them for that. However, this was decision made by the publisher Deep Silver, not 4A. Once this period is up however, I would recommend anyone who has an interest in this game to pick it up, it is excellent and I am currently eagerly awaiting the DLC expansions. I have played it 3 times through at the time of writing, and I still thoroughly enjoy this game.

_childDocuments_.review: Unfortunately, this game is riddled with bugs.To start with, there's a persistent post-processing filter that's laid over the game at different moments. It's unfortunately not possible to turn this off, and the filter makes the night scenes far too light, and the daytime scenes far too dark. I don't think this has anything to do with the new ray tracing features, because the filter sometimes disappears during cutscenes, when waking up, etc. Very weird. Wish they included an option to turn it off.There are a number of other bugs which damage the experience, too. For example, my subtitles got completely stuck very early in the game. The same two lines are stuck on the screen permanently, and no other dialogue will display. Very annoying...Despite the beauty of added ray tracing and the fantastic impact of DLSS 2.1 in the new Enhanced Edition, the graphical options are so bare bones it's almost laughable. All you can really change is texture quality. No anti-aliasing or other options.The big kicker for me, though, was that I am now at the end of Caspian, and the game crashes whenever I try to load my save. I've tried to load older saves, I've tried starting the game in safe mode. No dice, it's broken. I'm not sure what caused this, but it's pretty disappointing. I can put up with the graphical weirdness but this is obviously a dealbreaker.Since my save file was now effectively bricked, I decided I would play the DLC. A few moments into starting up Sam's Story and, guess what? Yup, can't progress due to another abundance of crashes, this time in-game. So I ended up giving up and just uninstalled this. Not going to waste my time any further by putting hours into a game that will randomly hard lock me.In any case, if you were waiting to buy this for Enhanced Edition, you'll probably be disappointed. It's a very unstable game, even now, two years after its original release. I like this game a lot but unfortunately I can't recommend it considering how unstable it is.If you liked this review and would like to hear my opinion on other games, please feel free to follow !

_childDocuments_.review: Metro Exodus does many things right, and by all means it succeeds on many levels. Graphics are amazing, especially with raytracing, the "semi-open" world is just large enough to prevent any unnecessary baggage (like filler quests), and of course the atmosphere is on point; especially the further you get into the game. The character writing and development was much stronger this time around, and if you wait on the train characters will talk to you for extended amounts of time, and it feels like a real conversationHOWEVER...While Metro Exodus does many things right, it also has it's fair share of wrongs. There are some mechanics that feel like they don't fit, or don't work out practically. For example, there is no "Save" option, only quicksave. Quicksave can set you back upwards of 10 minutes prior to where you were when you exited the game. Also, the game forces you to keep one gun in your inventory for almost the entirety of the game, which severely prevents the "play anyway you want" tagline. The game is also biased towards stealth, but I don't mind that.I also encountered a plethora of bugs during my playthrough, and let's not forget this game is officially over a year old. I had multiple crashes and freezing issues, I haven't had a game crash on me that much in years. Sometimes the game would stutter on levels with more detail (like the Taiga/Forest) frequently, but other times it would run completely fine. I also had many clipping errors, and issues with the player gaining airtime while running, which would launch me into the air, and wound me.IN CONCLUSIONEven though I just spent two paragraphs complaining about the game, when Metro Exodus succeeds, it does it astonishingly well. Even with it's shortcomings, I would still recommend picking up the game. I waited a year to purchase this game due to the exclusivity period, and because of these issues, I don't regret it one bit. Now that it's here and on sale though, go ahead and give it a try. Not everyone experiences the same bugs, so hopefully you'll have an easier time than I did.

_childDocuments_.review: Ten years ago Metro 2033 was an unexpected pleasant surprise. It was a scripted linear stealth FPS that cared about its storytelling, its world and characters more than about making you feel cool, something that was commonplace for the tightly scripted big budget titles of the time. It was as if Escape from Butcher Bay was based on a Russian post-apocalyptic sci-fi novel. And despite a lot of its issues, it was unforgettable and wonderful.Ten years from then, Metro Exodus is trying to turn Metro 2033 into Far Cry. Results are far less disastrous than one might expect.I simply do not understand why anyone thought that basing Metro Exodus almost entirely on gameplay would be a good idea, without rethinking said gameplay completely. But that is what happened. Exodus has several story sequences/levels that work almost exactly like the previous games - highly scripted stealth FPS with forced action moments. And then most of game is set inside open maps/open levels which are essentially tiny open world locations with several locations for you to explore at your own pace. Except, most of those, if they have any kind of quest attached to them, work exactly like what I've described with the older games. Which is completely at odds with the open nature the game is trying to have at the same time, simply because that core gameplay was never particularly fun in the first place.See, Metro games were never good FPS or stealth titles, if you boil them down to mechanics specifically. Those worked to create the tension necessary for the situation, for the story. Those worked in conjunction with the moral choices you had, with understanding that you must ration your ammo, your filters, your medkits. Mechanically, it was boring and basic. Stealth, as mentioned, was almost always the "intended" way to go, but it was relatively not annoying specifically because you just had to follow the "intended" path and everything will work out. Shooting was fine for short sequences, because the unorthodox weapons had neat little touches to them that made them unique. Metro 2033 and Last Light were great because these mechanics served a purpose of telling the story.Metro Exodus jumps between telling a genuinely atrociously stupid story and outright refusing to tell the story unless you beg it to say anything. The story, as it is, is just boring, but the fact that you essentially have an all new cast, while the main character is still a mute dummy isn't helping. The obnoxious "love interest" from Last Light returns and is, in fact, the main focus of the story in a way, her dad, redesigned completely yet again, returns as well. But apart from them, the rest of the cast are all new and all forgettable, all lacking personality. With Artyom being the biggest personality void of all. In 2033 he was just a guy who suddenly got an important task assigned to him and went on a journey that changed him and who managed to change the lives of those around him as he went. In Last Light he was closer to your typical soldier character, a "hero", yet it still fit the story. In Exodus, he is simply not a character at all. He has all these relationships, all of these desires, yet he, as a character, is just absent and nothing in the story or the gameplay builds him at all.What's worse is when you need to ask the game to tell you things. Do you know how most character developments, most critical expositions that build the locations you visit happen? You need to find a character who is willing to share those and stand near them. Just literally stand near them. Doing nothing. For up to 5-10 minutes. Listening to Exposition Podcast. With things mentioned there that are vital to understanding the situations and motivations. Who thought this was a good way to tell a story in a story driven game?But then again, Metro Exodus tries hard to not be story driven and to be gameplay driven and it just doesn't work. The joy of Far Cry, or Just Cause, or whatever other similar titles is in the fact that you can do really fun things with the core systems, the core mechanics of the game. Heck, even Gears 5, with similar open level design, is good because its core shooting is, and always was, good. Repetitive, but good. Very few things in Metro Exodus are mechanically interesting, yet the open level design forced the studio to cut down on the actions and the weapons, so they could reuse those in the most efficient way, as often as possible. And it's just boring to go through. And on Ranger difficulty, which is, as usual for the series, in many ways the intended experience, the scripted sequences feel about as fine as they used to before, except now in the open exploration you can randomly die to something unexpected and then learn that the last checkpoint was 10 minutes ago and before you did all of that boring "collect crap, craft crap, upgrade weapon crap" stuff that is common to the Far Cry games. No challenge, just annoyance.There are good things in this game, however, as little as there are. Some of the stories you encounter are genuinely interesting. The whole "morality system" is least obtuse here and feels surprisingly well integrated into the story. Visually the game is astonishing even without the Ray Tracing features and locations are consistently beautiful at any time of day that is dynamic as is the weather. And even though it's considerably less inventive with its storytelling than the original was, it still has some really good moments.Two story DLCs for the game aren't particularly exciting either. The first one, The Two Colonels, feels closer to what Last Light and especially its DLCs were about, but otherwise tells a rather unimportant part of the backstory. It has some interesting moments, it has a flamethrower as a main weapon, but otherwise it's not very good. Also extremely poorly optimized for Ranger difficulty where you will most likely often randomly die to something. The second one, Sam's Story, does the same open level design as the main game, but its story is as bland and unimportant as of the first DLC. It is essentially just "more of the same", except with an even stupider story.Oh yeah, also the game can still be incredibly buggy. I personally encountered mostly animation bugs, with characters and things randomly teleporting around or things getting stuck in other things, but a few times things went completely off rails and I had to restart the checkpoint. Also, it's been 10 years, and the PC settings in the game are as basic and crap as they were in 2033 - just a couple of presets and no manual control over what enables/disables what. It doesn't even say what each preset does, which is especially obnoxious since it seems that the last 2 presets are basically the same in terms of settings and its just that the highest one uses supersampling (renders the game at a higher resolution and downsamples from it).I didn't actively dislike Metro Exodus, but unlike the previous two entries in the franchise, I didn't enjoy this game at all. Most of the time I just wanted it to end so I could move to something else. It looks great, it has a few good moments, its post-apocalyptic world, while expanded, is still curious and Tihar is still one of the most interesting guns in gaming history, despite its simplicity. But it's also primitive and bland as a story driven game, rather limiting and linear for an exploration focused open level game and not particularly exciting for a stealth action title. Also, the music is downright terrible this time around. How far from the wonderful music of 2033 we have come. Honestly, instead of playing Metro Exodus I'd suggest checking Metro 2033 again, in original or Redux versions. I kinda wish I did.

_childDocuments_.review: Criminally underrated series, all 3 games are nothing short of masterpieces of the modern times. With that said, this time Artyom and his crew finally break out from the haunting dark tunnels of Moscow metro and travel all over Russia (or whats left of Russia) to find a place to call home. The base game is 25-30 hours long if you are like me and prefer listening to every conversation and checking out every corner. The DLCs too are definitely worth the money and made with the same effort as the amazing base game. The Two Colonels is completely linear (veterans of metro will feel more at home) and tell a great story which I am sure nobody wants me to spoil here, its around 2 hours long and you can easily finish it in one go. Sam's Story is more like the base game in the sense that it gives you a map to explore. It follows the journey of the only American crewmate of Artyom who's trying to get to his home country, its around 5-6 hours long. Sam's Story starts right from the point where the base game ends, so its definitely better to play the base game first before jumping into any of the DLCs (even though Two Colonels is mostly set in past. it does contain massive spoilers for the base game). I still can't wrap my head around the fact that this game wasn't even picked as a nomination for GOTY. Single-player shooters aren't dead. Thanks 4A Games. <3

_childDocuments_.review: This is a tough one to review. There's a good game,under the grime,and the problems. I adored Last Light,I loved 2033,so much so I bought the books. But Exodus? For some reason,I just,can't get my vibe on with it. I really wish steam had a middle ground button more so than a thumbs up,or a thumbs down. I'm not finished with the game yet,and I plan to rewrite this once I complete the story(I'm currently in Taiga)Lets start with the good!The game looks so great.The weapons feel good mostly. They're punchy,they feel solid,the Ashot feels like a proper handcannon even if it's not my trusty Duplet. The maps are fun to explore.There's lots of neat little things to find. The crew is interesting,the Aurora is rather nice to just hang out on and listen to the various people chat.And that so far,is about where my praise stops.Metro Exodus feels like it was taken out of the oven far too soon. It reminds me so much so of Cyberpunk 2077. If you watch your shadows you have the goofiest animations.  I observed plenty of odd animation and texture bugs or issues(I.e Katya has a habit of..teleporting around for me,or oddly sped up animations). Plenty of animations look choppy in the Aurora. Especially if you observe certain characters. I have noticed in combat,the enemy humans play sort of strange animations when running and ducking into cover. This wasn't something that I noticed in Redux. The weapons that Artyom uses,have excellent animations,it's just odd that you can see your shadows,and the way the character moves,is so rigid,and clumsy.  The animation problems are often jarring I find because so many look plain unnatural.The enemy AI,I've noticed,has,weird problems. Between pathfinding to cover,to detection. There's times I shouldn't have been discovered (I.e hiding in a sandstorm in the dark) and I still get found,even though the bandits flashlights can't see me. Theres many,many bugs. The worst offender has been in Caspian Desert where I was unable to open my inventory. Especially near the end,where you are fighting in the Rig. It would've saved much aggravation and ammo had my backpack been functional. I find it especially odd,to see the weapon diversity enjoyed by Last Light,is suddenly gone.  The Mongrel is terrible as it uses Pistol ammo instead of assault rifle ammo.  There's no VSK,and nothing really to take it's place. There's many holes in the weapon library now,and it's sad to see them now gone. Especially now that your 3rd weapon slot,is restricted to the Tikhar or other Ranger weapons.While my PC surpasses the specs required for Enhanced Edition,I couldn't get it to run properly without CTD'ing. So I gave up and uninstalled it,and just played the standard edition. Mind you I did attempt the Windows update and it still failed to work for me. Even new GFX drivers as well. I'm not sure what the problem could be.Enemies are..hit and miss.Normal human enemies are generally fine(even if they blend in a little *too* well. The armored enemies can go burn in a hole,because they are the worst thing ever I've fought in a Metro game so far. Yes it's good to have them be strong,but it's annoying how they can sometimes shoot you through walls or cover you think is solid due to awkward hitboxes. They are horribly spongy,and you should always have a couple of molotovs ready for them. Storywise,it's fine. Nothing really too stand out,nothing bad either.  Buy it on sale,beware the bugs,the game is fun when it's not twitching out or freaking out in some manner.  But it's not worth full price,and I'm glad I waited a year before I bought it. If anything it showed that it needed more time in the cooker. This will be updated upon story completion.

_childDocuments_.review: Metro games are made with passion. The series expounds on what was previously derived from the novel  by Arkady and Boris Strugatsky, that was later produced into a movie, , by Andrei Tarkovsky, that inspired the Metro book series, before it finally making its way into video games. Metro Exodus is the third entry in this series. And it might be the greatest.Whether it checks that box for the consumer depends on if returning players, or newcomers, can handle the holistic changes that come packaged within Exodus. It’s a different game from its progenitors. It provides fundamental Metro gameplay, but it is now expanded within the context of open-sandbox environments. Which is a stark contrast from the on-the-rails story beats returning players might expect. Metro Exodus elected to give the player the power to create their own set pieces. And it was a risk, but a calculated one.The creators were most certainly attempting to broaden their consumer base while also being mindful of those returning (although Epic Store–timed exclusivity kind of screwed that up anyway). But alterations from the norm were a success. Metro Exodus is fantastic.  In the wake of apocalyptic nuclear war, the Metro series follows the surviving inhabitants living in the old Moscow Metro, or subway system. Metro stations have become towns and the remaining populace has formed collectivist ownership over these towns. Over time, each station established its own unique identity. Some friendly, some not. Previous Metro titles (Metro 2033 and Metro: Last Light) tasked the player with navigating the metro, warring with self-radicalized stations, and dealing with irradiated monsters that now stalk the tunnels.Exodus is about Artyom, the series’s protagonist, leaving Moscow with a squad of series regulars on a year-long journey across Russia. The game opens remarkably similar to previous entries. The player traverses a frozen Moscow landscape, journeys through a metro station, and is otherwise exposed to linear narrative threads. None of this is tedious though. The Metro series has already showcased how adept it is at handling linearity. Mostly, it does it through atmosphere and mood, which continues to be exhibited in Exodus. Artyom has always been a silent protagonist, the exception being his journal entries that are voiced during loading screens. Exodus keeps the same format, and in doing so, handles expository information well. It is difficult to competently and realistically disseminate exposition in a meaningful way with a mute character, so it’s amazing how effortlessly Exodus does it. The player naturally learns of the events that happened between Last Light and this current story, the most important of which is that Artyom’s lover, Anna, remains as such.Events take place that cause Artyom and his crew to leave Moscow for the Russian countryside via locomotive. After that, familiar linearity of old metro systems is mostly abandoned in favor of successive, unique sandboxes that change as each chapter progresses. And they’re all astounding.After leaving Moscow, the story proceeds through four unique chapters that all feature different playscapes. Mostly these areas offer aesthetic differences that revolve around the seasons in which your crew visits them. Basically, expect the summer area to feel hotter and the autumn area to feel colder. The first three sandboxes, in particular, elect to give up control to the player to create their own action within the various locations constructed. It is obviously an enormous risk to create a Metro game that doesn’t take place in, well, a metro. But they had reason to bet on themselves.The creators were able to split the difference between their typical, linear narrative structure and popular open-world exploration. This was achieved by not making any one area have  much to do or be  big to explore. Artyom has a map of each region, and that map is highlighted with areas of importance. Some of these highlights feature a monster’s nest to destroy or a bandit’s camp to clear, while others contain pertinent story points.  It really works.  Exodus swapped tunnels for open landscapes featuring a day-and-night cycle. The same emotions that the player previously felt exploring the darkness of the metro is again achieved through this approach. It is still extremely immersive, and surprisingly eerie, to traverse Exodus’s landscapes in intense darkness, surrounded by things that want to kill you. The environments are different. The atmosphere is the same.An absolute must when developing sandboxes is that there exists an inherent mechanical reason for the player to explore them, in addition to narrative motivations. If not, the game is just as on-the-rails as before, only now watered down with unnecessary fluff. Fortunately, Exodus does provide a reason. Not only do the environments look interesting, they usually contain important crafting materials within. These resources are used to upgrade, modify, and clean Artyom’s equipment. And equipment can degrade rapidly depending on the situation. Which means nearly every collapsed building, dark tunnel, or campfire in the distance is worth checking out. Occasionally Artyom will run into members of his own squad while exploring these ruins, which adds to player immersion. The world just feels alive.Exodus tells a wonderful story. It features terrific characters, some of which were introduced in the previous games, and expands on their personas. There is, admittedly, a trope-ish element that exists here somewhat—there are tough characters, funny characters, and sweet characters. But if the player spends enough time listening to their conversations, they will eventually observe personalities that exist beyond their archetypes. Especially with Anna. Anna engenders immense pathos by the story’s conclusion, partly because the player is granted so many different, immersive ways to interact with her. All of which are extraordinarily additive. Maybe you’ll put your arm around her, or hold her hand, or brush her hair back. And while all of this is completely optional, it is hard to imagine any Metro player electing not to. Their relationship feels honest. Which is doubly an achievement when you consider that Artyom never utters a word. When certain circumstances arise that place Anna in extreme danger, there is an emergent need for the player to deliver her safely and as quickly as possible. By the time Exodus’s train reaches its final destination, the player will have experienced one of the more immersive stories in recent years. A story that, much to its credit, features multiple endings to increase replayability. I have beaten the game twice (once on console), and both endings were different, excellent finales. One of the endings was the  ending. But it didn’t seem bad to me; more like good storytelling.Metro Exodus is the third part in the Metro series. It is a mechanically sound, first-person shooter that takes place across a litany of areas that the player will explore. It is a blast to play. It contains a strong story that perfectly balances gameplay with narrative beats. While it may lack some of the spectacle seen in more well-known franchises, it more than makes up for it in its polish and atmosphere. In fact, Metro Exodus surpasses nearly all of its contemporaries with relative ease.

_childDocuments_.review: Metro Exodus is awesome. But not as good as the previous two games.It has most of the elements I love from previous games like, pretty fun combat, fantastic atmosphere and level design, great story.There are some things that sucks though:- Pretty poor stealth.- Awful movement physics, possibly the worst I've ever experienced in a video game. It is very unsmooth, you stumble on everything, sometimes you move freely, sometimes you slow down heavily (not counting walking through the spider webs), you can slow down by walking on as tiny things as cables and wires too... Often you can stumble across a tiny rock and shoot a few metres forward often landing in a water and drowning or in some hole and fall to death. Or even worse, sometimes you run and then suddenly shoot yourself like a rocket into the air like 60 metres and then fall to your death... These happen very commonly.- Once saves got corrupted for no reason at all. Fortunately, the previous save worked and I lost like only a minute of progress.- Sound mixing is awful, couldn't make the game sound right no matter how much I played with the volume settings, it was always either the background effects too loud, the speaking too loud/silent, the music too loud/silent... It's as if every sound in this game has different sound volume on its own. Even in the same dialogue of two people standing next to each other sometimes there's like a 2x volume difference between the both of them.- Night/day cycle can be annoying. It changes way too often and sometimes there are no beds anywhere around.- Sometimes it is hard to tell whether you can walk on something or is it muddy water in which you can drown. What is even worse, sometimes an enemy can grab you in the water, you break out with a quick time event and then still drown...- Poor optimisation, at times it runs extremely smoothly, but most of the time it performs poorly.- Some of the worst product localization I have ever seen (for a big budget game that is). Most of the writings on the walls which are in russian, aren't translated (a few of them have translation pop-ups, but very few), also some of the russian dialogues aren't translated in English as well, they're just written in Latin alphabet in subtitles...Anyway, this game is an awesome journey with tons of nuisances.8/10

_childDocuments_.review: I've been playing games for over 20 years now, and the older you grow, the more you have already seen. As a consequence, it becomes harder and harder to be flashed by shiny graphics and action sequences and really dive into the world of a game that is believable and keeps you wanting more.Many games nowadays, in my opinion, are polished very well, but lack a soul. This game may not be perfect in all aspects, sometimes it feels a bit clunky. But it feels alive and real, despite or maybe even because of its little imperfections. It's one of those rare games that come along now and then that has something of a soul. 10/10 in my opinion. Great work and kudos to the development team! Personally, I don't know and care too much about the Epic store vs Steam store battle. That's how markets work. In the end, I know one thing: I would have bought this game on both the Epic and Steam store if I needed to, just to give the developers double of the money that they expect, because that is what they deserve.

_childDocuments_.review: After a few weeks I was finally able to get through the bugs and finish this game. The gist of the story is that after years of living in the metro, Artyom discovers theres' life outside of the metro and looks for a new radiation-free place to live. As a conclusion to the metro trilogy, I feel like it leaves off on a satisfying note, but I'm left with the feeling of "what ever happened to X". The Spartans have a lot of personality and don't feel like generic NPCs travelling with Artyom. I actually like and care about his companions. You will only get to know them if you actually go out of your way to interact with them and listen to their dialogue though. As for the gameplay, it's pretty much identical to the previous two titles. You can go in stealth or guns-blazing. Bullets are not very scarce this time around, however I only played on hardcore. Hardcore Ranger may be different. There's a decent amount of mutant variety, but they're not as dangerous as human enemies. Gun customization is pretty insane. You can get a variety of scopes, magazines, barrels, etc to customize guns as you see fit. The graphics and environments are phenomenal. This is definitely the best looking FPS I've ever played (sorry Crysis 3). The game itself would be solid if not for the atrocious bugs. The biggest one is hard crashing at the Desert lighthouse. Sometimes when sneaking up on enemies you aren't given a prompt to stealth kill or knock them out, resulting in death or being discovered. Random crashes can result when enemies discover and engage you. The game sometimes auto-saves when near hostile enemies or doesn't auto-save at all, resulting in having to redo 10 minute sequences. You are not able to create hard-saves, only quick saves. You can load up to 5 previous quick saves, but if you want to load one further than the most recent you have to quit to the main menu.I enjoyed the game, but the bugs can make it completely unplayable. I'm not just saying to say it. There is a high chance that you will not be able to finish this game. It really is jarring for a game of this quality to have these kinds of bugs, especially considering 4A has made two other Metro games without any issues.

_childDocuments_.review: I feel Metro Exodus is a step forwards and two step back....For those who love open world exploring then you're in a treat, because Metro Exodus offers that. But at the same time I feel this in't Metro anymore. When I first play Metro, it's because it's literally inside a Metro, it was so unique and mind blowing how people built their new life inside a Metro system. There was nothing like this even till today. Only Metro game you get to see it. Now having an open world is nice, but I feel the developers were lazy, because the world is fun to explore yet at times feel dead and dull, since there's no real form of missions or any sense of requirement for you to explore. Sure it's better to explore it and get all the best equipment, but you don't actually need it to complete the game. It's like you have to use your own imagination to have fun with it....if I were to do that I wouldn't be playing a game, I would learn to be a game developer instead. Battles / gunfights are lot more mediocre too....even on the Main Story line, It's not as epic and engaging as the previous two games. Hard to put it into words, but as I said when I play Metro Exodus it doesn't give me that sort of engaging and sense of a SP, but rather more like a MMO RPG Online game...It feels " dull " yet the game have so much potential....I actually had more fun in the DLC called Two Colonel...that's the easiest way I can explain my dissatisfaction with Metro Exodus. In a Nutshell, the game is great, I had fun, but It could have been better. And If I were to recommend a Metro game, I most likely would easily recommend Last Light / 2033 Redux instead, not because those are the Prequel, but I find those overall a better Metro games. Even when it lack the mechanic and gameplay Exodus offers. But I'm still gonna thumb it up. It's a Good game, but definitely not a Masterpiece or the Sequel I was expecting.

Their are probably one or two things I missed but these are the best elements off the top of my head.Cons: *Unskippable intro sequence. Every time I start up the game I am unable to skip the intros even when spamming "E". This is incredibly annoying... I know this could be considered petty but this really is annoying.*One of my biggest gripes is with a character in the game. Specifically Anna... Yes Anna. Don't get me wrong Anna is fantastic. _childDocuments_.review: As a fan of the previous two games and the books, I can without a doubt recommend this game. If you're a fan of the previous two entries, you owe it to yourself to see where the story takes Artyom and his wife in this Russian post-apocalyptic epic. If you haven't played the previous games, you could still enjoy this one but I urge you to play the others first as all three of them are part of the same story. I've played the game twice now, once on normal difficulty and once on Ranger Hardcore with all the hud turned off.Unlike Metro 2033 & Metro Last Light which were known for their linear gameplay and claustrophobic levels, this one has much wider and more open levels since our crew is leaving their life in the metro behind  in order to to persue answers about what life is like outside Moscow. The game still has underground levels that made metro so good in the first place, but the majority of the game is spent up in the unforgiving Russian Wasteland in what could be described as a Semi-Open world game.This is the most refined version of the gameplay that we know and love from the past games. The survival mechanics have been turned up to eleven. Mask filters are rare and  ammo is scarce. You're forced to count every single bullet and think before getting into an encounter. You wanna sit far away because you saw a mutant and you're scared ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥? Too bad, doing so will use all of your remaining gas mask filters so you have to man up and get it over with.  The gunplay itself has been improved drastically since Last Light. The guns feel much more real and impactful and you can really tell that you're firing a Kalashnikov when the gun starts to kick like crazy. Take care of your guns because if you don't do so, they'll get damaged overtime and they will jam. There's a huge amount of attachments  that completely change the identity of each gun.The bullet  economy has been changed this time around. In this game, there are no bullets that will get you anything. You'll have to make due with  the stuff that you find on the surface. Only then will you be able to craft things like bullets and so on.The AI itself is quite questionable. On my first playthrough (normal) I found both killing enemies and sneaking past them rather easy, while on my second playthrough(Ranger hardcore, hardest difficulty) the NPCs would grow a third eye and always spot me. They were also super deadly in combat and would kill you in 2-3 shots. If I had to choose a difficulty for someone who plays the game for the first time, I'd without a doubt choose "Hard". The number of enemies felt way too low on normal and way too high on ranger hardcore, so I feel like hard would be the best balance out of all the things that I mentioned.As far as mutants go, this game easily has the most variety out of all three games. You have your usual flying demons, you have your lake monsters, our friendly watchmen patrolling the wasteland, creepy underground spiders, mutated animals and of course a few others that I'll let you explore on your own.The maps/chapters are very varied as well. You have the huge caspian desert that feels like you're playing mad max, you have an underground bunker that feels like playing Wolfenstein, a far cry-like forest level, or the Volga level that Stalker fans will love. Dont get me wrong though, the final level of the game is classic metro on steroids. Absolutely mental.The replayability of the game isnt too bad either. Without getting into spoilers, the game has multiple endings that require different playstyles. Also, thanks to the non-linear levels, there's different ways to approach each objective and many things that can be easily missed on your first playthrough.The story of this game is loosely based on the Metro 2035 novel but 90% of the story is new. It only borrows some book plot twists in its first hour and thats it, everything else is new. It's a continuation of Metro Last Light and you see the effects that the ending of the second game had on this world and its characters.The plot itself sounds like a typical post apocalyptic Odyssey on paper but the subtle political messages and the characters are what make it special. My biggest complaint is that just like the previous games, our protagonist, Artyom, does not speak. He speaks in loading screens so you can hear whats going on in his mind but he does not speak in the actual game. That's really immersion breaking when people talk to you and ask things of you and you dont say anything, but they somehow get on with it anyway. What I dont understand is that since Artyom is already a very established and interesting character in the books, and since he already speaks his mind during cutscenes, why shouldnt he speak in game ? The other characters consist of Artyom's wife Anna from the second game, her father Colonel Miller from the first game and a few comrades from the Spartan order and people that you meet along the way. I was pleasantly surprised at how much of a backstory each one of them had. You can read your journal and learn more things about them and confont them on the aurora to hear optional dialogue that builds their character. All in all, great.The story itself with all the plot twists and stuff I thought was great, although I did see a few twists coming from a mile away(But again, I had read the book which the game drew inspiration from). The game slowly builds towards the big finale of the game which had me on the edge of my seat and was truly breathtaking. I legit had no idea what was going to happen in the end.Another thing that I feel like I have to mention is the lack of supernatural elements in this game and the story. If you've played the previous games then you're  familiar that the games can get pretty nuts with all the supernatural stuff but for better or worse, they are mostly absent from this game. Which, again, is because the same thing happened with the 2035 novel. The game though focuses on some political messages that were present in the book too which I enjoyed. Its a story of how you can best manipulate a nation, conserve it underground and make it follow false leaders who all they have to do is point their finger at a plausible enemy so you can blame them for your failures and be doomed in an eternal war. The 2035 novel itself is dedicated to this theme and how man needs enemies to find purpose in life and identify himself. It's a story about being afraid to look at the truth and take actions.TL:DR: This is a great entry to an already amazing series that thanks to its survival mechanics, gameplay and unforgetable story make Exodus a must play.+Great Story+Interesting Characters+Immervise survival gameplay+Shooting feels amazing+Satisfying ending+Very detailed Journal about the world and its characters with lots of lore+/- A few nice plot twists that might feel disjointed if you can sense them coming+/- AI can feel uneven+/- Silent protagonist (Which is a personal prefference)NoneScore: 8.8/10

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of those titles that stuck with me long after I finished it and that I kept thinking about for several days.The game is set 2 years after the events of the previous chapter.Our protagonists, Artyom, Anna, Miller and some former Spartans, tired of life underground and after discovering that there are other survivors living on the surface, embark on a journey on board a train in search of a place where they can settle a colony and start a new life outside the metro.This "exodus" will mean that throughout the storyline we will visit a variety of different places, each characterized by its own peculiarities. The bombings occurred about 25 years earlier and therefore a large part of the territories are still highly irradiated, inhospitable, infested with mutants or in any case difficult to inhabit.The game will let us discover many small settlements, each of which, following the wars and the absence of a central government, has had different events and has evolved and adapted to the circumstances as best it could.This allows for a very varied narrative that is free from the setting of the tunnels, which bored me a bit after Last Light. And towards the end, when we’ll have to return to another subway and visit its tunnels, we will discover that even there events took a very different turn compared to what happened under Moscow.Initially I didn't appreciate the first "open" level (The Volga), coming from the linear gameplay of the previous chapters I found it a bit distracting. However, once I got past the first adaptation phase, the game hooked me. In fact, it is not so much the gameplay that popped, but rather the various stories that we will gradually discover. Each chapter is somewhat comparable to one of the Fallout vaults, and so the thing I found most exciting was trying to understand what happened and how it got to the current situation.The environmental narration also helps a lot in this, very carefully crafted, full of visual clues as well as the classic fragments of diaries scattered around. All this captured me and immersed me in the stories, I felt right there, sometimes inside and sometimes alongside Artyom, while I explored All the characters have endured extremely hard stories, and are the often tragic fruit of their experiences. Despite everything at the end of each episode, however dramatic, there sometimes remains a glimmer of hope, perhaps reflecting the vision of Dmitry Glukhovsky (not having read the novels I can't say for sure, but I can certainly say that I felt like to read them while playing this title).To all this I would add that aliens are not present in the main plot, unlike the previous chapters, and this makes it in my opinion much more linear and simple to follow, and ultimately I appreciated it much more than that of 2033 and Last Light.Speaking of pure gameplay, however in this chapter we will have more freedom of movement thanks to the introduction of semi-open world hubs, where in addition to being able to decide whether to have a stealth or more aggressive approach, sometimes we will be able to choose the order in which to face the objectives.This might be a bit reminiscent of the immersive sim genre, although in reality everything will be much simpler and more linear. The result, in my opinion, is quite balanced and enjoyable, and contributes to immersion in the general atmosphere.Moving on to the graphics section, I must say that I also found this to be exceptional. I played the version with Ray Tracing and I found everything really well done, non-repetitive and with great attention to detail. As already mentioned, the environmental storytelling is really effective, also thanks to the beautiful graphics. The artistic direction is excellent, all the settings had a strong visual impact on me, without ever boring me, really managing to immerse myself in the atmosphere.The same thing I can say about the sound, whose well-crafted effects amplify even more the emotions gradually transmitted by the environment, the tension of walking alone inside radioactive tunnels full of corpses or in a sandstorm. The soundtrack is also excellent, discreet and effective.In conclusion, a game that I approached because I felt the need for a bit of a post-apocalyptic “fix” and which definitely exceeded all expectations, leaving me more than satisfied, and above all intrigued to finally read the novels on which it is based. Highly recommended!

_childDocuments_.review: Amazing metro experience, however not as good as the predecessors.Metro Exodus gets a lot of things right, but sadly misses a lot of what made it good in the past.The story as a standalone is a great experience and holds up quite nicely, however as a sequel it disregards aspects such as the Dark Ones from previous instalments. The new take on "open world" is refreshing and quite a fun experience, however it does not hold up compared to previous metro world designs. It takes away from the "metro" feeling and lacks depth.Gameplay wise the movement & hand-to-hand combat feel clunky at times while the stealth & shooting aspects of the game are great and feel satisfying similar to previous titles.Graphically the game looks great, but didn't make huge leaps. Some limited graphical options are frustrating such as no FOV (similar to previous games). The game is decently optimized and runs quite well.Overall Metro Exodus is a great experience with some limitations holding it back from being as good as predecessors. Would recommend, but not worth installing another storefront.

_childDocuments_.review: WARNING - I WISH THERE WERE A WAIT OR CAUTION OPTION!51hrs, 2 playthroughs, one on hardcore, roleplaying Artyom, and one run on Ranger Hardcore Full while getting all collectables and etc and getting alt ending and completing stealth challenges missed. Game is fantastic, thoroughly enjoyed it and have 100% the challenges etc within the 2 runthroughs...would be cool if some were a bit harder, but regardless it's great. Hope all that want it can wait for it to 'launch' next year as I cannot recommend anyone downloading the epic launcher in it's current state, for any other games either (The sale being pulled and pushed onto epic is a separate issue that does not inherently have any connection to the issues with the epic launcher, but the practice that was used in doing so). Personally never ran out of ammo, or felt like I 'needed' to scavange around...that may be just because the type of player I am, but I was always on at least 150 of each resource and had plenty of ammo, only dropping down when I hadn't bothered crafting any, but then after the engagement I would just craft more and still have over 150 of each. The upgrades are all useful, but I find that there are 2 that are just blatantly more powerful than the rest. The extended filter and the throwables pouches...light is up for personal preference although I found the IR/Thermal goggles useless, so generally ran the extended battery, as it is always useful/usable. Along with the detector for any resources I stumble across and to pin point them, I did not find the compass necessary at all. Ranger hardcore full was awesome, if you have a good memory as a lot of the numbers and prompts are not visible unless at a workbench or in the backpack. Most interactions have audio queues and weapon alt ammo types have a visual difference that can be viewed. There was only 1 QTE I missed because I forgot it, but the rest are rather intuitive to remember, but I do recommend changing the QTE to PRESS not mash... I may be a lot more conservative and careful than the average player...."maybe" Overall, the game is a solid 8.5/10 for me, with 2033 being a 9/10 and last light being an 8/10 (which some may dispute, I know a lot of people prefer last light over 2033...but meh) These are ignoring any content over the initial campaign btw and do not include the extra content in last light, nor any additional content from Exodus.All I hope is that more people are going to be able to play the gorgeous game sooner rather than later.
