_childDocuments_.review: Metro Exodus is a great game with great post-apocaliptic atmosphere and amazing graphics and story telling.Metro Exodus takes place after events of Metro Last Light. The story is mainly focused around Artyom and Spartans searching for a new home with help of their train: Aurora. The gameplay is similair to previous Metro games, but it has slightly changed and eaven made a bit easier at some times. But it still is amazing and eaven better, than ever before. The world is greatly detailed and features few semi-openworld areas. But the atmosphere suffers from more open areas. Where Metro 2033 and Last Light had amazing atmosphere inside the tunnels, Metro Exodus has big open areas, that don't create the great claustrophobic atmosphere of the tunnels of Russian metro. After the opening few minutes inside the tunnels, I can only wonder what would the tunnels look like in the new engine. (It would be awsome) But the atmosphere isn't the only thing that suffered. The gameplay suffered from making the game mainly for consoles. (The interactions require holding a button and some options are navigated through d-pad like interactions)But at the end of the day I would still recommand this game. The gameplay and story are just amazing. And my rating is 8/10.

_childDocuments_.review: Metro Exodus is one of the few games that I would play again and enjoy even though I already know the story, a game in which I didn't check how much time do i have left every few hours, it is simply amazing. It is another game that succeeded to prove my misunderstanding of stealth games, I got the wrong impression of how fun stealth can be from the chaotic game in which you rob banks, fix drills, shoot cops and stuff like that. I slowly becan to like the small stealth elements in Sekiro, got more into it in the second half of MGSV and Dishonored 1 & 2. Stealth depends on how it is applied, and it is done damn well in Metro Exodus.I am not a newbie to the Metro game and book series, but I didn't play/read Last Light (2034) yet. Even so, Metro Exodus was friendly to me, so it should be the same for newbies. The player continues playing as Artyom, the hero of the metro, who is sure that there should be life outside Moscow and randomly finds the truth that starts his journey into finding his "destination". The main story lasts long enough, took me about 35 hours to finish it. The Two Colonels DLC took me 2-3 hours, and even though it was small, it is a lot different from the main game and not in the bad way. Sam's Story takes a bit more (10-15h), it looks like Dishonored: Death of the Outsider done right to me, instead of a completely different  game it is just a DLC, this is great.The visuals and sound effects are stunning, I found myself glaring at rotten muddy wood from the ground, rust and old paint on iron and other very small details, can't help but wonder how many i have missed too.There are lots of russian songs that remind you that you are in Soviet Russia like Дорога by Аукцыон, a song I have heard in Brat 2 a long time ago. It was a surprise, but surely a welcome one. The sound effects are of pure quality, once I even got fooled by the wind sound and took off my headphones, thinking that there is storm going on outside.Sadly I couldn't run it on my laptop (i5 8250U, GTX 1050 4GB, 8gb ram ddr4) at more than 40 average FPS with all settings low , but it ran nicely on my desktop (I3 8100, GTX 970 4GB, 8gb ram ddr4) at 50 average FPS with all ultra settings. It could help some optimization, but give credit to all the details too, I think it's worthy of such hardware requirements.The gameplay in Metro Exodus is a a huge upgrade to its prequels. It has a few open world elements and danger is everywhere you go, consisting of mutants and humans. There is a karma system in the game. The Spartans is the small group of people trained by Miller (Your wife's father) brought together for Miller's wish to save people, which means you can't hurt innocent people. Even if someone can shoot to kill you it doesn't mean they are bad people, they could be manipulated or simply just defending themselves. You can't kill them, doing it makes you lose your friends and get the bad ending (Also known as the fake ending).Besides the main missions there are a few side ones and some interaction with NPCs. Some of them don't benefit you with anything, but it brings the role playing to the next level. I love listening to my character's friends, celebrating with them and optionally helping them out. I enjoyed it to the fullest and never hurried. As i said before, I didn't check how much do I have left till the game will be over. There are quite a lot of guns and modifications to fit your necessities. You can now modify them and create some types of ammo and consumables on the go with Tokarev's greatest invention, a backpack, and it is easier than ever. It is not only visuals, the modifications actually change your playstyle quite a lot, in my opinion it mainly oscillates between short and long range, damage and stealth.Artyom doesn't talk at all, except when he writes in his journal in loading screens. It feels weird when people call for him on radio stations and he doesn't reply even though he got no reason not to.The bug (not the bugs)! _childDocuments_.review: It was worth waiting until it was on Steam, lads.A fitting end to the Metro trilogy; Metro Exodus does a near-perfect job in tying up any plot holes left by Last Light, while being able to weave an intricate plot of its own in a stunning setting.The plot is arguably my favourite of the Metro games, and indeed one of my favourite plots from the FPS genre in general. To go into my favourite bits would undoubtedly spoil it, though. The world feels well-fleshed out, and even usually-monotonous things such as listening to NPCs chat is interesting and intimate- you really feel as if you are Artyom, rather than just his body pilot.The Metro games have always looked good visually, but Exodus' graphics are like nothing I've seen before in a FPS. I don't often screenshot in games, but I found myself stopping at least once every 15 minutes to capture a stunning mountain vista, or gnarly badlands scene.Weapon customisation is improved from Last Light significantly- which is no mean feat. By putting some time into scavenging and spelunking, you can change your weapon to be anything you need it to be. I found myself often using a Revolver that I had heavily modded to work as a sort-of sniper rifle. Customisation can also be done on the fly, which allows you to attach suppressors as you see fit if you're going in quietly, or a Night Vision scope if you're fighting at night or inside a dark building, and don't want to reveal your position by turning on your flashlight.Combat feels challenging and fulfilling- the scarcity of ammo promotes a stealth-heavy playstyle, which I feel is how Metro should be played. However, when you get into a firefight, the combat feels satisfying and well-fleshed out, and is a challenge even on the Normal difficulty. You really have to think about how you want to play encounters, rather than just going in guns-blazing. My only down point is that enemy AI can be a bit off when sneaking- it isn't all the time, but often the enemies will 'spot' you and start shooting very easily, even in situations where you are behind full cover and in darkness. While this isn't a regular thing, it can sometimes force you to take a fight on guns-blazing, which detracts from the stealth experience, and will use up materials you may not be able to afford to use.Other than that, this game is a near clean sweep. 9.5/10- one of the best games I've played in years.

For a AAA game, I think that is just atrocious, especially this late into its life cycle. If you're an avid fan of Metro series, get it at a discount, otherwise just ignore this and play the previous titles.

_childDocuments_.review: As of writing this Im planning on doing a second playthrough some time in the future       If you're like me and only heard about metro through the Metro Exodus E3 announcement, so you bought both games and played them for context, you're going to love this one.        Compared to the last two games this is really the most "open world" I've seen in  a linear shooter before, at some times it felt like I was in a better Fallout environment wise, the graphics aren't on the level of the Frostbite engine but they have gotten a massive over-haul, especially in a section where you spend time in "the valley", however its not just there , the game is beautiful at times and each map has its moments, especially at night, ill also add the day and night cycle is a much needed improvement, combine that with the random packs of mutants that spawn on the map really helps to keep this world alive in its own way, this helps them later on in the game really hammer home that an area is "dead" in one of the later levels     A Complaint I had in the last game was how Anna felt sort of forced,although I'm not sure if that's just a limit of the technology of the time, here her character is fleshed out much better since there's just more room for it and she feels more natural.       I loved the level of weapon variety and customization I found myself restarting levels just so I could get every kill as a stealth kill, similar to Batman Arkham.     My playthrough was on the normal difficulty level and the Survival mechanic has been vastly improved, vs the last game where you could potentially have 60 minutes worth of filters, they also introduced a crafting system to create your own med-packs instead of just hoping you find some which i really do like.Everything they did here feels like a massive improvement, the game is a 9/10 for me, it would be a 10/10 if i had not encountered some rather annoying bugs, it is definitely worth the 60$, its such a shame a great game like this has to be out-shined by a poor publisher decision

_childDocuments_.review: Metro 2033/Last Light meets open areas you've seen in games like Deus Ex, Dishonored, etc. Big areas that you can wander around in or do the main stuff and continue at a brisk pace. I find the new weapon customization to be a breath of fresh air, as it allows you to play around with guns beyond just what you use, alongside being able to carry a tertiary weapon now. Only issue I have so far is that if you wander around the open areas before doing the main stuff, you'll end up running into a lot of trouble. The trouble being enemies that overwhelm you and the potential lack of resources to fight all of them off. It adds a lot of tension, and I like it. However, it does feel a little wacky. Enemies respawning for instance...nah. I don't like that. Not for me in a game like this. So far I'm liking it more than the first two games, perhaps because of the gameplay improvements. People have said that the setting and flow are different but that's all subjective on whether you enjoy it or not. Many people will loathe this game because of how unforgiving the combat can be. Many people will love it. I mostly like the unforgiving combat, because it's not Dark Souls. It's not about memorizing enemy and boss patterns. It's about picking your fights, and taking advantage of situations where you can use less resources, or none at all, and by extension preparing for the next encounter. It's great. The crafting system lends well to it. Gives the player choice on what they want.

_childDocuments_.review: What I'm going to write in this review is purely my opinion I have of METRO Exodus, after I played and finished the base game story and many optional things. It is very likely that you won't agree with the things I'll say, since it's been proved I have a different conception of the entire METRO series from most of the videogamers out there. I also have read the books: METRO 2033, 2034, 2035, if you have questions, please leave a comment below.In Metro Exodus we have a complete innovation of the entire franchise.Guys at "4A Games" decided to go ALL IN, changing almost completely the setup of the previous METRO games, offering a few semi-open world maps combined with some new graphic features, including the all new nVidia RayTracing technology, which is absolutely stunning on ULTRA Quality.The game feels so immersive, which is the main positive thing of the entire game, and combined with the  (great musician), makes the entire experience really something else, especially for fans of the METRO franchise.Characters are so well made, giving options to the player to know more about them, or simply know the basics to follow and enjoy the story line. Enemies are also different in each map and location, and some of them will really offer you a good challenge and killing them isn't always the best option, this because Metro Exodus is not really a shooter, but a Survival Game, that will force you to take care of your ammunition, weapons, and your armor. You will need to craft your ammo if necessary, clean your weapon if it starts to get a bit rusty, and craft your own medikits and mask filters. All these items are not available in large quantity across the maps, and in most cases you're forced to loot around to gather the essential items to survive, which can give you a sense of frustration if you prefer action games like Rage 2, for example.The customization of each weapon is really well made, giving the change to the player to create tons of different combination, starting just from a selection of almost 10 different base weapons. Another important aspect of the game, is that your choices will change the progression of the game.A bad action during your gameplay can cause the death of one of your crew members, for example, and the majority of your actions can lead to two different endings.Tons of collectibles are available accross the map, that will give you some extra lore, and sometimes some extra items useful to proceed in the game.The graphic isn't exceptional or perfect, but it is very good indeed and very well enjoyable especially if you are lucky to have the possibility to turn on the Ray Tracing on ULTRA. If you love to explore and you're a fan of the post apocalyptic environment, you will have TONS of chances to make some great screenshots, that's guaranteed.A "New Game+" option is available at the end of the game, and new dlcs are coming thanks to the expansion pass.A new chapter of Metro will arrive in the next years with new stories to come.METRO Exodus isn't a game for everyone. But instead, for quite a few I would say.It wasn't even nominated to most of the game awards of 2019, and imho it was very bad damaged thanks to EPIC GAMES, since it was the first title to have this kind of "exclusiveness" of their platform.But it is indeed one of my favourite games I've ever played, for the immersion and the feelings I had playing it, the fun I had to listen their conversations (which most of them are optional), and the excitement I had to proceed towards each single side and main quest, and in each location of the maps.""(Fyodor Dostoyevsky)

_childDocuments_.review: I'm probably in the minority here who disliked the game not because of stupid publisher greed, but how little of Metro's identity is actually present in this game.Let’s be fair and square. ? Yeah, pick it up.It plays really damn well, has a lot of nice exploration bits and allows you to make it a challenge or a fun shoot-the-things journey. The story has nicer, quieter parts compared to the original two, and by the time you’re done, it’s easy to feel satisfied with the ride. There's an undeniable impressive level of attention to detail, not to mention the entire setting is presented with so much authenticity that immersion is practically given in a silver platter. The audio is pretty much excellent the whole way, with the lovable stock sounds making a cheeky appearance as well. The only jank I dislike at all is how if you run you slide across the floor on dead stop but that's the slavish specialty.Gameplay basics aside, both the dub and original dialogue is well directed, and it's unlikely you'll not love the brothers in arms that are along with you for the ride. Every scenario is full of stuff to see and are distinct from each other, and some have their own special elements that make them stand out, even if Caspian outstayed its welcome.So, yeah, to make it short, if all you want is a good, solid game, just pick it up. Enjoy it.? Oh, I have bad news for you. The core issue is that 4A changed, tweaked or outright ignored everything that made Metro distinctively unique. When theoretically asked "what's special about Metro" compared to say, Fallout, Stalker or the like, three things would instantly come to mind :1- Ammunition Economy2- The Supernatural 3- Central theme of humanity's love for self-destructionFirst, say goodbye to trading. Like, at all. Remember having to think whenever to use crappy ammo or grade rounds when in fights, or save them to purchase weapon mods? Well not anymore, they outright aren’t a thing now. While the dynamic approach is welcomed, it was such an essential aspect of the first two games that missing it makes something feel off to me.Weapon mods you ask? You can swap on the go, don’t worry about what suits you or making choices before heading on the field, and when in drastic lack of resources, just pop the bag and you now care prepped for whatever the game throws at you. Also check this crafting system that basically showers you with easy resources, making being conservative with your supplies even less important. If you explore a lot, you will never run dry, when in 2033 and LL even the most conservative runs had me hardly scraping by at points.In a similar note, they completely nerfed the visual identity of the bastard and the shambler due to the weapon customization. They massacred my boys.Second, gone are the mystical, more unexplained things that pitted Artyom against things beyond his grasp. The supernatural elements of Metro blurred a line between science and fantasy that was the most original aspect of both games, enhancing the narrative’s themes and giving the series something truly distinct from every other post-apocalyptic setting. Without saying much, for 95% of the game, there is absolutely nothing, and even then there is extremely little.And last, a central theme of the original story was that humanity was either going to have to learn understanding or was doomed to kill itself for good. Both games use a morality system that encouraged you to be invested in the world, the execution was questionable (cue the jokes about guitars) but the point was that to save humanity from repeating it’s mistakes, taking it slower and listening was the way to go. This is especially relevant in Last Light, where the child would beg for your peaceful discretion and resented the inevitable fights against your enemies. Exodus does something similar with the message of humanity coming together to save itself (if you know how the good ending is determined, you’ll know what I mean), alongside trying to make judgement calls interacting with other communities, but to me it failed to also show compelling contrasting factions save for the cult in Volga. None reach the level of tragedy of circumstance like Pavel, or pure evil such as Korbut. The moral dynamic of Taiga's children is compelling but it still ends up being interesting worldbuilding rather than an exploration of this theme. Not only that, all of the small scenes were you can sit and just listen to an NPC dwell on and on with stories, while mostly compelling, don't expand on this much either.The best thing about the handling of human flaw in the series was that it went at lengths to show there were not always inherently bad people outside your group just because they were different. None of the factions you find in Exodus have that element implemented as strongly, if at all, because for the most part you only interact with them for a single chapter.So yeah. Overall I was quite disappointed with this game. If it is the last game in the series, this is a considerably low note for me to end it in. They strayed too far to make a more appealing game that I did enjoy as it’s thing, but is devoid of the heart and soul that I expected from this franchise.

_childDocuments_.review: Ok, hear me out......The game is, story-wise, amazing. It continues with the story of Artyom, Anna, Miller and company, in a way that feels much more human even though Artyom never actually says a thing. Every interaction between the characters feels grounded, and since it is so "organic" ala Half-Life, nothing feels forced (though there are a few scripted sequences which honestly didn't bother me). The feeling of staying just a little bit longer just to LISTEN to what someone has to say is not something to be understated, specially considering I'm the type of gamer who may even skip cutscenes if he's not interested.. 4A Games really have stepped up their game in terms of narrative and character development. Obviously Dmitry Glukhovsky's work shines through as well.Graphically speaking..... DAMN, the game is simply stunning. Their implementation of Ray traced global illumination brings the levels and characters to life, with a lightning system that is mind blowing. Sure, its performance takes a huge hit if you're not running an RT enabled card, and even then you won't be running the game at 4k 60 unless you have the best of the best, but trust me, that alone is worth the effect.Gameplay wise, the game is defined as "open world" for a reason. While the game is divided into sections, these sections are open enough to let the player explore the world and get lost in its visual storytelling, as well as finding emerging gameplay such as imminent threats, a secret that can help with the upcoming battles, or sneaking (with a rudimentary system mind you) through an entire camp which really put your skills (and looting) to the test, since ammo is scarce, as well as medkits.Sadly, the gameplay is marred by some very wonky controls, which give off the feeling of floating around constantly, to the point where I wouldn't even recommend sprinting while going over an incline, as you'll just... fly out. I'm guessing it's something to do with Artyom's acceleration... Too much radiation perhaps?Controls are not the only negative however, and this is where the game almost made me rage quit and ask for a refund even though I was on my 25th hour of gameplay, and that is the HUMONGOUS amount of hard chrashes which forced me to reboot my computer. At some point it got so bad I couldn't even advance a few meters without one. Eventually, I had to disable pretty much every overlay possible, as well as disable any and all Overclocks I had (even though they are rock solid), and even then crashes would still occur, even in the ending credits.What really pissed me off about that is that the game is definitely not new, and its story and gameplay are really really worth it, but DAMN the amount of issues the game has, and the fact that the devs didn't even bother fixing them is a big screw you to the consumers who just want to enjoy this incredible story.So... Would I recommend the game? Sure, at its core the game is incredible, but the amount of crashing alone can cause enough frustration to uninstall it before you finish. Be warned.

_childDocuments_.review: If you find this review to be helpful, my curators page is here: This is the third game in the Metro series, and is an easy sell for previous fans. It's the same mixture of environmental hazards, scavenging, melee and ranged combat, tense set-pieces, and boisterous OTT story-telling that the series has consistently delivered. The open world setting does make levels freer to explore, and allows for the game to expand in a pleasant way that doesn't dilute it's best qualities. It's not fundamentally all that different to play, but it does freshen up those aspects that were perhaps in danger of getting stale, and without sacrificing their talents at making intense or scary directed moments.For those who are unfamiliar with the Metro games: They take place in Russia, after a nuclear war has left the landscape uninhabitable and the survivors have fled underground into the train tunnels. Life is tough, and above ground has radiation and mutants, but there are relatively comfortable communities making it from day to day. You play as Artyom, an optimistic every-man who gets drawn into the fight for survival against foes that range from men to monsters, to advanced beings with control of time and space. Y'know...the usual post-apocalyptic USSR stuff, which is solidly constructed rather than anything ground-breaking.It's voice-acting is usually overdone, and the characterisation can be a tad iffy (most Russians are apparently a bit loud and blustery?) so it has never been totally convincing on the narrative front. However, it has also never failed  to deliver an engaging mixture of FPS combat, survival elements, and exciting sequences of tension and terror. You're not a cyborg super soldier, or roided up bad-ass military guy, and this is a world where your gun is powered by a bicycle pump, and whether or not you have any ammo for it will depend on if you want to eat your last potato for health, or use it as a projectile to try and brain someone with it.I'm kidding about the potato, but bullets are both your money, and...uh...well, things you shoot with. The most potent weapons will be guns, and so are costly to actually fire, or you can have air-powered weapons that are cheaper to produce ammo for, but don't pack as much punch. It's a game where lots of little touches add up to a fairly unique flavour: some areas require using a gas mask, and finding top-ups for it's filters. You can get dirt and blood splattered over the visor, and will have to wipe it off. Your torch is powered by cranking the handle, and bringing up the map is an actual "physical" object Artyom retrieves and looks at.This isn't Fallout, or Dying Light, when it comes to it's crafting mechanics. You don't just get some wires, a few Duracell batteries, some double-sided sticky tape, and a gun, then slap it all together A-Team style to make a rail-gun that shoots beams of energy. It's not Call Of Duty where you're firing off a gun so powerful that it takes bionic arms just to carry it, and then you call in a death-beam strike from an outer-space satellite. Generally you'll probably be going down the stealth route, and are shooting them with a cobbled together air-rifle that sounds like a duck politely farting, or getting up close for some stabbing / neck-breaking.Fire-fights are for bourgeoisie capitalist pig-dogs, with money to almost literally burn, as it goes up in smoke with every bullet fired. It's a balancing act trying to get by with the cheaper, less effective weapons, so you can eventually afford to purchase upgrades to improve them, or save up for something better, but that is also more costly to use. On the higher difficulty levels it's a tough enough challenge that in the first game of the series, I couldn't ever afford to buy a new weapon throughout the entire campaign. On this third game they've softened that challenge a little bit (in some ways, at least) and searching every nook and cranny will yield all the items, or all the bits and pieces for crafting useful additions. It's smoother to progress, but limits to your inventory, relatively scarce resources, and the levels of enemy opposition, mean it's still not easy.It can be played as a run-and-gunner, and the combat is slick enough to satisfy. Though stealth is a viable option too, and enemies have varying states of alertness and responsiveness to threats. Mechanically this is very polished across all of its elements, and by now is super-slick with it's set-pieces. With plenty of capacity for tension, scares, and thrills, these nicely break up the "loose" action for more tightly controlled sequences.Story-wise it's engaging enough, but I'd be lying if I said this was ever it's strongest suit. This is about immersion in it's world, the sense of place and atmosphere that the excellent graphics and soundscape help to convey, and all those things that ground you in it. The involvement with your weapons and utilities, as you pump them up in the heat of battle, or furiously wind up your torch to see in pitch-black locations. Hearing your character desperately sucking in handfuls of corrupt air as your last filter runs out, and you're stumbling around searching for another before suffocating. Around you there's weird phantoms of long-dead people going about their business in an echo of the distant past, and there's no time to pay this bizarre anomaly much mind when there's the somewhat more pressing matter of ensuring you can breathe.The adrenaline rush of hard-fought encounters, or nervously creeping through the shadows unseen. That huge sigh of relief as you make it to a quiet moment after all that tension. There's a stretch where mutants aren't trying to tear your face off, and people aren't shooting at you, and the only thing you have to pay any mind to is the hum of a geiger counter. Just as you get comfortable, something bursts out of a nearby lake, or out of the ground, or from the sky, and you are reminded that you can never be truly at ease in this world. It is possible to appreciate this without playing the previous games, as it doesn't riff particularly heavily on events from the first two. Though some familiarity, and connection to the characters, will make it's twists and turns that extra bit more poignant or involving. For the most part this release is a very enjoyable final to the trilogy (the voice-work, whilst not bad, isn't great either, but that's it's main flaw), and I highly recommend it.

_childDocuments_.review: I have completed my first play through in 30-40 hours.  I tried to complete as much as possible and wanted to get all of the gear.  I ended up getting the good ending.  The good/bad ending system I enjoyed a lot more than the previous games.  In past ones you had to avoid killing creatures or animals.  In this one it is based on your decisions interacting with the societies you encounter and how much you help the companions you travel with.  This was much more engaging since I didn't have to worry about a random creature/human attacking me as much.  It also felt more justified with this.Visually everything looked amazing.  I am running this on a 8th gen core i-5 and a geforce rtx 2070.  It all ran smoothly and I never had issues with the lag or jittering.  The lighting from my head lamp & lighter were amazing.  There were definitely moments where I watched the lighter burn the spider webs away and particles and light blazed across the screen.  The textures and models also looked incredible.  After killing creatures for the first time I actually crouched down and just studied the beautiful models in the spectacular lighting.  The environments are also great.  They are interesting to look at and feel like a real place in the world.The dynamic weather system was beautiful and dramatically changed the way I interacted with hostile creatures/humans.  This also helped blend the world together.  The open world aspect of the game is incredible since I could go anywhere in the map and explore at my own desired pace.  The game also had the metro tunnel feel in multiple areas and integrated well with the open world.  The new factions were interesting and were a fresh breath of air when compared with the typical nazi & communist bad guys.  New creatures were also added to many of the old list of creatures.  They also integrated those creatures into the different environments & seasons.  The entire time I played the game I felt engaged and had a desire to continue forward.  I was initially upset that I didn't get to go and collect bullets and buy the new guns.  It was exciting to save up and get the new gun.  After an hour or two I was completely on board with the new system.  In the previous games I avoided using the pistol.  The shotgun and a long barrel rifle were always my favourite choice.  In exodus I used it all the time.  Being able to have a silenced sniper rifle with a massive clip & a short range pistol was amazing.  With the new system it made all of the guns feel valuable and versatile.This is a great game.  The mechanics are amazing and work well in this universe.  The combination of open world and closed tunnels are great and offer a new experience this universe has never had.  It has also allowed the story to expand in new ways that staying in Moscow would never have.  This has allowed the developers to tell an incredible & engaging story.  All that being said, a lot of the negative reviews are about the game being released first on Epic and later on steam.  It is fair to be upset, but the game is solid and should not be punished for this.  The developers clearly found it was in their best interest to go this route.

_childDocuments_.review: Well, the review will be exclusively about the game «Metro Exodus» and  not about any other aspects and scandals associated with it. It seems to me that if the developers screwed up at least in something, gave the slightest reason to bury their game (at least in optimization, at least in the plot, at least in technical aspects), then many people after the recent events would gladly do it in their reviews. But the rating of the game is steadily high, they play it. That is why I want to evaluate only what the developers have done, what has already taken away several sleepless nights and will take many more.«Exodus” - this is the torch that illuminates the bright future of single-player games, which took the best things from the previous parts and has changed with the help of many innovations. The conventionally open world gives the player a sigh of uninfused air outside the Metro, see what the torn Earth has become without the harmful influence of mankind, meet people returning to simple life, living next to monstrous creatures, but seeing the Sun every day. The player is given to visit various climatic zones with different nature, different living conditions, and each locality has its own interesting features.The game still skillfully deals with the plot, replacing the dizzying action scenes moments of peace, intimate conversations with members of their team, each of which as a family member for Artem. All the secondary characters are incredibly worked out, Anna is the best girl Artem could meet and marry, and is incredibly human, each of the team members has her own character, I want to worry about them in every difficult situation. Graphics and optimization at the highest level, the game flies like a feather and feels like delicate silk. The system of crafting weapons and components is implemented perfectly, it feels necessary, but not so much as to turn the game into a blunt grind of resources for crafting, but only encouraging the player to thoroughly research locations. The weapon feels realistic in all that relates to the physics of the shot and the system of damage to enemies. You really see how much damage is caused by shots from one or another weapon to different parts of the body, how distance, your position, etc. affect the shot. Monsters are much harder to kill and fighting with them requires serious planning and tactics, understanding their weak points. It's easier with people, even though I try to solve problems with non-violent methods and stealth.If we talk about moments that are not performed at such a high level, here we can say about the not always perfect facial animation of the characters (although most of the time it is quite good), several times I caught non-critical bugs, a mini-map could be more convenient, Artyom's silence is a bit depressing, enemies sometimes see you from an incredible distance.Metro Exodus is a great project that worthily completes the game series. A game in which it is equally interesting to shoot monsters with a shotgun at close range, and sit with your beloved girl in a reserved seat and listen to the AuktYon and Viktor Tsoi on the radio, looking out the window at the running life, thinking about the eternal.

_childDocuments_.review: As a big fan of the Metro franchise, I am in love. I'm extremely happy to say that it exceeded all of my expectations and delivered an unforgettable experience. The level of detail put into the environments is absolutely mental; each location felt like a living, breathing world with its own unique set of challenges I had to come across. I found myself constantly in awe of the beautifully rendered landscapes and dynamic weather effects, which in itself made the game so much immersing. The storyline was equally impressive, with well-developed characters and an engaging plot that kept me invested from start to finish. The game's blend of action and stealth mechanics kept things fresh and exciting, and I was constantly on the edge of my seat as I navigated through dangerous parts of the levels. What really set Metro Exodus apart for me was its emotional impact. The game tackled some heavy themes, and I found myself genuinely caring about the fate of the characters and their struggle for survival and the eternal "freedom" from all the post-war chaos. Though I got the bad ending, I am still happy with how the whole experience turned out. Overall, Exodus was an unforgettable experience that I will never forget. Thank you Metro, what a ride it was!

_childDocuments_.review: The first 2 metro games were fun survival games with great world building and some truly great moments of terror and atmosphere. The mechanic of using bullets as currency was great and the story while nothing revolutionary was interesting enough to keep you invested in the dark ones and the post nuclear Moscow factions. Exodus takes us out of the metro in the very beginning to explore other locations in Russia upon learning that the outside is actually inhabitable. This game ditches the claustrophobic setting for an open world and I think the game suffers for it. I am not against the developers trying new locations but the open world is a bit odd in a series famous for close quarters underground adventures. Also the world design is very rushed looking, certain forts and settlements look like fan made settlements in far cry 3. The texture work in the game also ranges from excellent to shockingly low res at times. Crafting in this game along with weapon management is a chore and along with the open world nature of the game I cant help but compare it unfavorably to far cry 2.  The locations, at least the first island are interesting enough at first but are filled with annoying bullet sponge mutants in a series that is suppose to be about ammo conservation. I dont like exploring and finding ammo only to use all of it on some monsters right after I obtain it. The story of the game is pretty bare bones and lazy, the writers just needed to come up with an excuse to have our hero leave the metro and it seemed very rushed and forced to have him do so. There are also long sequences of standing listening to NPCs talk while your character remains silent just like the first 2 games and it is very odd considering he speaks in the loading screens. The game has interesting ideas like the anti technology fish cult which was a fun experience but they are few and far between. Unfortunately I was finding that the game felt like busy work to get through and so I uninstalled it prior to this review. I am glad that I got this in a humble deal instead of paying full price because I did not have fun for 90% of the time I was playing. I think this game tried to be a far cry clone and it fails miserably at emulating it. Open world games are only fun if the gameplay, characters, and locations are fun to explore in it. tl;dr A game that tried to copy far cry instead of refining what worked in the first 2 games and fell flat in terms if fun exploration and writing.3/10

_childDocuments_.review: Metro Exodus is just about outside of that "Masterpiece" range. There's just a couple of not-so-tiny things keeping it down.First, let's get the good stuff out of the way. The graphics and artwork are absolutely phenomenal, there's an insane amount of detail in every level, and that's especially stunning when you realize that Exodus now went out with some of the more open world type of levels, but there's no lack of detail in those either. Everything was carefully crafted to seem as immersive as possible. That's also supported by all of the tiny interact animations of Artyom, such as whipping out the map, climbing ladders, checking your geiger/compass and so on. All of this has tiny little animations which show Artyom physically interacting with the environment around him and it all adds up to create this insanely immersive experience.Add to this the epic music and all around quite immersive voice acting, whether you choose russian or english, it's mostly great, except for some of the characters. There's all this "russian-english" going on and it's kinda funny. The sound design itself is fine, but what's a little weird is some of the cutscenes, it sometimes feels like as if there's missing audio, or the voice acting overlaps in places, it's a bit off, as mostly it's good, but especially at the beginning it's rather noticeable how the cutscenes sometimes feel weirdly silent.Speaking of the beginning, make sure to get a few hours in before setting your judgement on the game, as the beginning is probably the weakest part of the game, once you get to your first open area - the Volga swamp, it gets better. And then by the time you get to the final level, you'll get all that classic Metro atmosphere you were starving for, trust me, the final level is epic and so is the ending, it's just the game starts a bit weak, then gets good, then a little weaker and then good again, kinda strange I know.But yeah the main two things aside from the weird audio at times, is the movement and the bugs. Artyom's movement is just extremely "floaty", jumping around or going down stairs has never been more dangerous. Artyom might slip or slide off at any moment and since the fall damage in this game is bonkers you might aswell break your leg at best. And these aren't a very good combination to have in a game where there's occassional platforming or very dangerous and slippery cliffs, roofs, floors and so on.As for the bugs, I personally didn't encounter any game-breaking ones my entire playthrough, but there still were a couple of funny bugs, mainly regarding the NPCs, they sometimes teleport around, stutter, or their equipment starts floating, it's a rather common sight in games regarding bugs, but here it's kinda everywhere, so try to not look at the NPCs too much, it might break your immersion lol. But I've read people encounter countless game-breaking bugs, such as NPCs getting stuck, the inability to interact with some core elements and more, so hopefully most of it was fixed now and you're good to go, as I didn't encounter anything fatal, no crashing or errors either.

_childDocuments_.review: My God 4A, you really hit it out of the park. I absolutely fell in love with this game; it just exudes beauty and depth in every square inch of game play. Movement has never felt so smooth, and balanced with the absolute JUICY weapon mechanics makes this one of the best feeling FPS titles I've ever played.The world building is done with impeccable attention to detail, making it come across as a finely polished hand-crafted experience. The amount of professionalism displayed in the artwork is staggering. I haven't felt like a kid in a candy shop in a VERY long time in video games. The closest might have been 2016's DOOM. This game knows what it's doing. Every character has their own unique personality and I find myself growing more connected to them as I play. You can really feel the struggle and comradery between your fellow survivors. Your decisions matter, and they play up to the ending of the game. The horror elements also come up later through the story and Exodus delivers the same anxiety inducing tension that we've experienced in 2033 and Last Light.I really cant express how much I appreciate Studios like 4A. From watching the developer commentaries and tracking the release, I couldn't help but feel a strong attachment to the team. These guys put their noses in the grindstone, toiling for years over every line of dialogue, every line of code, every texture, every polygon, to produce the best experience they are capable of. It ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ worked. I have so much respect for hard working artists that craft such an amazing vision like this. I had an absolute blast.I hate endings. They make me sad.I cried at the end. I did. This project connected with me as an artist myself and I experienced a swelling of emotion as the credits rolled in. What a culmination of talent. I really wish luck and success to 4A, despite the controversy created by their publishers. They are a group of people unanimously devoted to their craft and it shows. I can't wait to get my hands on whatever they come out with next. I hope the story of Artyom doesn't end here, and even if it does, Exodus will most certainly suffice as a book ending.Thank you 4A.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR: This is no longer a Metro game. Worth playing once, wait for a sale. Or watch a Let's Play on Youtube, you won't miss the gameplay much.Although I had some criticism towards the former two Metro games, in general I liked them. I was looking forward to play the third game, especially given that it was supposed to be very different from its predecessors. And that it was. Unfortunately, I can't say all changes were welcome.First, what I liked about the previous Metro games is the atmosphere of the metro and remnants of humanity. There was a fine balance between spending time in the underground and on the surface, there were quality horror moments with a dose of mysticism. And for the most part, all of this is lost in Metro Exodus. Except for the last chapter (which, I think, is the best part of the game), most of the time you spend on the surface, underground bunkers are rare and optional and are not even close to replacing the metro. The suspense moments are simply nonexistent. The authors tried to set the mood by the post-apocalyptic scenery on the surface, but that is a poor replacement, especially given the gameplay. The game feels and plays as an open-world survival, with lots of resource hoarding and crafting. Looking at another crumbled shack or a rusted shipwreck you're thinking what kind of resources you might find there, not what kind of story is hidden in there. This simply kills that depressing atmosphere I was so fond of.Second, the first two games had reasonably good stories. The first one was especially good, it even had a moral choice in the end. But I can't say there is much of a story in the third game. Basically, at the beginning of the game Artyom and a small crew of spartans leaves Moscow and travels around the country with no real goal. Sure, at certain points the game offers a reason to move forward, then, at the end of the chapter, it gives you a reason for the next one, and so on. But there isn't an ultimate goal or a feeling of progression towards it. Besides the simple kill/don't kill decisions, there aren't any moral choices in the game. What's worse even, there's no moral of the game, at all. In Metro: Last Light, there were kill/don't kill moments too, but you had a moral obligation to the Dark One, and the characters in M:LL were more complex and more familiar. All that made those decisions not so trivial. In Exodus, you barely even know the characters beside your crew, and there's barely any reason to make one choice or the other. Barring some details, the ending is more or less predictable, and, given how unattached you are to your companions, is mediocre. There are good and bad endings, depending on your choices during playthrough.Speaking of the characters, they are one of the weakest parts of Metro Exodus. Some of the main companions are straight annoying in their sheer blind stupidity. () Every character in the game is 1D, shallow, straight as an arrow stereotype. You know them for 5 minutes, you know them to the end of the game. No shades of grey here, we are the good guys, most of them are bad. Aside from a couple of obvious main companions, the rest of the crowd are so unremarkable that you can barely tell them apart, if not by appearance. The dialogs, with the speechless Artyom and these dummies quickly become a farce, and you wish you could skip them. I have to say, stereotype characters were bad in the previous Metro games, especially M:LL, but even there they had some depth to them (remember Pavel?). In Exodus, it got much much worse.What is good about this game is visuals and sounds. The game is beautiful, and in that regard it continues the Metro tradition. Although level design has bugs in quite a few places, like grass or objects hanging in the air or objects you can clip through. The game has dynamic day/night cycle, although at key points in the game time goes non-linearly, which can be apparent.In conclusion, should you buy and play this game? If you're a fan of the Metro series, you don't need my answer - you will likely buy and play it regardless. And you might be slightly disappointed, like I am. Still, I think the game is worth playing once, especially if you like the more open-world direction the game is taking. Just don't get your hopes up and maybe wait for a sale on Steam. For the ones new to the Metro series, it is difficult to recommend starting your acquaintance with Exodus. I'd recommend playing Metro 2033 and Metro: Last Light first. Having played those first you'll have better understanding of the story and background of Metro and you can then decide if you want to play Exodus.

_childDocuments_.review: This game makes me a bit sad. I was a huge fan of the first two metro games, especially the first one. The setting along with the terror-action vibe it had. So it saddens me that Metro has become more of a shooter over the years. The little details that made the first one special has slowly been diluted with a bunch of generic stuff.I'm actually a bit surprised at how many people like the game. But then again it's clearly a game made for a wider audience this time, and it seems to have worked out. This is just my opinion.My first big gripe is the setting. It's a Metro game, but it's not set in the Metro. For some people this probably seems interesting, seeing the rest of the world outside of the Moscow Metro, but for me that setting is what made the previous two games so interesting. The open levels when you wandered the tunnels alone in the first two games are some of my favorite moments of the franchise. Not to mention that going above felt so special because of how dangerous it was.In Exodus that tension is almost completely gone. There are a few select moments (which all take place underground btw) that still make you feel that claustrophobic goodness of the first games, but most of the time is spend on the safe surface not doing, or worrying about much.The different places that you go to are nice to look at for the most part, but it does get old searching through similar looking buildings for scraps that you use for the obligatory modern game crafting system... In the end I just went from mission to mission, not bothering to scavange anymore.The story isn't much to talk about, that has never been a strong part of the Metro games in my opinion and this one is about on par with Last Light, so not exactly good, but not bad. Also, the voice acting is worse than ever. It's actually cringy. A word I hate to use but listening to some of these dialogues was painful.The game is also plagued by the same moral choices that you faces in the first two games. Killing people = bad ending. No fun allowed. Hyperbole aside, it is better than in the first two games, but feeling restricted just because you want to get the good ending has never seemed like a good idea to me. Special objectives? Sure! But asking people to not shoot stuff when we got all these lovely weapons is such a sin.We need to talk about the bugs as well. I thought, that after a year on Epic, that it would be pretty polished by the time it got to Steam. But no. In the 16-ish hours I've played I've had somewhere around 10 crashes, and too many in game bugs to count. Small stuff that doesn't bother me, to me getting stuck on the terrain, or in the middle of a mission, camera losing alingment in certain situations and more. Really disappointing.Overall Metro Exodus takes away what I liked most about the first two games, that being the Metro. It has it's enjoyable moments, but the weak story, uninteresting cast, bad VA, bland enviroments, just makes it feel like so many other games out there today. It has lost the special flavour that the Metro games once had. I can only hope that they bring the franchise back into the tunnels, and maybe slope the linear storytelling for a more open experience. I think an open world game set in the Metro could work really well. Fingers crossed.

_childDocuments_.review: Metro Exodus is one of the best FPS games ever made.The gunplay is too satisfying. The environment and atmosphere stands apart from any other games; the detail and gore of the interior buildings, factory and underground tunnels is just insane. The story is heart-touching, and is very relevant. The urge for survival and to continue the humanity has been depicted well through the journey of Artyom, and later in the DLCs through Colonel and Sam. The weapon customization system is well-made too, alongwith satisfying gunplay where every bullet of your gun hits hard.But yeah, not everything is too good, rowing a boat here can be a frustrating job, and the movement and sprinting of the character is very clunky too; and, the human enemy AI is just trash, and also, the facial animation of characters are not impressive.But still, it's an immersive experience, and a must play for everybody.

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic Game, i personally felt the chapterwise divison and inclusion of a few open world levels in between linear levels really made the gameplay shockingly refresing, especially since almost no area overstays its welcome and most encounters are well designed and varied mini sandboxes inside the giant sandbox of the level itself, except for the final are but that's to be expected, and it stays far more ludonarratively coherent compared to games like Far Cry and most other open world games. The Story and Graphics were my main driving force, which is very rare for me personally since i usually get hooked to gameplay, themes, music etc. Having Playing the Previous Metro Game, I had ideas about how the game will go and it exceeded expectations, especially when you actually genuinely started caring about characters. Having a small ragtag team go on a Train Trip is as fun as it sounds. My favourite part was the train rides section between missions - Very nostalgic, the scenes were very similar to what i used to see when i used to travel a lot on trains as a kid and i loved every second of those looped scenes. For those scenes alone in various different biomes, i feel like the price i paid was justified. This was a Constructively short review based on a Purchase of the "Gold Edition" of the game at 75% off on a steam sale, that would be about $10(US). After completing only the base game as of now, i can recommend anyone to pick this game at nothing less than a 40% discount, ideally 75% or more. I feel like the game genuinely justifies its price even on full price, especially since according to SteamDB they have implemendted Regional Pricing so nobody's getting ripped off with unfair prices either. Game's Pretty Demanding though, both on your PC and You, as the game can get quite stressful and difficulty can be over the roof if you're not careful. I played on Hardcore and Mutant encounters were fine for me as an fps Veteran, but gradually human and other enemies got stronger and i had to tone down it to normal in certain parts to finish the game. Also, Better make good use of benchmarking tools provided with the same and i also suggest talking a look at the requirements before making a purchase. Being a single player game, some performance drops didn't bother me and the few bugs i saw were mostly animation related, and i found them quite funny tbh. These 26 hours were well spent, i got at least 3x the value of what i paid for the game in the first place. A AAA Studio made a complete game on launch, we all steam gamers scrutinized the publisher a lot for the epic exclusivity back then, but looking back its easy to see why they took the game from steam for a year. Even if the Publishers made questionable choices, there is no denying that this game oozes love and respect for the source material, the previous games, the playerbase and its own legacy to deliver a quality game and the marketing trailers of the game match so well with the actual game. The Immersion is surreal and gameplay is fantastic. I'll be trying out the DLCs too at a later date, but i have feeling they hold a high regard for quality just like the Metro Series has always been. Thanks for wasting precious hours of your delicate life reading this. I appreciate your ducking time and hope you have a ducking nice day or night or evening or afternoon or whatever the hell your time dictates.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is currently in the Humble Bundle for May  2021. If you are interested in the game and it's before June 1st, 2021, consider picking up the game as part of the current monthly bundle.This is an excellent first-person shooter with stealth and survival elements, though neither of those categories is as strong as the words may seem.  Players can sneak around behind enemies and will have to scavenge ammo, filters, and even gas masks in a post-apocalyptic setting. The story in Metro Exodus has taken a huge step forward in how they tell the story.  From an opening train ride that gives you the back story or short but efficient cutscenes, I was hooked almost immediately and wanted to know more.  There’s also a big action set piece about an hour into the game, which got me to play a little more. The graphics are especially good and will probably look better with the enhanced version that came on the 6th.  I accidentally played the original version for the video and it still looked extremely good.Pick this up if you like the Metro Series, or want an FPS with more story and an adventure.  Though this is not a run and gun shooter, and the story here will be depressing with the post-apocalyptic setting.  This isn’t necessarily a happy story, but it’s a well-told one. _childDocuments_.review: Ahhh where do I start with this...First of all, the game is amazing, the weapon animations, shooting mechanics, the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ graphics are beautiful! Faces look photorealistic most of the time, and the global illumination looks so natural and real. The sound and atmosphere shines big time too, the developers took big notes of what made the STALKER games so good, Shadow of Chernobyl in particular, and implemented that into the Metro experience. I really like the game, I really do, loved Last Light that even played through the entire campaign it three or four times.That said, Metro Exodus doesnt play like previous Metro games, not even the Redux versions, this game is sometimes a very good enjoyable experience and some other times a complete rage inducing mess. Remember when you played Last Light Redux on Hardcore Ranger mode and only had trouble at the beggining? Remember how enemies were as fragile as you were during firefights? Remember how well the stealth system was? Well now forget all that because in Metro Exodus Hardcore Ranger the enemies take 6 AR boolets do die and sometimes take 1 shotgun blast to the body or ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ 6 SHAMBLER ROUNDS TO THE FACE TO ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ AT THE VERY LEAST FALTER BACK. Seriously, my biggest complain about the game is how easy shotgun enemies popup in one corner and instantly blast your ass back to Moscow with a single shotgun shell. Or how they can snipe you with a barebones bastard from 20 meters away with perfect accuracy, putting 10 bullets in your skull before you had time to acknowledge their position because they have this pseudo STALKER Anomaly ultrahardcore aim. Their field of view changed from like 100° wide (Last Light) to 200° because they can ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ see you when you're behind them, oh and they instantly start shooting your ass when they see you, no more alerting their friends or giving you a window to run up and perform a kill to shut them up. Sniper rifle bullets somehow dont connect to your telescopic sight reticle, they go off a little bit enough to either side of the reticle to avoid headshoting an enemy. _childDocuments_.review: When I played Exodus for the first time last year at Gamescome, I thought: It looks great, but ... is it still Metro? No more dark tunnels in the bowels of Moscow, no more abandoned busy, no anomalies, transfer stations turned into small settlements or, in most cases, burial grounds full of horror. Nevertheless, the uniqueness of the series, as well as its name, drew the most from where it was situated - into the post-apocalyptic metropolis, more precisely, its underground train system.But now I realize that Metro is much more than just ... metro. Glukhovsky's bestseller describes the morbid and violent renaissance of humanity, the rebirth of civilization, which, however, is basically only a return to the primitive era, moreover full of repetition of old mistakes. While Metro 2033 and Metro: Last Light revealed that man's need to stand over others is alive in a corpse, where governments have taken over the revived Nazi and Communist factions, Exodus goes further. During one game year he will transfer the player not only to different parts of post-apocalyptic Russia, but especially to cultures that arose - or only returned after hundreds or thousands of years - after the bombs hit. Sectarian religion, cannibalism or slavery; wherever you move, as the Christians in the new Subway, there is a separate, very sad, and convincingly drawn chapter of the human “book of survival”. And it is full of horror, often not even horror intestines of the Moscow underground full of corpses, monsters and huge spidersEach part of the game, which is stylized not only to different locations, but also to different seasons, is associated with the previous and following predominantly linear story. The 23-year-old Arťom, now an experienced and respected member of the elite Spartans unit, as a combat group's main explorer, is being broadcast to unexplored parts by a nuclear shootout of a mutilated Russia. The game starts in the subway, but it is only a fraction of this sandbox visual feast. If there is something that impressed me after just the first ten minutes, it was the great atmosphere of post-war Russian mother wrapped in luxurious graphics. Visually, Metro Exodus is a beautiful ode to destruction and disintegration, plus you don't need strictly high-end cards.It's hard to tell if Metro Exodus is the best game in the series, but it's definitely a great post-apocalyptic title. It is different from the previous parts, much more massive and less solitary, but at the same time it is a sharp departure from the atmosphere of its predecessors. Luckily, however, the game is closer to titles such as Far Cry, Rage or Mad Max, fortunately, without boring cotton pads in the form of casting camps and basic or revealing the map. It is a linear but profound experience and a natural evolutionary step in the chapter of the amazing stories of the Moscow metro settlers. All thumbs up.I personally rate the game 9/10Postive+ impressive atmosphere of the world+ very good story telling+ nice variety of environments and types of gameplay+ visual ballad with great, alternating atmosphere+ an engaging, albeit predictable story+ diversity also in the case of weapons and their adaptability+ sympathetic main characters to whom you create a relationship+ dynamic weather and day / night cycle+ large sandbox maps including Madmax Caspik+ stealth option for most missions+ game lengthNegative - it would want a more varied range of enemies- the environment is large, but besides the story deaf to activities- often labyrinth design of levels- there could be more open environments

_childDocuments_.review: The game looks absolutely gorgeous, even at 1080p non-Enhanced edition. Even on a dated PC it runs well at Ultra quality. The production quality is through the roof, AAA stuff. It's very apparent that this is the most ambitious game they have ever developed. The wanted to create an epic conclusion, grand in scope.Two major areas (Volga and The Caspian) in Exodus are semi-open world, i.e. there isn't one huge map, but several smaller which can be explored. It's also a game where having no ambient music during exploration actually works. For example, in Dragon Age Inquisition, it made exploration a bore. Here it builds atmosphere. However, the gameplay loop of the open world is painfully average and serviceable. Though there are a few elements that were just plain bad: using the boat in Volga is slow, cumbersome, and being attacked by the fish creatures is a chore.Gameplay wise:Finally! Quick saving, huzzah!... but it's a single slot shared with checkpoints... also still no FoV slider, boo! At least the default is 90 degrees, which is perfectly acceptable.The physics are weird. You can accidentally bump off of the environment or slide off a cliff while walking. Jumping is very floaty.Ladders are contextual now, so no awkward "aiming for the ladder when trying to go down" moments. Stealth is virtually the same from the Redux versions. It was fine there, but no improvements at all should be pointed out: - You cannot move bodies. - Enemies either don't know you're around or know exactly where you are at all times, just - because somebody saw you for a split second.- Using a flashlight even for a moment is a coin toss. You either won't get noticed, or everybody goes into instant alarm.Additionally, the hitboxes sometimes just do not work. You will shoot them in the head but nothing will happen. Except, of course, a building wide alarm.Story wise:I'm surprised at how much dialogue there is in this game. In 2033 and Last Light there was a lot of talking, but in Exodus it's just too much, especially in the first few hours. The dialogues just go on, and on, and on, for several minutes at a time. What's worse, Artyom STILL does not talk outside of loading screens. This makes the dialogues extremely awkward.Mind you, there are some great scenes in the game, primarily on the train, but overall it's just talking. At times the NPCs are even talking over each other.Anna comes off as overbearing. I understand she loves Artyom, but sometimes it appears a bit creepy, and if she had any doubts, she'd cut Artyom's junk off for perceived cheating. Read: it's unhealthy.DLCs are much better than in Last Light. The Two Colonels is short, but serious. Sam's Story is longer, but very lighthearted.Overall it's good, but a bit overrated.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is well worth playing. This is marred by a few bugs here and there such as getting stuck on ladders, not being able to navigate certain parts of the terrain, and enemy AI.The boss fights seems rather oddly placed and more like a chore to get through.The protagonist is very uninteresting and lacks any depth, simply being formed by the characters around him. Sam, however, in Sam's Story is a great character and should probably be explored more in future games. I'd put my money down to see his story as he travels through the USA to get to his father.If you enjoy sneaking and assassinating, or even running and gunning, you can do either. If you have arachnophobia, you should probably not play this game.It's worth buying at a discount with the dlc.

_childDocuments_.review: After beating the game on Hardcore, Ranger Hardcore, and New Game+ with Ironman modifier, I'm left with mixed feelings about Metro Exodus. Although it wasn't a strong negative, it still was mostly a negative experience for me. This game is a massive leap forward for the franchise in many ways. The game is much bigger and longer than its predecessors. But the game also stumbles in many areas and feels very tedious at times. I'll first start with the good.Immersion, atmosphere, and story:Like the other Metro games, Exodus places a large emphasis on immersion. But Exodus takes this to the next level. There are many opportunities for you to interact with other characters, learn their backstories, and make choices. The atmosphere is much more upbeat than other Metro games, which is fitting considering you don't really spend any time in the metro itself. The story also supports this with the theme of hope being front and center.Much better morality system:The morality system is completely overhauled. Although, it still isn't always clear at times, it does a much better job of signaling how to get a certain ending. You won't be getting any moral points for watching a woman shower this time. This makes getting the good or bad ending much more predictable and logical.Good weapon customization:The game lets you swap between any weapon you've found for free. You can add and remove attachments to make your guns more powerful or to suite a certain playstyle. The weapon cleaning system is certainly immersive, although it consumes to many resources so on Ranger Hardcore I never cleaned my guns and didn't have any issues making it kind of pointless.These are very strong points for the game. But there are several nagging issues, some big and some small, that really hold the game back. These issues compound each other, turning what should be a few annoying sections or mechanics into bigger problems for the game.Clash between linear and open world:I'm not completely sold on Exodus' open world sections. The linearity of the first two games is a well known criticism and I assume the open world sections in Exodus exist to address that. But it doesn't, at least not completely. The game switches between three linear, highly scripted levels, two open world sections, and one that's a mix of both. But the open world sections don't fully commit to being open world. The game still expects you to tackle the objectives in a linear fashion. Often there is only one way to approach and complete a task in the open world. Most of the open world is boring wasteland with a few annoying ghouls or watchmen. So what's the point? It just makes running from one objective to another take even longer. The open world sections feel very static and nothing like the dynamic world of a game like Stalker. I wish the game had fully embraced the open world sections, but instead it feels like the worst of both worlds.Horrible stealth system:Stealth is pretty broken on Ranger Hardcore, and not in a good way. Enemies spot you through walls, can kill you through surfaces, hear you walking 2 floors above them, see you crouch walking through bushes, etc. In general enemies will sometimes get alerted for seemingly no reason and once alerted almost always know at least your general location if not exactly where you are. This makes stealth extremely tedious and unfun. During many sections in the game, I wouldn't even bother being sneaky. I found it was more effective to headglitch some cover and pick off enemies one at a time rather then try to kill them in stealth.Prompts sometimes don't show up for melee:Several times I would walk behind an enemy to knock them out, press the key, only to sit there and have them turn around and kill me. This further adds to the tedium of stealth.Bullets don't always hit your target:I'm unsure of the mechanics behind projectiles in this game. But something is just off with many of the weapons / scopes. I will aim directly at an enemies head and somehow miss. The 4x scope on the AK is zeroed wrong and bullets always shoot higher than they should. Enemies in cover often cannot be hit, even if they are exposed. You can spend a ton of time sneaking around, only to "miss" a point blank headshot, alert the enemies, and have to start all over. This on top of the scope glare and depth of field which makes aiming a pain in some lighting conditions.Random annoying encounters:As an example of this, at one point I found a "safehouse" in the Caspian level and slept until morning. The game spawned two enemies at the same location and one of them "heard a noise" as my character woke up. He then proceeded to spot and kill me faster than I could ADS.Very long scripted sequences:Instead of traditional cutscenes, the game keeps you in first person. This should add to the immersion of the game and in many cases it does. But the sheer amount of time you spend listening to other characters talk, completing scripted sequences, or otherwise not being able to do anything is staggering. It's pretty annoying to just sit there and watch your character complete some scripted sequence. Having no option to skip is an issue for repeat playthroughs. If you're "lucky" you'll get a quick time event and that's about it.Horrible movement physics:Your character seems to float when going up or down stairs and other elevated surfaces. It's like he's skating on ice anytime there's a little bit of an incline or decline. This can lead to you taking damage as falling 3 feet takes half your health and can even lead to your death on Ranger Hardcore.Awkward dialog:At several points in the game, a character would speak, then pause for a second or two with no one else talking before continuing. It's like they're waiting for your character to respond, but of course you're a mute so it just feels weird.DLC:The Two Colonels DLC is fine. Pretty short and completely linear but it adds extra context to the last part of the game. Sam's Story, however, is downright awful. For some reason the performance on my system was terrible and I struggled to get 60 FPS in many sections while having over 100 in the base game. It's also very sparse with the checkpoints it gives which means that, on Ranger Hardcore, when you die you'll be set back 15-30 minutes at times. You really don't have many options for fighting enemies, meaning you'll have to fight head on. This really sucks, as the enemies are very accurate and can oneshot you even through bushes when you can't see them. Getting set back to before a scripted sequence, and replaying it over and over is such a slog. By the way, enemies that "surrender" can unsurrender themselves and you'll have to kill them, but if you kill them while they are surrendering you'll get a negative moral point.Conclusion:Exodus' story and atmosphere is just as great as the previous games. It was awesome moving out of Moscow and exploring other places. But, for me the gameplay just wasn't very fun. I always had this nagging feeling of "I cant wait to get past this section" but there was no fun section to get to.

_childDocuments_.review: Despite the huge fiasco with the publisher and all the crap that came with it, the game itself didn't fail. It's better than the previous Metro games in every aspect, in my opinion.1. Story. The overall plot is solid even though a bit predictable sometimes. Characters are convincing, they feel alive. Even generic NPCs have a character, although I believe it's always been that way in Metro.2. Gameplay. It's very solid; the guns shoot well, the enemies aren't bullet sponges if you aim correctly and use a good weapon. Sometimes, guns overheat, which is a good mechanic, but it happened a bit too often for my liking. Cleaning them is another good mechanic that is a bit illogical. I need to collect medicine-related resources to clean it. Where's logic in that? At least it doesn't eat too much of the precious resources. The gun attachments really help with choosing the right tool for the job even though I prefer to choose loadouts before going out like in previous Metro games.3. Performance. I have AMD Ryzen 5 2600x, 16GB 3200MHz RAM, and GTX 1070. The game worked almost flawlessly at High settings with some minor weird dips that happened less than five times. Basically, I think the system requirements are correct, and I was almost able to play the game on Ultra without many problems.4. Levels. The design is top notch, their size is just enough to not get lost or have nothing to do. The amount of environmental storytelling is very good as well. I'll definitely be replaying a lot of this game.5. Enemies. A lot of them return from the previous Metro games, but now they feel even more alive and less than just mindless hordes of NPCs to throw at you when it's time. Some enemies are annoying (those with slime stuff), but other than that, it's fine. As for humans, they can sometimes be dumb, but sometimes they're precise and smart. 6. Audio. I noticed some sounds returning from the previous games, and I think it's fine even though they're from the sound libraries. We already know the sounds of different things, so I think it was a good decision to leave the old simple sounds in. 7. Bugs. There were some lighting glitches in a few places, flying helmets and disappearing hats, plus a funny one. Somewhat major spoilers ahead!8. Graphics. They're pretty good, although transitional levels could use an upgrade. Fire looks convincing, which isn't an easy feat. Characters look good, although facial animations are still not very good. The big levels sometimes have bad textures in places where most wouldn't look, but that's understandable – if the minor textures were better, it'd fry even newer GPUs, heh.Conclusion: despite the giant mess that Deep Silver made, the game is good, playable, and definitely enjoyable.
