_childDocuments_.review: Factorio is a simulation game. It's also a real-time strategy game. It's also a logic/programming/engineering primer. It's also a survival/crafting/building game. You would think that with so many genres it wouldn't be a focused piece of gaming software. On the contrary, it is laser-focused and requires you to constantly improve at streamlining production systems.The basic gameplay loop consists of gathering materials, refining materials, and using those materials to build other crafting structures and quality of life improvements. You can build weapons, armor, turrets, a cool car (with questionable controls), a complex train system, and a space rocket. As you advance in the game, you must research technology to open up higher tiers of crafting. In this way, it's very similar to other survival/crafting games. It doesn't stop there, though.From each resource point (iron ore, copper ore, water, oil, wood, stone, etc.) you can sometimes gather materials by hand or build machines to gather the resources for you. But, the resources don't just fill up in the gathering machines. Take iron ore, for instance. You place down a mining structure to pull iron ore up from iron ore patches. The mining structure outputs a single piece of iron ore and it sits there. Add a smelting structure to it and you can turn the iron ore into iron plates for use in crafting. Or, you can place down a series of conveyor belts (called transport belts in the game) to transport the iron ore to another location where you can smelt it and create those iron plates. From there, you can use the iron plates to make items for yourself or you can use mechanical arms (called inserters) to remove the plates from the smelters and send them on even more transport belts to be sent to multiple factories using splitters (splits one belt of material into 2 belts) to make something from those plates. Some items require only a single material input. Others require multiple, refined material inputs to create additional items for use in making more advanced pieces of crafting components.Eventually, you'll have a very complex system of conveyor belts, refining equipment, splitters, inserters, etc. to make higher-tier technology items. Trains can be used to transport the player or materials over long distances or to bring items to a central production or research hub. Almost everything in the game can be automated and many items must be manufactured in factories.At certain points in the game, unless you are completely familiar with the crafting requirements for various bits and pieces, you'll find that the previously "perfect" setup you had is now obsolete and you might need to adjust your transport belts or start entirely from scratch. Then you get access to transport and repair robots and they add a new form of challenge and quality of life.At first, you are limited to powering your machines and structures with wood or coal. This works for the very beginning of the game but becomes impractical as item requirements increase and vary over time. So, you start building steam engines to create electricity. Eventually those become impractical or insufficient and you create solar arrays or more efficient power-generation structures. And all of those have their own unique requirements for production. Late in the game, you start building nuclear fuel rods (and more advanced systems) for generating power.The game is really a series of short, incremental increases in productivity and efficiency followed by long plateaus of wrapping your head around the new crafting requirements. The material costs for research steadily increase until you are using dozens of complex components to create the research packs required to generate research points in your science labs. Finding out how to maximize your efficiency is one of the charms of this game. That is, of course, if you like that sort of thing.This all occurs while groups of enemies frequently storm your base(s) and probe for weak points in your defenses. In fact, as your production increases, you generate more pollution and increase the rate and power level of the enemy spawns. In a round-about way, you are the enemy in this game. The creatures are just trying to protect their planet from the dirty scientist/manufacturer. This leads to the main dichotomy and source of conflict within the game.Your goal (as indicated by a single dialogue box at the beginning of a new game) is to reach the end of the tech tree and build a rocket to fire off into space and escape the planet. To do this, you constantly increase your pollution output to the point where the enemies attack very frequently. Fighting off the smaller-sized raids isn't too difficult. Some of the late-game raids are a bit more punishing. So, do you simultaneously increase your defense/offense budget (in research, materials, and manufacturing time?) as well as attempt to improve your infrastructure? You'll be doing everything a lot slower if you devote your resources to defense. But, you will have to do both if you want to win. You can also fiddle with the options in the game start menu and make it a peaceful run where the planet doesn't respond to toxic levels of pollution. It's your choice.If all of this sounds great or intriguing, then get the game and give it a shot. There are constant updates and content patches from the developers.As far as a downside, there is a major one. The tutorials in the game are a bit simplistic and don't give a complete example of how systems work. The developers have done some work to increase the quality of tooltips for the items in the game, but they aren't quite sufficient for the complexity of most systems. Several recent patches have added more information to various system status screens and this helps some. I still frequently have to refer to external sources for tips and tricks on how to properly set up a system that isn't horribly inefficient. The train station/stop/automation system is especially complex and overwhelming at first. There are a bunch of options and tweaks available. On the plus side, the game doesn't punish trial and error too much and the tooltips do a good job of explaining the speed at which certain systems can gather, refine, and manufacture materials.Some best practices from the community run counter to the spirit and expectation of game mechanics. A good example of this is early coal mining. You can take 4 extractors and link them together in a 2x2 square in sequence. The first feeds the second feeds the third feeds the first. Put coal in one and it will then extract and transfer excess coal into the next extractor in the series and so on. Sure, the coal extractors run by burning coal, but this runs counter to the spirit of the game (using transport belts to move materials from one place to another.) However, if you need coal in the early game, this is a quick way to gather lots of coal. Just remember to pick it up before the extractors are full.I played for many hours before I found out you could feed extractors directly into other extractors or smelters without the need for inserters. I played for many more hours before I realized that transport belts had two distinct sides, inserters fed materials to specific sides of a belt based on placement, and that inserters could transfer items from both sides of a belt into a smelter or factory. None of this will make sense if you haven't played the game, but you'll soon know what I mean.There are a lot of these "a-ha!" moments in the game. This, more than anything else, directly affected the fun I had while playing. I'm sure this is one of the major reasons that people enjoy this game so much. Do yourself a favor and avoid the wiki and walkthroughs as long as possible. Try to figure out things on your own, if possible. You'll be surprised by how different your solutions are compared to other players.

_childDocuments_.review: EDIT: It has been four years since I wrote this review. I currently have logged over 350 hours in this game, and I still feel the way I did four years ago. The game has changed dramatically, in a lot of ways; most importantly, the devs have kept the endgame criteria in, but you're able to continue playing afterwards, in case you want to keep building your base, and make something ridiculous. They have reworked a lot of the science and tech; it's now possible to automate all of the science! They updated the visuals, and they were very responsive to player feedback! Currently, they're reworking the tutorial to really streamline the way it communicates information.Also, the game runs a lot smoother in multiplayer now, though there's still some latency from my network connection. (That isn't the devs' fault, obviously)And every Friday, they have consistently, without fail, provided their Factorio Friday Facts, letting all of us know what they are up to, and the direction they are taking the game.This game is a gem.Original: Early Access games can be hit or miss sometimes, and this one is definitely a hit.tl;dr Absolutely the best $20 I have spent on an Early Access game. The devs update regularly and are very transparent about the behind-the-scenes stuff, and I am very excited to see where it goes from here.This game is all about logistics and automation; getting resources from place to place, and feeding them into machines to build large quantities of stuff, and even research cool new technologies.While there is a very rudimentary story (crash landed on a planet, have to build and launch a rocket with a satellite to call for help), the game is very much a sandbox game with a win condition, which I love. The one problem I run into with sandbox games is once I get to all of the high-tier stuff, I'm left asking "...Now what?" But Factorio provides a fun, but very challenging, way to end it.You can also mess around with the generation settings via a GUI that is super easy to figure out. Want hostile alien nests to spawn everywhere at ridiculously high rates? Want large patches of resources so you can build a ton? Just mess around with the drop-down boxes a bit, and voila! A game customized however you want it.The tutorials are fun and teach you the basics; the controls take a little getting used to (or at least, it took me a bit to get used to them), but it isn't hard to get the hang of how the game works.I've found that multiplayer lags a little bit, which makes it hard to drive cars or tanks, but it's entirely possible that that has more to do with the network I'm using than the game itself.I haven't even messed around in the map editor, but the idea of setting up a challenging (or otherwise entertaining) scenario is always cool.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is one of the best games I ever played. A friend originally showed it to me about a year before it came onto the Steam platform when I purchased it on their website. Your goal is simple: Escape from the planet with a rocket. Somehow this leads to your next big problem: You just stand there, without anything! While only the plan to get to the rocket is already hard, you'll soon realize that the biggest problems were your earlier decisions. And your demand for raw materials is skyrocking! So you need to upgrade again and again. New technology needs to be researched to approach your goal in small steps. There is always plenty of work to do. Even factors like the pollution you influence in the aggressivity of the Natives. And you always have not enough iron!!! +Game recieves constant updates and is always improving+Very balanced+Steep learning curve +You decide how fast you play+There is always something to do+Vast field of actions (raw materials, crafting, transporting, getting electricity, oil, combat, ...)+Well done campaign, you learn step by step all mechanics+Good Multiplayer System+Mod platform+/- Very addicting (you start playing at 6pm and suddenly it's 2am or so...)- Free mode can feel pointless when you start a new world, especially when you're new to the game- In the free mode, tutorials are non-existent. Therefore, play the campaign first or play multiplayer mode (with friends explaining you the basic steps). For further help ingame, factorio wiki / youtube is going to be your friend.All in all I definitely recommend you this game. And be prepared, the game is very addicting ;-)

_childDocuments_.review: Honestly, when I first got this game I didn't play a ton, mostly because the game had a decent learning curve and carries some time commitment to it.That being said, I started playing with friends and it brought all of this game back to me. It's lovely and just complicated enough that you constantly feel like there's another thing to do, but not overwhelmed. I highly recommend finding some people to play with to start, as there's a lot to the game that isn't super obvious in the tutorials or instructions.Very good, thought provoking, and rather peaceful.I'm added now with 2.0:I've played for an additional 500 some odd hours at this point.... Game's pretty dang good.2.0 redid a lot of the things that gave me the most pain with 1.0, (redid fluid behavior, added a BOATLOAD of quality of life features, added a bunch of functionality to train networks!). Space exploration is super fun. I've not gotten super far, but the planets don't feel more complex while still being very different to approach, which is super duper fun.The modding scene is alive and booming, especially if you want to beat the game and then make it harder and more complicated. Bob's mods are wonderful, and Angels was too big for me to ever finish.

_childDocuments_.review: Pros:Addicting gameplay that generally provides you clues about what to build next. Nearly endless replayability thanks to a multitude of built in game settings, plus a huge modding community.UI - makes it easy to accomplish everything you need to do, provides good player feedback about current status, easy to read, and modders can hook into the UI to make all sorts of fun changes.Sound/Graphics/Music - all are top notch for this style of game. Rustling leaves of trees, waves of water, chemical plants whiring, biters angrily screeching. Little graphical details brought to life like parts of your base being destroyed are still visible, the glow of your laser turrets at night, and foot prints in the snow and sand. One of the few games I leave the music on because it is unobtrusive and really sets the mood.Devs - receptive to feedback, quick to fix bugs, passionate about the game, respect the gaming communityMods - this is why you play on PC right? for the mods? Unlike most games, the modding portal is built right into the game and the devs go to great length to support mods. They make it easy to add/remove mods and to ensure the right mods load with your save. No dealing with Steam Workshop, Nexus, et al. And the modding community was already huge before 1.0 release. Dont like some aspect of the game or wish something was easier, chances are there is already a mod for that. Try the game first w/o mods, because it is still very complete and bug free. Unlike many other games, there is no need for an "unofficial bugfix" mod with Factorio.Cons:Addicting - like "one more turn" in Civ, only its "I'll just reroute this real quick then goto bed" and next thing you know the sun is rising.Update: If you really liked the base game, the expansion "Space Age" is totally worth. A lot more complex, so if you struggled with plain Factorio, the expansion might be too much.

I haven't put more than a hundred hours on any other game in the last 5 years. I *make time* for this game. Amazing mod community and S-tier mod support adds literally hundreds to thousands of hours of gameplay. _childDocuments_.review: I had a great time with this game, complicated puzzle where you try to design and build this beautiful machine but have to run around putting out fires constantly. The core game loop is the iterative design of increasingly complex industrial processes and logistics systems. I've played the game a lot but I still find new ways to improve efficiency all the time. The designers did a wonderful job of creating moral tension in this game. The player character crashes on an alien world with nothing but a wrecked space ship and some simple tools, then has to try to climb the technology ladder all the way back to space flight so they can escape the planet. The pollution generated by resource harvesting, processing, and assembling more and more complex machines pollutes the surrounding land, air, and water, kills the plant life, and it causes the local fauna to attack the player and the factory. The pollution also pressure the local dominant species to evolve and become stronger, faster, and more destructive. The players endless battles against attacking xenomorphs could feel like a simplistic tower defense game or a minor annoyance, but for me, they don't. There is something heroic and tragic about seeing these aliens throw themselves endlessly into battle to save their home world. The aliens also just keep coming, and like Leiningen vs the ants it evokes the fundamental struggle of humanity against nature. Can we humans reshape the world as we please and deal with all the consequences of our actions, or must we sometimes bow to inexorable forces of nature when they come against us?There is also something heroic and tragic in the role of the castaway engineer(the player character), fighting desperately for survival against impossible odds as they try to return to space. To go home? To complete some other mission? The game does not tell us, and is better because it does not tell us. We know only the struggle for survival and mastery.This game is fun and engrossing, but it also a work of art that explores themes of environmental destruction, the struggle for survival, colonialism, specism, and unintended consequences.

_childDocuments_.review: I probably have over 600 hours combined and I have yet to create a review!  (Standalone client included)Edit: Oh, I had over 600 on the steam side... Oh..oh.  I need to re-evaluate my life.. right after I set this refiner up.First off, I'd like to talk a little about the company.  When you buy the game on steam, you can also create an account on their website and get a copy from there to download for standalone use.  Works great for multiple mod sets!  There are frequent updates to the game as experimental (option under the properties of the game like all beta stuff, or their website), then you get some major updates that drastically expand the game.  Now about the game.  The game is cheap enough to just try it, it should honestly be higher, but its alpha.  In the game you build a factory from nearly nothing, you can automate everything from loading ore from a belt into a furnace to make plates, from a logistic drone network that carries the plates to other areas of your factory for building anything from ammo to solar panels.  There is a blueprint system where you can copy layouts of your base and put them elsewhere or simply store them.  The game has captured my attention for some time, from the infiinite world to the infinite complexity your factory can be.  There are no limits in this game, you would think the game would say "you already have 1000 robots moving stuff, you can't have more." Nope.  6000? 10,000? who cares, just be ready to charge them.  Or say "Congrats you built your rocket, good job."  This game: "Hey you launched a rocket, [end game screen: continue?]" and then you see people with 6000 rocket launches and launches every minute, gigantic mega factories, factories just using robots, factories using no robots.  There is a train system you can see in the trailer, they don't tell you theres no limit to the number of trains on a rail, the length of cars on them, or the distance you can send them.  This game is turely a game without limits.  The best part of all, they've been working heavily on optimizations, so your mega base with 20,000 bots or 100 trains, doesn't notice a FPS drop.  I'll be realistic here, you can get a FPS drop eventually, simply due to size.  However the game runs great far past end game, and continues to run better with each update.TL;DR, It has 98-99% positive reviews, if you like management games, just get the damn game.

_childDocuments_.review: For the love of god, don't buy this game; it's not a game, it's a curse.Sure, it starts out innocent.  A couple of transport belts here, a robotic arm there.  Oh, what's that? I can unlock more things to build, you say?  Sure, why not?  All I have to do is connect these miner thingies to a furnace array, then sort the metal output to a couple assembler factories and put the results on a train to go to another assembler factory, where the product will be taxied by drone to my rocket silo so that the resulting white stuff can be transported to my research facility and voila, my automatic missile-shooting train can now shoot 12% farther.Suddenly, it's daylight.  That 12 hours between shifts you were supposed to spend eating and sleeping to keep yourself well nourished was instead used to play this "game".  You reluctantly get in your car and go to work.  Your colleagues say they're gonna hit the bar later and ask you to join.  But alas, you tell them you've got to stay late to finish up this couple of assignments.  In reality, however, there are no more assignments-- no, there is only Factorio.You get home in a fit of panic, desperate for your fix.  It's been invading your brain the whole driver, thinking about how to optimize your main bus split-offs, making deadlock-proof junctions for the copper transport rail system.  You get a text from this girl you started seeing.  Asks if she can come over.  Exasperated, you pause your game, only for a minute, so you can come up with a lie about taking night classes at a community college 5 nights a week for the next two years.  She says it's cool, goes out to a bar alone, where she hooks up with one of your colleagues.Weeks go by.  Months.  You've lost complete track of time.  You've taken off of work for the past three weeks citing some sort of infectious disease.  You can't remember the last time you left the house, even your computer.  But alas, the day has come.  Your steadfast dedication and unwavering determination have finally paid off.  The inhabitant's of this alien world have almost gotten in, almost destroyed all your hard work on so many occasions.  But alas, their efforts were for not as their noble warriors lay by the hundreds, no, the thousands, at the foot of your base-- your megabase.  You have finally done it.  You are now launching 60 rockets every second, science coursing through your veins by the hundreds of thousands.  You control everything.  Not a tree stands on this red planet you can now call yours.  You exit the game, reminiscing over all the good times you had in that base as you watch the replay with teary eyes.  Then, back on the main menu, you slowly move your mouse towards the bottom to exit this "game" and return to the real world.Suddenly, something catches your eye.  That button.  You never really paid attention to it before.  How could you have missed it in your zombie haze?  What's this?  This game... has mods?

_childDocuments_.review: Everything you've heard about this game is probably true.The hours will escape you. The days will pass. Maybe even years. And yet still, there is more to be done. The factory isn't going to build itself. (Unless you design it to)I spent my first 20-50 hours of this game blindly stumbling among piles of wet noodles. (conveyor belts)Learning to experiment with all of the machines, their ratios, and necessities to function efficiently, the game made me feel like I've actually grown, like it has actually expanded my capability to manage and solve things to some degree, both on a logical and creative level.Even when I wasn't playing, I was thinking about it. "How could I improve this..? Maybe I could put this here and.." My idle times were filled with "Aha!" moments, which drew me back in every time. One-hundred hours later, I launched a rocket, and was finally done with the first half of the game.I have yet to learn how to properly use trains, the curcuit network system, or even logistic robots.I know that at first glance, it looks complicated, and daunting, but there are plenty of settings to make the game as hellish or lax as you feel is necessary. Player opposition is optional. You decide what to build, how to build it, where to build it. If you don't know how, figure it out. And when you do, the reward-feedback from this is like high-grade crack. Except, it's even better than that.

_childDocuments_.review: A game like Factorio will send you on an emotional rollercoaster with heartwarming happiness and severe anguish. The sensation of achievement is unfathomable, from the thrilling beginning of a crash landing on a foreign planet to creating a vast manufacturing empire. The thrill of streamlining processes and automating whatever you can is comparable to enjoying a properly cooked steak while listening to your favourite music.But don't be fooled by the seeming simplicity; Factorio's challenge is just as genuine as walking barefoot on a LEGO block. When you believe you have everything under control, the game throws a wrench (or a dozen) into your well-functioning system. Your factory is invaded by alien biters, which causes a panic similar to a cat chasing a laser pointer. The balancing of the electrical grid turns into a unicycle juggling show with flaming chainsaws.The dark comedy of Factorio will have you second-guessing your decisions and considering a simpler life as a hermit in the woods. But in the middle of frustration, innovations occur, and your factory once again hums with productivity. The delicious win justifies the nerve-wracking times.This game takes pleasure in both your triumph and your misery. It will simultaneously make you feel smart and stupid. But despite everything, you'll be enthralled by the game's compelling gameplay and the prospect of building the ideal mechanized paradise. You'll laugh, weep, and undoubtedly curse like a drunken pirate on Factorio's gloriously chaotic trip.I sincerely urge any daring factory builders to check out Factorio. Accept the happiness and the sorrow, and remember that they are all a part of the experience. Happy engineering, and long live the spaghetti-free factory!

_childDocuments_.review: TL:DR Okay long time coming. Its 9/7/2020. Been a bumpy ride, and i've been around since factorio version 0.10.xFactorio is inshort a builder/engineering simulation on a 2D platform on windows, linux, macos (yes even raspberry pi with wine on the raspberry pi3/raspberry pi 4 which will run like garbage on pi3, somewhat bareable on pi4). If you wanna read the long winded review, then well go ahead its after this text.||VAnyway first off, Huge kudos to the devs! Those folks from WUBE studios have literally set a standard when it comes to PR, and how to keep the community informed when it comes to EA titles. We've finally made it to the 1.0.0 finalization build. And the optimization is unbelievable! Okay now onto the finer points.Thanks to modding, this can literally transform the game into literally whatever you can imagine. Going as far as PvP, PvE, and PvPvE. Mods are written in anything from LUA to c++. So much compatability and capabilities. Another huge selling point, is the game is DRM free. You buy it through steam? You can still go to  and login connecting the game site to your steam account to obtain a DRM Free installer build, and more resources (including authentication means on the DRM Free platform if you so choose, and other goodies, like the mod portal, etc...).Besides having the mentioning portion mentioned above and below, you can also buy factorio through their actual website giving more money to the devs (yay for the devs!) if not just link and get those extra goodies.Now moving on, the whole story behind factorio is, things got real, your ship crashed, and your now trying to get off the planet. You need to launch a rocket to get the heck off this planet. Now this 100% reminds me of a game called StormRunner by Lego's MindStorms project which you can find out more if you google it. Anywho this game has a similar concept except it was more like the pioneering of the first generation of such simulation games (except in this case you get to play as the player instead of utilizing programmable drones, which you can do in factorio's vanilla builds {Means to play with out any mods}).That said, story aside, your way off, is automation. Building massive mega bases, mini bases, whatever you need to do to get resources, and get the heck, off that planet. The game has a unbelieveably robust "blueprint" building system, where you can save or migrate old blueprints (dating back to 0.13.X with the blueprints mods) to current 1.0.0 build of factorio. This means no more reinventing the wheel, you figure something out once, and you blueprint it for future use later (make blueprint book and save it into your blueprints library ingame). Anywho thats the simplicity of build and forget. Now.. if you do wanna reinvent the wheel or just try playing a whole new way tackling new challenges at a different pace (you can change map generation and difficulty to your hearts desire), go right on ahead. Its super addictive, and super fun. Either way, everyone has a favored playstyle. Inshort, this games a ton of fun, i personally play with the bare minimum of a deployable portable fusion reactor (that can be installed as infinite energy supply on ground at a hefty ingame resource cost) with (new game+) and factorissimo, amongst other qol(quality of life) mods, so that when i beat the map i can start all over, but with all my inventory (or using clustorio for example i can travel from server 1 to server to with all my resources in my player inventory, or as a "care package" drop off to the other servers "map".All in all this games a ton of fun, try the demo out first. If you like it, i suggest you buy it! Im also willing to part with my giftable copy (i originally had a few i bought prior in 2016 and i bought a few last minute before they stopped selling at the $30 price tag) so if you wanna use paypal to buy the extra license its $25 my way for the steam giftable copy i have remaining of the 8 overall copies i've bought through steam/factorio. Then yeah reach out to me or post under here as interested(i only have 1x left). If you wanna buy any of my other giftables, just well make a offer, im usually selling them for less than their worth on steam.P.S. You can play on a drm free build, if you didn't buy factorio you can still enjoy local lan, and gameplay on servers running their own authentication/white listing system (authentication added in with users own homebrewed mods) with out needing to authenticate with steam, or  --------------------------------------------------------Old review below New atopAlrighty Review as promised, 7/1/2016After playing around i found 0.13.0 to be quite pleasing. Given it was rapidly updated within the last 3 days to 0.13.2 some noticeable improvements, for me the core difference was the reworking of their network, offering much needed stability vs the old fashion p2p networking.Alongside that, flamethrowers! Flamethrower turret, and the flamethrower itself was beautifully done, although LAGGY if you spam it hardcore (in multiplayer that is), its amazing, and the server easily stabalizies within seconds of stopping the jetstream of death you shoot. Now you truly are a mobile tank, with or with out the tank and destroyer capsules.This being said though, you'll enjoy improved game stability, alot more features that were corrected/patched in the 0.13.2 build. Personally, you'll love the new network scheme, if you buy your game through  or through steam (i suggest steam, and then link it to  but either or), you will gain access to a new online hub, where you can see others who host servers, and hop in. Thats a major convience given now you do not need to know diddly about port forwarding, let alone configurations to host a temperary non headless server. Alot of new commands like kick, ban, promote, etc.... the admin commands are definitely a start.All in all, i personally enjoyed this game, if you like games that involve low taxing of the machine, runs on windows xp (32bit and 64bit builds), the fact you can run it on a low end gaming rig (raspberry pi Mk3 can play this through the linux steam build), you will certainlly want to take a crack at this game. The games that involve survival is what makes this game fun. But like games like minecraft, terraria are your thing? You'll like factorio. The game truly is limited to your imagination, and the cool part? All the infinite number of ways to optimize your own factory. Its a amazing idea starter game. Once you demo it, or really get into it, consider buying a copy. As for me, i bought 5 copies altogether, and i still have 2 in my steam inventory to gift out randomly. Think you like it? Respond with your most favorite like about factorio. For the next two weeks ill give out 2 copies of factorio, 1 copy a week. Consider this my Early Happy 4th of julyCheers

_childDocuments_.review: --- GAMEPLAY ---If I'm being honest I think I probably spent more time outside of the game planning how I am going to make my creations than I did in-game. I'm not saying that the gameplay is bad it's actually really good but ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ did this game have me thinking about it more than most. Starting off from manually mining ore deposits and eventually end up with a machine so complex you can't remember how half of it works. The gameplay is really good. Each time you get to unlock a new machine your mind starts racing thinking of all the different ways to use it. Then you also have the aspect of the bug colonies. I think they really bring a good aspect to the game by being one of the main reasons I was progressing so quickly. At first they were to difficult but it doesn't take that long to start getting overwhelmed. Working on my defences I found to be really fun and s good change from constantly having my brain bombarded with ways to try and create the most efficient machine I could.--- DIFFICULTY ---I'd say the game is pretty difficult in terms of getting used to and wrapping your head around the mechanics to make your machines as efficient as possible. As I mentioned I spent an awful lot of time outside the game planning out my machines from ore mining to science creation. The combat I don't find too difficult it's more just an arms race to try and overpower the bugs before they overpower you. The combat slowly scales up and especially at the beginning it's all pretty easy.--- Worth The Price ---At the time of review the price is: £21.00Worth the price? Yes--- SCORE ---9 / 10TLDRPros:Really great mechanicsGameplay so interesting you will be thinking about it outside of the gameCons:I'm not a huge fan of the limited amount in ore deposits (modding can fix this)

_childDocuments_.review: Very engaging, don't see a whole ton of replayability but my hours played should speak for themselves.Kind of like those factory-esque puzzle games, but fused with a sandbox-survival game. There is technically a goal, but you can achieve it pretty easily (still quite a few hours if you don't know what you're doing). You spend nearly all of your time expanding an ever-growing factory that produces the necessary machined parts to either research further in the research tree or defend your base from the angry inhabitants of the world you landed on. Your path to the goal is kinda the same every time you play, there isn't much of a difference between the different world types to me, mostly just speedbumps. You start small but soon you are automatically mining minerals, smelting them into plates, then crafting those materials into things that either expand your factory, kill the insectoid bad-guys, or research more things for you to craft. The gameplay is pretty cyclical though; you set up an area to craft something you need, find you are lacking materials somewhere else in your factory to do so, follow the problem & fix what is slow until you are crafting a surplus, then start crafting the next thing.Don't get me wrong, the game is really fun, I just don't see myself spending a thousand hours playing it... maybe just a few hundred. It's very tech-focused and supply-line oriented, and there is no story, very little exploration, and only as much combat as you want. There are lots of options that tailor your world or gameplay to your liking, and great mod support if you want something else.PS: the tutorial is kinda bad but you still need to know how to get going, so I'd recommend watching a video or something instead.

_childDocuments_.review: The true genius of this game is that it's actually a masterclass in logistics programming that tricks you into wanting to eradicate aliens for their resources. It's the agony of always being one part short to complete your fancy new subsystem that's connected to a main line of cargo that you've already spent hours carefully connecting only to realize that you could move something just 2 tiles and add one more inserter here or there to improve it by only 0.25%. That's a huge number in the world of this many moving parts and most players of this game would likely agree.The sense of progression is something akin to Civilization where the start of the game provides you with 2 sticks that you can rub together to make your first furnace glow that will have to be powered by fuel you hand gather. By the end you'll be in charge of a giant series of machines that spans across a literally infinite map that just simply wants more and more. Your robot army will help put fuel in your tank so that you can drive to site, destroy all of the aliens around it, design a new system on top of it, add it to a blueprint and plop it down with one mouse click right next to your new train depot that's piping ore into smelters 10 minutes (in train speed) away in the other direction.If you get lost, there's a lot... and I mean a lot of information out there from other players that also realize this game is as much of a theory and programming language as it is a game. I personally think experimenting until everything on fire is the best kind of science so I've spent quite a few hours now just hooking things up to things and trying to figure out exactly just how far I can take the programming circuits. Sure I could have played the game and won several times over, but this very much the hybrid between real-time strategy base building and Transport Tycoon I didn't know I really wanted until I just blew almost a whole week of free time playing it.Of course YOU can play this game exactly how you want, because after all it's multiple games at once. It's a formidble tower defense game and turtling is a viable strategy. You can turn the aliens off and just build a fancy factory that hordes resource, or you can play the game the "right" way and work towards building a rocket to get off of this alien infested rock. A very supportive mod community makes a ton of completely optional enhancements that do very minor things like improve quality of life, or add complete overhauls that seemingly have created expansions for the base game. I just experimented with a mod that overhauled how the game generates resources, which drastically changed my entire strategy. Again, I say option because the base game already offers 100's of hours of enjoyment if you find what it is that I personally enjoy: Destroying an entire planet.. 9.5/10 mechafistsside note: if this were an Early Access alpha standard, I may not regret 97% of the other abandoned trash fires I pointlessly invested in. This game is still heavily supported and maintained each week after FOUR years.

_childDocuments_.review: Factorio is amazing.The most similar things I can think of are certain varieties of modded Minecraft, and Factorio is better than them in almost every possible way.    Graphics: Not particularly high quality, but with the amount of bits and bobs that end up floating around, you can't really have super fancy graphics without hurting FPS.     Speaking of FPS, Factorio manages to simulate the MASSIVE machines, items, and other entities any decent factory will have without suffering any noticable lag whatsoever. It's an amazing feat of programming, and it greatly improves the quality of the game.    Sound: As with most sandbox games, I consider Factorio's BGM to be appropriate. Not particularly good, not bad, but fitting. I still usually choose to listen to other things while I play, but something is playing enough of the time that someone who requires auditory stimulation (like me) will probably be satisfied. The sound effects are similar: acceptable quality, and appropriate for the game.     Gameplay:       Pros:    -Factorio is a sandbox game based around automation. Most such games (in my experience) have less building complex systems and more waiting for resources. Factorio manages to mostly avoid this pitfall through careful balancing, meaning that you have to spend less time waiting, and can spend more time making and fixing things (which is the fun part of the game).    -Very active modding community. The large amount of mods available adds a lot of replay value, and the community shows no signs that they're stopping any time soon. It also help that you can install the mods easily by pressing some buttons in game, rather than having to fiddle with files manually.    -Active Developers that care. As is, Factorio could easily be released as a full game, but the Devs continue to add to it and improve it. Weekly rundowns of what they're working on let users be involved in the development process. The best part? Like the modding community, the devs show no sign of slowing down any time soon.    -MULTIPLAYER. While it's still not 100% optimized, you can play online with your friends. I've yet to try it myself (all of my friends that own Factorio have gotten bored of it somehow), but games like this are better played with friends. Just having the option is a plus.      Cons:    -Addictive. The vast majority of other reviews mention this, AND IT'S TRUE. Factorio progression requires you to set up large systems to produce and process various goods. As soon as you finish one project, there'll be another one ready for you. It's fun, and it draws you in.     If you have trouble remembering to do things like eat, drink water, sleep, go to the bathroom, go outside, etc. when gaming, it might be a good idea to stay away from Factorio until you figure out a solution to your problem.Overall:Great gameplay and a decent amount of replay value make this game one of the best games on Steam.Don't forget to take breaks!

_childDocuments_.review: Factorio is a phenomenal game, if you're the right audience for it. And if you're looking at its store page, you probably are.I'm an old gamer. Played thousands of games since the Atari 2600. I have to admit, nothing really keeps my attention right now: heavily-modded Minecraft, some RPGs like Divinity: OS2 & Pillars of Eternity, shooters like the Battlefields and a bit of Apex, the occasional drop-in to old MMOs like EQ2, and even Satisfactory - a very similar product - I'll play them for an hour or two each, but Factorio is what I always want to play, what I keep coming back to. It's just right for me. I played GTNH (Gregtech super-hardmode industrial modded Minecraft) for a few years, but that was developed by a rather incongruent medley of modders. And you could compare it to those chemistry-style games that were popular some years ago (SpaceChem, et al.), but those are pure, dry, open-ended logic puzzles. Satisfactory is great but feels rather incomplete and lacks depth, while also being bereft of the mechanical simplicity you need to satisfactorily lay out a large, complex floorplan and troubleshoot it. Factorio is so simple on a basic level that it makes coming up with complex, compact, even symmetrical solutions feel easy, if you have a logical mind. And the game's purely 2D, so you'll never have to worry about performance even if you go absolutely nuts with a long-play world.Add a bunch of mods to make it more challenging whilst giving you something novel to work towards, and it's like a fine 5-course meal; you don't want it to be over, but you don't want to stop enjoying it. Magnificent.(I recommend Bob's and Angel's mods (there are several of each) to start if you're looking for a longer game)If you'll excuse me, I must return to the new playthrough I've started since the big quality-of-life patches. The game feels even better now.

So to put it simply, I absolutely cannot stop playing this game (which rarely happens).Overall Impression: Factorio feels like a strategy game, but may not be for everyone. You basically wonder around gathering resources (which is and understatement, because the point of the game is to automate the resource gathering and managing). To me, it's like re-living the days of playing Age of Empires against a few bots, but MUCH more satisfying. Factorio is addicting, and I have yet to remember a game that has kept me playing until 7:00 AM. Overall for the price, it's worth it.PROS: -Lightweight, no issues with game crashing, or bugs, or anything else that negative that is outside of gameplay-A Great game if you like thinking about managing and automating resources. Tis an odd thing to enjoy, but it's 10/10 in giving you the ability to basically do whatever you want when it comes to building your factories.-A Great game if you are patient. Enjoyed planning it out again too.-You get the complete factory experience without having to work a factory job (wouldn't recommend working a factory job).-Lots of fun, the game is challenging in a lot of ways that doesn't make the user want to immediately quit. I imagine there could be a bit of improvement with that so the vanilla music is at least tolerable, if not catchy.-Visuals could perhaps look a bit better (better close-ups, some icons are not distinct enough, better effects). Bonus points for being actually pretty dang good for being Early Access.================ UPDATE 11/29/2024 ================I've been playing since Early Access for several years now. _childDocuments_.review: An incredibly solid and well put together game for anyone who likes logistics and design challenges.  The game challenges you to constantly build and create in order to expand your factory and create more advanced machines through researched technology.  You need to constantly look for more resources to keep your factory alive, and come up with your own solutions to problems as they appear.  Your little factory will grow and become a huge mess, but that's part of the fun.  The native monsters don't like your factory and will try to attack, but base defense is usually a secondary component to augment the main goals, so if you're looking for an action game or some kind of shooter, this isn't that game.  If you like automating your factories to produce ever greater quantities of materials to expand your factory and conduct tech research, in an infinite loop, then this will definitely tickle your fancy.  For those so inclined there is even some rudimentary circuit logic you can create, making basic computer systems and even infinitely expanding factories with construction robots.  You can play alone or with friends (which can be a ton of fun if everybody can get along and not grief!), and build basically whatever you like, from the smallest production line to the biggest industrial manufacturing hub you can dream up.Personally, I like to play with friends, but when I'm by myself I find the game plays best in short bursts.  You load in, fix a problem and expand your factory, maybe get inspired to make that new iron refinery you were thinking about, and then log out again.  It's a very easy game to play for any length of time, from 15 minute break sessions to multi-hour marathons.The game sprites are all extremely well-drawn and the game mechanics are solid.  The devs provide constant progress updates and fairly frequent updates and patches, implementing new ideas on a regular basis.  Some fairly new additions (at the time of writing) include nuclear power and updated ore sprites, among other things.  The world generation tools are highly customizable, allowing you to play any setting you like.  Don't want to fight monsters?  Turn on peaceful.  Don't like building new mines?  Turn up the ore richness.  And that's just a couple of examples of what you can do.One problem I can see with the game is that it's not always intuitive.  That is to say, the tutorial system to explain things is very rudimentary (at the time of writing, though it is something the devs are working on) and somewhat incomplete, making some features and concepts somewhat difficult to pick up for the beginner.  But overall, it's a fairly easy game to get the hang of once you've played for a couple of hours, and it's not a huge thing to get hung up on.Overall I solidly recommend this game, if you're creatively inclined and/or enjoy problem solving you will almost certainly have a good time.  Hell, even if you don't like those things you'll probably  have a good time.  The devs have clearly put a lot of time into making the game really good, and they deserve your support.  Unfortunately though, as far as I'm aware, the game has never gone on sale.  It is also still in Early Access, though it generally avoids the pitfalls so common of the type.

_childDocuments_.review: Factorio features very satisfying and fun gameplay of constantly expanding one's base and acquiring new resources.The devs are expanding the game's content for years at this point and most changes they made are sensible and actually enhance the game in so many ways.The really impressive part about the game is its implementation code wise.In contrast to what you see with most games, the devs actually cared and have gone the extra mile to optimize the game's code to a very high degree.- Factorio is able to use all 16 threads of my PC.- Multiplayer runs seamlessly and makes an awesome coop experience.- Modding is supported. Changing the attributes of an entity in-game is easily done in a single line of code (LUA).- The game can be set up to run out of a single folder (portable).- To host a dedicated server, you just run the game's exe with some params (single line .bat file on Windows).Factorio sets its standards higher than any other game I have ever modded.It is the example I bring up for good code in games if the topic ever comes up.

As these thoughts race through your mind, the latter part of you wins out. You accept the stranger’s dark gift. At first, everything seems fine. This isn’t so bad, you tell yourself. _childDocuments_.review: I'm certain this has already been said, but the amount of grief I've seen this game get lately due to the price change is absolutely unwarranted.The current gaming industry is overflowing with toxic and anti-consumer practices that make me sick. There are more studios than ever before with access to better technology than has ever been available, yet pre-orders, micro-transactions, cosmetics, and subscriptions plague games that are over-marketed, lack content, release while unfinished, and remain unsupported. These are the "greedy practices" that have ruined a depressing amount of potentially timeless experiences.I have yet to see any of this nonsense from Factorio or Wube Software. The game continues to be updated by the developer. Wube strongly supports and incorporates a modding community that has drastically increased the value of the base game over time. In this case, never putting your game on sale is overwhelmingly pro-consumer. Fallout 76 went on sale a month after release, which just meant that everyone that had already bought it had over-paid for that game. Anyone who bought 76 overpaid for the game. The value of the game is protected when it never goes on sale because when you buy it, that's it. No subscriptions, and no grief over not waiting one more week for it to drop 50%. Then the price is increased by $5. They say because of inflation; I don't know about that, but really who cares? Are you forced to pay another $5 if you already owned it? For anyone who has been enjoying this game any time between 2016 when it came out in early access and January 2023, it's irrelevant. You already own that value. It is absolutely mind-boggling that people are upset over this. If you cared about the game enough to be upset about a price hike, you would have already owned it. We should be celebrating a developer who has continued to refine a game to the point where it warrants a price increase, not saying ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ like "don't reward bad practice". This is the opposite of bad practice.Rant complete. And since this is a review, yes, the game was well worth the $30 I paid for it in 2018. It would be worth $35 if I were buying it today. Wube will continue to have my support as long as they continue to treat consumers and their community with respect as they have so far.

_childDocuments_.review: The Pauli exclusion principle is the quantum mechanical principle which states that two or more identical fermions (particles with half-integer spin) cannot occupy the same quantum state within a quantum system simultaneously. This principle was formulated by Austrian physicist Wolfgang Pauli in 1925 for electrons, and later extended to all fermions with his spin–statistics theorem of 1940.In the case of electrons in atoms, it can be stated as follows: it is impossible for two electrons of a poly-electron atom to have the same values of the four quantum numbers: n, the principal quantum number; ℓ, the azimuthal quantum number; mℓ, the magnetic quantum number; and ms, the spin quantum number. For example, if two electrons reside in the same orbital, then their n, ℓ, and mℓ values are the same; therefore their ms must be different, and thus the electrons must have opposite half-integer spin projections of 1/2 and −1/2.Particles with an integer spin, or bosons, are not subject to the Pauli exclusion principle: any number of identical bosons can occupy the same quantum state, as with, for instance, photons produced by a laser or atoms in a Bose–Einstein condensate.A more rigorous statement is that, concerning the exchange of two identical particles, the total (many-particle) wave function is antisymmetric for fermions, and symmetric for bosons. This means that if the space and spin coordinates of two identical particles are interchanged, then the total wave function changes its sign for fermions and does not change for bosons.If two fermions were in the same state (for example the same orbital with the same spin in the same atom), interchanging them would change nothing and the total wave function would be unchanged. The only way the total wave function can both change sign as required for fermions and also remain unchanged is that this function must be zero everywhere, which means that the state cannot exist. This reasoning does not apply to bosons because the sign does not change.Build big factory, cool.

_childDocuments_.review: Factorio is the quintessential logistics and automation game. You start by doing some mining to get enough iron, copper, and stone to make machines to mine for you. Then you smelt the resources so it can be turned into other useful machines like transport belts and "inserters" (robot arms that move items both in and out of machines) and now you can automatically move ore from your mining machines to your smelting machines. Then you scale all this way up, most often with some of your previous work being in the way of where you want to do something now, so you make some "spaghetti" to make it work, and it's beautiful.Factorio is a bit like Minecraft in that one can spend a lot of time just doing fun things because one finds them fun. Like optimizing a build or making use of the "logic gates" the game has to build a computer in game...And now for something completely different:Digital goods doesn't need sales, there are no physical space restrictions that mean having one item listed restricts another from being shown. Sales on digital goods are manipulating you into buying stuff you don't actually need or wanted that much because you see that shiny "-50%" instead of thinking through if you  want the game at that price. And if they can have sales on their products that means they overpriced them to begin with (just like Steam recommends: "Are you pricing with future promotions in mind?" (from the Pricing page on the Partner pages for Steam)).It takes cognitive effort to recognize how much big corporations are trying to manipulate us, and it's very easy to forget it at times. Stay vigilant, and only buy games you actually want to play at the  you see, not the percentage off.

_childDocuments_.review: My first time writing a review - but this game is worth it.  Absolutely love this game.  If you like building games, planning, problem solving, resource collection and management researching tech trees, and spending long periods of time obsessing over minor details, then you should definitely buy this game.  It is fantastic value for money. If you're not already, this game will likely instil some masochistic tendencies.  Constantly wanting to refine and re-engineer things, or build a new, bigger, better base that maximises resource gathering and production will undoubtedly lead a player to experience bouts of immense frustration, probably long bouts of social isolation, and perhaps even despair.  Such feelings are dwarfed however by the immense gratification in watching your automated systems get you to places you want to get to, build the things you want to build, and go to war with the bugs. There is a lot to learn in Factorio.  The tutorial gets you orientated enough to get you started, and to intuit other parts of game as your factory grows.  The tips function, is also very useful. There are other aspects of the game that are well worth looking up for help/tips online too (especially in how to make your automation more efficient).  The game, although challenging at times, is always immensely fun to play.  There is an enormous amount of depth to the game, and there is lots of replayability because there is a lot of scope for creativity.  Learning new systems, implementing new tips, foments a desire to constantly improve, recreate, rebuild, and expand the factory.  Also recommend the co-op mode.  Game is even funner shared - especially when engaging the biters.  Though unrelated to the gameplay, I have noticed in recent weeks that driving through industrial towns I have developed a proclivity to take photos of factories, conveyer belts, smoke stacks, large power lines, and silos and share them with the friend I have played this game with.  Prior to playing, I did not have this tendency.  In turn, he sends me videos of smelting processes, and robotic arms being used in factories; something new for him too.  So a word of warning, because it is so fun, this game does things to your brain.  You may get funny looks from friends or family when you enthusiastically share your newfound fetish for automation, or where you needlessly over-engineer various things around the house to maximise efficiency, or be uncharacteristically intolerant towards an obviously inefficient process observed in everyday life, and/or make it known that while your friends have developed green thumbs during these pandemic months, you have developed a compulsion to uproot every tree and concrete everything in sight.  Hope you enjoy it!

_childDocuments_.review: This game is just incredible. It is at its core a "casual" game, I believe. To me it is very relaxing to play. But, it is a game of automation and puzzle solving where you get to decide how easy to make it for yourself. You can do so many things with the tools that are available, and those things make the game easier to play, but at the same time the game works well regardless of how many of these things you do.To gets far more meta than Minecraft, although I wish the ambiance was better. It would be great if there were a variety of beautiful biomes in this game, like Minecraft. The planet you are on is pretty drab, so the damage you do to it in your attempt to launch the rocket is not as jarring as it would be if there were lush, flowery fields being destroyed by acid clouds or oil spills.Still, it is one of my all-time favorite games ever. It is both engaging and relaxing and I could see myself playing this game 15 years from now.

_childDocuments_.review: Factorio is one of my favorite games. It's also one of the most polished and fun alphas I've ever seen. And it even have mods that make it crazier already!I played it a lot outside of Steam, so don't be fooled. :)Factorio is a Sandbox-Survival game where you play someone who crash-landed on an alien planet inhabited by a hostile race of primitive aliens that seem to, instead of going to the gym, simply breathe Carbon-Dioxide to get pumped up and angry before trying to steamroll your base.What? Read on.Initially, you'll have to gather resources manually in order to craft the tools you need for basic automation and basic research. You'll then start automating resource extraction, smelting, refining, production and research as you try to steer clear of the angry aliens. Eventually, you'll have automated trains loading up cargo on automated stations that's being automatically filled by automated extractors and smelteries. And as it reaches your main base, that train will be unloaded by automated cargo drones that will help you sort out your huge storage system and bring you whatever you need directly to your inventory.And let's not forget about the construction bots that will automatically build blueprints you design. It's a simple, great feature that will make you do the "Feel Good Man" face every time you build a new Solar Array.Of course, you're free to play, build and progress as you wish. Make your designs as compact as you can or as large as you want. Design storage and sorting systems, optimized smelting/refining/research/transport designs, or just load up your tank and troll the wildlife.(Personally when I first started playing with trains I completely forgot about the rest of the game and simply tried to weaponize them for a few hours.)The game features a World Generator that really lets you fine-tune your experience. You can go for a game with passive and weak enemies filled with resources, or a scarce planet filled with angry mobs. You can even make the map really narrow, only generating terrain horizontally (Linear Factorio), which is a different gamemode by itself.The default settings are balanced and challenging enough for most people, so you can quickly jump in on a new game. And even though the game has a learning curve and can be rather complex at times, the tutorial will get you covered, for the most part.There's also a mechanic in the game called Pollution. As I mentioned before, Pollution will make aliens (more) agressive, and they will get stronger and evolve faster as you pollute more and more. This can make you adapt, plan and upgrade your factories for lower footprint or higher production in order to progress faster before the aliens spread everywhere.This is a really interesting feature that keeps you on your toes, and makes it so having radar stations and keeping an eye at enemies is actually useful, and sometimes necessary.The game is already really fun as is, and features multiplayer. Hopefully it will get further expanded and polished. If you enjoy crafting, survival, automation (especially Minecraft Tech mods), you'll definitely have a blast with Factorio!

_childDocuments_.review: This is a warning: Just bypass this game if you value your time and your mind. In this game, you build stuff to build other stuff that builds other stuff until you launch a rocket. Seems simple enough. Well, grab your notepad, because this game will suck away your time. The highlight for me was after 309 hrs, multiple game restarts I was able to finally launch my first rocket at 80 hours into my last game. That was 80 hours just to create a simple main bus with a plethora of spaghetti just to launch 1 rocket. Big deal you might think, and what a dummy, 80 hours? Well, put into context, their are brilliant players who spend 100's/1000's of hours on their mega-bases that can launch 100's of rockets per minute. The factories are huge! I found myself constantly learning something new and a better way to do things, so I would start over and incorporate my new knowledge. Even after launching a rocket, the game is not "done" you can continue and research everything in the tech tree, you can expand and build your own mega-base, you can hunt biters, whatever. This game has replayability - I mean you have to apply all that knowledge you gathered from sending off your first rocket to make a better more effeciant base the next time, right?! At $30.00, and not even launched yet, this game is a steal. This is one of the most challenging and rewarding games I have ever played (I started with Pong back in the day). Do yourself a favor and give the demo a try, although I don't think it will do the full version justice. BEST GAME EVER!!!PS. Wife hates it, so you know it's the bomb!
