_childDocuments_.review: Exceptional puzzle game that follows in the footsteps of others by blocking your progress until you've overcome simple puzzles, then uses your newfound understanding to pose more and more ruthless puzzles as you progress.The trailer is representative of the game. You navigate 2d platforms, pushing boxes, throwing switches and the like, then head for the exit. Many of the puzzle involve dropping out to the real world to alter the route for your stickman. There are a few timing based challenges which are thankfully very simple to execute; nothing more stressful than jumping and pressing a button - a good thing for those not seeking a game that requires practice and precision.You will spend the majority of your time planning, visualising all or part of the solution and conducting a little experimentation, until you figure out what should happen and in what order to get out of the room and on your way with whatever gadget you need next. Later on, you'll need to incorporate new mechanics and relearn where all the boundaries lie.Puzzle games can suffer from tutorial syndrome, but The Pedestrian never comes close to this. Every time I learnt a new mechanic, the game followed up with half a dozen unique puzzles that went beyond the scope of the dedicated tutorial areas, and each incorporated things from previous areas - just how you want it.All tolled, the game should take around 4 hours give or take a bit, but that all depends on how much time you spend solving problems. A better indication might be that there are roughly 50 puzzles that can halt up your progress.This was a Kickstarter game; there's been plenty of eyes on it. I can't speak to the update history but found no bugs as of summer '21. There isn't anything to do after finishing, no bonus levels or extras, no achievements to track down or alternative routes to exploit, and the credits read like graffiti on a passing freight train. Hold LMB to skip... you're welcome.On the plus side, it appears the game's levels were also crowd-sourced, which is a great choice and explains why the difficulty curve was so smooth and the challenges so varied. I'm guessing here, but I'd wager the backers were offered a level design tool and the producer then cherry-picked from submitted levels to build out the game.If you like puzzle games, this is a must own. It'll give you a good challenge and make you feel justifiably smart.
_childDocuments_.name: The Pedestrian

_childDocuments_.review: At the end, all I wanted was more.  Not in a bad way, not by any means, this game was so great that I wish there was more.  The Pedestrian is a puzzle-platformer where you can rearrange and connect street signs to solve puzzles and get to the next area.  Set in many gorgeous, loving-rendered 3D environments with a great soundtrack, you’re left wanting to continue exploring and solving.  The game effortlessly teaches you its mechanics, with its puzzles so cleverly designed you’ll get the rush of success every time you manage to solve one.  I want to say more, but I feel that the game is best described by playing it yourself.  As with many puzzle games, to say any more about it would be a disservice to what they have created.  Some may believe the game is too short given its cost, as many of the other reviews point out.  If you strongly believe that a game’s worth is dependent on its hours per dollar you get out of it, then this game would probably only interest you during a sale.  I used to be that way as well, and for some games, that’s a fine metric to measure by.  However, if you’re willing to put that aside, I promise you that the game is worth every dollar, if not in time, then in everything else it has to offer.
_childDocuments_.name: The Pedestrian

_childDocuments_.review: The Pedestrian is a very good example of a well-made puzzle game. I'm not going to spoil, but nearly all the mechanics make logical sense, and they're designed in a way that makes them recognizable in an instant. Said mechanics seem simple at first glance, but as the game progresses they're mixed with old mechanics and played with in such a way that it never feels like you're doing the same solution (keep an eye out for those big doors you see in the trailers!). The final mechanic the game shows you is purely awesome. I wish there were more puzzles like that, but again, maybe less was more.I like the world building, too. Each area has a feel to it, and despite the fact that you technically only see one person (you!) the world is still alive, from the hustle and bustle of the city to the eeriness of the subways to the sleepiness of the alleys. If you keep your eyes peeled, there's even some measurable activity. For example, in one part, there's a burrito that has a bite taken out of it each time you return. When you're about to finally leave that part, the burrito is gone, with only some beans left for proof.Would I recommend buying it for full price? Not really, no. My playtime was just short of 3 hours, and considering I carried over my save from the demo, the game SHOULD be about 3 and a half hours long. I got it for 60% off ($8.00 USD). As with anything on Steam, just snag it when it's on sale. If you feel generous, though, there's nothing wrong with paying the whole 20 bucks (USD).
_childDocuments_.name: The Pedestrian

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely incredible. The Pedestrian combines old flash puzzle platformers with The Witness. It's one of the few games that I found myself completely unable to pull myself away from until it was over. I did happen to encounter one soft-lock, but it was quickly fixed by saving & quitting and loading back in.
_childDocuments_.name: The Pedestrian

_childDocuments_.review: The Pedestrian is a fantastic puzzle game with light platforming elements. I absolutely love the aesthetic and theme of the game. The Pedestrian perfectly implements the concept of a stick figure roaming through the world via street signs and digital screens. The music fits the journey well, but it eventually fades out instead of looping. This is a minor complaint, but it is especially noticeable during more difficult puzzles where the awkward silence becomes oddly distracting. The best part of the game is of course the puzzles which are creative and satisfying to complete. The puzzles are constantly adding new mechanics to test your problem solving skills. My only regret is that I finished the game hungry for more.
_childDocuments_.name: The Pedestrian

_childDocuments_.review: My all-time favorite puzzle games off the top of my head are Talos Principle, The Witness, Antichamber, Gorogoa, and of course Portal 2. And I am not exaggerating when I say The Pedestrian is up there with all of them in my book.The puzzles were inventive and always had me guessing, The difficulty was a literal perfect balance across the board. Got frustrated a couple times, but it was never the games fault. Visually it was always fun to look at and the perspective was so unique and charming. The actual quality of the 3D graphics at points could have been better i guess, but it never detracted from the experience. Maybe my biggest critique is that i wish it would have lasted just a bit longer. Maybe 30 min to 1 hour longer as (no spoilers) the ending was satisfying, but I could have definitely spent just a little more time in the world and been just as happy.As it stands though, it's difficult to think of negatives with this one. I'm so impressed. I saw the trailer for this game and was sold, but I still did not expect something this wonderful. Highly recommended, honestly a must-play imo, for anybody who likes platformers and puzzle games.
_childDocuments_.name: The Pedestrian

_childDocuments_.review: Quick Description:-The Pedestrian is a puzzle platformer w/ a gorgeous visual style, a very fun story that will make you smile, and a very unique premise.  This is a game I've been excited to play for quite some time.  However, I was a little disappointed w/ the actual puzzles themselves, which makes up a majority of the game.  The puzzles actually remind me of the puzzles from Cocoon quite a bit.  Most of the puzzles felt either too easy or tedious due to the long list of steps that they required.  I also found the paint mechanic confusing at times, b/c I only really learned the rules through lots of trial and error (do the objects go back to original location or do I go back to start or both?).  At the end of the day, this is such a charming and like-able game, but I'd recommend picking it up on a hefty sale.Consensus:-Middle of the Road Game (Tier 4 and makes up 25% of my reviews).  I really want to give this game a higher score, but I just didn't have nearly as much fun during my 6 hr playthrough as I was expecting.  I think the game length is fine (4-6 hrs for most fans of the genre), but I realize that others may expect far more content from a game w/ a $20 price tag.  I do think that this game may be a good choice for those looking for a more beginner friendly logic puzzle game as this game is far more forgiving than most of the other games in this genre.  Wait for a 50-75% sale and see for yourself if The Pedestrian is a worthy addition to your library.
_childDocuments_.name: The Pedestrian

_childDocuments_.review: The Pedestrian is quite the mind-bending, but very fun adventure! The core mechanics of the game sort of remind me of the old flash game Continuity, but The Pedestrian builds off of that and expands that idea to a world of fun and unique possibilities. Every area you explore comes with new mechanics, beautiful scenery, and a true sense of immersion that really makes you feel like you're apart of the adventure.Now with everything I love about the game I will say the performance has had some hiccups all throughout. As a life long Mac user I've come to expect there to be small issues here and there, but I've found this game to run really badly on higher graphics settings, which I find a bit unusual because the specs of my Mac more than meet the recommended requirements. I suspect this is likely an issue of the game's optimization and if the devs were to consider looking into this I think it would be very beneficial, because I would LOVE to experience this game in its intended higher definition.Overall though this is a really good game. If you enjoy games like The Witness or the aforementioned Continuity then you will feel right at home here!

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a complete delight on all fronts. It is a shining example of "more than a sum of it's parts".The puzzles themselves are pretty good honestly. Quite a few made me scratch my head wondering how they could be solved. Every area introduces a new mechanic and a new way of interacting with the environments which is always neat. The game is also a bit open ended in that you can choose which puzzles to solve in an area. My one problem with the puzzles is that the difficulty curve is a pretty wild graph where certain puzzles will make your ears blow smoke but the next one you would breeze through.The visuals are absolutely gorgeous. The world around the signs is vibrant, colorful and beautifully realised. You definitely feel like you're moving through the various places in the game rather than simply being limited to the signs and papers and stickers. The very pause menu itself is made of actual CRT TV screens placed discreetly in various places. You even control the motion of real world objects in a limited fashion which affects the puzzles themselves which gives me the fuzzies every time I trigger it.The music is fantastic and a neat mix of jazz and a melodious orchestral arrangement and is a very gentle accompaniment to the experienceMy one hang-up would be the the length compared to the price. I bought it at the launch discount and felt like I got every penny's worth out of it but it may not be as attractive at full price. Nevertheless, I highly recommend you pick this up if only to appreciate a really well made polished, fantastic little romp
_childDocuments_.name: The Pedestrian

_childDocuments_.review: This is an amazing game! the puzzles are not easy, but not so hard that i ever had to look up a guide to finish the game. The environments in the game look awesome, and the music is beautiful. I plan on buying the soundtrack when it gets released for sure. You may see the other reviews that say that the music "cuts out" or something similar. The music fades out if you are taking a while to finish a puzzle. I think that having any song going the entire time you were struggling with a puzzle would get annoying or frustrating fairly quickly. The music does come back when you finish a puzzle and move to another area though, so it feels a bit like an additional reward on top of making progress. The music waits for you :)Overall I'd say that this game is worth every one of the $20 it's listed for - zero bugs, great puzzles, and great polish.The only thing I could really ask for is a level select after the game is over, since I'd like to look at some of the environments again  , but you can play through the game again after you're done.

_childDocuments_.review: I typically don’t consider myself a big fan of puzzle games. The time it takes for me to go from “considering a solution” to “I hate everything” is far too short. However, when I see something innovative and visually appealing, it always manages to catch my interest. Recently, Superliminal (which will come to Steam eventually) impressed me with its perspective based puzzle design. Now let’s see if The Pedestrian attempts to do the same with puzzles based on signs.Abbreviated Review: The Pedestrian, at its core, isn’t a particularly crazy puzzle game when considering the puzzles alone. What you solve usually involves the typical affair of moving the stick figure protagonist to areas using bouncing platforms, switches, and engaging doorways. While this expands a bit in the latter half, I don’t think anyone will be too overwhelmed by the methods and tools you use throughout the game.What makes The Pedestrian so interesting is how it all goes together. Your character is the generic blocky-limbed round-headed human-proxy that is used in signs around the world. The same guy you see breakdancing on the “wet floor” signs. This simple protagonist was chosen because the puzzles you’ll be solving are on various types of signs.The signage you’ll be traversing is spread across numerous environments and is reflective of each location. You’ll be working on cork boards and whiteboards in offices, street signs along the roads, chalkboards outside restaurants, and so on. You transition between them using cables that you connect via an overview perspective – connecting doors and ladders that you can enter when in the ‘platforming’ view. It’s also often possible to move signs to both allow these connections and make use of other puzzle elements.The most compelling parts of The Pedestrian are the backgrounds. That’s a strange thing to say, but after just watching the trailer, it was quickly apparent how spectacular they were. The juxtaposition of playing the game on simplistic 2D signs with rich detailed 3D backgrounds and foregrounds moving around you makes the whole game seem more alive. It may have just been a serviceable puzzle game focused only on the signs, but the environments add a layer to the aesthetic and even the gameplay.It doesn’t take long for the puzzle-solving to expand beyond the boundaries of the signs alone. Soon after starting, there will connections between switches on the signs and parts of the environment. It starts simply with the opening of a garage door or moving an elevator but eventually progresses into driving a train and moving pieces of machinery. While this is mostly used just for cool visual effects, it’s also integrated into some puzzles by unlocking areas to allow you to move signs for different solutions. However, the visual component on its own is still very rewarding.The way that the camera moves you between the puzzle sections has you floating through these well-crafted background environments in cinematic ways. It gives you a charming view of these interconnected areas designed mostly just for their appealing looks. I always found myself excited just to see what new location I’d end up seeing as I progressed through the game. It became just as much as part of the experience as the puzzles. The Pedestrian drops you into the gameplay without much explanation of why you are this stick figure or what you’re trying to accomplish in the end. It drops some hints here and there, but the ambiguity is present throughout the game – up until the very end. This did make the ending more interesting than it probably would have been had it been heavily foreshadowed.  However, it might not have worked out if the game wasn't so entertaining.One thing that did ultimately stand out was that you’re manipulating a strange little modified Gameboy-looking device. When you first encounter it, it just seems like another part of the background/foreground, but after some time it becomes apparent that you’re adding pieces to it with each central puzzle area. This item plays a much bigger role toward the end of the game, which is both unique and surprising in its design.Toward the end of The Pedestrian, the difficulty ramps up quite a bit. The introduction of some mechanics like the ‘green paint’ that prevents triggers on a sign from resetting when you change connections adds a notable level of complexity to the puzzle solving. This is a common element of any extended puzzle game, but for some reason, it took me a while to wrap my head around how the ‘green paint’ really worked. My limited puzzle game patience made this part of the game much tougher to complete.  I might have given up if not for the great music.I don’t know what it is about the easy listening jazz-styled music, but I loved it. It reminded me a bit of Sim City and, of course, that’s a big win in my book. The only disappointing part was that it would always fade out in the middle of puzzle sections. It was so disappointing and made those frustrating parts even more frustrating. I didn’t enjoy having only the relatively silent background noise to keep me company while I contemplated how puzzles. I'm fully capable of turning off the music if I get tired of it.The Pedestrian was an enjoyable experience from start to finish across it’s five or so hours. The puzzles were mostly competent without being too easy. Yet when they were tough, they didn’t let up. The quality of the backgrounds, the transitions through them, and their interactivity made every piece of the environment feel distinct and well designed. Even the music is wonderful (when it’s playing). If you are remotely a fan of puzzle games (I’m talking even Portal here), you owe it to yourself to try The Pedestrian. It’s practically a master class on what makes this genre enjoyable.

_childDocuments_.review: Lives up to expectations, a nice puzzle experience.The game has you thinking outside of Euclidean rules in a way I haven't seen before: Generally, you have a bunch of rooms (laid out as 2D segments) and you need to figure out how to logically connect them to reach the finish. Generally, you can only use paths once, so efficiency and clever placement is essential. The game twists its own rules constantly, sometimes letting you reuse links, sometimes letting you go through a portal that you can't return to, etc. The game does start out slowly (I was worried it was going to be too simplistic for a while), but the tutorial sections get to the real meat soon enough -- there were plenty of challenging puzzles that required some careful planning (although never to the point where I was extremely mentally taxed).To build upon that last point of having a relaxing experience, the scenery is quite beautiful. You move around from street signs, chalk boards, street lights, notices, etc, all with the backdrop of a city (subway, warehouse, main street, rooftops, cafes, etc etc). Nothing is ever chasing you, you can just relax while you ponder the puzzles at hand. Each puzzle moves the background smoothly from one area to the next (except a few times you activate a subway and end up in a new area, which is fine). The game also augments the experience with a calming cafe jazz soundtrack, mixed with cityscape white noise.I do wish the game had a "reset" button for each puzzle, and that you could rebind your own keys, but these gripes were never too frustrating.All in all, a great experience, and a worthy addition to your library if you're a puzzle fan.

There are some doors you can't seem to access first time round, so maybe there's more replay value there. We'll see. Definitely worth your time, but maybe wait for a sale to be worth your money.

_childDocuments_.review: 2020’s Game of The Year probably pissed quite a few people off. The Last of Us 2’s overall reception could be described, at best, as all over the place. You have people like me who praised its level and sound design while also thinking it’s story could have used another draft, but you also have people who will bite their fingers off in frustration calling it “the w0rst gam evr” despite the fact they’ve never played the f*cking thing. Granted I do share in their frustration as there are plenty of other games that deserved the award far more, one of which is “The Pedestrian.” Which I assume will be my game of the year at least until I can afford a PC that can run Half Life Alyx.The Pedestrian oozes charm from top to bottom. The game is stylish without ever losing its depth, its mechanics are polished to a mear shine, and its puzzles are so well made that it gave me flashbacks to my first playthrough of Portal all those years ago. The whole concept of controlling one of those bathroom people across the Manhattan area via signposts is so ingenious that I’m surprised this hasn’t become a genre on its own.  Every location the player visits is obscured just enough to prod their imagination at what the world beyond the stop sign has to offer. From construction sites, to small coffee shops, and subway terminals the places you go to feel lived in. As stated before the games mechanics are polished to a near shine, granted it's not like there was a lot to polish but simplicity is key. Jumping feels weighty, objects are easy to distinguish, and objectives are almost always clear as soon as they enter frame. I especially love how the game sometimes will introduce location based mechanics like its a retro Mario platformer (I know this idea is an obvious one, but I felt it deserved recognition). The art style may not be original (as it is just ripping off sign posts) but it was effective in adding to the sense of whimsy the game was going for. The story is non existent but this kinda works. I hate to say it but I would have had a very hard time relating to the dark silhouette of a platforming crossing person but hey… that's just me.In summary, though I don’t see the Pedestrian as a 10/10 masterpiece I do see it as the most deserving for game of the year. Its gameplay, level design, and pacing all work together to provide a seamless experience, and the creativity of its puzzles make the gameplay loop endlessly entertaining. But the fact that it is a “storyless puzzle game” does limit its replay value somewhat. Still, definitely worth the price of admission.
_childDocuments_.name: The Pedestrian

_childDocuments_.review: The puzzles in this game are well balanced and fun: solving each one feels like an accomplishment. I played a lot of this game in small chunks, carefully pulling apart a couple levels, solving them, and then stopping for a bit. Even so, coming back to this game after not playing for a while was easy: overall goals and mechanics are clearly spelled out and easy to return to, even if individual puzzles are tough.It's all well-balanced so it feels tough without feeling annoying, and each new mechanic is interesting and fundamentally changes how you solve levels in fun ways. Even up to the very end The Pedestrian found ways to surprise me. And, it just looks really good.

_childDocuments_.review: Great game! The mechanics keep building on themselves and often the right answer is a move you thought would be illegal - and that feels great - feeling like there is nothing stopping you. Your solution might seem out of the box but the game itself doesn't hide the answer - doesn't make you feel like you are stupid. Devs also made a great effort to teach you as you are playing.  I personally had a feeling of urgency but there is still so much detail in the world itself that you see passing by in between the puzzles. I was looking to play this game for a long time and the anticipation didn't leave me disappointed. Enviroments are intersting but the core interactive parts feel the best. The only think I would change is the death animation - it feels too organic. Based on the achievements, I'm in the middle of the game - I don't sense any big story so far, but it might reveal itself in the end. Even if it doesn't - it's a good game.
_childDocuments_.name: The Pedestrian

_childDocuments_.review: This is a fantastic puzzle platformer with a really cool style. Even though there isn't necessarily a story, there is a certain playfulness to the progression of the level that carries you through the game and makes you want to keep playing. The puzzles are neither too easy nor too hard. The best thing about them is that, because the puzzle resets when you switch a path that you already used, you have to think about the solution before you execute it. This prevents you from brute forcing the puzzles, or at least it makes it a lot harder. Each puzzle is also fairly short, so I did not feel like an undo feature was really necessary. Lastly, yeah, this is a 3-4h game that costs $20 and doesn't have much replay value. That is pretty much the only reason some people have given it negative reviews. I think that's a bit unfair, but if that's gonna bother you, then you should know in advance.

_childDocuments_.review: A novel concept that blends 2D platforming and jigsaw-like puzzles, almost always maintaining a comfortably balanced difficulty throughout. Clever level design, stunning visuals, and a beautiful score make for a great experience, though one you might wish lasted just a bit longer given its price. A must-play for fans of the puzzle genre, even if it means waiting for a sale first.  is a side-scrolling puzzle game in which you navigate a sprawling metropolis by way of hanging public signs in order to find components to rebuild a mysterious machine. The levels are this mix of platforming and jigsaw puzzles, as you need to rearrange and form connections between nearby signs in order to move across them and reach your goal. New elements are gradually added to the puzzles as you progress, like new objects to collect and use within the signs, signs locked in place to limit how you can connect to them, and ways to make connections inside the signs affect the outside world.  , including getting all achievements since they're just unlocked through normal gameplay. I'm really glad I played this one, but as someone who didn't grab it until it went on sale, I can understand if the short length makes it hard to justify the full $20 price tag. If you're on the fence, give the demo a try and pick it up next time it goes on sale, because it's definitely worth your time to play.  From visuals to music to level design, this game certainly put the "art" in developer Skookum Arts' name, and I hope that this won't be the last time we see their artistry on display.

_childDocuments_.review: I don't have a strong opinion on puzzle games. It's not my favorite genre, but I definitely don't dislike a good puzzle, and this game did not disappoint me. Each area in the game had unique and clever ways to add to the challenge of the puzzles set before you, and they felt satisfying to finally get right. Nearing the end of the game, the puzzles got more challenging, but I found myself learning how the game can trick you into thinking the puzzle is solved one way when you're supposed to think outside the box, which is definitely vital in a good puzzle game.The visuals of this game is also very stunning. I loved that each area of the game had unique scenery and the signs were different colors and materials. I also liked how the signs we journeyed through never felt out of place in their environments. They all seemed as if they could exist where they hung, even if I would question what these signs would say if there wasn't a 2D world in them.Lastly, I found the ending to be a surprising one. The last puzzle was something I never expected to see happen, and I wish there was more to that section, but it was good while it lasted. I'm interested in what the ending represents, but I like to keep my reviews spoiler-free, and I'm glad I went into this without knowing what the ending had in store.
_childDocuments_.name: The Pedestrian

_childDocuments_.review: Rarely do I find myself smiling so much when playing a game as I did with The Pedestrian. This is simply a masterclass in game design. The whole game introduces new mechanics that expand upon what you previously learned, and it continues to surprise you throughout. If you're interested in unique gaming experiences, or are a fan of the Portal games, do yourself the service of playing this game. 100% worth it, even on full price. I can't wait to see what these developers do next.

The game starts off pretty simple and gets progressively harder but not too much to give you a headache. The puzzles were relatively enjoyable and was just the right difficulty imo. I was actually surprised by the amount of variety in the unique puzzle mechanics. It made the game so much more enjoyable and fun to play. What I really loved about this game is how it takes you through these different environments. The transitions were really smooth and helped to enhance the experience. The music was soothing and the ambient noises were just the right touch. My favorite part was definitely the ending. It took me a good minute to realize how the puzzle was incorporated - I had a moment of amazement and awe. The abstract ending was a nice touch too.Overall, this game is definitely worth the money and you can really see the love the devs put into this game.

_childDocuments_.review: I really enjoyed this game, the 3D environment to a drawn on platformer is really good. I like how each puzzle progressed and gave good times to take a break after a set. It is fairly short, which I wasn't expecting, but at the same time it wasn't so long I got bored of it. I wouldn't get this at MSRP, but it is worth it on sale, which on steam happens a lot.There is one issue I had that should be noted **SPOILERS** At the end of the game the puzzle turns first person 3D, which I was not expecting and really let me enjoy how pretty the 3D world is. But it made me very motion sick for a couple hours once I finished the game. That is one thing to look out for if you get motion sick. The rest of the game was just fine for me.I recommend this game. If you get motion sick, maybe don't do the last puzzle, but all in it was a lot of fun.

All in all, The Pedestrian is a friendly little diversion and, generally speaking, a good time.

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely brilliant and ingenious puzzle-logic game, quite likely the best I have experienced yet! _childDocuments_.review: Great puzzle game. The only real complaints would be the same as everyone else's, the music stops sometimes, and the game is far too shorty and it leaves you wanting more. A lot more. At four hours I'd say the experience is worth twenty bucks, but that doesn't stop you from wanting more.As for the puzzles: None get too insane. Most people could probably complete this game without using any kind of guide. There might be more trial and error depending on the person, though. There were a few frustrating parts where screwing up meant you had to do some monotonous stuff to get back to where you were in a particular puzzle, but there wasn't much of that.My final thoughts are it's a cool puzzle game with good presentation and fun platforming mechanics. I think there are probably some secrets in the game I never saw, but I don't particularly care to replay puzzles I've done before to try to find them if they do exist (though I got all 10 achievements, so there may not be any secrets, but I swear I went through some rooms with exits that I never took, but maybe the game wrapped back at some point and I didn't realize it).I will say this, if you want more puzzles in a relaxing experience you should try The Witness, it's much longer. That is all.
_childDocuments_.name: The Pedestrian

_childDocuments_.review: Fun and creative puzzles. I feared it would be too simplistic in a way where you'd only have to advance linearly, just walk a straightforward way as you simply reorder panels that obviously fit like a jigsaw puzzle, but it wasn't the case. You have to think it through, using the simple yet deep and engaging mechanics in a clever way as they are introduced at a proper pace. The content is unfortunately on the short side, with a completion time of 4~6 hours on average. The difficulty is moderate, it's not a complete breeze, but you probably won't get stuck. For reference, another puzzle game that got good popularity, Baba Is You, was harder after about halfway in.That doesn't stop this game from being a pleasant and enjoyable experience though, it is nice to watch the world as you interact with it, and the puzzles were good enough to feel satisfying when completed, requiring some ingenuity nonetheless. I always have respect for a good puzzler that can bring that out of its players.The price is a tiny bit high for the play time, but for a puzzle game, it's still a somewhat decent ammount of content. I'd personally value the game between $10~15, but i don't feel like it wasn't worth it. The game is polished enough to make up for what it lacks.
_childDocuments_.name: The Pedestrian

_childDocuments_.review: So, first off: I really liked this game! This sounds pretty contrary to my negative review, but I'll try to explain why I gave this rating.The Pedestrian is a calm and magical puzzler. It's not too hard, but a few levels will be tricky. Throughout the game, there seems to be a story going on in the back, but it keeps you guessing as to what it's all about. There are a few neat little twists at the end there, and the finale gave me a really nice, melancholic feeling.So far so good.My problem is that, having played games like The Witness and others, this title leaves a lot of opportunities to be a REALLY good game untouched.The look of it suggests that there would be some original interactions with the 3D environment, but the game doesn't give you that connection until the very last level. For 90% of the game, you stay in your 2D format, which really is a bummer because in itself, those puzzles have been done to death in simple, free browser games for the past 20 years. There is no twist to it.I enjoyed the little story it tells, open ended as it is. But the creators also missed the opportunity to put some more hints to what is going on in the environment. Games like Portal are full of non-essential hidden corners filled with unexpected storytelling. You stumble across them and they explain the world you're in a little better. With The Pedestrian, I kept looking for secrets in the background, alternative routes or easter eggs to interact with, but didn't find any.And finally, the price. As I write this review, it's "down" to about 16 bucks. I got it during summer sale for 14 I think. It's still too much for a 3-4 hour game that doesn't really offer anything new.I strongly suggest trying out the free demo (which they might've added recently, I didn't see it myself before buying it) to get an idea of whether or not this game is enough for you, for its price. Sadly, it's not going to be much more than what you're about to see. Then buy the game during a sale if you're still convinced you want it.If it had a stronger soundtrack, if there were more new ideas about how to combine those 2D and 3D environments, if there was a stronger story or worldbuilding, or if at least the puzzles themselves were really interesting, I'd have probably given this a good review. But with all that lacking, it's simply not worth the money.
_childDocuments_.name: The Pedestrian

_childDocuments_.review: A short, simple, and sweet puzzle-platformer.  The game has you moving signs around in order to progress through each level.  Although I found the puzzles to be relatively easy until the very end, it was still an enjoyable experience seeing the detailed backgrounds and the nostalgia of long car rides imagining someone running next to the car.  Overall, I would recommend it if you're looking for a game to beat in a single night.
_childDocuments_.name: The Pedestrian

_childDocuments_.review: A lukewarm recommendation when this gets a heavy price cut. The Pedestrian starts out very positive with it's wonderful presentation. I have never seen a puzzle quite like this but I will admit I always had this sort of concept in mind when I was a child during car rides. It's wonderfully executed. The thing with this game is that it's incredibly short, and in that short period of time you're presented with delicious visuals but easily-solved puzzles, and it stays like that for half the game. However, during the last third of the game a switch is pulled in the level designer's brains and you're stuck in a dark environment for a long time where you're presented with a new mechanic involving paint that I could not for the life of me understand. I got stuck at almost every single puzzle involving this mechanic and had to resort to a guide on YouTube. It's explained to you very briefly in a tutorial that doesn't really give you a proper explanation and immediately you're thrust into puzzles that require a good grasp of the mechanic. At the very end of the game you're presented with an incredibly tedious final puzzle where you're required to support your 2D stick figure in a 3D space and even though that sounds exciting like it excited me when I first saw the puzzle, I was honestly genuinely relieved for it to end when I solved it. So in summary: - The presentation is literally style over substance. Only at the last 15 minutes does it involve the environment with the puzzle. - The first 60% of the game is dirt easy, while the last 40% ramps up with a difficulty spike that I could not overcome. - This game is depending on how fast you solve puzzles 2 to 4.5 hours long, so a huge chunk of the value is lost for me.

name: Manifold Garden
detailed_description: Join Our Discord About the Game Manifold Garden is a game that reimagines physics and space. Rediscover gravity and explore a beautiful Escher-esque world of impossible architecture. Geometry repeats infinitely in every direction, and falling down leads you back to where you started. Manipulate gravity to change your perspective and see the world in new ways. Master the rules of the universe and restore a barren world with vegetation and life. An expansive and visually striking world filled with mind-bending puzzles. Manipulate gravity to gain new perspectives and walk on any visible surface. Explore expansive architectural structures that repeat infinitely. Capture striking and beautiful images with Photo Mode. Manifold Garden has been nominated for several awards, including “Best Debut” from the Game Developers Choice Awards and BAFTA Game Awards. It was selected as one of the New Yorker’s best games of 2019.

_childDocuments_.review: Just finished playing this unique, challenging and amazing game! Having played a lot of puzzle and exploration games, I was intrigued to play Manifold Garden as well and wasn't disappointed! The gameplay is totally unique (as far as I'm aware) in that you have to constantly change your frame of reference to move around without falling off a surface. This can take a bit of getting used to but is a huge part of the enjoyment of the game. Comparisons with the artwork of Escher are well deserved and and understanding of working in 3D is key to navigating the many areas of Manifold Garden. The artwork itself is superb - I can't imagine how mind-bending it would've been to create this game, trying to keep track of all the level design as objects in Manifold Garden don't behave in way you might be used to. For example, a solid block when viewed from one side, becomes an infinite hallway when viewed from the opposite side! Speaking of infinity, it took me almost until the end of the game to be entirely comfortable with 'jumping off' into the abyss in order to land on the upper side of a building! I'm sure that's just me, though :-)The puzzles themselves are challenging and use the world to great effect, especially those involving water. It took me a while to find my rhythm with this game as it wasn't always clear what you had to do or where you had to go. However, after a couple of levels, I could navigate more easily and the time it was taking to complete each area and transition to the next became less and less. The only real downside was perhaps the first level where you encounter the Tetris pieces - I wasted a lot of time here as the game seemed to want me to line up all the blocks in the correct order to power them up but this wasn't the case at all. In that area and I think the one after, there were a couple of 'red herrings' that I spent a bit of time on as well. But, that's a very small gripe considering you have, quite literally, an infinite space in which to move around! All in all, a terrific and engaging game quite unlike any I've played before. The ending graphics are worth the effort to get there and there is an excellent, minimalist soundtrack to accompany you on your journey into infinite Escher-space.
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: Manifold Garden is a fantastic game. The first hour or so feels like a game that's an excuse for an interesting game mechanic - and the game may well have started out that way - but as you get into it, it starts to tell a subtle story, one that is very much open to the interpretation of the player. This game is highly metaphysical and speaks to you more philosophically than literally. And so a warning: if you like your stories explicit and straightforward, this is not the game for you; but I thought it was brilliant.
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: Outstanding non-Euclidean Bauhaus-like visuals combined with beautiful cosmic/eerie ambient music.Solving puzzles by exploring fractal/continous world is a great experience. Few puzzles where meh (especially near the end- I hate obfuscation as a puzzle) but majority of them were enjoyable.Adequate lenght of gameplay i.e. few hours, given its form.Highly recommended! Especially for fans of The Witness or Portal.
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: This is a very good puzzle game, the environments are amazing, the puzzles have a nice difficulty level where you are not probably going to spend a lot of time stuck in one, but you are going to spend enough time figuring them out to feel satisfied when you do. Best puzzle game i have played since portal 2 (then again, only  puzzle games i have played were the portal series and antichamber, so oh well) The ending is very pretty too. As for the story, nothing is told explicitly, but you can see some stuff trough the game that gives you somewhat of an idea about perhaps why you are doing what you are doing. Definitively not a deep story tough, but the gameplay and especially the environments are the stars of the show. The audio design is very good, when you pass near stuff at high speed you hear a woosh sound that lasts as long as it feels like it should, and the music is good too. In terms of bugs, in almost 8 hours of gameplay, i only experienced two bugs: a very minor one that was of the fun variety rather than gamebreaking or annoying variety, and a minor bug in a certain environment towards the end that was a bit bad but nothing major. They certainly did not hinder my enjoyment of the game. The game also ran perfectly, never dipped below 60fps with max graphics and vsync, which would be expected with my setup, but sadly, if understandably, in many indie games isnt. I hope we get another game like this in the future.
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: I don't really have words to describe how beautiful and mind-blowing this game is. The puzzles are nice, but they weren't the main attraction in the time spent playing. The world itself was. It was amazing to experience the way the space revolves around the player, but at the same time effuses magnificence and an infinity that is mesmerising, haunting and breathtaking. More, please!
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: Wow, this certainly is a unique experience. While the puzzles in this game aren't very difficult the general concept behind shifting gravity is very intriguing and the art style and general presentation is phenomenal. Even though the game is a bit on the shorter side (taking about 4 hours on my first playthrough) i still think it is worth the price.
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: Simply the best puzzle game I have played in my entire life. The whole gravity and map looping system is just perfect, the puzzles are challenging but not to the point of smashing your head against the wall, and the  aesthetics are just stunning. I've been a total fan of M.C Escher since I was a kid, so this game appeals tremendously to my sensibility. And those fractal, kaleidoscopic level endings are gorgeous, and everything is merged with a fabulous musical score. Unforgivable experience !
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: I remember following the game since 2015 and finally hearing it release in 2019. The price was a bit steep when it first launched and I was a bit hesitant on purchasing the game because of its short nature (around 3 hours for me). But now that the game is often on sale for less than a meal, I would highly recommend this game!The game is gorgeous, has some pretty thought provoking puzzles, and builds on basic game mechanics. The puzzles aren't particularly difficult, but enough to make you think especially in a spatial manner. Though short, I think this game really pushes the boundaries of novelty, execution, and pushes the envelope of game mechanics. After playing this game, it really makes you think about "huh, what if we introduce this engine in this other game?" Very mind opening experience!
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: Let me start of by saying this game deserves a lot more recognition and attention than has been received. By far the most unique puzzle game of the decade, not only because of the art style, the gameplay, the music, but design and effort going into the making of this game. I am a big fan of the "Puzzle" genre and I think William Chyr did a great job keeping the player interested all the way into the end of the game. There is some mystery behind this world and what you (the player) are exactly doing. Maybe I'm thinking to much about it, but I believe there was a lot of thought into the sound and music design to go along with the unknown "narrative" of the game, perhaps it is all just open to interpretation. Gameplay is a mind warping, gravity manipulative, first person experience that keeps you so curious about the world and the solution to solving the puzzle up until the very end of the game. If I had to pick one word to describe the entirety of the game, I would say .If you have an appreciation for puzzle games and the art style of games in general. I think you will find this to be a very pleasant, euphoric like experience.9/10, Will more than likely play it again.
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: A short, sweet, beautiful experience, with an interesting postgame/alternate playthrough for an extra challenge.The visuals in this game were really what drew me in and kept me in, they're absolutely incredible throughout. One thing I noticed and appreciated immensely was the distinction between the environment and puzzle-related objects. The environment is kept very flat, with very desaturated colors and very gradual shifts in hue that help to convey the immense scale of everything you see. Objects you need to interact with to progress are generally very brightly colored and pop out from the scenery, which feels like a necessity given the scale. A comparison keeps sticking in my mind wanting to call this game's environments a combination of the monolithic, monotone greys of NaissanceE and the highlights of Antichamber put together with a twist.Mechanically I want to compare Manifold Garden to Portal. They give you the means to break a rule we're accustomed to, and expect you to learn new ways to exploit that rule being broken. In Portal's case, we skip straight past B on our way from A to C. In Manifold Garden, you get to fall down to go up. Or whichever way you need, if you try hard enough. It forces you to approach moving around the environment in a new way that's incredibly interesting, and they've managed to make it surprisingly intuitive. Definitely recommended for a unique and at times psychedelic adventure.
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

Thats just me though, it was a really great game and i loved the puzzles i was just really put on edge by the God cubes and the black substance. I'd recommend anyone to play it. I don't know why i found it scary, maybe it was just the fear of the unknown.

Everything revolves around you switching the direction of gravity, with infinitely repeating patterns and portals.It is a very easy and very short game. The puzzles are trivial. _childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: You are trapped in a tesseract where space folds in on itself. The cage you must escape is small yet infinitely vast. You will feel insignificant as you plummet through the endless void of your tiny prison.The puzzles aren't that difficult, but the experience is completely mind-bending.Some people may be turned off by how basic the graphics look, but I can assure you that the world of Manifold Garden is exceedingly beautiful.It is very short, but if you are a fan of first person puzzle games (Portal, Anti-chamber, The Talos Principle, The Witness, Obduction/Myst, Quern) then this is one you don't want to miss.
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: Any game that can scratch my Ender's Game itch by making me think in zero-G is a win. Not that Manifold Garden is zero-G, but you'll need to redefine your definition of what is "down."If you want to see my first impressions as they happened, watch my video above. Manifold Garden lets you walk on walls and change the direction of gravity. The few blocks in the world will maintain their sense of down, but they also won't be affected again until their down is your down. Makes sense? Explaining occasionally non-Euclidean geometry is like explaining calculus: you'll need to experience it for yourself. And, if you're in doubt, try falling. The first time I fell I thought I made a horrible mistake, but the world loops on itself, and you can change your direction while falling.The soundtrack serves its purpose, but pass on buying it. And you can see how beautiful the game is for yourself. I'm looking forward to finishing Manifold Garden and having it break my brain a few more times.
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: This review will look at the game through the lens of its Steam Achievements, and so is primarily targeted at those that strive for 100% completion, or otherwise enjoy achievement hunting. Are there any particular barriers of note, whether engaging challenge or boring grind? Are the achievements designed well enough to elevate the game-play experience? Or are some poorly designed enough that you'll be forced to choose between a miserable slog or stopping just shy of 100%? If this all sounds like pointless nonsense to you: you are probably objectively correct, and there's plenty of other reviews for you. For those of you that embrace the madness like me, I hope this will be helpful!Nearly every achievement in this game is linked to standard progression, and so is 'free' just from beating the game.  The exceptions involve figuring out the purpose of a mysterious room you may well have come across in your play-through, and doing a second run of the game where you discover hidden 'back routes' through the game.  If you enjoyed the game and want more, these are great incentives to make new discoveries and challenge yourself to new puzzles.  If not, as one would expect from a puzzle-game, guides are available, so there wouldn't be much impediment to checking them off.As a minor technical disclaimer, there is also an achievement for getting all others that some people have reported having issues with.  In my case, closing out of the game then relaunching after getting all others caused it to trigger without further issue.If the concept of this review was relevant to you -- whether it was helpful, or if it seemed like it could be helpful but ultimately wasn't -- feedback is very much welcomed!

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of the most fun puzzle games I have ever done. Not only does it completely change how you go about solving the puzzle. _childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: With a brillant use of a non-euclidean engine, Manifold Garden takes us to a beautiful realm where gravity can be bent in six different ways to advance in rather dazzling puzzles (I must admit that I was a little bit dizzy at some point relatively close to the end). Gameplay is challenging and authentic. Graphics are astonishing in a way that promotes patterns. I would certainly not hesitate to recommend this kind of experience to anyone who is looking for some unearthly physics puzzles.
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: Would I recommend this game? Yeah, sure, if you're craving a physics 3D puzzle game. A lot of people compare this game to Antichamber for some reason, but the similarities end at the line that there is a lot of white architecture and the puzzles are about putting cubes in certain places. Most of the time, I found the puzzles that Manifold Garden put forth were extremely simple, or about turning yourself around until you see a door you missed somewhere.There are certain puzzles that shine in Manifold Garden, but it felt like they were running out of ideas very quickly, since there's only one action the player can actually do, flipping gravity. The game didn't introduce enough external concepts (there are only three, really: water, dual-direction blocks, and the really annoying large blocks) to keep it interesting all the way through, and I say this when the game is only 6 hours long.I think the game does what it set out to do correctly, which is be a very pretty game with puzzles in it, but it doesn't really bring it home the way I was hoping it to.tl;dr You'll probably like this game if you like any other 3D puzzler, but I wouldn't expect it to live up the "Overwhelmingly Positive" rating.
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: This is a genuinely absorbing puzzle game! Visually it's like walking around inside an architectural sketch, which is exactly as calming as it sounds. The difficulty is not very high; you never have to keep more than one or two moves in your brain at once. Solutions require you to re-think what you are seeing, but only slightly. Therefore you get a nice balance of feeling smart without actually needing to be extremely smart. Plus, it's tremendous fun to walk off an edge and come into the environment from a different direction, or to frivolously change the gravity so you can fall down hallways rather than walking along them.
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: This game is one of the best puzzle games I've played in the last 5 years. It reminds me heavily of Anti-Chamber yet stands on its own. Gorgeous visuals, seamless non-euclidean geometry combined with creative reuse of classic puzzle mechanics, as well as mechanics unique to the fractal landscape. My only problem is I wish it were longer but its all made up for in the raw creativity and beauty of this game. Highly recommended.
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: Amazing puzzle game. Looks beautiful and is confusing at times. If you have never played a gravity changing puzzle game before, you may find a challenge in this game, however, overall I do not think this game was that difficult. I only got stuck on a couple of puzzles. However, it was very enjoyable and I would definitely recommend it.
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: Holy S*** I am normally really hesitant to spend money on any game, but I love the concept of infinity and shifting gravity so i bought it. I just beat the game and it took 5ish hours. Its hard to describe the feeling of watching the credits after beating the game, but its amazing. First you have to assume that you are real and just spent a long time solving puzzles and going through doors in infinite rooms and finally can escape. The feeling is equal to the feeling of reading the ending of a good book. I don't cry, but I do get sad whenever I finish a book. I love the character and will miss them and its sad knowing that they will be gone and not exist if nobody reads about them, and the story ends and dies when you put the book down after the last page. Its a mostly sad feeling, I felt that as I watched the credits/end screen visuals roll. I wished i hadn't beaten the game so quickly, I wish I was still playing. At the end the screen fades to white as you fall into infinity and its sad. It is the sweet release from puzzles, but being locked into an infinity of falling and looking at weird visuals. I'm not gonna tell you to get the game, but if you have 20$ to spend it is definitely worth considering.
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

Brain needs fixing. Brain says it's okay and let it happen. I'm now on ceiling. Dog looks worried. Brain took talking power away to solve cube. We worship the cube. we are the cube. The cube is all seeing. It knows. Don't let it see you. It sees you, you go bye bye.
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic style, brilliant soundtrack, fun puzzles. Got stuck for 10 minutes maybe 2 times trying to solve a puzzle, but once I solved it solution was actually quite simple. Otherwise, game has nice pace, amazing locations and it's really beautiful. You want to stare at the distance all the time cuz it's very fascinating.
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: I've only played for a brief moment, but I am already feeling woefully unmotivated to open the game up again. The gravity mechanics were intriguing, but I was put off by how "Antichamber" the game is, whereas the steam page left me more with an impression of exploring an MC Escher-esque world with trippy perspective and visual puzzles. There isn't really much reason to keep going, other than to keep going. For being such a unique game, it's interesting how...stale it feels. It's like a boring gravity level from Mario stuffed with boring puzzles from Portal. If you loved antichamber and want more, I recommend this game. If you're just a casual player looking for an interesting puzzle game to get into, I think I would try something else.
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: It's quite beautiful and intricate. Comparison to Portal and Antichamber seems inevitable, but Manifold Garden's aesthetics and puzzles very much set it apart as its own unique experience. After you play through it there's an optional non-linear second run with its own more complex, obscure, and difficult puzzles. Great if you love trippy visuals!Edit: last night after finishing the game my dreams were just gameplay of new areas that do not exist 😔
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: A wonderfully fun puzzle game, it makes great use of the simplicity of its core mechanic with puzzles that reach a level of difficulty that leaves you satisfied when you figure them out. In an ingenious way, in order to complement the puzzle solving, the art and level design too has a simplistic look to it, that is not to take away from the fact it is still very much capable of being beautiful and mesmerizing at the same time. Lastly the score is wonderful, building an atmosphere that fits just right and leaves you fully immersed .
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: A fantastic game, from start to finish. manifold garden focuses everything on aesthetics and atmosphere, and it succeeds great. the puzzles are quite easy, only at the last the game brings out more complex puzzles than the ones we face during the previous areas, but don't expect all that complexity here, rather manifold garden shows its "true teeth" through a very specific achievement, which i can say is quite tricky without a guide: 3/4 of my game time was used to wander all over the place looking for a way. .. alternating between eurika moments and "I could never get there". I would still recommend trying it without using a guide, but I can understand if some people aren't fans in getting lost for hours (I used it in a particularly stubborn puzzle with the ball).ultimately this is a beautiful visual experience, somewhat less fulfilling on the puzzle side (without pursuing the achievement mentioned above) but overall it's a pretty enjoyable experience.However, it's a fairly short game for 20 euros, so make your own considerations
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: I absolutely adore this game. Not only is it a unique puzzle game, but it doubles as an actual art piece you navigate and roam through. There is a certain feeling in this game that I have not gotten anywhere else being the isolation and the imposing nature of the infinite space you occupy, however with a strange warmth and coziness that stops it from making you feel unnerved or alone. The music also adds to this effect, with some tracks being quickly added to my playlist.This is an experience that I believe everyone should try at some time.
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: Ok, after just 10-20 minutes of several gameplay sessions my two thoughts always end up being "it's so dull and aimless". It's like an open-world walking sim that, yes, has the slightly faster running function, but it barely alleviates that problem. Nothing is more frustrating in first person games than artificially limited maneuverability, especially when you lack the means of either jumping over tiny curbs or doing 180° gravity flips, if the ceiling is low enough, which forces you to run all the way to the end of the room, step on a wall, then step on the ceiling and run the same distance back.The looped locations are kinda cool at first, but the effect very quickly wears off and leaves you in a wide-open area, exploring the world by switching between the planes and doing fetch quests. It legit feels like a chore.Too cubic, too abstract and too aimless. The game tries to impress you with large scope geometry, but it lacks diffused lighting or textures to make it pop or leave a lasting impression.For the closest comparison, Antichamber is basically a blank canvas with soundscape as invisible ink and, occasionally pretentious, tutorial strips doubling as your silent narrator, upon which you can infer a meaning for your journey (it also has a hub that lets you quickly go back to unexplored dead-ends that you missed or left unresolved, which this game could use), whereas in here it feels like you're a speck of dust, lost in a drafty filing cabinet.I bought it at 50% discount and if I could refund the game - I would, but it's past 14 days so I might go back to it later to justify the purchase and try to push through to the bitter-sweet (and, I fear, pointless) conclusion of this thinly veiled walking simulator.
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: I have been following and looking forward to Manifold Garden for some time, and while it's certainly technically very impressive, with a great aesthetic and creative design, most of the puzzles have either been astoundingly easy, or have been basic platforming challenges (or even platforming gimmicks).Overall I think it might be worth picking this up if you're really into the look of the game, but I think that if you're looking for a really good puzzle game you should look elsewhere.
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: As an upfront disclaimer, I received this game from free as a giveaway code from the Dev that I won while watching a streamer playing, this in no way affects the following review, but felt it a good idea to state.This was an experience unlike any other game I've ever played. The visuals have a distinct style and the mind-bending aspects of how they are implemented are engaging enough that at times i had to remind myself to actually progress to the next puzzle instead of just looking around and interacting with the angles.The puzzles are fun and I feel are a good balance between challenge and entertainment. Some I would grasp intuitively and others would leave me scratching my head until something would finally click to have it make sense. The extra dimentionality of them can really throw you for a loop.I applaud the Devs, this was a fun ride!
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: Just epic! Beautiful aesthetics, sound design and great gameplay.Only cons I can come up with are missing toggle run (felt like I was holding shift for the majority of the game), and the first one of the sliding block levels: I think the area was too large and there was too much going on in the area to see the "big picture" without lots of effort. The subsequent block puzzles were much better designed in my opinion.I see complaints about the length, but while it was short, it was also cheap. Perfect bang for your buck in my opinion

_childDocuments_.review: Stunning visuals and great sound design but the game was mostly boring so I will try to explain why.I have a problem with description the developers posted on the store page because it is misleading in my humble opinion,Here are some things that I find a bit misleading- An expansive and visually striking world filled with mind-bending puzzles.- Explore expansive architectural structures that repeat infinitely.Mind-bending puzzles might be interpreted in many ways but after more than a decade of playing all kind of puzzlers I can interpret in only one way really and that is that the puzzles are not casual. Well most of the puzzles are casual and they are more orientation based and pixel hunting based. In closed spaces you will at least see right away what you have to do, in open spaces you will just have to detect where all the cubes,doors and switches are. There are only few types of puzzles and after you figure out one type you will figure out the rest. So the puzzles are mostly boring and repetitive. Mind blowing, no chance.Explore expansive architectural structures that repeat infinitely. I did and you know what I found, nothing. Maybe I didn't look hard enough but the exploration and reward aspect is non-existent.So these 2 factors are misleading for the reasons a stated above. I am tempted to say that this is borderline false advertising, just my opinion of course.Don't get me wrong. it is not a bad game if you are looking for a game that has stunning art style and great sound design with some lite puzzle solving than this game might be your cup of tea.I can't recommend this game because I got almost nothing from it. _childDocuments_.review: A stunning and unique puzzle game that makes you use your brain! The graphics look amazing, a piece of art. The mechanics are a lot of fun but you can get disorientated quickly, which is part of the fun. I totally lost my bearings on the stairs and buildings, which reminded me a lof of the Relativity lithograph print by M. C. Escher. So the video is basically me trying to figure out where I am, where I'm supposed to go and.... did I already visit that place? Or am I going in circles? Either way, great fun! If you love puzzles, get this game!The Good:+ Amazing graphics and mechanics+ Great atmospheric sounds+ Well designed puzzles that really make you use your brain while being completely disorientated.+ Feels like a trip while you're in a loopThe Bad:- I don't know how, but one of the puzzle blocks got placed mid air and it just kept falling. I must have done something wrong.The game can be completed in about 5 to 6 hours, depending on your puzzle skills.A must play if you like games like Portal and Antichamber.15 minutes of gameplay so you get a good impression of the game:

_childDocuments_.review: Manifold Garden takes games as artistic works to a new level, and demonstrates exactly what makes this medium unique. The puzzle difficulty is perfect throughout the entire game, never getting frustratingly difficult, not too easy, and follows a reasonable curve as you progress. There are tons of secrets to discover. Every new area is a work of art that makes you stop and take it in. The reward for solving any puzzle, was more puzzle. No handouts or empty rewards, which makes figuring out each level (and especially the secrets) incredibly satisfying.One note, there was one puzzle in the achievement path that required knowledge either from a previous playthrough, or from later in the sequence, and therefore I have no idea how you are meant to know what to do, besides guessing. Other people have apparently had this issue too, I solved it by using the photo mode to see the puzzle (since its hidden behind an opaque wall). Other than that one instance, all puzzles seem fair and don't have fake solutions. Incredibly impressive.
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: If M. C. Escher was alive today and working on computer games, this is the game he would have made. The looping level geometry, the use of portals to create impossible spatial relationships, and the stylised, edge-lined graphics are like an Escher piece brought to life. The sound design, level design, and art are excellent, bordering on awe-inspiring in a few places - literally raising goosebumps.How hard you will find this game will depend entirely on how good your sense of direction and spatial reasoning is. If you struggle to keep track of where things are in relation to you, you're going to have a hard time getting through this. Otherwise, some of the puzzles do take a bit of lateral thought, but usually fall into place pretty quickly.While the game does rely on colour cues for the puzzles, there are options to allow the colourblind to change the colours used for each of the 6 gravity directions, with a variety of presets and the ability to adjust them.If you are sensitive to flashing lights, you want to avoid the ending - the rest of the game is largely fine, but the ending involves sequences you may want to skip.
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: A beautiful fractal puzzle game that has you exploring set pieces infinitely repeated upon themselves. Within these minimalist renderings you can explore by moving to any adjacent surface, find interactables, and try to figure out how to proceed to the next area - normally just by finding a switch, placing objects in set locations, or redirecting a flow of liquid to another location.This game really blew me away with the sheer scale of its infinite spaces. It oozes atmosphere from its surreal liminal sandboxes, and the puzzles are just as fascinating as the solutions are devilish creating some mind blowing physics interactions that make use of the infinitely tessellating space.While there is no real story to speak of the abstract goings on throughout each level are well worth the price of admission as you're treated to some wonderful visuals from start to finish, and for the avid puzzler every stage has an alternative solution which gives a great excuse to replay such a unique and interesting game. High marks for creativity, a truly unique experience, and clever but simple mechanics that draw on the fractal world making you think in entirely new ways.

_childDocuments_.review: This game be like "yo antichamber players, I heard you like puzzles with cubes, so we got you a world of infinitely repeating non-euclidean cube structures, so you can look at your infinite spans of cubes, while you solve puzzles with your cubes"In all seriousness, this game is almost therapeutic, so far its been a fairly simple puzzle game at a slower pace, that messes with a non-euclidean world but I think its most standout feature, is the sound design. _childDocuments_.review: This is the case, when Steam’s binary “positive” or “negative” is not enough. So I’ll write what I like and don’t like about this game and finish with who I think will like this game.First: this , yes. But I think it lacks on theside. Specifically, the gameplay largely consists of two parts:1) Gravity puzzles in enclosed space - those are nice, but mostly quite simple and take comparatively little time of the game.2) Navigating open tiling/looping spaces - this takes the majority of the first completion play time and this part is quite boring: you walk and fall trying to look for where to go next. There are some puzzle elements in some of these places, but for the most part there is little logic here: you just explore until you luck out finding what to do next.I watched a video with alternative routes - they require more thinking, probably too much, but even they contain some obscure passages, which require you to navigate and navigate until you luck out to find them. For example: one structure repeats dozens of times, but one of the copies is not exact, but contains a hidden passage around the corner, so it is not visible from afar among repetitions and you’d have to navigate through every repetition to find it and there is no indication that there even is a secret passage somewhere nearby. I find this kind of obscurity bad, contrary to “The Witness” where everything is in plain sight and exploration is about you learning to see it as a player, not looking for obscure hidden passages.itself (which, again, you have to do a lot) is in many parts unpleasant: you see all the intricate geometry on the screenshots? - it sure looks beautiful, but it makes the navigation unnecessarily tedious. You can’t jump, so every single “increase in height” (for which a small jump would be enough) except stairs requires you to switch gravity at least twice. I say “unnecessarily” as it doesn’t make puzzles/exploration more difficult, it just makes it longer and more awkward.My playthrough would certainly be less tedious if I knew that , you can switch gravity while falling (if other surface is close enough), unlike some other games with similar gravity switching mechanic, but the game never teaches you this (I learned it from watching YouTube after completion).The game seems to prefer visuals over gameplay, another aspect of which (besides intricate geometry) is the “black matter”, which has zero gameplay element: it’s just visuals, which obstruct your view and make exploration unnecessarily less pleasant (yet again). Black matter is not that bad, but there was zero reasons to have it in the game: it doesn’t influence game mechanics in any way and the game doesn’t have any story, which could potentially justify it.I had a few “aha” moments while playing, but those were sparse (2-3 in the entire ~9.8 hour playthrough).I completed Antichamber (although some years ago), which looks much worse, but as far as I remember was more interesting to explore and had more puzzles, so I enjoyed it much more overall.If you are looking for a gorgeous chill game, with some puzzles, but mostly about navigating tiling spaces and you don’t mind this navigation being somewhat tedious - grab the game.If you are looking for a “big brain” game (which requires you to think and improve as a player), it’s probably not for you.

_childDocuments_.review: If  had us thinking with portals, then William Chyr Studio’s  has us thinking with gravity. This game is based around the mechanic of manipulating gravity to solve puzzles in levels with impossible geometric designs. If you’ve ever been fascinated by Oscar Reutersvärd’s optical illusionary designs (e.g., Penrose stairs and triangle), or wondered what it’d be like to explore the surreal world in M.C. Escher’s various works (i.e., , , ), then  may just be up your alley.The seemingly infinite environments in , drawn in ligne claire style, are simply mesmerizing to behold. The looping design of the set pieces, which play a role in the puzzles’ solutions, add to the mysteriousness and wonder of the game. This visual delight, along with the dizzying gravity manipulation puzzles, make  a unique puzzle-solving experience. With each change in gravity and direction, the same level can look completely different with new physical challenges to overcome. This game really deserved an award for level design.It’s difficult to describe how much thought went into designing the game’s detailed set pieces and levels, which are essentially the puzzles. Without spoiling too much, I can reveal that  can be completed by following the prescribed path, which in itself is already a mind-bending joy, as well as via a secret path. The secret path involves not using a key object, forcing you to traverse the same rooms or levels in a different way, and to think beyond the immediate space you occupy. It’s so complicated that I needed a video walkthrough (not a written one!) to guide me. I would not have figured it out by myself. is a puzzle-centric game aimed at gamers who solve puzzles for the pure challenge and/or enjoyment of it, so don’t expect a narrative to keep the proceedings going. Aside from lacking a story to hook casual gamers in, the game’s gameplay, sadly, also makes it less accessible to most people. Gamers who struggle with spatial orientation will find this game challenging; those who tend to get dizzy from playing games presented in first-person view will likely feel ill from the changing perspectives during gravity manipulation. Increasing the FOV and turning off gravity-changing animation (toggling from S-Curve to Instant) alleviated nausea for me, but it may not work for everyone.Although  is a niche game, it is one that is unique, extremely well done and very appealing visually and in terms of gameplay. There is sophistication in its simplicity, and elegance in its beguiling, complex level/puzzle designs. While it may lack a story, let alone some humour and tension, to appeal to more casual puzzle gamers, I think those who love solving puzzles will find  extremely entertaining and challenging.
