_childDocuments_.review: Coolest game ever! Every puzzle is a fractal that contains itself. The sound design is amazing and perfectly parallels the visually stunning graphics in every way. The primary atmosphere that resonates throughout the game's entirety is one of surprising simplicity yet mind-bending complexity, and it is created fantastically by allowing the player to traverse an infinite space of geometry that bends into itself. Puzzles are as simple or as complex as how you think about them, which is what I think creates an amazing gameplay experience. It also introduces wonderful intuitive clarity to the theoretical situation where you meet yourself in the real world, allowing you to realize that actually no paradox would be created if there is only one version of you.

_childDocuments_.review: Among all of the other reviews for this game, you will see a plethora of words expressing its absolution in presentation: stunning, gorgeous, mind-bending. Those qualities cannot be overstated. The puzzles are simple, but the laws of the Garden continually obscure their nature.Once you get into a rhythm, you can easily speed-run, but I caution you against it. _childDocuments_.review: A masterpiece. If you're a fan of first-person puzzle games, this is a must play. opened the door to the genre,  enriched it, but  distills the formula to its beautiful, raw fundamentals. _childDocuments_.review: There's an inherent distance between how architecture is molded in real life and in video games. The idea behind architecture is creating forms from establishments in a pre-defined space. Those forms are walls that make a room, textures that wrap pillars, and shapes that elucidate the inner and outer space. From that, you start picking out the more specific forms, a bedroom, a basement, a walkway, a garden, and together, they become whole, an establishment formed by physics, space, and of course, blueprints.But, video games don't need to follow those rules. In a 3D software, we can create anything, a human model with no arms and cheekbones spiral from eye sockets, a fluffy 8-legged dog, or whatever Cruelty Squad is. So, what if we do the same with digital architecture? The idea behind Manifold Garden is simple: what happens when architecture is no longer bound by the limitations of real life? The concept that one would call "impossible architecture" is depicted in a very thoughtful and shockingly non-abstract way in this game, in which falling down a building will loop you back to it on a Y-axis direction, as if you are alone in a non-physics-defined playground. Manifold Garden is full of architecture that is impossible to be sketched like that: mirrored stairs, identical floating towers marching towards or apart from each other, humongous halls with nothing but glass. Because of this, puzzles in this game are often just as unorthodox as how the game itself looks: you need to grab a cube above you but there's no stair or any path that leads to it, but because the building loops itself when you leave it, you can land right on the place with the cube just by jumping down.This is nothing short of genius, especially when Manifold Garden starts putting you in the exterior space around objects that make you look like an insignificant lone matter. The puzzles don't progressively get more challenging; they become more involving with how the world evolves. It began with simple cubes and yellow-ish flat walls, to harsh color shades, gravity, and probable constructions that resemble mother nature elements. The deeper you dig into this place, the more unsettling you might feel, because architecture is meant to create order, and anything that defines order will bear an uncanny vibe to it.In short, Manifold Garden is a brilliant and somewhat terrifying example of how digital construct can dwarf our perception towards the nature of reality.

_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: Elohim must be so proud if his robot got out of The Talos Principle, passed The Turing Test, played the games Hue and 140, got high and fell into the Portal, eventually landed within Manifold Garden. Many times, the sense of space-time doesn’t really make sense. It feels like 2010 movie Inception. 3D is just relative, different perspectives, door or window, would lead you to different places.Those stairs reminds me of Chand Baori step well in India and Maurits Cornelis Escher’s artworks, probably where William Chyr got his inspirations from. My nerdy self told me that it’s similar to El Naschie’s theory of Cantorian space-time, then I realized that it’s actually conformal cyclic cosmology where your ending is a new beginning (Homecoming and The Game is not Enough trophies). Anyway, this piece is one of a kind artwork that you just got to try it. However, this game is not designed for those who have megalophobia or acrophobia. You should feel comfortable falling from the top of skyscrapers into the abyss, in order to get to the next gate, and it’s unavoidable. The Game is not Enough trophy is so hard to figure out by oneself without YouTube. Who would've ever thought to play the game this way?
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: Its a beautiful relatively short game but its an experience I can recommend to anybody with a cursory knowledge of video games. _childDocuments_.review: This game is pretty special, and I mean that in a kind of existential-perspective way.The puzzles are pretty challenging, and the transitions between levels are pretty awesome. The game looks and plays pretty beautifully, and I admit I only looked up other peoples' solutions a few times because I got stuck; not because a puzzle is broken, it's really that I lacked imagination to get the solution on my own, which is saying something about the depth of the gameplay. There are some places where I feel like geometry is actually *too big*, and some of what you are meant to do isn't obvious (it's very easy to get lost if you aren't focused), but I believe that the game is 1000% worth your time.Definitely play this game even if you aren't into puzzle games or games where time-space-warping is a main feature. Even if you don't make it all the way through, I think the visual exposure is kind of it's own reward.

_childDocuments_.review: 11 out of 25 acievements. I really wanted to love this game... but alas I have vertigo and I have to aknoledge I will never finish this game. I tried. I tried when it first came out on Steam and now I just have to aknoledge that for as much as I love puzzles and for as much as I apreciate what Mr. Chyr has done, this game just isn't for those of us with vertigo.I love the concept, I love the puzzles, the environment... _childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: Manifold Garden is an incredible piece of work, a genuine work of art. This game gave me a few headaches, but there's no denying its genius. A platformer exploring and articulating the boundless, dizzying reaches of infinity, while at the same time disguising itself as a simple block-stacking puzzle. The navigation in this game is as much of a challenge as solving these incredibly difficult yet immensely satisfying gravity brainteasers. I won't lie, Manifold Garden had me stumped several times, but I steadfastly refused to look up a guide and with more patience than I knew I had, the game opened itself up to me. No spoilers here, but be warned: the giant tetris block puzzles are real killers. To be honest, I can't fault this game at all, you should play it as soon as you can.
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: Manifold Garden is a stunning achievement. I don't really know where to begin here. I can't even begin to comprehend how this game was made. It's the kind of experience that really pushes the boundaries on what we can do in the medium of games. You can call it a puzzle game if you want, but this really is a unity of light and sound and interactivity and I felt like a 10 year old kid experiencing the joy of games again. It's not really difficult as far as games go and I suppose I would have liked a little more challenge in some areas to really push my understanding of the rules here, because the ceiling on what you can do in a game like this seems endless. That being said, it never once felt frustrating and I hope that will lead to more players sticking with it and enjoying it so that we can popularize this kind of creativity. Just a huge round of applause to everyone who made this a reality, you all really made something beautiful here.

_childDocuments_.review: Eh.Completed it in 3.4 hours, most of the puzzles were barely even puzzles, more like 20+ versions of the first few test chambers in Portal 1 where you put a cube on a button, they barely got any harder towards the end, most of the time it's just looking for the box receptacles.overall really weak, minimal puzzle design, plus a lot of leftover cubes for some puzzles, which I assume and hope are used for the 0% playthrough, otherwise bad design and may confuse players who are unsure if they should bring the spare cubes with them or not.Like what other reviews have said, the visuals are nice, but that's kind of it really.Surprised some people are claiming up to 6 hours of gameplay, lmao.One major negative thing for me is there's a number of components in the game that made me feel really uneasy and anxious, and freaked me out, due to what i think is agoraphobia;-The stupid-huge spaces, infinite voids, etc. made me uneasy. -The eerie glitchy deterioration of the world gave me anxiety.-The shockwaves that occurs when you completed an area and enabled the dark cube always freaked me out for some reason, every time. Really put me on edge.I turned the music down before i even started playing, but it was still always SO DAMN LOUD, and the soundscape in general added to the sense of unease and anxiety.On the plus side, I like how the game clearly uses realtime raytracing to render everything, presumably all done through compute shaders, the true reflections and special effects and stuff were neat.Also I'm a sucker for non-euclidean space in games, I can wrap my head around it pretty easily though, so that probably made quite a few of the puzzles easier for me.Use of world portals was surprisingly seamless, presumably due to the nature of everything being raytraced, since lighting can be cast through the worldportals. I only noticed one slightly misaligned worldportal somewhere, so I could see the transition between areas when I was close enough to the surface.All in all.. uh... yeah, neat little tech demo of the concept, but I'm never playing this again, not even for the extra achievements.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is intensely beautiful in both graphics and sound, but the gameplay doesn't do the game justice. You see, Manifold Garden leans heavily into being a puzzle game, but the puzzles are really disappointing.On a normal run, the game presents itself as fairly linear, and most of the puzzles are solved before you can even figure out what it is you have to do: You see a cube, you grab it, you see some water, you put the cube on the water to re-direct it, you grab another cube, follow the stream, see the water wheel, redirect the water into it, puzzle solved. Most of the puzzles take about as long to solve as putting all of the pieces together, with not much time required for thinking. It's really quite disappointing.Doing the 'Game Is Not Enough' route turns the game into a frustrating experience revolving around navigating infinitely looping environments, looking for portals to let you progress (four pillars, all of the passages between them loop infinitely save for one) and for cubes to let you solve the 'puzzles'. For example, near the end of the route, you have a yellow socket and a green socket in the back-ass middle of nowhere. You have to find a yellow cube, a green cube, or two yellow-green cubes to fit in there. I managed to find one yellow-green cube, and within a few minutes, dragged it across the map, through two nexus areas, to the puzzle. However, I could not find a yellow-green cube, so I resolved to get a green cube, and 'walk' it across the map using two red cubes. After some time 'walking', I reached a large staircase, which prevented me from using the 'walking' method. I ended up coming up with a way to 'walk' the green cube up using the two red cubes as well as the green-yellow cube from earlier. After forty minutes spent tediously getting the cube up the stairs, I was home free. Some fairly tight platforming and a bit more 'walking' later, I was able to progress.This took over an hour. Over an hour of lugging a cube across the map. The stairs thing was the only time I felt smart when playing the game, but it was not worth spending an hour getting the cube across the map.Overall, the game is really pretty, but the puzzles are a big let-down — the infinite looping nature of the environments starts to count against the game when exploration becomes completely nonsensical, so it's impossible to navigate the environments unless you have a guide, or you are willing to scour every corner of the map for portals. The game would have been better off as more of a walking simulator and less of a puzzle game, but as is, the frutration of the purposeful obtuseness of 'The Game is Not Enough' is enough to make me give this a negative review, because running around the nonsensically connected 'open world' looking for cubes and ways to bring them across the map is essentially the opposite of what having large, infinitely-looping areas would wncourage — in a game where you can navigate freely by changing your gravity, restricting the player by forcing them to stick to one specific orientation and forcing them to find ways to slowly drag themselves across the map in this manner is the opposite of what should be done.

_childDocuments_.review: I will start with the reason of why I played this game. I once run across videos showing various non-euclidean spaces. Those seemingly unintuitive topologies seemed fascinating to explore through, so I searched for games that employ this concept. I came across Antichamber, which was quite amazing. But this is not a review for Antichamber, so I'll just say that I was so amazed by the experience that I was thrilled when I saw this game coming up on Steam. Basically I purchased it as soon as it became available.Now for the game, it is a magnificent piece of art. A very relaxing experience with puzzles that are not frustrating or annoying to solve, yet still fun to think them through, with brilliantly made otherworldly music that enhances your immersion. It takes you away from the mundane constraints of your real-life spatial experience, and dives you into a fascinating; infinite open world of spaces folded together in all sorts of ways. The sound effects and music really heighten the feeling of exploring a transcended world. You cannot die in this game and there are no enemies. Just you and the world.As for the gameplay, the game is essentially a series of puzzle rooms. Unlike Antichamber, you don't have to bring stuff from some rooms to other rooms; instead puzzles are self-contained. Also, unlike Antichamber, this game is more linear rather than branching out to multiple paths. The main mechanic you are gonna play with and that you are introduced to from the start is rotating the world when you reach a 90 degree angle with a wall. There is a lot of gravity play, and as simple as this mechanic sounds like; the change in perspective can be sublime! There are other mechanics seen as you progress, but I won't go through them to not spoil.One note on the paragraph above, the gameplay description I gave is for the normal progression of the game. There is a (much) harder path that avoids certain parts of the game; which basically exists for a steam achievement. THAT path WILL require you to think more outside of the ..box, use stuff from other rooms, find shortcuts between rooms, and do some (fairly frustrating) actions in order to progress through it. But this is a choice for a second play-through for people who like the challenge.Final thoughts: If you liked Antichamber or Portal, you're gonna love this (well, and vice versa..). It can get trippy as well! Overall, a relaxing experience with good puzzles that also amazes your mind. I like the concept of 'growing' this space like a garden, with all the atmosphere related to that. I hope there will be more great topological puzzle games such as this one, but one can only hope :p

_childDocuments_.review: Wow what an amazingly produced game. First and foremost, this is a non-euclidean puzzle game that revolves around the perception of gravity. Due to its infinite scope, there is not a truly right direction or right way to solve puzzles. To solve puzzles within the game, you need to constantly change gravity to either get to your destination or to solve somewhat sophisticated puzzles. The floor that you currently reside on is the direction in which gravity is active. As of posting this review, I am not done with the game but will update this with the difficulty of the puzzles themselves.This game takes what portal, fez, antichamber, the witness, monument valley, switchball, and talos principle do best. The puzzles are difficult but they won't stump you like the more advanced puzzles in the witness or talos principal. With enough thought or experience within the genre of these games, you should be able to solve the puzzles. Due to the nature of the games that inspired this one, I am lead to believe that there are some hidden easter eggs within this game that I will do my best to unravel. The levels themselves are extremely spacious yet easy to traverse. If you find that an objective is far away or you just want to get a better grasp from an outside view, you can change gravity in your favor and fall where you want to go or fall infinitely.The graphics of this game are incredibly minimalistic, yet bolster an impressive fractal environment. You will see the space you occupy from all directions around you. At times it is rather disorienting and changing surfaces may cause motion sickness. Trying to purely understand the geometry that you are enveloped in is enough to give you an aneurysm. The sheer amount of thought that went into producing and creating such a design must have been insanely difficult to accomplish.Although everything so far has been great, nothing compares to the soundtrack. The sound design for Manifold Garden is impeccable! It really emphasizes the sheer vastness of the environments you are in while also driving you forward to your next destination. It doesn't scare, stress, or enforce the player to finish the game quickly. The serenity and peacefulness that it creates makes exploration seem less of a task and more curiosity.I have two major complaints about this game. If you easily get motion sickness, I would not recommend playing this game. The constant changing from surface to surface while trying to comprehend the surface you were just on is difficult to stomach. Many directions you look will be disorienting and you sometimes won't be able to tell which direction you are truly going. The next complaint is a spoiler: I give Manifold Garden a 8.5/10. An amazing puzzle game, however due to the level of motion sickness I received while playing I can't rate it more than an 8.5. I also expected much harder puzzles but this is a personal preference. I liked the difficulty of The Witness and The Talos Principle more. This game leads to more sense of quicker progression while those 2 games are geared more towards gradual satisfaction. Definitely worth the $20 ($15 on sale).
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: While  it's not the most difficult puzzle game out there, Manifold Garden is definitely one of the most interesting. With a heavy focus on environmental, physics-based puzzles, the setpieces are absolute top-notch.If you're scrolling down to read reviews, you probably already know the basics of how the game functions as an Escher-esque gravity flipping first person puzzle game, so I can get right down to the brass tacks.The game is beautiful. It's got a stark simplicity to it, with  sharp edges, straight lines, and only a few solid colors that are pleasing to the eye. It was made by a professional artist, and that shows  through. The music is likewise more ambient aside from a few swelling moments, and it's mostly to help accentuate  rather than fill in. It's rather nice, though not the most compelling soundtrack.As for t he gameplay itself,  it's very solid. There's only a few basic controls, the most important being the ability to swap gravity to pull you towards a surface that you're standing by, turning walls into floors. It's got a very well-built learning curve, easing you into each mechanic smoothly, attesting to the countless hours of playtesting Manifold Garden used in an absolute monster of a development period. Certain blocks can only be picked up when standing at specific orientations, which leads to some really interesting puzzles. The other main mechanic is that the stages are set in an infinite void, with infinite versions of the stage set in a perfect pattern, thus letting you leap off one area, drift through eternity, and fall back onto it at another. Between these two mechanics, the game turns into a delightful, if rather middling difficulty,  mind-bender. It's  also a bit short, clocking in at a bout five  hours for a standard playthrough, and some of the zones were a bit weaker than others, but for the most part if you want something interesting, are  a fan of puzzle games, and want to swear in awe every time you step outside, this is a perfect match. Would recommend.Also this might be a more personal thing, but I found the game to be scary. I'm not sure if it was intentional, but gazing into an infinite void is wholly terrifying at moments.

Overall just a disorienting movement style, but I can't offer any suggestions on improvement. Maybe a slider to help the sharp 90 degree rotation in camera angle- Some puzzles were so easy that it made them hard, at one point there is a random tree that was hard to spot and that was the entire section. _childDocuments_.review: Manifold Garden is incredible. At its core is an excellent first-person puzzle game in the same vein as Portal or Antichamber, but what puts this game on a whole other plane of existence is the breathtaking ambient soundtrack and the stunning fractal level design. There's nothing quite like the feeling of endlessly free-falling through one of this game's many towering environments as the psychedelic architecture flies by. Manifold Garden is perhaps the most unique experience I have ever had with a video game and I recommend it to anyone ready for the spectacle of a lifetime.

_childDocuments_.review: A really cool concept game, totally wicked art produced from the tiling of levels.This feels like a much more reigned in and honed Antichamber, the concept is similar but not balls to the wall and certainly more understandable. Yes most of the puzzles involve the tiling mechanic and yes there is non-euclidean geometry but it is used SPARINGLY and to an extent that you will be able to understand it without breaking out a flowchart. I applaud the game for understanding the limits of the what the average person is willing to subject themselves to with regards to spacial awareness and staying (mostly) within those boundaries. Very few times did I feel "lost" within the maze of self-referential geometry, which doesn't seem like a big feat when thinking about how every level repeats, but with 6 different gravitational axis and thus 6 perspectives in a world consisting of nothing except MC Escher inspired patterns and simple gradients, it can become a lot to handle.The puzzles are pretty weak, they are good enough to keep the game going, and around 2/3 of the way in there's a few puzzles that really explore some of the cooler mechanics. But there really isn't enough mechanics to create complex puzzles with complex solutions without completely overwhelming the player with information since the world repeating is the biggest mechanic. Remembering the spacial layout of an entire level in 3 dimensions and converting that into a solution to a puzzle is too much to ask for most people I would guess. It is a form of obfuscation which is great if you get satisfaction from exploring levels and spending a bit of time in them. I did not enjoy that aspect in this game as much. This might be due to the fact that there are no secrets to look for or any encouragement to explore, I am kind of thankful for this though. Largely, you'll be falling in one of 6 directions back to almost where you started trying to figure out what you're supposed to be doing. The most frustrating part of this game for me was that I spent just as much time finding the puzzle as solving it. I got stuck in the hub world for 20 minutes trying to figure out where to go because I didn't know that one of the doors would automatically open for me when I walked near it. There's a lot of emptiness in this game and while it adds to the beauty, it subtracts from the gameplay when you don't know what to do, and every level looks similar enough that if you backtrack you might not realize until its too late (I did this, I thought I was supposed to complete the puzzles in reverse to progress).There's also the problem that since every level is designed with tessellation in mind, there isn't an "end" or beginning.  Should you try to go back to another level or just load an old save and forget what you were trying to do or go, good luck remembering where the entrance/exit of a level is and which one is which. Thankfully, not many levels require that you bring an item from the previous level into the next, but it is possible to do so, the open-ness is really impressive.The best puzzles were the gravity blocks and the MC Escher waterfalls. They found a way to make use of the falls in really interesting ways and wish they kept on that path, they really did some advanced stuff and I loved that you could use them in like 4 different totally unrelated ways. The gravity blocks turned a tired 100 year old puzzle into something entertaining, and combining that with the falls with the tessellating levels was a perfect combo. The non euclidean aspect didn't help the puzzles as much as it did the level and artwork transitions. The only real use for the effect in gameplay was to obfuscate an objective or act as a semi-secret, or just move you to another place faster. I do appreciate that they used a small scope for this very hard to grasp element, and I think its a way larger step in the right direction than Antichamber which just vomited it all over the game.The soundtrack was not really a soundtrack but a low hum or drone with the occasional chords and heavenly organs, it just fit really well, everything sounded fantastic and it was as perfect a fit as can be for this game. Even the sound effects of you changing gravity was pitched to fit in with the soundtrack.Overall get this game for the art, the cool concept, the relaxing aesthetics and gameplay, your brain might be teased a bit too. One of the prettiest and well executed games in its genre. The best part about this puzzle game is that If you get stuck, it's probably not because you're an idiot, its more likely you just haven't explored the level enough, but that can be just as irritating. Who knows, maybe this game will help improve your spacial awareness.Update: The final achievement "The Game Is Not Enough" took me almost the length of the game, and I gave up and followed a tutorial to beat it. The challenge really amplifies all the weaknesses of this game. I could not imagine attempting to do this without a guide as there's no way you'd figure out not only what to do, but where to go also. Yes it did get a bit easier as I traversed the same areas more often and treated the non-euclidean stuff as "portals" or doors rather than what they are, but it was still very convoluted. This games biggest weakness is that is too focused on the beauty of the game and instead of having puzzles rely on your ability to understand the mechanics given to you, your ability to randomly stumble upon a secret. That said, the game itself is still pretty good, but this shows that mechanically there isn't a whole lot they could have advanced on without having the puzzle game be so unfair that it isn't fun.

_childDocuments_.review: Anyone familiar with  will likely enjoy this game, this one being less of a labyrinth and more of a dizzy dream world. This is a puzzle game that utilizes keys and gates that can only be modified under certain conditions, the conditions being gravity. You're able to freely change gravity in all 6 directions, but it won't make things any easier for you. The keys, which are colored cubes with directional arrows, can only be moved when their direction matches the gravitational pull of the world.I really enjoyed how straight forward some of the puzzles were, they sometimes fool you into thinking they're harder than they appear. However, with a little patience and thought, the puzzles will eventually come together. I also don't think the puzzles ever have a failure condition that can't be undone. The world design is both functional and artistic, like moving through a 4th dimensional maze of sorts. You can't really get lost as much as you lose track of where you were and which way is up. Falling off ledges will actually cause you to land above where you just fell, it seems foolish but it's extremely useful.Overall this was a great game to play and experience.

_childDocuments_.review: I love this game. I see it as a spiritual successor to AntiChamber. I've been waiting for this to come out since 2015 and it's been worth every second. The environments are fantastic to explore. Despite the simplicity of the gameplay, some of the puzzles can be extremely challenging, which is very rewarding when you figure out how they work. If you loved AntiChamber, you will love this.My only issue with this game is how the architectural spaces are often far larger than they need to be. It doesn't ruin the experience, and you can hold shift to run, but it can make things a little tedious at times. As a consequence of their size, there isn't always enough detail on smaller scales to prevent the environments from sometimes feeling sparse or even lonely. I strongly feel this should be addressed if a sequel (real or spiritual) to this game is ever released. Don't let that one issue stop you from playing the game if you're on the fence. _childDocuments_.review: UPDATE: After reading reviews and checking out the achievements that I missed, I found that there is a second, more-challenging way to progress through the game. Finishing these puzzles took me an additional 10.5 hours. The extra challenges felt mostly tacked on, and were more rough around the edges than the main game. I did not feel a sense of reward for beating them with the exception of a fun ball puzzle that requires you to listen carefully. The challenge route is confusing, but I must admit that it is more in the spirit of what I expected from this game, just with substantially less polish than I wanted.ORIGINAL: I enjoyed this game, but I went in expecting another Antichamber based off of the reviews. Because of this, I was a bit let down by the lack of variety in the gameplay. This is a 4-6 hour game. The game consists of a series of linear challenges that all involve infinitely repeating expansive environments with non-euclidean hallways snaking between each infinite area, whereas Antichamber trapped you in a non-euclidean maze and forces you to learn the logic and layout to find your way around.MANIFOLD GARDEN however does bring a fantastic atmosphere, cool music, and a mind-blowing ending. I was definitely impressed by the design of each puzzle and the environment it was contained in. There were a couple of times I had to play scavenger hunt to locate a door or couldn't figure out to do, and the puzzles do get a little repetitive at the very end.It's a fun experience for 4-6 hours. There is a deeper set of challenges, but they are confusing and will probably turn away most people.

_childDocuments_.review: One of the few games I like to refer to as a "wallpaper engine", where you could take a screenshot at just about any point during playtime and have a work of art on your hands. _childDocuments_.review: Manifold Garden has been compared to games like Antichamber, NaissanceE, Fez, and Portal. The comparisons are warranted, although MG is very much its own game. One could say Antichamber is more challenging, Portal is better because of this or that, etc., but it's a bit petty to judge a game in relation to other titles. Brass tacks: is Manifold Garden worth your money and time? In my opinion, yes. Absolutely.What to expect: First-person exploration and puzzle solving in recursive spaces. It's like being trapped in a box made of mirrors, except you can go through the walls of the box in every reflected direction, which creates a rather effective illusion of infinity. It's pretty darn interesting. It's also pretty darn difficult to put into words. In terms of visuals, the game looks downright beautiful, with its bizarre landscapes and floating architecture that repeats itself like atoms in a crystal lattice. Awe inspiring stuff.Length-wise, it's a short-ish experience (my first playthrough was about nine hours long), unless you're aiming to unlock every achievement without the assistance of a guide - in which case, best of luck to you. On a regular playthrough, the puzzles are rather on the easy side, but I believe this game was always meant to be more an aesthetic experience than something to rack people's brains. The music and sound design certainly contribute immensely in that direction.There really isn't a story there, at least not anything obvious, given the deeply abstract nature of the whole thing, but - all in all, it's a very interesting and unusual game. Definitely worth checking.

_childDocuments_.review: From the immediate impression, this game begs comparison to Antichamber. I would honestly say I like Manifold Garden more as a complete game. It has a similar sense of surreal non-euclidean space, but the puzzle mechanics are much better integrated into the game's core conceit. Where Antichamber, I always felt that the block puzzles were tacked-on to the non-euclidean level design and the two, while each very cool, didn't compliment each other very well. To the contrary, Manifold Garden has a very tight set of mechanics that all interact with one another in interesting and logical ways. The result is a much more cohesive package with much fewer one-off gimmicks and tricks. The visual aesthetic is clean and beautiful, the soundtrack is gorgeous minimalist music that I barely noticed at times, but at other times was hauntingly beautiful. This game conveys a sense of scale better than the vast majority of other games I've ever played, and gave me chills on a number of occasions. It also showcases some incredible architecture, using the tessellation and non-specific gravity to create bizarre and beautiful structures. The puzzles themselves were... extremely easy, *if* all you want to do is go directly from the start of the game to the end of the game (I'll get into this more later). I got through it in 5 hours on my first play-through. It never really had me stuck in one place for very long, except when I chose to explore but to be honest... I really don't mind. Every time I entered a new "outdoor" area, the sense of awe this game inspired was second to none, and between the minimalist soundtrack and visuals, I found the game very calming and meditative, never frustrating at all. A big part of this was that the game does an amazing job using increasingly complex puzzles to demonstrate the mechanics in a limited setting before using them in more complex puzzles. In this way, the game achieves the puzzle game ideal of never having to explain anything. However, the complexity of the puzzles never got to the point I *really* wanted it to. For example, I had many opportunities to smuggle puzzle components between areas, but never found I needed to-- I always had exactly what I needed in each room. I would have liked to see the game use the strange spatial mechanics to break the conventional puzzle room isolation, since those types of puzzles are my favorite (The Talos Principle and Baba is You are the best examples of this I've played).I have a specific gripe with the last level, However, something I discovered a number of times throughout the game is that there is a second game hiding beneath the surface-- I found a number of "hidden paths" throughout the game that make it possible to skip between levels in a non-linear fashion. Opening these is *much* more difficult than the main puzzles, and seems to be intended to create a challenge mode for people who grasped the mechanics intuitively or a sort of new game+. I am fully intending to go back and try again to see if I can find all the hidden secrets, and I'm hoping I'll find the challenge I'm looking for there.As much as I love what I got from this game, I think there's a *lot* more design space to be explored here in terms of puzzles. It feels like just the introduction to a game I *really* want to play. The conceit of the game gives the tools to make some really mind-bending puzzles and after that, I'm ready for it. Despite that, it's still a strong recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: In short, this is an excellent (non-combat) platform puzzler that blends visual, audio, and physics in a uniquely artistic form. My only real criticism is that it is short, took me about 5 hours to beat the game, and I'm not the best at puzzles.Features:This game uses something called "non-euclidean" geometry. That is, you can walk in a straight line, and come back to where you started, rooms can be bigger inside than outside, and a seeming infinite space is in fact finite in size. Imagine a Klein Bottle, but executed in 3 dimensions instead of the usual 2, and you are looking at the core principle in Manifold Garden's world design.This alteration on how geometry behaves is further highlighted by the architecture and design of the levels, creating M.C. Escher like scenes where you can walk on the walks and ceilings. There is a central "hub" area that literally unfolds as you lock in your completion of an area that is reminiscent of a Hyper cube or other geometry of 4th dimension (or higher) rotating along a 3d intersection with the world.The sound direction and music is top notch, reminding me a lot of 65 Days of Static's "No Man's Sky" OST with great heaving textures of sound and melodies that swell and fade as you complete levels. All of the audio effects and music match up extremely well with the visual aesthetics to create an incredibly beautiful experience while wracking your brain on the new realities of physics.The Puzzles can be broken down into a few simple mechanics:Pressing buttonschanging GravityPutting blocks into holdersRe-directing water3D sliding Tile puzzles (Manipulated by changing gravity)Navigating between objectives.These elements are brilliantly integrated into the way the world behaves to create situations where you're trying to figure out why 5 90 degree right turns produced a single 90 left turn, and just how is it that the tree right next to you is simultaneously hundreds of feet below your position.One of the nice features is that it is 100% 32:9 ultra-wide compatible. With a 2080ti and max settings I am getting about 60 FPS with a 5120x1440 display. Bumping it down to 3840x1080 I am getting about 90FPS.If you enjoyed Antichamber and Portal 1&2 this will definitely hit on the mind-warping puzzle aspect that those games featured.*below is some nit picky stuff that in no way should dissuade you from experiencing this game*I was hoping for rotational displacement and/or chirality transformation of levels as you looped around, but the spaces are "Simple" linear loops. Perhaps in Manifold Garden 2? The "corrupted" cube's distortion effect meant that often times I was setting it down just to admire the scenery around me.  While you can look into the infinite loop and see the cube you are carrying, there is no rendered player avatar. A minor disappointment when I first encountered an area that allowed this.I encountered a single bug that most people will not ever see: I have 5 joysticks/accessories plugged into my computer for flight sims, and if I accidentally nudge a directional axis on any of them, the game thinks I'm using a game pad and that the movement stick is stuck walking backwards.

_childDocuments_.review: I was kinda afraid to even start this game but I'm also fascinated by endless geometric patterns so I had to try no matter how confusing it will be.Game starts easily inside with gravity shuffle puzzle mechanics which reminds Portal games. True mindblowing experience begins "outside" when you look and see infinity. Well it's more like endlessly repeating architecture which gives feeling of infinity but it worked on me as I experienced moments of sacred awe everytime new colossal architectonic piece was unfold before my eyes. Yeah game looks amazing, it's mostly just simple geometry but there is a beauty in simplicity. Also I have to mention awesome soundtrack which makes some moments even more memorable and thus adding another dimension to this game.So game is mostly about solving puzzles by using gravity shuffle mechanics and repeated geometry which gives you new traverse options. I guess it's not so hard if you are used to puzzle games but with adding confusing element of repeating architecture you can easily lost sense of where the hell are you. _childDocuments_.review: A nice little puzzle game, where you continue on your way by changing gravity.It has a great OST and a nice art style. The world is interesting, since sometimes falling down means you're able to get higher up. It has a weird psychedelic feel to it.But that's sadly where my praises end. The game is simply too short to warrant the price tag for one. 16 bucks for 4 hours of gameplay. That's literally the same price as something like Hollow Knight with less than a tenth of the content. On top of that, while the game looks interesting, there is next to nothing to do. The puzzles are very easy to solve for one. _childDocuments_.review: Manifold Garden is a gorgeous puzzle game... but one with very little puzzle depth to it. I managed to complete the game in 4 hours, and approximately 1.5 hours of it were spent floating around the same room after completing the first "chapter" because I didn't realize that I was missing a box from a previous room.The visual and sound design are both extremely well done, but the core gameplay is just lacking. Every puzzle is extremely basic, and many puzzle solutions are reused of the short course of the game. For what could've lead to some incredible non-Euclidean puzzles like in Antichamber, Manifold Garden only abuses its infinite world in one puzzle over the course of the game.I don't hate the game. If Steam had a neutral option, this would definitely be it. I'm just surprised more people aren't upset by how simple this game is, considering it had such high potential.

_childDocuments_.review: It is a very cool concept and in some ways it's a pretty game, but ultimately it falls short for me.The game often leaves you fumbling to find stuff in the puzzle instead of actually letting you focus on solving puzzles. Too often I'm left with the sense that I don't know where I'm supposed to go or what my goal is. Often I also find myself looking for a slot for a cube without knowing where to start. This leaves me aimlessly wandering about until I find it. That's not solving puzzles, that's just obscuring the puzzle elements. I don't feel clever finding the needle in a haystack, I just feel like I wasted a lot of time.Perhaps the game could've benefited from a map similar to what Antichamber has. Having more linear puzzles where you can focus on solving the puzzle instead of finding the puzzle elements would also have been nice. Having a sort of hub world would've been great as an anchoring point.While the graphics and environments are initially quite stunning, they quickly become bland and there is very little urge to explore as every corner looks similar.All in all, the feeling of aimlessness is the biggest problem. The lack of any story also makes me struggle to get any motivation for going through these puzzles in the first place. A story might've helped keeping me going to discover what was coming next.If you want a better puzzle game, try The Talos Principle instead.
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: People really have the gall to compare this to The Talos Principle, Portal, Obduction and even Antichamber. Sure, the OST adds a lot to the game, and the game itself utilizes infinity and impossible geometry in impressive ways, but the mechanics are just too simple and repetitive. The world is huge, infinite even, and yet there is nothing to do. Every rule is taught in the first part of the game. The entire game is just you doing the same thing over and over. The ending and secret ending are abstract, in fact, the entire game is abstract. There's no story, no goal. Even Antichamber managed to have a predictable goal - something to work towards. Manifold Garden has no goal despite what reviewers say. There's no enemy, no tower in the distance, no mystery to solve, nothing. You just keep solving the same kinds of puzzles, and maybe you take a different path, and then it's over.

_childDocuments_.review: Manifold Garden is a kaleidoscope. It is stunningly beautiful, and looks like it's probably rather cleverly constructed on a technical level. However, you can experience just about everything about it in only one or two sessions with it, and after that you'd have to have been really smitten with it to want to go back.This particular first-person puzzler's main conceit is the ability to redirect gravity in any of the 6 axis directions, in effect replacing jumping with the act of changing which way is up. It's quite fun to fiddle with, and I found it not very disorienting (so long as you keep the gravity change animation setting to "S curve" and not "instant") so very quickly it develops into a fun little game of parsing and solving puzzles couched in geometrical and non-Euclidean architecture.I found the level of difficulty of the main game to be very casual, more so a test of your ability to notice all the parts of the present puzzle than to recombine those parts in spicy ways. So I breezed through it somewhat unsatisfyingly quickly. But after that main ending, Manifold Garden also has a secret ending, which is orders of magnitude tougher to get. It requires a rather intimate knowledge of all the standard puzzles and their relative locations, as well as an insistence on exploring some rather unintuitive nooks and crannies with extremely few breadcrumbs to point the way. I don't think I can call the difficulty spike unfair, but it is certainly very demanding relative to the rest of the game.My bead on it is that it was probably intended for people who played the main game a lot more than just once, which I think is why it leaves such a sour taste in my mouth: I had absolutely no compulsion to play it a second time (beyond hunting down those last few achievements) and I have trouble imagining that other people would, either... much in the same way that I have not had the desire to peer down a kaleidoscope a second time.
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: Fun little puzzle platformer that took up a weekend, reminds me a lot of Antichamber in it's visuals. There were a few puzzles that had me running in circles, but nothing that had me rage-quitting or looking up a guide. Puzzles often were simpler than expected, and I'm sure if they really wanted they could use the mechanics to come up with some truly mind-bending challenges - but as it is, there's nothing too taxing on the brain. A fun journey.
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: One of the reasons I play games is so they take me to places or times I normally can't go. Manifold Garden took me to places I could barely even imagine!Overall the puzzles were very enjoyable and even made me feel smart at times. I did have to look up a few that involved specially large areas with many options, but it was all there if you analyzed it in simple terms. I wonder what people like Frank Lloyd Wright would've thought of this game. Some of the architecture was mindbogglingly evocative, even more so because of the freedom you have to experience it. Concepts like up and down or beginning and end have a different meaning here. I recommend this game if you like puzzles, if you like architecture, if you like relaxing music, and if you're not afraid of getting disoriented and overwhelmed with reality. Think Inception meets the Interstellar Tesseract meets Portal meets Kula World.

_childDocuments_.review: WARNING:  A non-Euclidian brain is required to play this game.Manifold Garden is what happens when a develloper takes his previous game, learns what parts worked and what did not and makes annother game in the same spirit.The style is kept simple with some monotone blocky objects, but injected with a caleidoscope of hue and configured in a repeating fractal pattern, giving this world a pristine and alien look further rinforced by a plethora of other effects that tie into the gameplay, like colouring the surfaces you could stand on, or inverting colours and seeing some distortion to comunicate danger or unusualness.Gameplay is simple, pick up boxes and put them down in a certain spot, the complexity comes from non-euclidean spaces and the ability to mutate how you are affected by gravity like you are in some M. C. Escher painting to allow you for otherwise impossible tricks.A complaint is that some levels later down the line start to drag on, since the game hits you immediately with a lot of visuals in a short span of thime it may leave your mouth dry seeing the dame style of the same room for an hour straight with nothing else, but besides this i ended up playing it all in a single sitting so for all i can say thet the game is repetitive it must have done something right.Story isn't even there but I appreciate more a missing element than a badly realized one.Think with portals... with broken general relativity, and gravity to engage in an ahestetically and technically impressive puzzle game.

_childDocuments_.review: Like trying, as a mere mortal, to traverse the realm of an AI god who feels that physical laws are just suggestions.Is it worth full price?  If you've enjoyed other first-person puzzlers like Talos Principle, Antichamber, The Witness, yes absolutely.  Took me <5 hours to finish but worth every dollar because it felt so much longer (in a good way).  And if it were any longer it would start to feel tedious instead of awe-inspiring and fresh.  If you're new to FP puzzlers and not sure, get it on any kind of sale. The mind-melting premise alone is worth it, even if you don't finish.Btw, I see a lot of reviewers talking about "non-euclidean" space or geometry.  Just for those that might not be familiar, this is referring to architecture/geometry that is impossible in real life; for example, you could find a doorway that you could both walk through and walk behind, and be in 2 separate places.  WARNING: you have any problems with vertigo while playing video games or falling great distances in-game (on purpose), DON'T BUY.  In this game you constantly switch which way is up, and are constantly falling as a game mechanic.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a great game. In short, I highly suggest it for its intuitive mechanics and beautiful design. In Long...     I came to this game through my search for indie games after beating through Outer Wilds- my now-deemed favorite game ever- for the fourth time. It piqued my interest because of the interesting and foreign mechanics. It was tagged "exploration," so I came into it hoping for a controlled open-world (like Outer Wilds, of course), but with an open mind. Open-mindedness was a good decision, since as it turns out, the game is a somewhat-linear puzzle game. There are two chief differences between this game and others. In one case, there is no jump mechanic. Instead, your space bar flips gravity 90 degrees, making the walls your new floor. Second, every level has an infinitely-recurring functionality. If you go off a certain part of the map, you can fall onto a completely different side of the map. These mechanics are combined with a "3.5-dimensional" experience to make a wonderfully challenging game simply about ridding corruption and finding peace.     No matter how much I love it, I have two issues with it. First, I came into the game with high hopes for strange recurring loops and visual tricks. The game employs that sometimes, but, honestly, not as much as I hoped for. Second and more importantly, it's very short. I finished (NOT 100%, I still have a few achievements to hunt out.) the game in a slightly disappointing 4 hours. It was really good while it lasted, but I wish there was more.     In summary, this was a very good game- one I very much recommend you get. Although it is a short game, it makes up for it with a very thought-provoking game with multiple amazing and new mechanics, all packaged in a beautifully simplistic, very clean (I only remember one serious bug on the last level where two moving blocks collided very awkward) game.
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: I'm kind of conflicted here. I was initially going to give this game a negative review...but it does just enough to cross the wire.What is the game? At its core, its a puzzle game that explores non-euclidian physics. In layman's terms, the laws of our physical world in terms of direction and orientation go do not necessarily apply. Portals lead to different areas, most world spaces loop in on themselves, and most importantly, the player can shift gravity to any of the six cardinal directions, and often must do this in order to traverse the world. While the game does do this well, there's not as much variety as some other puzzle titles. No combat of any sort either, if that's something you are seeking.What this game excels at is atmosphere. It has an amazing soundtrack, and vast feats of architecture present throughout the game. Most of the architecture is there for show, but still, its nice to see these grand feats of engineering that, unfortunately, is not really possible to build in the real world. But where this game really falls short is...well, there's not really much more to the game. It has puzzles, and a good atmopshere, but that's pretty much it. There is no story of any sort, characters, not even basic dialogue. "You are here, do the thing in front of you" is pretty much it. This game really could have benefited from even a vague contextual storyline of some sort, something for those of us interested want to pursue and unravel.Still, at the end, I felt good about completing the game, so it did its job. Worth a 10-15$ pricepoint if you ask me.
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: If I could describe Manifold Garden, its like Inception physics while on a DMT trip trying to unite 6 biblically accurate angels with music from Blade Runner 2049. I found that the levels are ironically pretty linear pathing, with the most difficult part being just trying to orient yourself. Would be awesome if they included a "multiplayer" with user submitted/rated levels, time trials, etc for game longevity similar super mario maker. Amazing game and so happy I discovered it.
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: i've been hyped for this game since i first heard of it. i watched some of the dev videos and played the heck out of the demo when that became available. the game did not disappoint. it's absolutely breathtaking at points. i was able to complete the game without a walk through because it does a really good job teaching you how to play and solve the puzzles. the game is just full of "ah ha!" moments that feel very satisfying. every time i was stuck for a bit and starting to get frustrated i'd suddenly notice the one thing i was missing and it never felt like it was the game's fault i was stuck. i'm now playing through to get the game's not enough achievement plan on 100% the game. i am using a walk through for this when i get stuck because while the first sneaky bit was actually pretty easy because it's something i'd noticed when combing over the demo and realized how to get past the thing i'd noticed.... some of the other sneaky solutions i'm kinda glad i had some hints. i'm sure if i had more patients and was willing to be lost exploring every inch of every area i can access at any given time for very well hidden things.....i mean... i'm probably gonna come back periodically and wonder around and take photos of different areas.i was kinda sad that it was coming to an end as i approached the end of my first play through. i wanted more... and really there was more.i really love this game. i love games like this. i want more games like this.
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: Neat portal-esque puzzle game with amazing aesthetics and cool mechanics, none of the puzzles are too difficult (if they feel difficult, you likely missed something). The styling is cool, but the fact that it leads to HUGE game worlds makes it tedious to do some puzzles due to the amount of walking (if your puzzle game needs a run key, you may have gone too far).
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: What an amazingly beautiful, confusing, and satisfying game. Technically brilliant, visually unique and mechanically well-rounded. The puzzles aren't necessarily the focus, this game is as much of a walking simulator as it is a puzzle game, but that isn't a flaw. There's certainly enough to scratch a puzzle game itch.
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: Solving the puzzles is fun. Figuring out which puzzle I'm supposed to solve next kind of sucks though. I'm currently in the third color level, and I just put a lot of effort into gathering five blue blocks, but I can't figure out at all where I need to put them. I found solution I guess, but I have no clue what problem this solution is supposed to solve. I've been running and flying around for half an hour now and I guess I am just overlooking a small thing somewhere, a tiny little square that indicates where it needs to be dropped. It's a pity that with such a good concept, progress in the game relies so much on searching where to go next.
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: I love this game so much, it is not so complicated in comparison to other IQ games but the way it tricks your brain is very very new and welcomed, the concept is very very creative and odd and I loved it so much.also, the audio and the art style both are amazing, that is what all other puzzle games lack.In short terms, this game is so worth it, and I think it should cost more, buy it and enjoy, you will thank me and the developer of this game later.
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: Wow. When the 4th dimension meets the infinity, you end up with a game like this. Beautiful, to those who like endless straight lines. Probably not a good game for those who dislike mazes, distorted cameras, or are easily lost.The game would be a lot worse with "better" graphics. The simpleness of the world gives a sense of perfection and makes it a lot easier to do cool effects.Would be a great buy at $5 but the sale price of $10 so far seems fair.Update. After completing the game and finally getting all of the achievements, here are my thoughts.If this game was free, I would suggest that everyone give it a try. At least the first couple of levels. Playing through the game and beating it normally was really quite enjoyable.However, trying to get the last few achievements kind of tainted the game for me. I ended up having to use a few guides because some of the hidden paths were essentially hidden behind invisible walls. (You had to look at the wall in a super special place to see it wasn't actually a wall.)But I think the worst of it is all the tiny bugs and glitches scattered throughout the game. Playing the game normally, you mostly don't see them. Hunting for hidden passages, you see them all over the place. I tried to send a few bug reports out, but then realised the game stopped getting consistent updates a while ago. Check the Discord channel, and you see its mostly dead in there. Even getting the "I got all the achievements" achievement required going to the Steam forms because that was bugged too.So its a good game. It just lacks the shiny polish that would make it a great game. And the way things are looking, its just going to slowly fade away over the next 5 years.
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: I have yet to fully complete the game, but I do feel I've gotten my impression; this game is great!! I was unsure at first but soon fell in love with this title. The puzzles are challenging and great for spatial thinkers. I myself am so-so in that field, so I find these mind-boggling, but oh my, do I love them nonetheless. _childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: 10/10Pretty cool game, just finishing the "story" -- getting the "Watched the Ending" achievement -- is relatively fast, I'd say 5 hours max; though as I'm typing this the achievement titled "finish the game without placing a single god cube" + 2 hidden ones are having quite the laugh.Very nice atmosphere, sound & music is great too.Has cubes, pressure plates, no incinerators, perfect.
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: Very beautiful looking game, and interesting puzzles. It was an experience of sorts.Don't expect any depth beyond that though. There is no perceivable story, no deeper meaning to the world, and nothing to explore beyond the puzzles.As a puzzle game, it isn't that great. There is no progression in difficulty, as levels can be easier or harder than previous levels. It is satisfying to finish the levels after solving the puzzles though. You are playing this game mainly for visuals, and puzzles second. If that sounds fine to you and you like how the game looks, I'd recommend waiting for a sale before getting the game.
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: So, admittedly, I was ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ around with cubes that I clearly wasn't intended to bring with me. But in the process of doing said ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, I found out that it's possible to arrange three cubes against a wall such that you will be permanently trapped due to the mechanic that prevents you from changing gravity if you don't have room to stand in the space you're trying to occupy. All right, fine, I was ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ about where I knew full well I shouldn't have been and as a result got irreversibly trapped. On it's own not really damning, even if it is annoying that the game design allows for such a broken game state.Then I tried to reload my save to get out of it and realized something two things that combined reveal a sobering truth. Item number one, it had been an hour since I last saved. Item number two, the game doesn't auto-save. At all. If you haven't saved your progress, you didn't make progress. So, basically, if I wanted to keep playing the game I had to start all the way back at the beginning. There is a 'reset to the last checkpoint' option...that overwrites your most recent save. No help there.If you're going to play this game, I guess you just have to break the beautiful flow of it every five seconds and spam that damn save button or else you'll risk losing your progress. Game, I could have used a warning about that one ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ hour ago. Or, you know, some kind of, "I've stuck myself please help" button that resets the room. A feature which is, in my opinion, the very basic entry-level requirement of any puzzle game. Just because the way forward is obvious doesn't mean people like me aren't going to try to cheese the system. And if we can cheese it so hard it burns a whole save file, your game is fundamentally broken.I want to be clear here, the game seemed fun, and it only broke because I was pushing at the boundaries of something I knew I wasn't supposed to be able to do. But it's a damn puzzle game. The whole point is to think outside the box...allegedly. Apparently the developers of Manifold Garden didn't get that memo, and what you're actually supposed to do is follow the linear path and do only as they intended when solving the puzzles. So I just can't in good conscience recommend the game. It's a decently mindbending puzzler I guess, but I never got to the hard puzzles so for all the fun I got out of it the thing may as well be a very buggy walking simulator. Hard pass.
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: i dont usually do serious reviews but this game was something elsebeautifully crafted game, looks absolutely stunning. the atmosphere of the entire game is perfect and the sound design is great. plus its just really nice to fall for a while and appreciate all the structures and geometry around you. the world this game created really left me with a sense of dread while playing. being infinitely small in an ever expansive world with towering structures all around you does that.completely worth the money to get. on top of that it has pretty good puzzles too!
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: This game hooked me immediately. I love 3D puzzle games, and the atmosphere of this one was so nice. The graphics are crisp and clean and fit the world very well. The infinitely repeating level design blew me away, was integrated so nicely into the puzzle solving, and was not just a gimmick. The sound effects are great. The first thing I noticed were the melodic noises as I walked across glass. The music is ambient and appropriate and at times I was expecting a breakout into full synthwave.There is very limited difficulty curve with the puzzles (first playthrough), but it is fun, interesting, rewarding, and unique. You can play the game a second time, though it is much harder and I am not smart enough to have done so without using a guide for most of it. The depth and complexity of this game on the second play through is bananas. I knew during my first playthrough that something was going on, as I saw a few places that I was like, hmmm, maybe the game will come back to that. But they never did. It's unlikely I would have figured this out on my own without spending a lot of time in the world playing around, and I wasn't committed to that, but I was glad to experience the second playthrough.With what this game has to offer, and how well it is designed, it is worth full price. If you figure out the second play through on your own, you would get your money's worth many many times over. This is an absolute gem of a puzzle game and a no-brainer to pick up if you like games like The Witness or The Talos Principle. It's just one of those games that words, a review, even videos won't quite help you to understand. You really just have to play it.
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: - Gorgeous abstract visuals throughout- Screenshots, while pretty, don't do the game justice. Traversing the world is a whole different level- The music is light background electronic music ranging from austere to ominous- It's an abstract puzzle game; there's no narrative- Instead, just enjoy the splendor- The puzzles are all perspective-based, so people with good spatial awareness will probably like this game- Besides running around and moving colorful cubes, you'll also shift gravity around quite a bit, both for moving around the levels and for solving puzzles- Not sure I'll be back for a replay- If you're a fan of pretty visuals and sometimes tricky puzzles, this is for you- Played the first few parts on PC, then finished up on the Steam Deck. Ran very well on both- . If it seems up your alley visually and you enjoy puzzles, buy with confidence. Keep in mind it's between 5 and 10 hours depending on how often you get stuck
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: Aesthetics: an absolute masterpiece. Manifold Garden has a crystal-clear vision and every visual and aural element works towards it. Many of the infinite environments are simply breathtaking.  It's probably worth the price of admission just to be able to wander around the world.Puzzles: a bit on the easy side. A couple puzzles were joyous to solve; many had a hint of cleverness; some were annoyingly fiddly, especially the .  I often reached the end of an area with a bit of a "that's it?" feeling-- after learning each mechanic, I usually found them to be a bit underdeveloped.  (Compare with e.g. The Witness, where every mechanic is explored to the extreme.)  The mechanics themselves are quite nice; I just wish they built up to something more substantial.World design: I frequently got lost, but with the mechanics in play, it's an absolute miracle that the world is navigable at all.  So, in that respect, I have to give huge props to the world design.Overall, I would call it a good game, not a great one.  Pick it up to enjoy the outstanding art, or if you want a world that will mess with your head along with puzzles that won't.
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: I got softlocked a mere 38 minutes into the game. I had to look up a guide to confirm - yes, I was supposed to bring some sort of 'God Cube' through a door that closed behind me. Exiting and reloading my save kept in the softlocked state. I had 0 interest in slowly 'sprinting' through the first set of puzzles a second time, and as such will be attempting a refund.The puzzles I played were simple, the mechanics were boring at best. Sure, maybe things pick up later on. I'll never know. Spending 15 minutes fumbling around in some black goop around a tower trying to find an objective that doesn't exist leaves one kind of salty.
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: It's super interesting but it does suffer a bit from being like... it's like portal but you don't get to step through the portals, you have to carry them around.It's fun to navigate and figure out the environments, but it feels very manual a lot of the time, but it's also a product of the puzzles, not the controls, so... it's like... metaphysics. _childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: I've gardened my manifold in one go and can say with confidence - this screensaver comes with some brilliant built-in puzzles (and interactivity, for some reason), I wouldn't mind just staring at it, but developers also allowed me to walk around and press things and move other things and jump on walls - I was pleasantly surprised with how much freedom of movement this screensaver gives. With that said, I'd be satisfied even if this screensaver would come without a stellar game attached to it, so can't recommend enough.This game yeahs and then some.
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: I had only played this game for about 10 minutes before I decided this is one of my favorite games of all time.I love puzzle platformer type games, and this one takes it to a whole other level. From the mind bending illusions, beautiful artwork and design, even the ambient soundtrack was amazing. After the ending sequence and credits started to roll, I will admit it brought a tear of wonder to my eye. 10/10 recommend, only wish there was more to play and explore!
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: wow.don't remember the last time I played a game that is a gallery-tier work of visual art but with genuinely fun gameplay.absolutely gorgeous, a surprising amount of story told solely through architecture, some genuinely upsetting abstract visuals, incredible sound design, interesting puzzles that never get too unreasonable or sacrifice either visual appeal or gameplay clarity. the relatively short length might be a downside to some people but I found it just long enough that it didn't feel rushed or overly dense but also doesn't overstay it's welcome, plus there's bonus puzzles if that's your kind of thing. a rare 10/10 puzzle game for me.
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: It was inevitable that a game like this would get made and I'm disappointed with how it turned out. The developer may be quick to assure me it was for mercy's sake that orientation changing was locked behind physically looking at and also being near a surface, but in practice I felt like much of my playtime was wasted looking for low ledges to abuse when all I wanted was to be upside down.I wanted to be upside down because I was using gravity to my advantage to cover the enormous empty distances that make 's 6-axis kaleidoscopic world work. But what is nice to look at from a distance can be tedious at hand, as evidenced by all the time I spent climbing stairs instead of just turning the room upside down.Many puzzles were relatively straightforward, but the ones that additionally required giant tetrominoes were torture. Water had the potential to be a neat mechanic, but despite maybe two useful instances of water-as-bridge, was mostly wasted on lining up complex pathways over tediously long distances. None of the puzzles felt fun or satisfying to solve; I only felt relieved they were done and I was one step closer to being done with this game.I think that  is important in being the high-water mark for this genre by being the first infinitely recursive world, but except to show off I have zero interest in playing it again. It would have worked better at smaller scale with decorative elements designed to be walked over rather than constantly trapping the player in ankle-high prisons without a jump button. Player movement in this world could have been something really special with that sense of taking the training wheels off as the levels get bigger, but instead there were just a lot of stairs.
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: I almost refunded this game.  So so close!PROS+ Art style+ Infinite landscapes that are are a bit stark, but also capture the imagination+ Sense of "which way is up?" puzzles.  I.e. the puzzles depend on your ability to rotate the direction of gravity and which pieces are active or locked depending on what direction is down.  So far I have only seen 6 "down" directions: +/- X, +/- Y, and +/- Z axes.+ The puzzles are satisfying, even though they are not brutally difficult - sometimes getting my head to switch orientations to have the foresight of finding the solution takes some time.CONS- I get a headache playing this after a while.  I think because changing the orientation, or having to think in terms of changing orientation makes me dizzy.  I have a physical reaction to the game.I didn't refund it after all.  I decided the art style was cool enough to keep this game around and explore the different puzzles.
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: I never knew that the infinite could give me that feeling of dread before I had played Manifold Garden.  That vastness is definitely the primary reason why I would recommend this game, as it's truly unique in that sense.The puzzles are alright.  A lot of them, especially towards the end, commit the cardinal sin of physically taking longer to solve than mentally.  That is, I knew what the solution was, but because of the aforementioned vastness, it takes some time to actually solve the puzzle, which makes going through the game feel really tedious.  The physical/mental ratio needed to be worked on.I think the game is fine for as long as it is; any longer and it might have just tired me out from having to move forward SO MUCH for what is ultimately a pretty simple puzzle.  But I'm glad I got to experience it.
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: Manifold garden is a puzzle game that utilizes impossible Geometry, switching gravity, and Fractals. I have never seen a puzzle game like Manifold Garden. The puzzles were fun to solve and the soundtrack was extremely good! (The soundtrack alone is worth buying). The visual art style was a delight to play and everywhere i looked i smashed the screenshot button. Seriously this game will hurt your brain in its mind boggoling puzzles, it goes a little into the forth dimension but honestly you just need to play it. I had a smile on my face the entirety of this game, and the ending was Beautiful. Every time i got familiar with a mechanic the game always introduced another one. I highly recommend this game, it is sooooo gooood!
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: I wanted to play this because the screenshots looked cool and I liked the idea of playing in an environment with vast open spaces. Overall, I think this game is pretty good. More than anything, it's the sense of awe with which I am filled when immersed in the game environment that keeps me playing.I've almost finished the game, and I'll probably do another run-through just to check out some things I may have missed. _childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: Very cool puzzle game...the puzzles are well-constructed and feel really good to solve.
