One time I walked around for like 15 minutes with a god cubeThe atmosphere is really cool. Sound design and music an obvious highlight for meOverall, I liked it...I think I'm glad I purchased it on sale though, because it's rather short and I'm not sure how much I would want to replay it given that a lot of my time was spent looking for things rather than solving puzzles
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: The Style, the music and sound design are all excellent. The gameplay on the other hand, is certainly something you do while playing the game. If you are getting this game because you are hoping for a challenge or difficult puzzles that require alot of time to solve, then skip this one.If you are getting it because you think the visuals look hella good, then go for it.
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: I really, really hated this, and I'm surprised, because I thought for sure I was the target market, considering I love Escher, psychedelica, and puzzle games.But I disliked almost everything about this game aside from the music. The graphics are ugly and not even pleasing to the eye in a retro way. The controls are uncomfortable and never become intuitive. The puzzles are just dumb, tedious, predictable, and pointless. Like they were designed by a computer. An  computer. Probably using a tape drive.Thank goodness the suck began at once, because I shall now recoup this conceptually interesting, functionally uninteresting nonsense with a refund.
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: Cool concepts, cool experience. Not much of a puzzle game.  Puzzles were easy and not always incorporated well into the environments.  Most of my time was spent running between levels or looking for things.  To people saying it's about the experience/ambiance, then why did they introduce puzzle elements that clashed with that aesthetic (looking at you tetris blocks).  There could have been many more puzzles using only the simpler puzzle elements.Yes, I did stop to look at some of the cool gateway rooms between puzzles, but I prefer to be incentivized by the game
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: Took me 3.6 hours to complete.Manifold Garden is a great non-Euclidean/impossible geometry themed puzzle game. No real story, and feels like it builds upon what Antichamber got going way back in a fantastic way. It removes the inane quote-hunting that Antichamber does and creates a phenomenal linear puzzle experience similar in difficulty to Portal 1/2.The puzzles themselves have very simple mechanics that the game builds upon in extremely interesting ways. It's the mark of any good game, and I'd have to say Manifold Garden is a very good game.I took a long time to play this game, and I'm not sure why. It's a very awe-inspiring experience; it does much more for the eyes and ears than most triple AAAs could hope to achieve. Don't let the short run-time fool you; Manifold Garden doesn't waste your time. It knows what it is and how long it can stay.All in all, this game is an excellent and short puzzle game that is a treat for the eyes and ears. Overall, the game is phenomenal and has a lot to offer, with incredibly few shortcomings. If you're a fan of Antichamber, buy this game. It's kinda worth full price, but I'd say wait until it goes on any sort of sale. Thanks for reading.EDIT: Formatting overhaul!
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: Visually beautiful, some simple and straightforward puzzles. Replay value seems pretty low, and will deliver around 6-12 hours of puzzle solving and exploring. This isn't an absolute 'must play', but it is enjoyable nonetheless. Play does start to feel a little monotonous by the last 20% in my opinion. I'd recommend to buy this game on discount, say $10 or below unless you really want to support the devs. This game was surprisingly resource intensive (caused my PC to crash). I ended up getting a new power supply and nothing has crashed since then.
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: A trippy, wonderful little puzzle game. Above the gameplay itself, the most striking and memorable part of this game is it's unparalleled visual style. Infinite, endless fractals and mind-bending architecture make for an incredible visual experience. The puzzles are fun and take advantage of the unique way that environments are navigated, but vary greatly from fun and intuitive to confusing guesswork.A great experience for the pricepoint, especially if it's on sale. Above all else, it's a uniquely beautiful experience with some of the most memorable vistas in modern gaming.
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: A very relaxing puzzle game ( more a discovery game with light puzzle elements ) with a really nice minimalistic graphics style. The game starts with the basic premise that you can walk on any walls, using cubes to open doors and introduces new elements gradually during the game that kept it interesting until the end. I will add that if you are really looking for a true puzzle game this might be a bit lacking, but if you are looking for a good experience with puzzle elements you should really consider this one.
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: Awesome game. If you like puzzle games get this game. If you like Antichamber (or The Talos Principle), get this game! Note the puzzles in those games are stronger than in Manifold Garden. However! Manifold Garden is an *artistic masterwork*, and worth getting for that reason alone. Support awesome games like this.
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: ..1st you wont get the value of this game unless you finish it.. and if you do you will know why it was worth it..As for the game it self, its a puzzle game where you have to manipulate "gravity" and cubes to open door to progre3s there is a learning curve to it, you are likely to struggle (like I did) in the 1st levels after I got the "hang of it" it seemed easier with every level.The graphics are "simple" yet effective, the music is cut just right to create a fitting atmosphere - I wont rate this from 1 to 10 because this game is so peculiar that I cant do that its basically a binary choice either you will total "get it" or you wont..If you consider you self a "gamer" its a must play.. prefferably to the finish
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: This non-euclidean puzzle ♥♥♥♥ fries your brain like an egg.There's a lot of first person puzzle games out there in a post-Portal world, but this one sets itself apart from the rest by coupling exceptional premise with exceptional presentation - no game world I've inhabited has fascinated me quite the same way as the impossibly infinite fractal architecture of Manifold Garden, and no approach to problem solving has fascinated me quite the same way as jumping off a ledge to reach a place above me.If you like puzzle games this one gets an enthusiastic recommend.
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: It's a very enjoyable puzzle game that relies heavily on non-eculidean space and repeating spaces, tesselation and arrays. It is worth playing for the aestethics alone. The puzzles are not too hard and the game flows comfortably.I picked this up because it reminded me of antichamber. The two are similar but also quite different. I feel like Manifold garden took the most enjoyable sights of antichambers ending and explored those concepts further.
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: I am kind of blown away by this game.  For what it is, this, this is a perfect game in my book.  Absolutely breathtaking and I feel a bit emotional that my journey with it has come to an end.  For only 10 hours of play time like the game play, it felt infinite.  My recommendation is not whether or not to experience this, but on how much at a time you should.

_childDocuments_.review: very cool visuals and music.  the overall presentation is great, i love itthe concepts are neat, but they got stale quick.  not much is offered beyond a mechanic's initial introductiongameplay?  easily one of the most boring games ive ever played.  every level is massive, recursive, and most key points are not distinct at all.  it makes for some cool visuals, but its an absolute nightmare for actual gameplay.  its very easy to get confused, lost, and frustrated.  it takes ages to get from point A to point B, even when youre constantly sprinting.  theres a stupid amount of tedious back and forth.  the puzzles themselves arent challenging at all, i solved most of them instantly.  the real challenge comes from the rooms being far too large and confusing to actually tell what youre looking at, and keeping your patience as you do nothing but WALK for minutes at a time.  its a walking simulator.  it felt like they were forced to add gameplay, so they made 10% of the game simple block puzzles with miles of empty space between the locks and keys just to add empty length to them and pretend they have any complexity.  your only rewards are long empty corridors between puzzles, the same sequence copy-pasted six times, and a 4 minute video of shapes spinning around.  wow, how artsy.  if youve watched the trailer, youve played the game.  do not buy.  watch a playthrough if you want. _childDocuments_.review: Manifold Garden is similar to games like Antichamber and Superliminal in that it is a non-euclidean puzzle game with special attention towards foreign topologies. However, of the three titles I feel this is the inferior. It's lacking a certain "humanity" that the other two possess, Superliminal more directly with its premise and story, and Antichamber more obliquely by its allegory. Speaking of which, like the other two games, Manifold Garden is allegorical, though I'm not sure for what. This game has a unique treatment of infinity which I quite enjoyed. The spaces are expansive and awesome (in the formal sense). However, this use of space also made some puzzles frustrating by the time it took to reach some locations, possibly as a form of padding as the puzzles aren't too difficult once you wrap your head around the mechanics/physics at play. I would say I quite enjoyed the game, but I did find the ending slightly pretentious. It has just as much conceptual meat as Superliminal and Antichamber, but as I said, it's lacking in the human or philosophy department. Not a particularly thought provoking game, as the underlying theme seems to be either environmentalism or nth-dimensional transcendence (whatever that is). An aesthetic delight which doesn't overstay its welcome (which considering my hours played, should tell you something).
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: Beautiful puzzler that takes you through various abstract landscapes full of geometry and fractal goodness, with great music to further inspire awe. Of course you shouldn't come here looking for story since this is purely a journey through mesmerizing geometry. Personally I think the game's better without it because you don't really have to "justify" what you're experiencing within a rational context.Would be neat if future level packs were in the works, or even a level editor for players to come up with perhaps more bonkers puzzles that push the game to its limits?Also those who are prone to motion sickness might want to at least watch someone else's playthrough a bit first, because this game involves a *lot* of falling and changing orientation. _childDocuments_.review: To make a good puzzle game requires three things:1. Simple mechanics.2. Exploring how those mechanics interact.3. Not overstaying its welcome.Manifold Garden is an absolutely fantastic puzzle game.The basic mechanic is changing the direction gravity goes. Cubes only fall if they are the same colour as the gravity (this sentence does not make sense on its own, but will as soon as you start playing). Cubes can redirect water by 90 degrees. The game takes you on a journey exploring these mechanics, and then ends after an appropriate amount of time.The game is full of secret pathways, some of which still have me completely stumped. There are some pretty difficult puzzles in them too, and I wouldn't recommend searching for them on a first playthrough.The photo mode is incredibly versatile. Some of the effects end up creating images you never would have though would come out.As a challenge for anyone who wants it, I've managed to collect . I'm not sure if it's possible to get more, but if it is, be sure to let me know.

_childDocuments_.review: A very unique exploration game disguised as a puzzle game. The main point of the game is to enjoy the infinitely extended geometry and abstract art. The puzzles themselves are mostly simple, with a few exceptions where exits and required actions are not clearly presented and might require a walkthrough. The main storyline took me around 10 hours, and I know there are optional hidden stages created for those who want extra challenges.Go watch some videos to get an idea how the presentation is, as that is the deciding factor whether you should consider the game. _childDocuments_.review: This game is beautiful. It's constantly mesmerizing, and honestly there were various moments where I felt in awe at the sheer beauty of the game. The colors, the sound design, the fact that everything is just... infinite, all of this caused my jaw to drop throughout the game. It may sound like I'm going a bit over the top, but this game is genuinely art. Especially the ending sequence. The vibe this game emanates is such a weird feeling. I think the best word for it is just awe. Awe at the insane vastness of the game. I'll say it again, this game is art.I haven't even gotten to the gameplay, but that gameplay is a great compliment to how trippy and beautiful the game already is. There were various moments where I was left utterly confused, as if I had genuinely just witnessed a glitch in the game or something. But no, those stairs leading up? They were going down too. Oh, and also nowhere. You're in the same spot you started. The puzzles are mind-bending, yet simple enough to solve once you change the way you think about the game and 3D space as a whole. The puzzles also incorporate the infinite-ness of the game very well, with many puzzles' solutions having something to do with falling through the infinite copies of the level to reach an area otherwise unreachable. There was also a nice variety of puzzles, with ideas slowly building on each other until they culminated in the final level.Manifold Garden is art. And if you're planning on playing it, approach it from that lens. Take things slow, appreciate the beauty of the game, and maybe take a few screenshots. I know I certainly did. The gameplay is fun, but more than anything the game's beauty is what will blow you away.

_childDocuments_.review: Relatively easy puzzler with a focus on exploring infinitely tessellated spaces from all 6 directions in 3D space. Your primary ability is to rotate the world 90° so that gravity points towards a new down, forcing you to think about the space from a whole new direction.If you dig the trippy, MC-escher-esque feel of the trailer → you won't be disappointed with this gameIf you're looking for a mind-bending puzzle game → tread carefullyThe biggest mind-bending challenge is figuring out how to explore each successive space to locate the elements of the puzzle and how they are positioned relative to each other in 3D space. Which is more akin to a challenging walking simulator than a puzzle game. Thankfully this is quite fun owing to the trippy environments, with enough variety to keep things fresh.The puzzles themselves are polished—like I don't think you can ever get stuck—but they're also, you could say, uninspired. Here are some comparisons: - many challenges leave you thinking "whoa, they kinda bent my brain solving that"; that never happens in Manifold Garden. In Portal, all the elements feel fully explored across the game; in Manifold Garden it's got portals too (albeit static portals) but they're barely explored from a puzzle perspective, and you can say the same about the rest of the tools you're given. -  so often you're like "how on earth am I going to solve it with only these 3 items"; in Manifold Garden the hard part is recognizing that the game gave you like 5 cubes but you only need 2 to solve it so don't overthink the solution. - the most direct comparison, as this was the first non-Euclidean-space, 1st-person puzzle game to popularize the genre. Antichamber is less polished and harder to get started with, but once you "get it" the puzzles are very addicting and it's hard to put the game down until you finish. Manifold Garden is significantly more welcoming to new players, but lacking in the "addictive challenge" department. a trippy puzzle game, but one that leans on🚶simulator elements to sell the game in lieu of mind-bending challenges

_childDocuments_.review: tl; drl(ol):  is an amazing puzzle game that delivers thoughtful design. If you believe that video games have potential as a non-verbal art form, just ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ buy it.1. WHAT IS THE GAME ABOUT?One of the complaints I saw in the reviews section was that the game was too easy or linear or something like that. While this is partially true, this is hardly an issue. Indeed, you’re not gonna find crazy hard-ass puzzles like those of . The game tends to a be a walking simulator with simple but interesting puzzles, and focusing on its architectural design more than anything else. Another two things can be said regarding this.First, the game was initially designed to be a much more ambitious in terms of level design, with inter and intra connections between areas. Check out his post in case you’re interested:And that would influence puzzles in general.2. IS THE GAME "EASY"? WELL, YES AND NOSecond, the impression that the game is “easy” is for the "main" game. There is “hidden” path in which stuff could get really hard. If you do it without a guide, it will require a lot (and I mean a lot) of observation an exploration. If you go this path (which can be done in the first playthrough if you are patient and attentive, although it is highly unrecommended), you will quickly drop the impression that this is a “casual” walking simulator. While I do not agree withs kind of design (of denying the player access to contents of the game), I cannot know if this was intended since the beginning or included as a “NG+” because of the restrictions imposed on the initially planned design.Anyway, I am absolutely convinced that difficulty is not a determining factor of quality. And I am not even talking about games exclusively. This is a suspicion that might arise when studying other art forms. For instance, Shakespeare is held as the greatest writer in Western literature (take my word for it). But his texts are not considered “difficult” in the sense of being hermetic. They abound with subtleties, but this does not make them difficult. It makes them (the texts) demanding. James Joyce and Thomas Pynchon, on the other hand, are considered difficult because they are hermetic. But that does not make them better than Shakespeare. Joyce, in fact, is often regarded as being as great as Shakespeare, but . Therefore, difficulty is not a factor of quality, even though it might appear in the final piece as a byproduct.3. CONCLUSIONIn conclusion, if you believe that the true aesthetic potential of video games is in exploration and non-verbal thoughtful design, then, I should check out this game.

_childDocuments_.review: Awe-inspiring, trippy, beautiful, and mind-blowing. I'd recommend this to everyone, whether you're a fan of puzzle games or not. Just understand that this is a somewhat short experience (~5 hours)The puzzle design here is quite solid and highly rewarding. However, it's not particularly difficult and it's basically a linear set of challenges. This is less "The Witness" and more "Portal 1". It introduces a handful of clever mechanics and develops them with gently increasing difficulty. This strikes me as the sort of game that has been playtested to hell and back - I don't expect there will be much frustration for most players. For that reason, I feel like this would be a fantastic introduction to the puzzle game genre for people who don't generally play these sorts of gamesIf you _are_ the sort of nerd that plays puzzle games, you still need to get this. Do I really need to convince you? It's like Antichamber, but EVEN MORE TRIPPY and with ten times the polish and finesse. This is an obligatory purchase, nothing is going to compete with this for another decadeAnyway, I feel like I've a disservice to the game by just talking about the puzzle design. Yeah, it's solid, but the real selling point here is the atmosphere and environments. There aren't words for how incredible it feels to simply navigate this game - just look at the trailer. Some ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ legend looked at *Relativity* by MC Escher and said "man I need to make this into a game... but also with a heroic dose of DMT". The absolute madman.The best thing about this game is just how polished it is. It's visually stunning. The soundtrack is fantastic. The controls work perfectly. This could very well have been a rough, low-budget game and it still would have earned a place in the obscure pantheon of mind**** puzzlers, but it's executed flawlessly and for that we are all incredibly lucky

_childDocuments_.review: Manifold Garden is a puzzle game inspired by, and faithful to, the artwork of M. C. Escher. It's similar to The Bridge, Disoriented and, to a lesser extent, Antichamber. What makes it truly unique are its awe-inspiring, infinitely-repeating worlds (achieved via seamless 3D world wrapping) and the clever use of portals to create the illusion of impossible architectures.The key puzzle mechanic involves altering gravity / changing your orientation. The puzzles are fairly intuitive and rewarding, though the difficulty curve is more like a hill with some trivial puzzles towards the end, while the more difficult ones tended to be in the middle. There's nothing terribly demanding in terms of timed execution or precise movements, although some puzzles can get tedious, especially when a desired surface is not immediately within reach. The soundtrack is great, especially the majestic pieces that play upon entering certain worlds (plus the credits song is excellent).Although it is a tad pricey given its short length (3-4 hours), Manifold Garden is an outstanding game that's well worth playing for all fans of the puzzle genre and/or aficionados of Escheresque architecture.

_childDocuments_.review: Game has the unique distinction of enabling HDR by default. In fact, this is possibly the only game I have ever seen that uses HDR that has no calibration menu (or option to turn off).(That, of course, means what we have here is little more than LDR -> HDR remapping to use the attached display's full luminance range with no advanced post-processing).Nonetheless, given the fact that virtually all games in existence are capable of LDR -> HDR and none have made it a policy to do by default, this is still pretty neat. Would like to see more games take this approach even if they don't make an attempt to do more advanced HDR-related work.----As for the actual game, my brain hurts.

_childDocuments_.review: This one has been a game i've had my eyes on for a while and finally got it gifted by some friends and safe to say I'm happy i got to play it. The visuals are stunning and the sound design is worthy of multiple eargasms, the puzzle design is awesome and stays good in every level, but there's only about 2.5/3 hours of game time for the main game. I say for the main game because there is ONE achievement that quadrupled this play time for me. Having a hard to get achievement is very nice for most games: it adds an extra challenge for those who loved playing it and want more of the good stuff. That is technically also the case for this game, but to me it was an absolute drag to get. Looking for the correct way to make sure you do everything correctly is a repetition of checking every little corner to see if there's a pathway there. I liked the cube transportation (which cost quite the effort) because you knew what to do, but the endless finding of secret tunnels had me looking up a walkthrough in the end.All and all a very nice game for those who loved portal and puzzle games of the like, it has both the nostalgic feel of the test chamber and an extremely refreshing set-up with more freedom than most other puzzlers fail to give you. That combined with the awesome sound and music makes it an awfully good experience.TL;DR Stunning game with one frustrating achievement

_childDocuments_.review: Not as mind-boggling as it may look, fairly simple once you get used to the mechanics. Not worth $20 for the length, though absolutely worth $10 or similar. Unforgettable concept, just wish it was a bit longer/had more levels, maybe a second pack of levels or something. Spent at least a half an hour stumped then double-checked the fruit tree and saw I missed a fruit. Very good game.
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: A nice and neat walking(Or running, the world is so vast) sim game with a hint of puzzles. The good mechanics never got elaborated. It's got potentials but the puzzles are just not challenging enough to qualify as real puzzles. The visuals are stunning and beautiful. Overall it's a bit underwhelming as puzzle game, but I would still recommend it for its graphical beauty.
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: This is a puzzle game second and an exploration of the concept of infinity and perspective first. The purpose of the puzzles are to provide context and motivation for observing this geometry.The most similar game to Manifold Garden that I've played is Antichamber, which came out in 2013. Both are abstract first person puzzle games that have minimalist aesthetics with solid colors and a lot of cubes. What makes this game different is its focus: Antichamber was a puzzle game where the player had to adapt to the changing rules and properties of the game, while Manifold Garden's rules are more simple straightforward. Structures are infinitely duplicated on 6 axis, and the player can change what plane is considered the floor/which direction gravity is applied. The main levels are large, aesthetically pleasing structures that you have to explore on multiple planes to solve.Manifold Garden fills me with more dread than typical horror media. Horror usually relies on the hidden and unexpected: monsters lurking in the darkness, unpredictable and sinister thoughts and behaviors. These things elicit fear because they cannot be easily perceived. While the visuals of this game are bright, simple, and clear, it is difficult for humans to comprehend the scale of infinity. This is the unique strength of this game. Portal is a puzzle game about connecting two points in space, Superliminal is a puzzle game about depth and perspective, Antichamber is a puzzle game about non-Euclidean space, Manifold Garden is a puzzle game about infinity. It explores a unique concept, and it does so beautifully.
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: Nice enough little puzzle game. Visually it blends the clean lines and bright colors of Antichamber's regular levels with the majestic, trippy, spacious design of its final level. The puzzle design focuses less on clever, mind-bending solutions and more on confirming that you know the rules it's teaching you and that you can explore comprehensively enough to find the parts of a solution. This makes for a less thinky, more meditative experience.It's not _short_-short, but it's shorter than I usually prefer in a puzzle-oriented game. At my own personal price sensitivity, the current sale price of 15 USD seems reasonable enough but I wouldn't want to go higher.
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: Manifold Garden is a first person puzzle game in universe with a peculiar geometry and controllable gravity. The puzzles are well designed. Many are on the easier side as they teach the mechanics, but there are also more complex headscratchers. I must also highlight there is not a single word of text in the game – everything is taught through exploration and interaction.
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: The puzzle aren't especially hard. The game world (infinitely repeating geometry) soon becomes dull.The difficulty comes from locating items/doors: If you don't have the same gravity-direction as an object, it'll appear beige (on a beige background). Hence, the game has the same kind of frustration as point&click adventure games: pixel hunting.I got stuck on very mundane problems: realizing that an object could be picked up, that two doors were not the same, that there was a door in a messy geometry.Besides that, the game world is very dry and unwelcoming, even depressing at times. I was worried about the game creator mental state: why all the black clouds?You don't want to linger in the game world more than necessary: solve the puzzles and get out of it. It's not a place where you would want to come back and explore. It's a bit like high school.
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: Phenomenal puzzle game, a fantastic visual style that is striking and absolutely insane in scope. The game's puzzles are well designed and very creative. Would highly recommend to those who want a chill, albeit complex puzzle solving experience that feels entirely different than anything they may have played.10/10.
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: Gorgeous and breath-taking game. The visuals alone gave me so much wallpaper-worthy material, and the OST is extremely calm and chill. The puzzles aren't outrageously difficult to work out, but there's some thought involved when working for the "The Game Is Not Enough" achievement.Good luck and have fun navigating the Manifold Garden!
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: The game managed to firmly grip my mind and pull me into its world with several good points: - The many complex and beautiful geometries always keep your vision occupied with something.- The generally rare tinges of color in the world always carry some meaning and make gameplay objects easily identifiable- Sound design is convincing and very fitting with the visuals.- Unique gameplay mechanics using the manifold principles.- The puzzles range from easy to medium, making use of all the unique gameplay mechanics.Overall this game has me wanting more. Sadly it is only a few hours of gameplay until you reach the end. For my taste it could have used a few highly challenging, complex puzzles at the end.
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: Friend got me into puzzles, including getting this one, but I ended up playing it before him.I wasn't disappointed. The visuals are pleasing if not a little disorienting. Once you realize how perspective functions in this game, you'll have to think in many ways how to approach the puzzle, some thinking within the box, some without. Definitely recommend for someone getting into puzzle games, but also great for those who want a good mental exercise.That said, a BIG warning if you get nauseous or suffer from vertigo: the game's sound design and FOV is so well-done that a large drop will trigger the latter. And I didn't know that my vertigo was bad until this game.That said, I'm grateful that there is no death in the game either. I managed to get myself squeezed between two giant bi-directional sliding blocks, but I'm clearly the Incredible Hulk or Stitch, because I could hold that ♥♥♥♥ on my shoulder until I'm out safe. Beautiful stuff. Please play this if you have even a slight interest, it'll be worth your while.
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: I saw this game, among others, in a youtube video and thought it looked like fun but it was only when i started actually playing it that I realized just how freaking rad this game is. Literally every moment of free time this past week I have spent playing this game which is astounding considering I normally hate sitting in front of a screen. Bravo and kudos to the devs!
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: If there was a game capturing how first Portal playthroughs felt, something easy enough but requiring you think. A, dare I say, "experience" rather than a game. and one in a puzzle genre...Beneath good graphics, awesome soundtrack and lack of a story, in usual sense of the word, there are a few curious bugs (not telling you what and would like them to stay) and plenty "what if?" moments. No mods and entire start-finish playthrough is rather short, but worth it. 6 hours of pure enjoyment at your own pace, whatever it will be.Manifold Garden is unlike anything I have played before and that could be a high praise on its own (provided good experience), but it somehow achieved what  games manage — received my personal seal of highest approval.
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: This game seemed reminiscent of Antichamber, which really excited me! Antichamber is hands down the best puzzle game ever made, so I had high expectations for this.From what I played, it was a glorified walking sim with gravity mechanics. It wasnt engaging, period. The most interesting part of the whole thing was the geometry of the levels, but that too got old quick.
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: its ok... super pretty game, great experience, but a pretty week puzzle game. the devs ended up reusing a lot of the same puzzle solutions/tricks over and over that really ruined the experience. super easy puzzling, too much so, the only times i got stuck was when i couldnt find the next box to use, they tended to hide puzzle pieces instead of making the puzzles more exciting. so eh... i wish it was better.
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: Amazing game. Short, but sweet - I felt like I got a lot out of it.The premise is simple: you play as an unseen and unheard character (or nothing, really) that can manipulate gravity in a world filled with various colors of cubes and the game's main selling point: its endless architecture. Manifold Garden is one of - if not the only - games to truly capture what it feels like to be inside of the infinite. For a more in-depth explanation as to what that actually means, I'd highly recommend Jacob Geller's video "The Shape of Infinity," which is all about how this game continues a long-standing tradition of non-euclidean, "infinite" architecture. It made me appreciate the game in an entirely new light, and also helped me understand the true beauty of Manifold Garden.All-in-all: I'd say it's worth the price. Obviously, if you can get it on sale, go for it. I do not regret supporting William Chyr and his co-workers on this wonderful game, and I'm very happy to have experienced it.
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: Other negative reviews summarize it well. The game works as an art piece, but not much more than that. There wasn't a single 'aha!' moment in this game, nothing felt particularly engaging or fascinating in any way. Further, the game is very, very short for its price. I managed to beat the game with most achievements in around 3 hours.
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: I'm gonna finish it but it's not very good. My main gibe with this game is that there's almost no gameplay. The entire game is you stacking cubes on top of one another in zany ways. There's really not much more interactivity than that. Your character has no abilities beyond walking, running, picking up cubes, and pressing buttons. It's really not a good use of the non-Euclidian environments. The only thing this game has going for it is the unique geometry of the maps. If you've already played Antichamber, the geometry really isn't all that impressive. In fact, I'll stick my neck out and suggest that the ONLY players who will truly enjoy this game are those that have not yet played a game with non-Euclidean geometry.I'm left wondering if the developer ever actually put a lot of thought into whether or not his game was fun to play. The dev may have been so enamored with his non-Euclidean creations that he forgot to build an actual game. See, I'm fine with minimalist puzzlers. But usually the devs of those games put in a variety of objects to pick up and put down.For me, this game is almost a total failure and not worth the 15 bucks I paid. I'm not usually this harsh with bad reviews but I honestly feel like almost any game developer could have come up with a few ideas to make the game more fun. The design is bad and there's no excuse.
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: A good game that delivers what you expect, but doesn't overstay its welcome either. Not flawless (a few concepts I think could have been introduced better), but very very good.  The puzzles mostly get into a "what haven't I seen/explored yet" rather than being too mind-bending, but that's good for the overall feel of the game.Worth it on a sale, probably not worth it full-price.
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: Manifold Garden is the videogame equivalent of trying to assemble a 5000 piece spiral puzzle while listening to Tool's Lateralus and so high on Acid you can't even feel your fingertips. Hell, you don't even remember you HAVE fingertips.It's been real hell with all the floods here in my state, thank you for taking my head outside for a while.I absolutely recommend this one.
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: Good puzzle game with interesting mechanics. They hit that sweet spot of not being too hard to solve that I was frustrated, but also werent so easy that they were tedious. It didnt overstay its welcome; It explored the different ways to twist the puzzles mechanics without doing the same thing over and over. The visuals are beautiful, interesting, and even interestingly unsettling. I finished the main story in 4.4 hours. I bought it on sale for $8 and it was well worth it.
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: manages to create uniquely intricate physics-bending puzzles whilst utilizing the same core gameplay elements from start to finish. Their synergy and how they complement the puzzles is the core reason why  deceptively simple gameplay loop was so enjoyable.And the very first puzzle establishes rule '' –  There are  you can shift your perspective to, each tied to a specific colour, in turn enabling you to interact with items corresponding to said colour. The game doesn’t tell you this; There is no long wall of text explaining every mechanic and instead utilizes the  approach. A perfect example is how the game handles . If you aren’t standing in the correct plane, their colour tells you they aren't intractable. They'll always be white, with just a hint of their true colour. This lack of hand-holding is something I personally love in games. While it can lead to some head-scratching moments, it also creates that "" moment once you finally find the solution. We are all very closely acquainted with , but you must rediscover it once more. In this physics-bending and seemingly nonsensical world, gravity works in a slightly unconventional way. It only affects the current plane you occupy whilst freezing everything in place for the other. As such, manipulating your perspective, constantly shifting it and manoeuvring items will prove challenging, but once you open your mind to the beauty of  physics-bending puzzles, it becomes oh so satisfying.  You can't jump, and sometimes no amount of plane-shifting will get you to the other side. Well, all it takes is a simple . Since each structure is endlessly repeated, taking that plunge into the unending abyss allows you to land right on top of it. As someone who isn't on friendly terms with towering heights, I had a period of adjustment to the game's rules. Entering a new puzzle room will often yield a familiar sight - a lonely power slot, coloured cubes dangling from a tree, and (another) locked door. This may appear simple enough; just pluck a cube, place cube in the slot, and (un)presto!!!...the door (still) doesn't open. Well, the game is a bit more challenging than it lets on. , and as such, activating it requires the . This frequently requires clever manoeuvring of two different coloured cubes;  The game later introduces a couple of new mechanics, that add to the already complex gameplay, complicating your life as you juggle cubes around. You'll be able to alter the path of a stream, grow your very own cube trees or even change the colour of cubes. The end goal will always stay the same,  Of course there is, as you are seeking the almighty . You see, a foul corruption has spread across the world of  and enthralled its many gardens. Restoring these  to each root slot is your ultimate goal and the only way to dispel this corruption and bring back the vibrant colours. With each new garden come new challenging puzzles. Despite a sense of familiarity between them, the game introduces new gameplay mechanics at the ideal moment. It's always the last puzzle of each garden that does so, with those leading up to it reinforcing your prior knowledge.While it was a marvellous experience for me, as a casual puzzle gamer, I certainly see how it could disappoint the more seasoned puzzle gamers. The lack of a real challenge many of these puzzles might probably pose could disincentivize them to keep playing. But the devs created a scenario just for this occasion –  So, if you fancy yourself a puzzle game connoisseur, take the plunge and re-explore the world of  once more, pursue the seemingly impossible, and finish the game without placing a single .The game has a minimalistic, almost completely stark aesthetic. Each structure is constructed out of simple textureless polygons. Looking at them up close might yield an unimpressive sight, but taking a step back opens you to the true beauty of . The clean, stark aesthetic lends itself perfectly in creating enthralling never-ending rows of simple, yet complex structures stretching to infinity. And throughout my journey, the sublime soundtrack was the perfect minstrel, capturing the sense of awe and mystery surrounding this strange world. is a stellar, physics-bending puzzler with the synergy of core gameplay mechanics keeping the game interesting from start to finish. It's astonishing how beautifully this game is, creating complex and never-ending structures out of simple polygons. Couple that with its marvellous soundtrack, and you get a serene experience that is hard to put into words.
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: Beautiful calming experience.  Great ending.  Literally worth watching just the ending if you haven't seen it.  The mechanic used for the main quest-  Place cube, start lasers, pick up god cube, take god cube through new door and place.   It's simple enough.   I got lost twice and stuck once, would be nice if the areas had names.   No single puzzle is terribly hard and they are mildly repetitive but not to the point that you dislike any of them.  Haven't done extra achievements other than the main ending. Highly recommend.
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic piece of art. Visuals are mind-bending and gorgeous. The audio design is superb and really adds to the ambiance. Features some great music that drives the momentum and atmosphere. This game really understands how to make puzzles fun. It doesn't feel like tedious work. Even traversal becomes a game in itself. This is far more of an experience than a typical grind it out puzzle game. If you shy away from puzzle games but are attracted to the art style you should absolutely give this game a go. Highly recommended 10/10.
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: A glorified walking simulator with good visuals and sound design. What really holds this game back is the lack of direction given to the player. Good puzzles are usually in confined spaces, allowing you to see everything you have at your disposal, so you can form a clear picture in your mind of what to do and how to proceed. The game starts this way but then quickly diverges. A lot of my time was then spent navigating the terrain until I found the next door to enter or the block I was looking for so I could progress. I love the design of the world, but it does more to hinder the puzzles than it does to make them better, and most of the puzzles that are there aren't really difficult, just time-consuming and mostly just involve picking up a cube and placing it somewhere else.
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: Holy wow. Incredible visuals, incredible sound and music. The story-line is up to the imagination of the player but I think it's better that way. The puzzles are playful and it's comforting that if you fall, you end up back where you started. The structures and landscapes created here are immense and beautiful and the non-euclidean aspect is constantly mind-blowing. Play this game (all the way to the end, you won't regret it)!
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: Fun puzzle game. I only have two complaints,First, at times it can be hard to tell where you have to go or what you have to do. In fairness, this is made difficult because most of the rooms are infinite and repeating. It does become easier as the game progresses as you learn a bit about the game's level design. My tip is that you almost never have to stray from the main path, and in fact if you do, that is probably going to be how you get lost. Second, I ran into at least one bug where a critical object didn't spawn in. This happened early in the game when I didn't fully understand what the intended loop was. So this combined with the previous issue left me wandering around the infinite level trying to figure out what to do, when in reality I needed to restart the game.
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: Solid puzzle game that thankfully doesn't outstay it's welcome.  The visuals and infinite nature of the world are the clear highlight and main reason to play.  Wouldn't recommend this to people to get motion sickness easily, are looking for a story-rich game, or really want to challenge themselves.  Many puzzles involve only one or two steps, with the answer blatantly obvious if you just explore the room enough.  No puzzles really pushed the boundaries of or effectively combined the mechanics introduced and nearly every one made me think "ok cool, but that's it?" Would probably be immensely more enjoyable on mind-altering substances, which might've actually been what the creator was going for given the trippy visuals and one-dimensional puzzles.  7/10
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: Brilliant game! Had me at awe at almost every level, envolving you in the impossible structures and mindbending architectures. Not to mention those perfectly timed blade runner-esque soundtrack to enhance that feeling of immensitude. Loved every aspect of this game's aesthetics, as it captures all those elements of non-euclidian geometry and repeating patterns a few games had toyed with and here are implemented flawlessly.About the gameplay: it's an improvement over anti-chamber, which is an obvious game to compare to for all the similarities in style. AC was a game I enjoyed immensly, but in it you quickly get stuck without a clue what to do since almost all the game is accessible at the start and the game confuses you more than it helps you. Sure this motivates exploration, but some of the puzzles from AC were a bit too obtuse and I couldn't for the life of me get through with without getting hints from the steam forums. Still, a great game.Manifold on the other hand is almost completely linear, and that helped at lot to grasp its mechanics, especially since entering a new room on Manifold for the first time is always a bit overwhelming. The puzzles have a great initial difficult curve, incredible design and engage you to learn about this weird world through experimentation, which is fenomenal!However, I do feel the later "half of the game" feels a lot rushed, very few puzzles compared to the beginning, and they stop exploring new ideas or expand more on the mechanics the game already showed you. To be fair, this happens after ~75% of the game, and until then the puzzles are really exceptional and well designed. And despite this apparent "drop" of quality in the last few puzzles, I still enjoyed progressing since just the puzzle-rooms themselves where amazing to look and walk around on.I was waiting a long time for this game to release, got super hyped, and it came through better than I could have hoped. Looking forward to more weird gorgeous gems like this.
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: I was waiting for this for quite some time to come out on Steam. And it was totally worth it. Great art style, mind bending architecture and a nice puzzle game.Also, while I'd love a native version, it does run decently via Proton, which was really a requirement for me, so I'm happy to confirm that it works quite well.Would recommend.Edit: Finished it, even though for some reason the last achievement didn't trigger. Really worth it and IMO one of the best games in recent years. The trippy ending is also quite fun.
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: So rad. This is what i'd expect to get if somebody told be that M. C. Escher made a puzzle game. The game makes great use of the impossible architecture in very fun & satisfying ways. This is easily the best puzzle game I've played since the Portal franchise. It is a little short, but not too short. it took me about the same amount of time to beat as it took me to beat Portal 1. Fantastic game. If you like puzzle games, give it a try.
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic game! Honestly, my favorite part of this is just absorbing the sheer scale of everything. You know that feeling you get when you stand on a viewing platform, overlooking a scenic landscape? That moment when your mouth hangs open a little. The game kept creating moments like that. Often you'll be traversing in tiny corridors, from puzzle to puzzle, but every so often you'll exit to one of many infinite landscapes. Seeing your world expand from a closed room to, well... infinity is an experience I wish I could experience again.I'm lukewarm on the puzzles. On one hand, the core mechanic of easily changing gravity makes for some interesting, and in a few cases, mindblowing concepts and solutions; however the execution and pacing could be better. While the game is good at introducing new mechanics as you progress, there is a point where it feels repetitive. There were stretches that unfortunately felt like padding, reusing the same concept seen earlier with minimal changes. Thankfully, none of the puzzles were overwhelming. Each "puzzle" is usually self contained with a very limited scope. So even if one stumps you for a while or is dragging on, it won't hold you up too long.I do want to highlight the sound design though. The soundtrack is mostly ambient with some melodic tracks mixed in, however the light synth combined with a handful of natural sounds completely meshes with the landscapes. My favorite moments were the rare moments of Overall, would highly recommend this. Manifold garden is a unique chance to experience infinity.
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: Manifold Garden is nothing short of a marvelous game full of perplexing mechanics, and beautiful scenery. Absolutely recommend if your a fan of games such as Outer Wilds or Superliminal; even more so if you just like solving problems that require outside the box thinking. It is quite short, but I think its worth the full price based solely on the one of a kind experience and definitely if its on sale. It's very rare you'll stumble across a game like this, it's best to treasure them when you do.
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: I'd say this game is art first, puzzle game second. An occasionally breathtaking world they have created here - all kinds of colours, and amazing geometry. It's like being inside a 3d fractal or kaleidoscope.The music suits the game too!I felt some of the block puzzles toward the end were too generic for such a great premise but they didn't take too long to solve.Never felt frustrated by any of the puzzles and enjoyed satisfaction when the solution was found.Sometimes like at the end there were multiple paths and by choosing one the others felt locked out - might go back in for secrets later.If you enjoyed Portal, Talos Principle, Light matter etc, get this for sure!
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: This was such an amazing and magical journey!! The geometry, the architecture, the colors, the soundscape and atmosphere: I've rarely been so immersed in a game as this one. The puzzles are sometimes tricky, but I've never felt frustration coming up. When I got tired of puzzling I simply shouted "farewell", jumped into infinity and enjoyed the hypnotizing view. And the ending is the cherry on top! Simply beautiful!
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: Challenging, beautiful, and rewarding. The world truly encapsulates you, and every aspect of the game ties together seamlessly to build the immersion.  I really have to give kudos to everyone involved. The music and sound design were fantastic, and really lend to the visual style. Give the programming team a medal, I have no idea how you could build something this crazy and make it run so efficiently. And to whoever added the orthographic photo-mode— thank you. My 5 hour playthrough was . If this ever goes on sale, it's a complete no-brainer.
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: If you live in a part of the world that allows recreational consumption of mind-altering substances, you owe it to yourself to play this game while on the highest dose you feel you can safely handle. If you're gonna be blowing your mind anyway, may as well get the most mind-blowingest experience you can get, yannow? The game isn't big on story, which makes sense as I'm not currently high enough to conceive of a story that fits the environments presented, but the puzzles are damn well designed for a game that contains no explicit explanations of mechanics outside the basics of movement and gravity control. There's no GLaDOS voice telling you what a laser is and how you can redirect them, that's all on you to figure out. But the puzzles are designed such that you tend to discover all the relevant aspects through just playing, which is good. The environments are what are going to make or break this game for you, they're what people are here for. Without the environment, it's just a bunch of block placing puzzles, which Portal did better. Hope you aren't afraid of heights, because there is no jump button, and you have an infinite way to fall in most rooms, if they can be called such. An infinite staircase may have walls and a ceiling, but will still contain enough space to fit infinite Earths, so can it still really be considered inside? In short, hearty recommendation of this game, especially under the influence of basically anything that doesn't fully divorce you from your surrounds. You'll need your eyes perceiving reality to enjoy this game to the fullest.
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: There is a certain thrill to this game - to setting gravity in the direction of your destination and then leaping into the void, hurtling down hallways and across expanses of space, flying past repetitions of the places you've been, to eventually crash feet-first into the wall of the location you wanted to go to - that really must be experienced to be believed.
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: An amazing puzzle game that forces you to think around the corner...literally.Unfortunately a little bit short but an experience noone should miss especially if you like puzzle games. I am honest with you guys: If you get easily lost in a city and have a bad sense of navigation you will probably hate this game.Another big plus is the great soundtrack used.
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: Very Unique, 100% completion is practically impossible without a guide unless you have atleast 3 genius' with too much free timeIt feels like the game is so large but so small at the same time, it would be nice if the game naturally suggested taking non-linear routes instead of the player having to go out of their way to find them or maybe this type of game just isn't my thing.
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: If you ignore the incredible aesthetics the game really only has one trick - its "modulo" repeating worldspace - up its sleeve. Thankfully it's a *really really impressive* and aesthetically pleasing trick and the gravity shifting along with no fall damage lets you play around with it to your hearts content. The visual style of the game is so striking and impressive the game knows it and supports it with one of the best photo modes i've seen.Probably not a good experience if you struggle with virtual vertigo and lack of spatial sense though.
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: The game is incredible. The end of the game just make me cry. A masterpiece for demonstrating computer graphics and art. And the game play also gives a perfect 'hacking' experience, you are in a complex and gigantic world trying to solve puzzle without explicit clues. After you figuring out the right solution, a door opens with a mechanical unlocking sound. Nothing can be more rewarding than 'unlock doors' for hackers. Great game, 10/10.
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: This is a decent although a purely mechanical and soulless puzzle game.Gravity alteration is already a well-worn concept in the genre but here it doesn't feel stale so points for that. The gameplay can give you a headache. The puzzles are cool, varying in difficulty, but for the most part they're not as hard as navigating the large environments. The game, with its infinitely repeating patterns and clean colouring, certainly looks nice but it offers no real motivation and by the end I just wanted to finish it. And is there a pay-off to all of it? If you like acid, then I guess there is.
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: In the beginning I was strucked by the beautiful and endless architecture. It was something completely new and unknown and it made so much fun to fall endlessly and never leaving the place. I also loved the idea to complete color levels for one part. In my opinion, it was very hard in the beginning to figure it out how to proceed but when I found out how to complete the color levels, it felt actually a bit too easy then. I would have designed the color levels slightly harder and focus more on that. Because when I completed all 6 colors I thought the finish line is near and was so anticipated to reach the ending it made me fidgeting. So I would have designed the final level somewhat shorter.But all in all I can recommend the game if you love beautiful architecture, colors and the feeling of transcendence. Also the ending firework was very fantastic. Absolutely worth it to finish the game and wahtch it.Thank you for creating this game.

_childDocuments_.review: Masterpiece, amazing, breathtaking, jaw-dropping and mind-bending are some words that can describe . I have been waiting years for a game to fill my "Antichamber" void and this game does so in spades. The world is infinitely linked together with impossible stairways and overlapping rooms. You have the ability to manipulate gravity and traverse on any surface you are facing. Solving puzzles involve moving colored cubes around that are linked to one specific direction of gravity marked by a specific color. Each world you explore introduces unique puzzle mechanics that can be combined to open new pathways. There are no enemies/threats in this game and falling is encouraged to help reach the next location or solve a puzzle by eliminating fall damage. The audio design is perfect, visuals are simple yet stunning, and the controls are flawless. There are two completely different routes you can take (God cube vs Non God cube) with the latter being significantly harder which extends the overall completion time. Included is one of the best photomodes I have used and a good chunk of my playtime was spent taking screenshots (See below). If you want to experience walking through a stunning MC Escher-like world or base jump into infinity, than this game is for you. Highly recommended. [100/10]

_childDocuments_.review: I'm not normally one to write reviews, but this is the most mind-bending game I've played in a long time. From the beautifully simplistic, yet impossibly infinite level designs to the reality warping puzzle mechanics and solutions, every step of the journey was filled with excitement and wonder. There's a whole other level of satisfaction felt when you have to defy everything you think you know to find the solution, and this game kept it coming. The ending sequence was beautiful, but it made me sad the game was over. Definitely running through a few more times for those hidden achievements. 9/10 the god cubes visual distortion and smoke/darkness particles made admiring the scenery hard at times.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is incredibly good. In the kind of specific, but quite well populated genre of "first person walking-about puzzle games with a big gimmick", this is one of the best. The only downside is it's not hugely long: I finished it in 4 hours. However just the experience of wandering through this world is excellent. In the downtime between puzzles you navigate these incredible infinite fractal like spaces, making the simple act of going to the next puzzle room a wonder. And the puzzles themselves are good, there's several different mechanics to learn, but each one is well designed and put to several different uses by the end.10/10, this is one of the game you'll wish you could erase from your mind and experience again for the first time.

_childDocuments_.review: Manifold Garden is a . It plays with the idea of gravity, after which you will get a lot of headache at first and you will feel like you are falling all the time when you close your eyes  This will subside after a few days, don't worry. Furthermore, you may experience pain from the psychedelic kaleidoscopic effects and caution is advised if you suffer from  After enduring these pains, you will have to engage your brain and think deep and hard about how to open and navigate through different portals, because this world is a seemingly endless symmetry .What I personally find a shame is the fact that the entire game presents a paradox of the laws of physics and does not explicitly reveal any story. Why did the garden find itself in this state?  What are the shadows that surround the architecture? And who am I? In the distance in the symmetry, the nothingness can be seen running with the cube to open another portal.It is appropriate to  the sci-fi music, which received nominations and honorable mentions at various competitions (eg Game of the Year at PGMGA, Independent Games Festival). Successful piano tones sound when building a garden, 80s synthesizers when grabbing a God Cube, hinting at danger.The concept of paradoxical gravity is, among other things, inspired by the well-known Dutch artist  and above all by his work Relativity.Ratings:Game Presentation: 4/5Narrative: 3/5Gameplay: 5/5Graphics: 5/5Audio: 5/5Price: 5/5

You look left, right, up and down and you can see this. The music is very spacey and calming, the visual style is simple and many areas of the game are non-euclidian. In other words, impossible to exist in the real world. It is pretty short, I beat it in around 4 hours, but it is mind-bending and I would recommend you try it when its on sale.

_childDocuments_.review: I really wish I had bought this game sooner and put a lot more time into exploring it.If you're a fan of games such as Antichamber, NaissanceE and Monument Valley, this game is perfect for you. The music, visuals, and architecture of the game are very well done. The puzzles themselves are well thought through, and pose a decent challenge, but never too much as to become tedious and exhausting. The mesmerizing non-Euclidean architecture of the world is itself part of the puzzle as you often shift gravity and traverse it on all of its sides.The main route itself might is straightforward enough and rewards you with a very decent feeling of satisfaction at the end when you finish it. But if you wish you could play a little longer, the game won't leave you unsatisfied in the slightest. The ultimate challenge and true test of your will is in attempting to get the "The Game is Not Enough" achievement. It's in this playthrough that you will discover the true depth of the game's puzzles, and the absurdly complex and hidden shortcuts and paths that you missed in the normal playthrough. You may have noticed some of these mechanics before but now they are not only essential but sometimes your only way to progress. If you manage to do it alone, I truly congratulate you for this accomplishment but I gave in and looked up a guide or two to help me along the way to get this achievement. Still, I could not believe what I just did when I finished the game and got the achievement and it made me appreciate the game a lot more. And that is why I write this review.Get this game, take your time and enjoy it to the fullest. You will not regret it.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a very ingenious and creative, yet orderly, game that gave me (at least in contrast to some speed demons) many hours of pleasure and thought.  One thing I especially appreciated was the ability to reposition and solve difficult puzzles without time limits.  It allows the player to do things that are relatively difficult in the real world, such as walking up the sides of buildings and falling from great heights without injury.  Oh, and it's very colorful!  It will be difficult now to look at prominent architectural monuments without imagining them sideways and upside down.  An update on the childhood pastime of looking up at the ceiling and imagining what it would be like to walk around there.

_childDocuments_.review: It's okay but worth way less than what it goes for. It can also drag on.I bought this game particularly for the "surreal" part which I see in the tags, even now, but surreal implies at least something with an attachment to reality, in the way of people or entities that do things other than participate in a puzzle (you could say this was the birds but that's a very small thing). I didn't get that though and that's completely fine, I played it to the end anyways. Another thing that isn't necessarily a problem but worth mentioning is that there is no story, besides a vague hint that you .This game has pretty environments, and relies on this. This is also why there is a camera mechanic. The environments are intricately detailed with arches and pillars and other architectural things that it is sometimes annoying to move. This contributed to my impatience but was only a factor.The levels were also very large, which both contributed to the prettiness of them and made them take much longer to navigate (sometimes; gravity can help you effortlessly fall to places you need to be). And to allow them to be seem so large, there is very little between point A and point B (besides architectural nuisances); this leaves a very barren set of worlds, besides some Toranas (the game has a theme of grandiosity and transcendence; the player can change gravity and uses "god" cubes to construct things) and other shrines. Sometimes these serve well to point us in the correct direction, but they are still underused and generally useless when they are used.An exception is that weird structure with the "snow globe" cubes, which doesn't add anything to the game but still feels nice to have around.Exploring got exhaustive, but it is also necessary to understand the levels. I'd end up going over the same platforms 20 times looking for something in plain sight, or trying to find a tree I haven't seen before. This is annoying due to the size of the worlds. The barrenness did not help this.Some mechanics are easy to get. I blinked when the "rotation" buttons came on screen during the first water section and connect the ideas in my head. I wondered what to do for an hour and explored the area over and over in this time. It's not totally intuitive where the prerequisites for a puzzle are.This sucks because the puzzles themselves are pretty quick to solve once you have the prerequisites. Sometimes I'd just follow the power cables without thinking and end up at the next solution without much thought. And, despite prerequisites being difficult to find, the actual puzzle's location is usually very easy to find. I found them using what I described in this paragraph. The game also has very little personality other than its "Escher-esque" architecture, but Escher actually incorporated a lot of tiny details into his work, and many characters, too! For example, in his infinite staircase, you can see some people sitting on the stairs at the foot of the building, and one contemplating the movement of these figures; strange foliage; the clothes of a jester; these characterised his work in a way this game lacks, and for that it fails to be so "Escher-esque."I really liked watching the birds, though. And the music was good enough that I turned off what I usually listen to. It reminds me of Nine Inch Nails' Ghosts albums.

_childDocuments_.review: I think describing the landscapes in Manifold Garden as "infinite" is a little disingenuous. They're infinite in the same way that the play area of Asteroids was infinite, in that you could move continuously in a given direction - but that's because the play area loops back around on itself. So the  play area is actually quite small, there's just the added navigation quirk of falling along a given axis being a useful means of reaching greater heights. Which, to be clear, prior 2D games have done. seeing this applied to 3D environments is still a game-changer. Gazing up or down a forever-spiraling staircase is still beautiful. The non-Euclidean geometry is still striking. This game is a visual experience above all else. The puzzles are decent enough; mostly straightforward with a couple of head-scratchers, and an extra set of post-game challenges for added difficulty (I chose to move on after beating the main game, simply because of my overwhelming backlog).I beat Manifold Garden in about three-and-a-half hours and enjoyed my time with it. It didn't blow me away but it was solid. If the dollar-to-time ratio seems high, remember that there's post-game content I skipped.Recommended.

_childDocuments_.review: Small rooms encourage sensory sensitivity. Try this at your grandmas small living room, the back of a stairwell, or a broom closet; inside the enclosure every detail is cataloged with ruthless expedience to the sensory deprived brain. Heart beats thump, thump with clarity, the walls seem a different shade of light. Contrast to the bustling center streets, without stopping to appreciate the detail, there is no detail. Manifold Garden is the biggest room. Mercifully it graces the biggest room with suitably sparse decoration. Eye twitches reveal little more than shape/color. Should other visual accents enter eternity, it would easily overwhelm the visual palette driving the player to turn their monitor off. Instead, smooth railings dress the horizon. Tumbles into the abyss become second nature with incredible speed, and the vastness of the fall, a moment of clarity might appear. For me, these bubbles of clarity always appeared as random flashes, not at all from me. In retrospect I believe that it only feels that way because an eternity of the garden squelches the detail of the self so thoroughly that the only remaining piece is the problem solving brain. These puzzles get devious, not Sausage Roll devious, but enough with enough to require nightly stopping points because of exhaustion. Puzzles deviously force new understandings of the space, realizations of exits appear, revisits become tempting, the game even rewards this thinking by allowing a clear of the game without using the end of level dark cubes. I have personally had enough vacant hallways to never go to an Olive Garden again, but this game is worth the money for the experience of truly becoming lost.

_childDocuments_.review: Manifold Garden is beautiful - it's like someone stumbled across a kaleidoscope dimension of iridescent fractal geometry, and decided to spruce the place up with a handful of light physics puzzles. The sound design, the art direction, and the level architecture all conspire to put you into a sort of trance, as you explore an environment that gently challenges but never outright breaks your perceptions - navigating the puzzles is generally more "oh THAT'S how I'm supposed to do it" than "I have no ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ clue what's going on." And in the few cases where I got stuck, taking a break and coming back the next day generally made the way clear, benefit of sleeping on it and returning with fresh eyes.There are certainly times where the fractal nature of the stages feels like it's more for show than for practical use - yes there are infinite iterations in all directions, but generally you don't need to travel far to find the next step in your path. But 'show' is part of the experience - the design and the engine *are* worthy of showing off. Game devs be proud!If you're into first-person physics puzzle games, then beating Manifold Garden may not be the trickiest task you set for yourself... but if you enjoy quiet exploration of awesome spaces, that aspect alone will be more than enough to carry you through the handful of hours it'll take you to reach the game's climax.

_childDocuments_.review: Amazing game! Relatively easy puzzles in the main route, but unique.The best way to describe it:You move by solving mostly gravity puzzles through a geometrical landscape in a 3d world in which every dimension consists of 2 opposite planes. (6 total: left-right, up-down, forward-back). You can shift through planes by 90 degrees when touching a wall, and then gravity shifts with you (the wall becomes your new floor), and objects on different planes become frozen in time. (except multidimentional objects)The most amazing part is the world exists in a pocket dimension, wrapped around itself, in a sense that if  you fall down, you will end up from above, and if you run to the left (or forward), you will arrive from the right (or back).
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: A creative puzzle game that makes excellent use of two central mechanics: changing the direction of gravity and "fractal" levels, where there are infinitely repeating instances of the structures. As far as I'm aware, there is no story / lore segments or anything of that nature, so if you're looking for that kind of experience, that might be the only con.Oh yeah, and turn on "toggle run".

_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: Manifold Garden is a beautiful visual experience, with some delightful puzzles.  I thoroughly enjoyed immersing myself in the bizarre, mind-bending world of the Garden; the visual and sound design is atmospheric and sets up effective puzzles. For example, by clearly color-coding each face it's easy to guess how unfamiliar puzzle elements will behave, even in the absence of a blatant tutorial.  However, for how much I loved the design of Manifold Garden, I find it challenging to think of it as a puzzle game.  In general, the puzzles are straightforward for those who have played games with related mechanics (such as FEZ) and seemed secondary to the artistic experience of the game.  I actually enjoyed this aspect of the game - the low difficulty makes it easy to recommend to others as a work of art, and by just completing a regular playthrough, one has experienced most of what the game has to offer.  For those looking for a more challenging experience, the game does offer a carrot - the 0% playthrough (hinted at by a steam achievement).  Unfortunately, I have a hard time recommending this portion of the game; instead of feeling like a challenging New Game +, I found this to be somewhat convoluted and unintuitive.  Without spoiling it too much, most of the 0% run hinges on noticing hidden doorways in an environment where, in general, exploration is not encouraged.  However, the puzzles hidden in these areas are generally good and some of the "cube retrievals" required to progress present exciting challenges that I enjoyed; I just wish that this method of playing the game was more obvious.Overall, Manifold Garden is an excellent experience that I can comfortably recommend to just about anyone thanks to its moderately low difficulty.  It is a gorgeous exploration of a relatively simple puzzle mechanic, accented by an incredible score and artistic style.Overall Rating 9/10

_childDocuments_.review: If you liked Antichamber. You'll like this too. If you like this, you'll like Antichamber as well. But even if you didn't like Antichamber, this might still worth a try. Moving and orienting around the puzzles are super comfortable, and aside from one single part, they all feel natural in either the way of "Oh, how didn't I realize that earlier?" or "Damn, that is satisfying". Although, headache and dizziness are real threats imo, I had to pause for 2-3 times along. Can't even imagine this in VR. There is no story really, but it is artistic and symbolic enough to keep folk entertained. The new puzzle elements always surprised me, and wanted to explore the possibilities with it. Aside from one such element, they were used extensively, so I believe all the design choices were well thought-out. The sound design is also super good. All in all this is a weird puzzle game, which is super unique, and I can't have enough of these type of games. Goes into my favourites!
