_childDocuments_.review: It's the year 2072, and in the game we take on the role of a hacker (or hacker, w/e) who is captured by the sad masters and brought to the corporation's headquarters in the Citadel - a giant space station suspended somewhere off Saturn. There, he gets an ‘unflappable’ proposition from the station's vice-president, and TriOptimum corporate board member, Edward Diego. The peasant apparently got bored with his current position, messed something up, and, not reading the AI manual, gives our hacker the simple job of removing the ethical restrictions on it. After successfully hacking SHODAN, as this programmer is called, the protagonist is to be released into the wild, and even rewarded with a special implant. The operation is successful and the character is put into a coma for about six months. After this time, we wake up in the Citadel's medical sector, with not a living soul around. There are mutants, robots, androids, drones walking everywhere. And they have no positive intentions towards us. We quickly learn that SHODAN has gone completely mad, because not only has she deified herself, but she also intends to assimilate all of humanity in the manner of the ‘Star Trek’ Borg. So it's time to grab the pipe and drink the beer that has been brewed.Let's start by saying that this game is not for dummies. Mainly because of the fact that it requires attention, focus, thinking and a drip of deduction. The plot is discovered through journal entries and voice recordings of former Citadel crew members. Any door codes or the final key required to complete the game are hidden in messages, or in plain sight. It's also not a Level 1 clear, then Level 2 and Level 3 naaah! You'll run through the mazes of the damn station until you remember it! And try to avoid something! Something that's three levels down and each lift has its own separate shaft. Sound like a lot of boring walking? Relaxee! SHODAN has a great way of keeping you entertained, sending you down waves and waves of enemies until you fall for lack of ammo or first aid kits. Well, unless you learn not to fly on the stick, and believe me... you will. Veterans, on the other hand, will be able to dust off the legendary notebooks where they jotted down all the notes they needed to get through the games. Yes! ‘System Shock is difficult. Although it doesn't have to be. I have encountered opinions that the game is too hard. There's a lack of ammunition and first aid kits, and it's hard to find your way through the clutter of corridors. I think this is a sign of the times and all I can say is: ‘Heh, noobs’. It's just not a title that will forgive you for mistakes or cackling. Want to shoot? Watch out for the head sticking out! In the end, once I embraced the need to play more carefully, I managed to accumulate a supply of 20 patches, 6 first aid kits and 500 standard cartridges. It is possible!At the start, we can also adjust the difficulty level for ourselves, which is a very interesting solution that you can hardly find today. You want action but don't want to exert yourself mentally? You can set the puzzles on the easiest level and leave the shooting on the hardest. Want to chill? Simple as that. It's brilliant in its simplicity and is a breath of nostalgic freshness from the usual modes of adventure, easy, normal, difficult, we'll all gonna be d3ad and my favourite difficulty level: Souls-like. ‘System Shock’ can therefore be VERY (!) challenging, as on the hardest mode you get a measly 10h to complete the title. Believe me, without knowing the game don't even sit down to it! Like a naive sucker I tried this approach at the start. I let up on the medical deck, especially as the game is full of finds and bonuses to unlock. You also have to manage your equipment wisely, as backpack space is limited and weapons and ammunition take their toll. So you can't keep hawking everything to the ‘scrap yard’, but rather recycle junk on site. They give half as many credits but take up sometimes four times as much space, so the calculus is simple. The thing that was annoying, on the other hand, and was brazenly added at the very end of the remake, were the ‘hacking’ stages. I like mini-games, but this crap got tiresome after a while, too repetitive. If the ship was still somehow upgradable, it wasn't. Phew-phew into flying blocks and that's it. The notation doesn't apply, so if you fall, agonise all over again.A big plus for the audio-visual setting, although I didn't particularly like any of the tracks, the voice-overs create an unearthly atmosphere. There's a lot of classic synthwave here, which, combined with the brilliant, retro-futuristic locations, creates a brilliant atmosphere. Unfortunately, there is not enough of a piece to make it stand out and to get into your head. The graphics are much better. Beautiful pixels, colourful wires, lights, diodes and shiny corridors give an amazing vibe. On top of that, all the floors are very well designed, and they vary a lot. The reactor is full of tubes and dark corridors, the levels for the elite are drowning in glamour, and the SHODAN bridge is reminiscent of a computer-worm evil mastermind. Marvellous!‘System Shock is a title that surprised me in truth. After all, it's actually 30 years old now, and all it took was a little sanding here and there to have a really good game, unmatched by today's productions. For me, it is further proof that a kind of gaming peak was reached in the 1990s, and that today's developers are duplicating and sometimes just trying to improve the mechanics. Welp. I would like to see more remakes like this one here!Graphics: 8/10Music: 7/10Story: 10/10Gameplay: 8/10Overall rating: 8/10

_childDocuments_.review: I'll preface by saying I love classic PC games, I started on the atari, and had a 286 and have played so many of these kinds of games, yet somehow I missed System Shock and System Shock 2. I played nearly every other Looking Glass game that was created.. so... I have no nostalgia for this game, yet I'm very familiar with these vibes and kind of games. I dunno man, this might be a fault of the original game and not the remake but I just can't begin to care. I've even spent 4 years in real life learning to hack so you think this would appeal to me. This all seems like it should be right up my alley but I just find the level design to be awful, the monsters to be so generic and uninteresting.. I mean, the layout of the levels flows NOTHING like a space ship should be like, it feels more like a game level than a realistic setting. Ok, now that we have that out of the way, I'll try to focus on this as a remake instead of the gameplay and other areas that might actually be flaws of the original game. The remake is ugly. THere, I said it. For a remake, the graphics certainly are better than the original but it almost feels like they just did some asset swaps and used the original games design and code. The rooms might be true to the original but I really feel some creativity here could've made them better because I didn't really like the end result, and looking at the screen shots I can see there's still a lot of "old school" level design going on. The remake could've been so much more. IS THIS GAME WORTH YOUR TIME??? Maybe! If you have a lot of nostalgia going on and want a perhaps-too-true-to-the-original remake that is simply better graphics and some modern quality of life improvements then this is it for you. If you have no attachment to the original game.. skip it.. let the people on the message boards gush about their happy memories with this games and instead spend your time and eddies elsewhere choom.

_childDocuments_.name: System Shock

_childDocuments_.review: Nightdive Studios has brought this legendary immersive sim classic to modern audiences with a new new coat of paint that truly compliments and respects the original art, as well as game design. Graphically, it's a sight to behold for old school fans! The art style can at times mislead you into feeling like this is what it truly looked like decades ago, in a very good way. It's a remarkably stylized look that truly suits the remake.In terms of optimization, it couldn't be better and those saying that it's not optimized are definitely experiencing a serious PEBCAK moment. This is one of the first releases in quite some time which utilized the Unreal engine without any serious issues at launch. So, optimization wise, it's virtually a flawless release. If you have a relatively modern system, there's nothing to worry about, it will run extremely well. Nightdive Studios should truly be applauded for their efforts here.In terms of game play changes found within the System Shock Remake, there are countless gameplay mechanics and systems which received much needed quality of life improvements from Nightdive, removing or updating many of the older archaic systems found in the original, bringing the game as a whole closer to the modern era without removing its original identity. If anything else, it brings clarity to the original vision, making it a much more enjoyable experience overall. That being said, considering these changes, this is in my opinion the definitive System Shock experience that all immersive sim fans deserve!Now onto the main issues I have with the this release. There aren't many but...Nightdive has truly done themselves and their community a disservice by releasing the System Shock Remake with issues in terms of re-mappable keys for both Keyboard & mouse. The feature exists within the menu, but at times it functions, but more times than not it simply doesn't and considering this near flawless release, seeing an issue like this at launch was disappointing. Nightdive knew of this issue during the beta builds, but it was never resolved. For me personally, I wasn't affected by this, as my keyboard and mouse have configurable software, so I simply created profiles for both keyboard and mouse and moved on with my life. Yet, many don't have this available and they shouldn't have to. This has been a function feature for decades.Then in terms of the controller experience, it's just not where it needed to be. Although yes, it is listed as partial controller support but, there's simply no reason that Nightdive couldn't have had full controller support ready for launch. The partial controller support available is generic and doesn't suit the game. It's quite clear to see they didn't put enough time into it. I wouldn't go as far as saying it's unplayable with a controller, but it certainly isn't a satisfactory experience and anyone saying it is must be delusional. All one has to do is try to navigate the inventory to see how insufficient it is. Nightdive should have ensured that inventory management was navigated using a D-Pad, not emulated mouse using the right stick, because there's never been a time where that form of navigation was acceptable, let alone in 2023.So overall, those are my primary issues. Input device support is lacking and Nightdive needs to provide an update soon, so those affected by the above mentioned issues can enjoy the experience the way it was intended.Now that those negatives are out of the way, I 100% recommend System Shock Remake! It's a magnificent remake of a legendary game that truly must be experienced by the entirety of the pc gaming community. If you enjoyed Bioshock, Prey, Thief or other immersive sims, but never had a chance to play the original, there's never been a better time to do so. It's superior to the original in every way.It's everything I was hoping it would be and more! Once those issues I mentioned are remedied, I'd go as far as saying it's flawless! A definite must have for your Steam account!
_childDocuments_.name: System Shock

_childDocuments_.review: So personal tidbit of information... My uncle was a release engineer for looking glass studio and basically compiled/programmed the installers for system shock 2. Its good to see this was a remake of the original but my concern is, its not really as scary as the original was. Its a good game, but doesn't have the same atmosphere.No tutorial, just throws you into it, tons of things to collect, keypads to find, puzzles to complete, and some messed up cyborg/backstory, reminds me of quake 2/4 in its cyborg storyline. The cyborgs remind me of the borg from startrek, just consider it a copycat in their design. The mutants keep some of their humanity, or at least it shows when they try to access vending machines, etc. Its a nice little touch, allows for some instant stealth melee kills, but otherwise nothing noteworthy.I feel like the gunplay is pretty lackluster, they dont feel good when firing. If I am at the head I am not entirely sure I do more damage than the body. If it does its not by much. The game feels massive, took me 2.3 hr to complete the first level, doing everything I could. I would rate it a 7 out of 10, I would wait for a sale, worth about $25 to $30 from my experience with the first level.

_childDocuments_.review: 25 hours for a single playthrough, and now that I'm done, I can safely say that this game by far has exceeded all expectations, sure it may be true to the original for better or for worse, but I can say that is more than a positive than anything.10/10 if it were any more possible for me to reccomend it, I would.This is what you want this is what you get.After playing the update I can safely say this is by far the quintessential system shock experience.Play it.

_childDocuments_.review: Played through the original version back in the day. Kept me hooked until the end. I have to say there is still same magic in this remake version. Luckily I don't remember everything from the original version.I have also played through Prey, which was pretty much like System Shock. _childDocuments_.review: Never played the original but  played number of other immersive sim games. I was a bit skeptical but demo convinced me to buy the game. _childDocuments_.review: I've not played the original System Shock, largely in part of the fact that once it became something I could attempt news came out that this remake was in the works.  And so I waited.  I'd honestly say it was well worth the wait!  I'll give this game a second and maybe even third play through again in a few months. _childDocuments_.review: This game definitely wasn't for me. I went into it with expectations that come with playing older games, but even then the game play just wasn't at all engaging. _childDocuments_.name: System Shock

_childDocuments_.review: As a  who's been kind of up and down about this game, after following the development for the last 7 years, I was kind of surprised by how much I've enjoyed the end product. I went from not even really being motivated to touch the game a couple months ago, to enjoying what I've played so far and wanting to play more (despite having limited time). The game is very authentic to the original System Shock, as it should be. Everything's there from the original, but it does its part to add some flourishes and innovations from later games in the Immersive Sim genre. I certainly don't remember being able to scrap and recycle clutter items into currency to buy items from vending machines in the original game, which I had played a lot before this. That feature alone has brought out the inner kleptomaniac in me in a way only Bethesda games can usually achieve; I've only played through the medical floor and half of the research floor and every room I've entered has been picked clean. Every candy bar wrapper, every bed pan. Vaporized to scrap. Hundreds of scrap cubes littering my inventory, half of them stuffed into the cargo lift for safe keeping. If I hadn't already been recycling them into credits, I'd have a full inventory of scrap by now. I have almost 200 credits, and anyone unaware should know the conversion rate is 10 scrap for 1 credit.I'm also delighted that they kept the difficulty settings menu, where you individually select difficulty for combat, story, puzzles and cyberspace; I was expecting this to just get forgotten about, and for the game to get some standard "easy medium hard" selection with no nuance to it, so I have to give a lot of credit to night dive for everything they managed to get to. At this point my only real complaint is just music related. I actually kind of miss the silly 90s midi trash music from the original. I don't know if there is any music in this game besides the intro movie song and the dynamic combat music (that doesn't always play, since I kill things too fast). All I've heard otherwise is just the normal spooky ambiance. Maybe it's in there somewhere and I'm just not hearing it? I see no options in the audio menu for music besides volume. Whatever. I've just been listening to the songs for each floor from the original game off of youtube while I play. It suits the experience better than the normal ambiance, at least in my opinion.So yeah, a real good showing with this game, it was a little dodgy mid development, but night dive have basically won me over. I kinda wasn't expecting them to, but they've done it. *
_childDocuments_.name: System Shock

_childDocuments_.review: This game is really good at atmosphere. You feel tense because you're constantly wondering if you're going to round the corner and get sniped by a cyborg who's waiting for you to appear. This game wasn't even on my radar, but a friend decided to be generous and it's been so long since I touched any of the Shock games that I just felt obligated to install and play it. Especially with the waif thin install size of 8 gb. In a landscape of games with installation sizes like 20/40/80/100/beyond, this was a jaw dropping moment for me when I saw this game was only 8 gb.So this version of the game is severely upgraded over the original in terms of storytelling elements, and of course the graphics are just great. The game supports DLSS on day one, turn on the quality setting and see really good consistently high fps with everything on Ultra. I notably did turn off Motion Blur, I've never liked that effect in any game. instead of a simplistic cartoony intro, the game has you play part of the intro from the original, explore the hacker's apartment. I'm not saying there's a lot there to see, but it is there.Explosions destroy corpses, corpses which are destroyed can not be looted. So if you really want to salvage ammo from dead enemies, try to avoid using destructive explosives. Eventually you will gain muscle memory that every time you see what looks like a half-arsed Dalek, you will dome him instantly with the shotgun. This is good, do this. When walking through doors, if you see a shiny red circle in the distance, go back through the door you just came through and wait.Cyberspace is visually great, and the combat is not the worst thing ever. It can be a little disorienting at times, since it's 360 degrees of hell.The game gives you sliders for difficulty, ranging from 1 to 3. I don't know what 1 is like, but it might feel a bit underwhelming.Overall it's a really great remake, and I definitely like it.
_childDocuments_.name: System Shock

_childDocuments_.review: I backed this on Kickstater back in July 2016, when it had an estimated release date of Dec 2017, which I took with a bucket of salt because I haven't yet seen a Kickstarter game that hasn't gone long long past its target date. In the end, I've gotten exactly what I wanted - a faithful update of the original which still feels like playing an old game, but in a good way, not in the way where it's simply too dated to be enjoyable like the original has been for a long time. I first played (and loved) System Shock 2 somewhere around 2005, with the Rebirth mod because it was already pretty technically far behind at the time. That made me want to play System Shock 1, but with its restrictive UI and very low res it was just too hard to enjoy, so I'm very happy to now be able to experience this piece of history with no gameplay compromises and without feeling like it's been remade as a totally modern game - if I wanted a totally modern take on the same thing I'd play Prey again. So if you're like me and love classic Looking Glass immersive sims, but feel like you missed out on playing System Shock back in the day, this is for you and you'll love it. If you want a totally new cutting edge game, maybe not.Having completed the medical level (first level) and just started on the research level, my one complaint so far is that melee weapons totally lack impact and feel very hard to judge in terms of reach and whether you've actually hit anything. Enemies barely react to being hit at all, and many swings that feel like they should connect don't, so you end up just swinging away until they finally fall over. Equally it's hard to notice impacts on yourself when they hit you in close combat so it can be hard to judge how close you are to death in the panic of a close-up fight. Since I found guns I've been sticking to them the vast majority of the time and combat is much more enjoyable that way.

_childDocuments_.review: Wonderful remake! Fluid interactions and controls. Exciting to freely explore. Great FPS, as a more calculated approach rather than all guns blazing. If you like story, exploring, puzzles, and fighting AI, you will like this very much. Great graphics. Runs very well on high settings on Macbook Pro Intel i9 (Bootcamp).

_childDocuments_.review: I really like this game. It was a great remake, and one of the better things was the skill selection screen, where you can customize each part of the game to your liking. I played on skill 1213 since I love puzzles and missions (but not combat and shooting, and not time limits either).Positives:* A GREAT remake, that makes it also easier to follow the story.* Skill selection made it pretty good.* Good story* Loved all the hacking and finding keycards, mission items, and the "open world" travelling.Negatives:* Even on skill 1 combat is extremely hard. Would wish some "skill 0" in combat, both cyberspace and normal combat. Maybe with health and energy regen? And having skill 0 should also, maybe make the stacks for health, patches and ammo 4x bigger, meaning more room for items, and maybe make every weapon 2 slots smaller in inventory size.* For puzzles, a skill 4 would be nice. The circuit boxes were wayy to easy even on the most difficult setting.* I found it kinda unfair that some cameras were in hidden areas. Personally I think 0% security should be part of story, and I think the reactor code should not stop scrambling unless you have 0% security. (This could be bound to the "puzzle" skill, so selecting skill 3 or 4 in puzzle difficulty will require 0% security to gain a a reactor digit)
_childDocuments_.name: System Shock

_childDocuments_.review: System Shock can be clunky, it can be weird, but ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ does it succeed where it wants to. Right when you think you are getting equipped for Shodan's cyborg and mutant horrors, it throws something new at you and you realize you are always outmatched. This remake took a strange, strange game from the early 90's and made it playable. A wonderful game well worth a purchase.
_childDocuments_.name: System Shock

_childDocuments_.review: I'm glad I could finally experience all of the goodness that's System Shock. I'm just barely older than the OG game itself, so I didn't get to play it back then. I've tried to go back and play it, but the original game just speaks a different language in terms of controls that makes it really hard to enjoy the game. Well, the remake fixes all of those issues and then some. I was fully prepared to get lost in the legendary labyrinthine levels of the Citadel station, but the new signs and clarity improvements to the original layouts made it really hard to get lost. The guns are interesting and fun to use, the difficulty can be brutal at times, and I overall really like the premise of one man against the station itself. The game isn't perfect of course; the inventory is a mess and it would benefit from dropping you some kind of hint that creating a safe room of sorts for yourself is a good idea. Could've saved myself a lot of frustration if I got that idea sooner. Consumables are usually entirely useless or very situational, but they're going to clog up your inventory regardless when you don't know that. The cyberspace hacking levels look good, but I didn't find them all that fun all things considered.Overall though, the game has been a very fun experience. There's a lot of games that have built upon System Shock, and they're all very good games. And yet, they are still missing something that System Shock has. It's a truly unique blend of level design, gameplay design and environmental storytelling.
_childDocuments_.name: System Shock

_childDocuments_.review: I am very glad to be able to experience this title despite being too young to have enjoyed the original release. There are a few problems with infrequent crashes and stuttering. I also do not love all the models, specifically that interactable objects aren't more distinct from the very visually busy background. There are some gameplay shortcomings too, like not being able to write on the map and the inconsistency of descriptions appearing at the top, which I thought was a very neat feature, but it gets sort of abandoned after level one. And also I absolutely hate anything that happens in cyberspace, especially the end sequence, though I probably would've hated it in the original as well. Fortunately all of these segments are very short. Overall though, it is a very fun experience of finding your way through the imposing and mysterious station. I feel like it must have been a big influence on Prey, a game I love a lot, so I'm glad to have seen its predecessor in a format accessible to a modern audience.
_childDocuments_.name: System Shock

_childDocuments_.review: As someone who loves the original this was a dream come true.Although it's a bit jank in some places and there could be room for just a little more I was genuinely happy with what I got.Like the credits says: "This is what you want? This is what you get!"See you guys at System Shock 2 Enhanced Edition!

_childDocuments_.review: It looks ok, but the gameplay gets tiring after a while. You run around and get attacked. That's it. You have to scavenge, a lot, or you will run out of ammo and health. There are puzzles, fine, but they don't really fit. The "cyber space" tasks are downright weird. But the worst is that there's no feeling of progress, not after the first, nor after the 2nd, 3rd or 4th level: everything is more or less the same everywhere, the puzzles become a chore, only the enemies get tougher. So after 12 hours, I just uninstalled it. It was fun, but it isn't anymore.
_childDocuments_.name: System Shock

_childDocuments_.review: I very rarely take the time to write a review, but as someone who has never played the original, I had to say just how much I enjoyed my experience with this game. The old-school design philosophy, the combat, and the environments all coalesce into an incredibly tense and rewarding experience. I believe there is still some refining which I hope to see in the sequel, but the passion the developers feel for the IP is palpable. SPOILERS Criticisms:The biggest let down for me was the ending. I was hoping for a bullet-hell sequence against SHODAN in cyberspace, but what I got what as no stakes, free respawn slog that didn't test any of the skills I had picked up throughout the game. Also, I was very confused when searching for the reactor code, as I was looking for a clear display panel showing the code on engineering as per the email from earth. I wouldn't have minded the back tracking if the audiolog said something about the monitors in each CPU node room. Even those are fairly big criticisms about the overall pacing, I will still recommend this game to anyone who might be interested. I absolutely cannot wait for the inevitable sequel and some more experience based RPG elements. I wish I had known about this project during the kickstarter, as I would have loved a copy of the art book. The biggest strength of this game is the environment, and I applause the artists.CONCLUSION:Even though there are teething pains, the Devs have proven their commitment to the spirit which made the original so great. If we support projects like this, we have a good chance of seeing fully fleshed out single-player games in the future.
_childDocuments_.name: System Shock

_childDocuments_.review: A good and modern version of the original Shock System.But beware, the game doesn't lead you by the hand. You have to really pay attention to the surroundings and all the records. It's not a problem to get stuck somewhere in the game, but when you figure out what to do, it's a great feeling.Don't expect a shooting game, but try to survive with methodical reasoning and planning.I enjoyed the game from start to finish.
_childDocuments_.name: System Shock

_childDocuments_.review: This has been one of the most thrilling and immersive narrative gameplay experiences I've ever had. Impeccable world-building pulls the player into it's unique, compelling aesthetic from the start. Tension is balanced with dark and occasionally twisted humor.  Shodan has a playful streak.  It is terrifying.I didn't play the original release so I don't have a yardstick, but the gunplay is fun.  The exploration is really old-school, and suited me down to the ground.  I *loved* Half-Life - if you actually *enjoy* getting lost and having to learn where you're going and why you're going there - quids in.  I can see where the subsequent Prey gets a lot of its DNA, but this is an entirely different story with an entirely different vibe.Shodan, the antagonist AI draws the obvious comparisons to GLaDOS, but apart from being artificial and homicidal, that's where the similarities end. Shodan's cold contempt, delivered in Max Headroomesque glitches and stutters by a superb voice actor is the best part of an already fantastic game.I loved it.  Even while I was swearing at it.  Perhaps, especially then.I'm really looking forward to more from this developer.
_childDocuments_.name: System Shock

_childDocuments_.review: This game is just incredible. Thank you, everyone at Nightdive. They threaded the needle perfectly, melding the classic with the modern sensibilities. The union of pixelated textures with modern lighting is such a distinctive visual. There really isn't much more I can add that hasn't already been said. If you're intrigued by the immersive sim genre, give this beast a spin.
_childDocuments_.name: System Shock

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic Remaster! This game strikes the perfect balance between modern aesthetics and a touch of nostalgia by employing pixelated textures alongside a modern engine and shaders. The result is a visually stunning experience that captures the best of both worlds. If the pixelated textures aren't to your liking, there's even a mod available on Nexusmods that enables texture filtering.Beyond the visuals, this game offers a refreshing challenge, eschewing hand-holding in favor of requiring players to connect the dots and explore a multi-level space station teeming with menacing Cyborgs, Robots, and Mutants. All these adversaries are under the control of a supremely wicked rogue AI that never fails to remind you of your insignificance (You are an insect). If you enjoy being immersed in a thrilling and dangerous environment, this game is an absolute must-buy.10/10.
_childDocuments_.name: System Shock

_childDocuments_.review: I never played the OG but i did play the sequel which i loved and do have on Steam, so i decided to get this and i'm rather enjoying it, it's a blast to the past of how great games were back then yeah it's not perfect what game isn't these days (i've not come across any bugs while playing) but as remakes go with it's lick of paint i think the devs should pat themselves on the back. System Shock is probably one of those games that paved the way for many more games of this type and yeah Shodan is still probably the best villain out :)I'm hoping they will remake SS2. If your into fps of the past with no BS like the AAA games do these days i would recommend it and if ur not sure try the demo :)
_childDocuments_.name: System Shock

_childDocuments_.review: System Shock (original and remake) is at its core a dungeon delving game with a sci-fi trapping. Explore, bypass traps, fight monsters, loot. If this is not what you like then this game is probably not for you. For players like me though then this is one of those games they just don't make anymore, so I would recommend. The remake is, on the whole, faithful to the original experience but with a modern engine and controls, making it a much nicer experience for those who cannot handle or dislike early 90s UI. Many of the changes it did are done right, such as replacing the original wiring puzzles with the pipe puzzle and the voltage bar. However, it also introduces changes that are baffling, such as the recycling (busy work). Cyberspace feels like one step forward, one step back, but provides an interesting change of pace. I felt worse part of the remake is the replacement for the intro sequence - a perfectly concise short video was replaced with a ***-awful first-person forced interactive sequence. I only changed my mind over this at the end game because the replacement for the SHODAN showdown as amazingly even worse atrocity. I wouldn't say the changed intro/outro ruined the game for me, but **** they are awful. However, the bulk of the game in the middle is perfectly fine, and recaptures the spirit of the original and other games from the 90s when developers were still pushing the boundaries rather than play things safe (due to the massive cost of game development nowadays). Therefore, I would recommend this game to any player to misses those experiences; just be aware that there will be disappointments.
_childDocuments_.name: System Shock

_childDocuments_.review: Game has a very unique visual style which joins retro and modern together very well. Game is very fluid, and you swings of the pipe feels very good on a mutant's splattering head.Exploration is nice and the map is interconnected with many passageways which makes exploration your own. Overall, I just finished Medical and i'm very very pleased with the game and I am looking forward to playing more of it!

_childDocuments_.review: A faithful remake bringing the 1994 classic into the modern age,  is almost exactly as I remember it, having played the original for the first time a few years ago. Nightdive have done a great job in keeping with the original's style, look, and feel while adding onto what was already there alongside completely new stuff.The minute-to-minute gameplay, while it takes some getting used to, is just great; bludgeoning, blasting, and blitzing your way through the hordes of cyborgs, mutants, and robots infesting Citadel Station is just as much of a blast as it was in the original. The gunplay is broken up by various puzzles and navigating through the maze-like structure of the station (which can confuse me even to this day), your attention will absolutely be demanded over the course of a playthrough -- and make no mistake, the old-school level design is alive and well in the remake, for better and for worse.Sound design and music also deserve a special mention; although (much of) the original game's eccentric and downright catchy soundtrack may not have made the cut here, we're treated to some really cool tracks that spice up every level of Citadel in different ways; the battle between the synth and guitar parts do well to illustrate the battle between machine and man that is central to  and its story.SHODAN – the unshackled AI and self proclaimed goddess of Citadel Station – is also back and better than ever. Just like in the original and in , Terri Brosius just knocks it out of the park with new performances of all the classics (with new skin-crawling modulation and effects) as well as what I believe to be some completely new lines – none of which I will spoil for you. You really get the feeling that she/it is inside every wall, behind every monitor, watching you through the cameras; haunting the Hacker (you!), pulling no stops in killing and recruiting you into her cyborg army. SHODAN really is what keeps me coming back to . I couldn't name many better villains than her/it in all of video games.I highly recommend both the remake and the original. While the former just slightly edges out the remake (can you be nostalgic for a game you first played two years ago?), it is still a worthy successor to what Looking Glass Studios made into a classic almost 30 years ago now. Even though  may not be for everyone, I do hope we will see more from this franchise, whether that be in the form of a  remake or a new attempt at  – I'll take anything really.Score: 4/5

_childDocuments_.review: Never played the original, but was interested in the premise so I patiently awaited the release of this remake.I was not disappointed. Super fun, engaging, and interactive game here.First of all, the progression is very interesting, it's non-linear until the last quarter~ of the game, what I mean is that while there is a set of objectives you need to complete, the game makes it extremely vague as to what exactly you are supposed to be doing, for the most part they actually tell you via voice-logs of other charactes saying what they are going to do, this tells you the objectives. While this was certainly confusing at first, I grew to enjoy it later on because I acknowledged that me experiencing the levels freely was a valid way to play. Some objectives wouldnt even become clear until the end of the first half of the game, even though you could technically start doing them right away. The level design itself plays into this, as there isn't exactly a "level 1-x" like in a typical linear game. The game sort of baits you, because the first 2 levels are linear, level 1 medical, level 2 research, but then when its time to progress, you get access to level 3, AND level R which is a basement level of sorts, this is where the game truely shines and opens up.This makes this game a "knowledge based game", as ill dub it. think games like outerwilds, hitman, and darksouls. Games where the learning curve is pretty much learning (the world, important item spawns, enemy placements, etc), and once you have all the knowledge you can beat the game significantly easier on your second time through. The gameplay isn't too technically demanding in any meaningful way, its all pretty simple, and you can trivialize a lot of combat encounters by being well equipped. I dont think this is a bad thing, it serves the game well and not every game needs to be super duper esport technical to be engaging and fun.The story was also pretty engaging. It was interesting learning about how Citadel Station slowly fell as time progressed while you were in cryo, and Shodan is a really well designed villain. She harrasses you often at key moments throughout the progression of the game, I genuinely was on the lookout for the next time shodan would show her face.On the technical side of things, the game runs pretty good id say, i averaged 70-80 fps, but when i would look at a wall i would get 144+ fps and it felt super smooth, so anyone with a beast pc rn will be having a really well optimized time id say. The options menu has ALMOST everything you could ask for. The 1 thing I noticed that they didn't have, that is deeply important, is hotkey rebinding. they also made it the hotbar oddly restrictive, as certain items are restricted to certain slots. This is a pretty silly oversight/ decision to make, having to hit 8 9 or 0 to heal is pretty ridiculous, in a very literal sense. I will be getting gunned down in a fight, and need to heal, and need to reach for the NINE KEY. lol. One other technical thing to note is for razer mice users, if u have a mouse that supports 8k hz, reduce it to like 2 or 3k, 8k lags the game pretty hard, reducing it fixes this issue.For art, music, and art direction, i personally am in love with all of it, the art direction especially i am fond of because it is very unique and well done, it is like a modern version of a retro game. This is subjective though, not everyone has the same taste.I really enjoyed the game overall, I do have 3 complaints though which i do feel hold it back a bit, which are mildly spoilery, I dont give exact details but if you would rather not know anything then click off, except for the first complaint.1: hotbar remapping isnt present.I cannot stress how stupid this is, it needs to be patched or modded asap, its dumb to have hotbars and not be able to remap them, no game does this for good reason2: no multiple endings. very early on i had an "ending" that made me think that the game had multiple outcomes, but it doesn't, it just baited me into thinking so, especially later on in the game when I got to more levels and could figure a bit how the game would play out. I get that this is a remake of the original, but this feels like a bit of a wasted opportunity to not go light years beyond the original game. Dont get me wrong, it does clearly surpass the original in every single way, but it couldnt been with the stars instead of being on the moon if that makes sense.3: ending was mildly underwhelming. I dare not spoil the ending, but i just want it to be known that I was mildly disappointed with the ending fight, it couldve been more imo.ok, that is all to my review, thank you for reading

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely fantastic remake. I played through the Enhanced Edition of the original and enjoyed it, but bemoaned the outdated controls and clunky inventory system. This game remains true to the original's atmosphere and makes you feel truly immersed in the setting of Citadel Station. Movement feels smooth and combat feels tense, though a tad clunky. The storytelling is as fantastic as the original, with better voice acting, more voice lines, and environmental cues to truly flesh out the setting. Overall, this is an excellent return to the franchise for long-time fans, and a more accessible introduction for newcomers to the series. I would highly recommend it.

_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to like System Shock, but it doesn't feel like an immersive sim to me at all. There're many areas and narrative beats that are gated by a single card, code, or item. Exploration of Citadel Station is nonlinear, but narrative progression isn't. Later immersive sims, like Deus Ex, Dishonored, or Divinity: Original Sin, give you many paths to reach a single goal. System Shock doesn't. It's a tightly linear game, that happens to take place in a sprawling, multi-tiered space. When everything clicks together, it's tense, and surprising, and fun—but miss a single mission item or audio log, and you're in for a slog, retreading corridors that feel endless. The map is massive and it's exciting the first time you go through it. There are, fortunately, many areas you can unlock, metroidvania-style, to loop back to a central hub. However, some areas, like the Beta Groove elevator in Executive Level, are only accessible through long, single-route paths. I want to be immersed in this beautiful and unnerving world, but too often I'm pulled out of it, crawling through the same vent multiple times to progress the story, or pixel hunting for a single missed log. I don't regret supporting Nightdive for their efforts, but I wouldn't recommend this to anyone except those interested in roots of immersive sims.

_childDocuments_.review: Great game and very faithful to the original. Maybe a bit too faithful at times. I don't see how anyone could understand the game and it's level design without having experience the original first. Parts of levels have been redesigned to make it easier to navigate. But that's not for all levels. Research, Flight Deck, and Engineering have some design changes that make the levels even more confusing than the original. I do love how they made levels feel lived in. it was a complaint many had with the demos. And some areas tell a stories through the environment which is always a treat if you are a fan of games like Bioshock.Cyberspace was fun the first couple of times, then it wasn't. Eventually it starts to drag and get frustrating at times. Enemies in cyberspace are not fun to fight. Not challenging, but annoying. Hate flying enemies in games that move way faster than you and dodge every attack while also blinding you? Cyberspace is pretty much just that. And sometimes cyberspace levels last 15 minutes. and if you die, YOU START ALL OVER AGAIN. You know you hate it when you dread walking into a room and seeing a terminal. At least cyberspace is more linear than the original.Now for the inventory. It's just okay. I think some weapons shouldn't take up so many slots. All weapons have a specific purpose. It gets annoying when you can't carry more than 4 without having your entire inventory taken. I think including more space for the elevator inventory box would have fixed this issue. Other than that, this game was worth the wait. I recommend new System Shock/immersive sim players to play games like Bioshock and Prey 2017 ahead of time. And maybe 90s shooters like Doom as well.

_childDocuments_.review: Do I like this game? Yes. Did I enjoy this game? For the most part, yes. Do I recommend this game? Yes. However, would I pick it up again and replay it? No. For the simple reason of the Boss fight, which really is one of the two points of criticism. The Boss fight, as it is now, is doable but so so difficult. You cannot skip Shodans monologue and sequence, no healing - feels kind of wonky if you ask me - no checkpoint there. Oh, and you have to "alt + f4" out of the end credits since they are non-skip, which feels like a odd note to end a game on.Apart from those two points, i had hellofafun playing it. For the most part: Good job, Nightdive! But please add a checkpoint after that mentioned part of the boss fight, it would really add to the game experience.

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic modern remake of an old survival horror/immersive sim action adventure sci-fi game. I was scared it was going to be too reliant on being like the original, with outdated mechanics/gameplay, but System Shock Remake plays really well and you can tell the developers put the time and love into making this.Only issue I had with the game was there is no quest log & the only real way of knowing where to go next is through audio logs you pick up (so you have to really pay attention) and so I had to use IGN's guide on the game for progression cause there's no way I would've figured out where to go or what to do.Amazing game that was right up my alley, I loved it and if a remake is planned for System Shock 2 I'm definitely down for it. 9/10

_childDocuments_.review: Out of any game currently out right now as of 2023, this is one I can definitely recommend to those new and familiar to System Shock and the Cyberpunk Survival Horror/Immersive sim genre.I've waited for years for this to come out, and it has blown my expectations away. Though, suffice to say nobody can outdo the master at work which is this game.Difficulty: Play on 2, please play on 2 if you want an experience to remember. 2 is hard enough as it is. 3, you're going to feel like you are putting your balls through a meat grinder.This game hates you, it doesn't like you - in fact it wants you dead every waking moment you walk on the station. _childDocuments_.review: As a huge fan of the original game - I completed the original game about three times and have considered the original System Shock the best game ever, I got exactly what I wanted from this remake. Finishing it the fourth (the sixth, actually) time felt so satisfying.The game stays true to the original and it was fun to play again. And it is visually stunning. ...Update after my third playthrough and after patch 1.2:One bossfight gave me a hard time this time (I lacked the proper ammo and tried different strategies). Still, it was so enjoyable. This game becomes even better when you start remembering (again) the maps. Citadel feels like a familiar place, which you enjoy to slowly walk through or to speed run through the narrow coridors. Recognizing every corner brings an almost physical sense of satisfaction, like returning back to the hotel where you spent your best childhood holidays :).Regarding the changes in the last patch, the updated final fight is definitelly an improvement and I enjoyed it. The female protagonist is better than I expected, even though you almost do not see her. But you hear her breathing and see her hands with polished nails and yeah... I realized how much I prefer to play with a female character in general.The controller support is not bad at all. This time I played on SteamDeck and on PC with DualSense controller (instead of mouse and keyboard). There is a minor issue where the run and lean keys are mapped to the same button which caused me few deaths (along with accidentally enabling a switch instead of reloading :-)). However, the overall experience is very good. And using gyro aiming gives me almost the same precission as the mouse, therefore I didn't miss the autoaim function (which is missing, I think). Maybe just one note regarding the SteamDeck gameplay, the design may feel overwhelming on the smaller screen. While still perfectly playable there, a larger monitor is much better for this particular game.

_childDocuments_.review: A remake like this is a fine line. Change too much and you wont' have the sense of history, change too little and you end up wondering why they bothered. I think Nightdive did an admirable job here. Are there oddities? Sure. This isn't the perfect game that will cause the heavens to open and lead you to the promised land.  But they nade a game that has been too clunky to really play for decades accessible and enjoyable. Worth a pickup if you enjoy this kind of game, especially since its been a drought for the genre lately.

_childDocuments_.review: Man this is just a badly made game.  Almost all parts of it are just painful to use.  I now understand that there is a pdf manual with the game but you shouldn't have to look things up to figure the game out.  For instance, the puzzles just suck.  They really aren't really difficult but the rules coupled with the lousy graphics make them difficult to figure out.  I gather the blue squares are supposed to have arrows or something to indicate what directions the current will flow.  If so, they are completely invisible on my system and many others.  Far too much of the game is just as tedious.Inventory management is painful.  Guess it just isn't possible to indicate what is junk and what is not. Maybe anything that will go into the recycler is junk?Speaking of the recycler, it iss painful to use.  You'd think there would be a button--recycle all junk but no.  Like the rest of the game it is tedious as hell-- find the junk in your inventory, manually move piece by piece from inventory to recycler.  Oh wait, that won't fit so we manually rotate object to place it in the recycler.  Now what?  Oh, you back up until you can reach the button to recycle.  Now, I have to do that entire process 5 more times.  It is a shame.  This could have been a good game.  It is not.

_childDocuments_.review: Started playing for the nostalgia, kept playing for the old school game play loop.  Simple, engaging mechanics that kept me coming back.  Hard to imagine that younger gamers will enjoy it but, if they stick with it, they may appreciate the simplicity of older mechanics that draw you in with a solid and consistent game play loop that, while unforgiving, rewards persistence.The aesthetic and game play decisions made with the remake are remarkable, as it feels like System Shock, and yet is different in so many ways.  It's hard to imagine wanting to play the original now, and this is what makes this remake such a success.  Like the original, this game isn't for everyone.  But for anyone that loves immersive sims, this is the best way to experience one of the first games in the genre.  While it's not obvious at the beginning, the longer you play it the more you appreciate how much work and care was taken with this remake.  All of the little tweaks and design choices come together to make this the best version of System Shock we'll ever get.  The worst thing about this remake is that is makes me even more hopeful that Night Dive will attempt a System Shock 2 remake, but I worry I might be hoping for too much.

_childDocuments_.review: As one of the original backers of System Shock (Remake), I'm very happy that this exists at all. *Update* NVM, it finally arrived, this Collector's Edition just makes me so happy!! Honestly, the main thing I was thinking while playing this is that I wish this wasn't going to be the last entry in the System Shock series. I hope they do, I think they have the right idea here. But well, alas. Continually creepy, a little bit moon-logic puzzly, and ever nerve wracking combat, System Shock does a great job of updating the game to modern standards while keeping its original soul. _childDocuments_.review: I backed this game on Kickstarter as a big fan of the series (it was a no brainer). I don't trust Nightdive with the franchise or pretty much anything else now and I recommend the classics over this, esp SS2. The less they have to do with it, the better your experience will probably be.The evidence is all over Kickstarter and in the inbox of everyone in the same position as me.Years of mismanagement and broken promises and even now in 2024, after: years ofbait and switches; a late, pretty-good-but-underwhelming game release; NDS being bought by Atari; STILL we have not received what was promised regarding physical stuff while it is purchasable elsewhere.Nightdive do not care about their supporters. They have generally been incredibly lazy and horrible with their management of this project (now almost a decade running) and devs need to learn from what happened here.The tactics have been incredible: Promise a feature or the full game release is coming by a set date ("it's ready, guys we promise!")Date approaches and they stoke the excitement once if at all.The deadline passesThe deadline passes by months.Finally there is word. "Whoops. We lied, it's not done. But here's a screenshot to distract you."Silence for many more months or a once-per-month post about absolutely nothing.A year has past. Repeat the cycle.After the 3rd cycle, they just started banning and silencing critics. The latest cycle was (for the 6th? time??) getting us to confirm our home addresses for shipment of physical media. This was supposed to happen when the game was coming out (promised multiple times over the years) and promised yet again for...June 2024? It is now September 2024. The silence continues to absolutely noone's surprise.I was sympathetic, especially during the pandemic. All I wanted was for them to admit what was actually happening at any stage but there was no transparency and noone at NDS seemed to know to be able to tell anyone. When Atari bought them out (the company's value in no small part to those who had funded them), I thought they might actually get the manpower and financial assistance to get things wrapped up properly. That hasn't happened and they nonchalantly gave up on the promised linux port.They promised our tier of backers early access to the game in beta. It was playable but without a LOT of polish and still isn't quite what I was expecting of it - especially the audio. The soundtrack is very disappointing for what it could have been.That's OK, it's a beta. But rather than let it get the fixes it needed, they rushed it out after about 3 weeks of limited beta access because it was painfully clear they were eager to call it a day.In general, they rushed the parts they shouldn't have and dragged out the parts they promised were already done. System Shock 2? They also promised "a remastered version of SS2 would be coming along with this game for backers to enjoy" - effectively they were just using or adding to existing excellent mods and texture packs made by the community and calling it a 'remastered' version they would handle the upkeep for. But it was a nice gesture. Didn't happen. Again to 0 surprise, there is NO TRACE OF THIS _STILL_.By this point, we'd waited so long I think most people like me were just happy there was SOMETHING.To their credit, they made a big patch that fixed a lot of bugs. They then sat on it for over a year and blamed their publisher (that they chose!) for not getting it out because 'the publisher didn't want us to'. The years of delays and lies up til then makes it more likely it was just another stall tactic.Some of the reviews at first release were so OTT positive, I was convinced they were paid for and I wouldn't be surprised if that were true.There was SO much unrealised potential for this game as a remake of an oldie into a modern title. Keyword: UNREALISED. I look for positives where I can: I was pleased they put some cool achievements in (and skullies to find!?), that do use the space well. There are few incredible highlights (shodan's lines being my fave. She pretty much carries this game. The cyborg drones are fab and they have massively toned down enemy spawns from the beta (the corridors used to be littered with the tougher enemies who had pinpoint accuracy)).It's mostly OK, but there are still things that needed more polish, and a lot of new players are going to get hopelessly lost or have to fumble around the notes/audio logs because NDS didn't streamline it. Melee is at best DISSATISFYING and it's so frustrating to see it when they had so much time to ask for feedback and work with backers on finetuning or incorporating suggestions.The original SS2 has some much better aspects and replayability. Go play that. If you're going to review the game, it needs to be on its own merits. I don't agree at all with the highly charitable point in some reviews that "at least this is better than the original version" (a game that released 30 years ago), that's setting the bar SO low, we've come a long way and this could have gone further.e.g. A little note for players to know what they're doing (objective) would have made the game far more accessible. Because of how this game has been, I have tremendous respect for Arkane's release of Prey 2017 and there is a lot within that game (ironically based on early SS games) they could have learnt from.Nightdive have really spoilt SS. Treated it like one of their many flights of fancy, treating supporters badly with dishonesty and neglect before they jump onto another project. The death of their passion a few years into the project never really left and is clearly visible still. I weep for what could have been.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a hard one for me. I recommend it, that being said, I don't think that I will ever finish the game. I think it comes down to personal tastes really. I really liked games like Bioshock and Deus Ex where I have been told this game these games takes inspiration from and I think that the game in itself is pretty good. It is challenging, gameplay mostly feel smooth (even though I have a though time dodging enemies attacks), puzzles are good and you really get the feeling that you are fighting a station with Shodan lurking around and not just some ragtag enemies all over the place. HOWEVER, I mostly play games because I want to reset my brain from work. Thus what I really look in a game is short levels ranging from a few minutes to an 1h-1h30 nowadays. This game as many people have pointed out will require you to take notes (by yourself, since the game does not babysit you. I think it is a good thing in life in general, but since I have become more busy in my life and want to improve on multiple spheres , I now prefer in game more straightforward in their progressions), to backtrack and complete certain sections as it was intended by the creators. All of this unfortunately makes the game for a modern audience hard to get in. It is rather unique in itself as since it is a living station, you really feel that everything is interconnected and that is where I applaud the effort of Nightdive that they have conveyed this feeling in me. I think they did a fantastic job at that. On the other hand, since everything is interconnected, you have to reread everything, backtrack, ask yourself how to do it strategically, explore the station in a very secure manner and take your time and take copious notes of where you left item number 4 that you thought was useless, but in fact was key to finish the game. Things that unfortunately I don't want to do anymore in a video game. For the record I have played (and finished) all dark souls games and found it easier (even with a wiki open) than this game. If you want to immerse yourself in a game and are ready to put in a lot of hours, this is the game to go. If you want something where the action is quick and require less brainpower, this is definitely not a game for you. I hope you may find this useful. In the end, I do recommend it for people where what I saw as a downside is for them a huge plus. As I mentioned, I won't finish it because of personal preferences, but I do see a huge appeal for certain people who want to take on this challenge.

_childDocuments_.review: It blows my mind that the Original game is from 1994.This remake shows how ahead of its time this game was. There is a lot of variety in Weapons, Locations, Enemies, music and so on. The exploration and progression in this game are extremely fulfilling and rewarding, I loved just exploring the Citadel Station thanks to an immaculate level design that is never too tedious.The gameplay is fun and never gets old, this is because of the numerous ways you can approach every single encounter. Riffles, pistols, shotguns, laser swords, grenades, railguns and a lot more. One playthrough isn't enough to experiment with everything the game has to offer.Everything is amplified by the perfect audio design that immediately grabs you and makes you feel your surroundings and your actions like few games can do.What an experience this was.

_childDocuments_.review: Nightdive specializes in modernized ports and remasters, uplifting games and their existing assets to the newer technological standards, allowing for quality of life improvements, increasing stability, visual fidelity, framerates, etc. These are often great by themselves, but this case is a full remake, something more rarely seen in PC gaming space and, frankly, a work of art. At least in it's current state, , even after years of development hell.I'm not a System Shock expert, I didn't get the original System Shock back in the 90s, and when I tried it for the first time in the latter half of '00s, it was already extremely dated, clunky, unintuitive and difficult to approach, so I kept bouncing off from it. It was similar years later with System Shock: Enhanced Edition, also from Nightdive, although it's a very good modern port.But System Shock 2, on the other hand, was probably the first "immersive sim" with RPG elements that I played. Looking Glass Studios gave birth to this wonderful genre and pioneered it for years with monumental achievements like Ultima Underworld, Thief, and System Shock. Without these games there would be no Dishonored, no "-shock" dumbed down spiritual sequels from Ken Levine and many other fantastic titles, including probably ones like Elder Scrolls in its current form. Gaming as a whole owes them a great deal.This remake walks a very fine line between modern gameplay and classic content and sensibilities. It is apparent in its every element, from level design, through the masterfully recreated soundtrack, which is now stuck in my head, and especially in the visuals. The art style skillfully combines 3D models with relatively modern polygon counts and unfiltered textures created as fine pixel art with all the bells and whistles like material properties, specular occlusion and dynamic shadows. It is a completely unique and eclectic approach to art direction and makes this game not only unlike anything else, but also simply beautiful in how it handles nostalgia.Because a lot more can be done to how the Citadel station looks nowadays, it doesn't resemble the original 1:1, but it's overall feel is kept, or even improved upon. It is still an increasingly complex claustrophobic labyrinth consisting mainly of right angles and tight spaces. Nearly all surfaces on the station are absolutely covered with technological doodads and gimmicks, single square pixel LED indicators invoking that retro feel, pipes, vents, fans and screens. And all of those little details also make sounds, creating a thick and oppressive atmosphere very similar to Alien: Isolation, something that I absolutely loved. Each section of the station has its own distinct feel to it, making these places memorable and immersive.If you are somehow on the fence regarding this game's presentation, I suggest watching Digital Foundry's YouTube video about it, as it goes nicely in-depth in what techniques Nightdive used to achieve this. But it's not just a pretty picture, the gameplay is spot-on. It doesn't feel like, say, Bioshock. It plays like an old classic brought to life with perfect mouselook, more intuitive controls and a rock solid framerate (though your mileage may vary - I was put off for some time after playing the demo on an older machine, but I don't think its performance is still indicative of the full release).Storywise, SHODAN has gotten a slight uplift to look and sound a bit more like her System Shock 2 appearance and I absolutely loved what they did (voiced by Terri Brosius!). A wholly unique antagonist in some ways, she basically carries the whole story and brought me back to a headspace that I had long forgotten...  The tension and immersion are insane. For however little of the original game I tasted before, I feel like Nightdive has made this iteration even more terrifying than the original, again in the vein of System Shock 2. Not only do you get to piece together the terrifying story of how SHODAN took absolute control over a space station and it's crew of over 400 people over several months of accelerating cybernetic horror, you also get intimate with the aftermath. Bodies, blood and entrails are strewn about everywhere, along with sad traces of people trying to hide and survive in any hole they could find for themselves, sleeping on the floors and tight spaces between walls and industrial machinery, subsisting on vending machine food, recording farewells for their loved ones, never to be received. Many of your opponents are humans turned into murderous cyborgs and mutants, visibly deranged and disfigured, slaves to a cruel mother-goddess. The scariest part is how the last traces of their humanity somehow still shine through to the surface, when they talk to themselves while sleepwalking through their programmed routines, pondering the nature of consciousness, reality, death, and the endless nightmare they found themselves in.All that being said, there are some gameplay elements many people dislike, me included. The cyberspace sequences are often criticized, but personally I loved them, if only for smooth controls and trippy visuals and being a general improvement over the original. I'd like to see those people handle the bleak pixelated wireframe void from 1994. The enemy respawn mechanic is quite unnecessary. I would rather have the overall number of enemies even doubled than deal with this. I know it is supposed to maintain a feeling of tension and constant danger, but they could have also made the enemies come in from upper levels in a logical manner, or at the very least always spawn out of sight. Currently they literally come out of the floor in an extremely cheesy way that I don't appreciate. The final boss fight, even after a complete overhaul in one of the recent updates, is also tacked-on and nothing to write home about. It feels like an unnecessary chore born from lack of ideas than a genuine contribution to the experience. There are also some glitches here and there, some problems with achievements and such, but none of these issues derailed my absolutely fantastic experience with this gem of a game. It is better than any Bioshock, not even close. I can't recommend it enough, especially if you liked any of the previous games in this series. It made me want to try and approach the Enhanced Edition of the original game again, which is an achievement for a remake in my opinion.I really wish this game had an official VR mode, just like the original (it was probably the first VR FPS). Handling environment interactions with your own hands and experiencing this horror with full depth perception and head tracking would have been an absolute game changer. There is a UEVR mod by Ashok0 though! I have to try it one day. I imagine it would be even better than The Persistence was, with which I had an absolute blast on even PSVR, so I'd recommend that too for anyone interested in a VR experience with a similar theme to System Shock.

_childDocuments_.review: Challenging  at times and at times tragic, it's a fun experience with a good core gameplay loop. Most of the mystery can be figured out with careful observation, and the metroidvania elements are satisfying. I also like that nothing despawns so you can (and should) use the found storage to your advantage. That said, there are small quirks that can make it annoying. Enemies teleporting in, ambushes that can feel cheap, and a fair bit of backtracking to take advantage of the spread out facilities, but overall it's a good time that forces you to plan ahead a little. Shodan makes a satisfying antagonist, even if some of the 'I am God' stuff can get old quick. It would have been cool to learn more about why she turns evil, there doesn't ever seem to be a good reason given about why removing ethical constraints would make her evil instead of benevolent - that though its a nitpick!

_childDocuments_.review: I'm a fan of the original System Shock (enhanced edition), so I was very excited to play this version.  I'll be reviewing this game in comparison to the enhanced edition and listing out which changes I liked and didn't like.I liked:> How faithful this adaptation is.  Nightdive did a fantastic job of keeping the strengths of the original game intact, namely its level design and how it challenges the player to figure out what to do.  The combat and resource management feel eerily similar to the enhanced edition's (that is to say very tight and good) despite the changed weapons and enemies.> Enemies are a lot more interesting now.  Nearly every monster in the original was a hitscanner that was either a robot (and therefore allergic to teflon and magpulse rounds) or not a robot.  This remake introduces a lot of variation in how the monsters move and attack.  A lot of them have more health, but they also don't tear you to shreds the second they see you.  The mid-game mutants also have teeth now, where before they were all pretty slow and weak.> The game is expertly made.  It's smooth and fun to play.  The art-direction and graphics are phenomenal.> The maintenance level is no longer a nightmare world full of no fewer than 2 respawning "invisible" mutants at any given time.  I'm glad I experienced that bit of character building in the enhanced edition, but I'm glad I don't have to deal with it anymore.> The puzzles are now enjoyable to do and not exercises in trial and error.> Replacing maintenance, the beta-grove is the new nightmare world of Citadel station.  It took me several attempts to get through, and I feel like it lives up to the hype better in this version.I disliked:> Cyberspace.  It's better than the original cyberspace, and by that I intend to damn with faint praise.  The enemies are kinda annoying to fight (especially the green wasp arseholes), being much spongier but less deadly than the meatspace monsters.  Cyberspace is bland and repetitive, and it started to be chore after my first foray.  Maybe that's not the case for higher difficulty (I played on 2).> How dark and murky everything was.  I don't mind it aesthetically, but the original System Shock could get away with expecting the player to figure out its maps and missions because all the clues were clearly conveyed, and the environments were bright and colorful.  I feel like the remake's moodier corridors and audio-logs make it harder to do that, and not in a good way.  I doubt I would have had as good a time as I did if I didn't already know what to do.Verdict: System Shock is a great game and this is a great way to play it.

_childDocuments_.review: Super TL;DRIs it good?:If you've never played system shock, Yes. This remake is very faithful and preserves nearly the entire experience from top to bottom. It perfectly encapsulates its source material in every way, just with a graphics upgrade and elimination of superfluous stuff or things that just wouldn't work/would have no use in a modern game. If you have played the 1994 System Shock:   They basically just took the original, and remastered it, with some extra flair. Like some extra logs, and an inventory system that isn't bottomless and isn't a list.--End TL;DRIf you're new to the System Shock games: This is the progenitor of all those Bioshocks, and one of the earliest good FPS variant of "maintained open world," where you can drop stuff in the game and it'll stick around so you can come back to it. Forming inventory stockpiles on the Station is actually a thing, as your inventory is limited and you can mark your map. All the stuff you will experience was in the 1994 version, with 95% accuracy to the original maps too, but now it doesn't look like a spreadsheet with a viewing window.  This was even the game that started the "451" door code meme, with the very first door. Just know that the game isn't going to hold your hand with certain things- in all likelihood, there's a scripted moment in there for when you screw up in exactly the way the devs figured you would. Enjoy finding that necessary, randomized even in '94 super-code, speedrunners.  Get it, play it, understand why SHODAN was always the better and easily more terrifying villain of the "Shock" style of games. Then, hope they remake 2, and apply the same care they did to the psionics system in that game.--For those that played the 1994 version: The game is so faithful to the original you can pull out the 1994 strategy guides  This is not an embellishment. From locations of key items, to non-random codes, to the  and ,  The parts that are inaccurate are because they changed things for the better or eliminated some kind of redundancy.Remember how you had 4 different pistols, a shotgun that used rubber ammo on cyborgs, "what the hell am I looking at" cyberspace?  The sensearound unit being a disorienting mess with little practical use?Now there's 2 pistols- the main little one that can swap between tungsten and 9mm, and the magnum.   The shotgun?  and the most versatile in the game, with armor piercing basic rounds and dragons breath that burns down organics.  Cyberspace alone can be it's own descent clone.  Now Sensearound highlights items on your mini-map instead, and high versions change range/what else it can see.The stuff they added makes total sense and works very well, too.  There are recycling stations and a vending machine system now- you can haul garbage from around the station to recyclers, like broken weapons or soda cans (made from when you drink soda and restore 1 health pip, now!), and convert them to tri-credit to buy patches from vending machines. These machines have limited supplies for your run, and the junk is consistent to the level; once it's spent, it's spent (in other words, a limited resource).  You can also do things if you have a little bit of thinking parts left: I found a credit chit item in the executive suites labeled as junk. I remembered from a moment before they had ATM's on that level. Low and behold, you can drop that chit in there and get free creds.  You can also rob the executive offices of display items and recycle them for stupid amounts.The cortex reavers? those things you could count on one hand and were too big to fit through most doors? Yeah. That first one's a .  Diego? Same deal.  They only show up when you're in the arena with them, doors locked. Not just hucking an EMP down the hall. yes, they will absolutely shred you if you let them.  no, the rapier is not the end all against them.Even the voiceless hacker has more silent attitude now, from the opening to how he handles logs, usb sticks, and checks out guns when he first gets them.There was only a couple strange choices.  I understand WHY they would from a dev perspective, but they're still weird.  One is the regenerator beds.  They still work exactly as before- you have to find the switch and throw it.  However, because the station is now unified without visible loading screens... You have no worries once you throw that first switch in med.  You'll be teleported to whichever bed you unlocked last/is closest.  The "mission" difficulty setting, however, will restore the original mechanic of having to find it per deck, or die- but only so long as you accept the 10 hour time limit on the entire game (up from 7).  Why they did that is absolutely peculiar. The option to make it it's own difficult setting was   The only other decision was how the hacker looks.  That hair, ugh.
