_childDocuments_.review: This game sat in my Steam Wishlist for about 6 years. There were times when I thought it was never going to be released. Now that I have played it a little I have to say that it was well worth the wait. I played the original System Shock back in the 90s and it remains one of the best games I have ever played. That game was well ahead of its time with lots of little things that gamers take for granted now. For example, it was the first game I ever remember playing with a "lean around corners" feature. Now, all these years later, it's very clear to me that this remake was a labor of love for the developers. I am really enjoying the game. The visuals are good, but retain the feel of the original game. The soundtrack is really good; very cyberpunky, techno, and creepy. I am so glad that the devs, while upgrading the visual and audio technology, decided to leave overall gameplay mechanics of the original game in tact. The game does no hand-holding. You are in a huge, yet claustrophobic, enviromment, with a HUD map and compass, but there are no "quest markers" to show you where to go or what to do next. You simply have emails and audio recordings from the dead crew of the space station you are on to give you info and clues in an in-world narrative way--passwords, objectives, locations of ammo and supplies, etc. I admit that some modern day gamers with little patience may have trouble sticking out out with this game, but from my perspective, it adds to the immersion of the experience. I am enjoying the circuit breaker puzzles for opening doors and taking down shields, and the couple of times I have "jacked" into cyberspace have been pretty enjoyable. I like how the visually protrayed cyberspace in the game, again with modern tech, but the old school aesthetics. I'm only a fraction of the way through the game, but I am guessing this will end up being my favorite game of 2023. If you've played any of the Bioshock games and enjoyed them, but never played the original System Shock, you owe it to yourself to play this progenitor of those games.

_childDocuments_.review: I've only played a moderate amount of the original game, but this felt like a pretty faithful remake. Being a checkers fan, this is the second hardest puzzle I would ever have had to do if I didn't just look up a chessbot to handle the problem for me. There's also a sudden need to backtrack towards the end of the game if you didn't realize you were supposed to be jotting down numbers sequences that had been appearing, but really that's on me for not noticing the things in the first place.Definitely worth it on sale if you're unsure about getting it, I feel like most fans of shooters will enjoy getting to run through Citadel Station even if you haven't played the original.

_childDocuments_.review: I really enjoyed this game. The graphics hit that sweet spot of looking old but not dated. It's a great looking game. The gameplay, like the original, are smooth with some wonky aspects. Though I only played the original long enough to get a feel for it.It took me 30 hours to complete this game without looking up any guides. There was also a point where I got lost and forgot what I was doing. Since this game doesn't hold your hand, you'll be going through and reading and listening to logs to figure out what's going on and where to go next.With the inventory system they have, you'll be back tracking and figuring out the best place to put your stuff. Or changing out your gear. (I highly recommend the maintenance level where the freight elevator is for having a centrally located stash.)I didn't play the game on the hardest difficulty since that's one life mode, and not something I wanted to do blindly. The one before it is the same difficulty but is not one life mode. However, I did have the other difficulties on the hardest difficulty and I never had any trouble with puzzles. They are unique, but not very difficult. Ammo is not an issue in this game, this game throws ammo at you. I had more ammo stashed then I could use on the last half of the game.Overall I really enjoyed this game. A dang near perfect 10/10.

_childDocuments_.review: The original System Shock was the basis for so many great immersive sims that came after it, and this remake takes all of the best advancements from the games that came after it and repackages them to enhance the original. The outcome is a truly fantastic game that remains true to the original whilst modernising the areas that benefit from it (and only those areas - nothing is lost from the original). This game is a masterclass in remaking something so many people adored the first time around, whilst making it accessible to new audiences.  But let's also be clear - System Shock isn't just a fantastic remake, it's a great game in its own right. Anyone who has played System Shock 2, Bioshock, Deus Ex will feel right at home on the reimagined Citadel Station.

_childDocuments_.review: The System Shock Remake is finally out, around 7 years after it's Kickstarter campaign. It's evolved a lot since that original demo, and I personally really enjoyed it.The story is almost the exact same as the original game, but with more fleshed out characters due to there being (if I recall the original correctly), over 10 times more audio logs. The original's animated intro cutscene was replaced with a short gameplay segment which tells more or less the same story, but with a small interactive portion at the start. The protagonist, a hacker, hacks into TriOptimum's servers and steals confidential information regarding cybernetic augmentations. He gets caught and captured by TriOptimum, and is transported to Citadel Station. There, a corrupt executive named Edward Diego offers to drop all charges and give you the military grade cybernetic augmentations free of charge, in exchange for the Hacker hacking into the stations systems and removing the stations AI's, Shodan's, ethical restraints. The Hacker accepts, does what he was asked, and is put into hibernation for 6 months. In the meantime, a now free to do whatever she wants Shodan developes a God complex and causes chaos on the station. That's all I can really say without spoiling the story.Shodan deserves her own little paragraph, because she's a great villain. She's always one step ahead of the Hacker, while you stop one plan she's already half way through executing another. She's more than aware of that fact, and will often communicate with you to mock you for it. She sees herself as a goddess, combining flesh and steel to create what she sees as perfection, and isn't willing to let humanity get in the way of her plans. During the game, you'll progress through Citadel Station with the goal of stopping Shodan and getting back to Earth. Citadel Station is a maze, a very dangerous one. If you just look at the automap, the different levels all seem like incomprehensible mazes, but actually navigating the environment is surprisingly easy, as each level is filled with landmarks. It's not always obvious where to go, System Shock really requires your attention. Key information is often hidden in audio logs, which isn't a big deal, but it's made slightly more annoying in the remake considering how many unimportant audio logs were added. Enemies respawn in places away from the player, so you're never fully safe. To fight enemies, you're gonna use a variety of weapons, mostly guns as there are only 3 melee weapons (all of which are weak). Unlike the original where only a couple weapons were good, here I felt like each weapon was useful. Most guns consume ammunition (which you can find around the station, loot from enemies or buy from vending machines which are one of the additions in this remake), but some use energy (which you can recharge with one time use batteries or recharge for free at power stations). The guns generally feel really good to use, and you can upgrade most of them with weapon mods (which weren't in the original game). The original game made you switch from interface mode to game mode constantly. Instead of just pressing R to reload, you'd have to press the button to go into interface mode (which would unlock the cursor), you'd have to go into the weapon menu, and click on the ammo type you wanted to load into the gun. Despite sounding weird, it was easy to get used to, and allowed you to do some cool things like shooting anywhere on the screen. The remake replaces this with a more traditional control scheme, which I'd say is probably an improvement.The only way to infinitely heal yourself is with surgery machines, and there are only 3 working ones in the entire game. Since there are 10 levels and only 3 have a surgery machine, you're often going to heal using one time use items, which aren't exactly rare but you're unlikely to ever have enough of them to truly feel comfortable.The original game used MIDI's for it's music, it was actually some of the earliest adaptive music in gaming. As cool as it was from a technical standpoint, 99% of the players didn't notice as the music often sounded like a child hitting random notes on a piano. The sound effects also weren't great, after a while of playing the original I was very close to muting it. This is one of the bigger improvements in the remake. The music is now way more atmospheric, and sound effects are way better. Some enemies can speak now, which in my opinion adds to the atmosphere.The remake is really faithful to the original, in both good and bad ways. Some issues with the original have been adressed, like making junk items useful (you can now recycle them for scrap which you can exchange into money, which you spend at vending machines for healing items, ammunition and weapon mods), and cyberspace isn't awful anymore (it turned from a headache inducing wireframe 6dof shooter with awful controls to a decent Descent clone) but some things are still just as tedious. I think the main change I would make is I would add something that would keep track of the red numbers. The player finds these on levels 1-6, but they don't stand out as much as they did in the original, and the player isn't informed about their importance until the moment they're needed. Keeping track of them somewhere on the HUD would save a lot of pointless backtracking.In short; the System Shock is a great remake of a great game. I'd definitely recommend it to fans of the System Shock franchise, fans of immersive sims like (Prey 2017), and fans of dungeon crawlers

_childDocuments_.review: I'd been waiting years to get into playing this, and I can't say it's worked out well after all the wait. The original is one of my favourite games of all time, and the first PC game I ever sunk a real lot of time into. The remake is .. almost a demake? It actually has fewer quality of life features than the original game in a few ways, and some of them are really quite impactful on gameplay - particularly the removal of nameable map markers. Many things they've just flat out removed, like the pose selector and being able to freely aim weapons, remove a lot of the fundamental character and charm of the original game. What has been removed was interesting, what replaces it is just boring tripe that makes it feel like a generic 2000s shooter.It's like someone remaking Doom, removing all the 2d art, all the original sound effects, all the original lighting scheme of the levels, and replacing them with some unity assetflip game quality placeholders, and going - "here's your remake". No it isn't, buddy. You messed it up. This is some cheap feeling crap.Ed - just from curiosity, I booted up the old SS1 Enhanced for a bit. Two things immediately stand out:1:  literally, from the very first room you're in, the changes in Remake are inferior, pointless, and remove a half dozen interesting pieces of content from the game. I knew remake was worse, but I didn't remember it being bad to quite that extent!2: Nightdive have left everyone who wants to play SS1EE with a choice of two delicious game breaking / experience ruining bugs (broken enemy movement OR inability to play above 30fps) since 2021. I simply can't believe these people get work - HOW can they be so bad at this? Architecting out the movement system vs viewport update frequency is ... really somewhere around the top 3 things you would need to do to rebuild the game? And in all seriousness, they've simply left it busted and told people "turns out that's a real pickle" years after finishing the work. More or less instantly explains a great deal about how the remake has turned out, I think.

_childDocuments_.name: System Shock

_childDocuments_.review: A very faithful revisit of a classic and genre-defining game. The things they changed mechanically and visually made a lot of sense and were solid modernization choices. The things they changed outside of that (level design, "quests", etc) were in my opinion, also done to the benefit of people who love the original game. As someone who did play the remaster of System Shock before playing this one, the changes they made to the game kept it enjoyable and made it so that my previous knowledge of the game was rewarded, while still sometimes making me learn new things to keep me on my feet. Solid recommendation for fans of immersive sims and science fiction. This is going to be my gold standard for any game developer revisiting an old game. They've kept the SOUL of the first game alive and well while making lots of changes to it. They knew exactly what they could and couldn't change to keep the core of the game intact and make it simultaneously a nostalgia trip and a new journey for people who loved the original.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a MUST PLAY remake, it is absolutely fantastic, needs next to no configuration at all to just get right-into play.  (i had to turn the audio down just a hair in settings so i could hear the voice chat of those who were in stream with me.) its so much better then the original, yet it pays respect to the second one (system shock 2) lining-up things that are all too familiar from that game. It adds little bits, not seen prior, that will make you recolect this version, when you proceed to play System Shock 2 afterward. Without making those little additions the Focus in this game. Easter eggs that you, if playing system shock 2, will get excited to see are brought more into focus in the second game.  That subtlety is HARD to achieve. It really is. Its often not even noticed by the player base. But those who become avid fans of their nostalgia later in life, progressing forward into the series, will appreciate the references. And it contributes the the whole experience of the series later on.Now The Original SystemShock was hard on the eyes.  This one can be difficult too, but less so, and for different reasons. Flat textures and LED's made the original difficult to view so much saturation and things looking similar, it was easier to get visually lost. In this version which is so much better, the strong saturation is reminiscent of the original as are the contrasting LED's on everything that are so strong. But 3d surfaces shadows and texture make it feel real.  So all the same feelings of the original are back. but with shading and darkness, making it much more horror and exhilarating then before. This might be the best Remake in HISTORY.This is better then the original, and better then the second game. yet balances that magical edge of not taking over or disrespecting either of those prior to it. This is some of the best work i have ever seen in gaming history poured into making the original game sooo much better, making it so much more real. For all its Draw, its maybe a bit Harder then the original., which works well, because there is a lot more drawing you in to keep playing and trying.  Kinda like Darksouls in the way that for as difficult as it may be, its fair and worth it, with enough interesting draws and pulls, that new players and old, will want to keep at it.  Which lengthens the play experience. Meaning you get a lot more out of your cost-to-game'time ratio.  Replay value is high.  Even though I've not reached the end yet, I almost don't want to. Because playing it, is whats fun. the Lore, is whats fun, Collecting and upgrading, hoarding, is whats fun. And trying the paths again even more efficiently then your first re-spawn, is whats fun. You know sometimes i consider leaving a negative review just because its what EVERYONE focuses on and reads.  Everyone wants to see why its bad. why its not recommended to play...  this gets a 5.5 stars out of 5.  this game is 120%. Because it was built based on something ALREADY great, and lovingly modified over a long thoughtful time, excellently and RESPECTFULLY reproduced, to improve on greatness.  Your group meetings and dev-socials paid off guys. Really!The original had flaws, and left me wanting for this or that. But only because of the limitations of the era and the hardware/software of the times.  It left me imagining my whole life what could have been better, or what would be taking it too far and detracting from the feel of the original with all the modern flashy-focus... the original was good, but limited by its era, They say copy-pasta is how we evolve and improve.  This team of devs, made that a matter of Fact. Clearly they discussed what taking it too far astray would be, and knew how to reel it in to maintain the original's experience. Bravo!I cant even express how much i am enjoying Panting and Sweating as i run through these Corridors.  It won't matter if the ending is short unepic or abrupt. I almost don't want to beat it, because how can anything compare with a perfect immortal Classic?I so much want to give this a bad review, just to get more cautious buyers to READ THIS REVIEW and give the game a shot. But i just cant click that 'not recommended" button. You devs have devoted time and torment to perfecting your respectful reproduction and making it even more emotionally impacting then the original, without damaging -anything- of the original. Breed and Reproduce you devs. we need more of your genes in the pool, Your lineage will prepare us for the day System Shock becomes reality.  Your magnificent grand children, will be the hackers that save humanity from something like Shodan!I cant even.   I cant even imagine better praise then this, You deserve it!

_childDocuments_.review: After playing this for 2 hours or so, the RE4 remake immediately came to mind. System Shock is also living proof of how a remake should be done: leave the game's essence, characters and plot untouched, just improve the graphics, make quality-of-life changes, and add some cool details. There, you have a good remake.Combat difficulty is still there, after all, you're just a human vs. armed robots and mutants. However, if you learn to use the correct weapons/ammo vs. them and master the leaning, you're good to go. Exploration and backtracking may be a little exhausting, you must learn the station's map very well or have very good spatial orientation. Cyberspace is a lot more fun than in the original and could be another separate game.Final boss fight was disappointing, though.

_childDocuments_.review: I never played the original beyond the first ten minutes of the demo version, but this is great! The sound design is similarly good, with each of the enemies distinctly recognisable before they've even come into sight. Full review:Oh damn, this game. Why didn't i play this earlier? I am a bit too young for the original System Shock but i am so glad this remake exists. This game is an absolute masterpiece. The story is nice and engaging, the combat is good, not groundbreaking but enjoyable.Though the Story was very good and the environmental storytelling was really nice. It was so interesting that every time i found a note or anything i read through it and i also listened to every single audio log i found. This is the first game that made me do this. Normally i skip this part because my adhd brain doesn't want me to read boring notes and wants that dopamin rush from combat or exploration. But this well made remake made me read though everything. It's really sad that only less than 18% actually finished this game. But i get it, always having to listen to audio logs to find where to go and what to do can be tedious for some/most. Just listen to what characters say to you and explore and use your brain.Also, the combat difficulty starts really easy and at first that made me a bit worried, but it gets harder the more you play it. Though if you explore enough, you never run out of ammo.Hope this review is making sense. I am not that good at writing stuff like this in my first language, so english is even harder for me.

_childDocuments_.review: Do I recommend this game to those who are familiar with the series? Yes. Do I recommend it otherwise? Maybe. This game is a faithful remake of the original SS, which was a product of its time. This means the game not only doesn't have quality-of-life updates like objective markers, it at times can seem genuinely obtuse regarding what to do next. The story and your next steps are revealed mostly through found texts and voice clips from the crew or even Shodan herself, but honestly I had to consult walkthroughs a few times to know what to do next or where to go. It can be very, very difficult to discern. You also need to do a fair bit of backtracking at times and return to places that are not easily recalled or marked on your map in any way. This leads to a fair bit of wandering empty hallways and areas you already cleared of all enemies, which isn't terribly interesting. The bottom line is that this isn't a game for everyone, but if you are willing to accept these caveats and okay with consulting the forums periodically, I think you will have a good time. With that said, here are some tips to make your playthrough more enjoyable: 1. Vaporize everything. The economy in this game can be managed pretty easily early on by just turning everything to scrap and recycling it. 2. Grenades home in on enemies. It's weird to say, but grenades will generally roll or bounce toward enemies in this game. Feel free to chuck them off walls/corners without being in the line of fire and you'll generally be on target.3. Non-health stims are whatever. Opinions may vary, but aside from the health-specific stims, I never bothered. You may want to stash the non-health options someplace or ignore them entirely to open up inventory space. 4. There's clear weapon overlap and preference. The first pistol you get can be replaced later by the Magnum or SMG (which uses the same ammo). The first energy gun you get can be replaced by the Ion rifle. While the laser rapier is mean af, I found there's zero need for melee weapons by the middle of the game (on normal difficulty), so just ditch it/melee in general.5. Have something to take notes on. As I said, objective markers don't exist AND there's no journal element in this game to tell you what to do. Further, if you see a number or a code that you need, nothing in-game records it for you. Write stuff down to keep things clear. It's unusual, I know, but trust me on this. It'll save time. 6. The junction box puzzles aren't explained. This was the case for me, at least. Honestly, watch a tutorial regarding how to do them and save yourself some time of trial/error. 7. Codes for doors/story elements are randomized. I mentioned using walkthroughs (albeit sparingly), but it's worth noting that a lot of the codes in the game are randomized, so what worked in one playthrough may not work a second time. Follow the steps in a walkthrough and ignore the code (in most cases) that gets reported therein.

_childDocuments_.review: It has all the elements of the original but instead of controlling like a mech game having an acid trip, this feels like a modern FPS. Don't expect a full-on imsim because System Shock is in the middle of different schools of design: FPS gameplay, the labyrinthic dungeon crawling layouts, some survival flair (enhanced with the newly implemented inventory system), the Descent-like hacking sections... it's a peculiar game in which various schools of design overlap while also pioneering its own, therefore the depth of something like Deus Ex isn't as present, just the beginning of it.It's still really engaging, and while it's more simplistic than more modern efforts, this Nightdive remake brings a ton of improvements that makes the whole experience a smooth ride. It's way less hostile and more approachable, gunplay is good, movement and exploration feel better, it's way easier to orientate yourself... and the presentation is pretty damn good. I was a bit skeptical towards the artstyle at first but it grew on me. The only major downside I can think of is the ending which tried to make something different with the battle against Shodan but it didn't quite pan out as smoothly as they thought, tho I applaud the artistic intent behind it and at the end of the day that's still like 10 minutes out of 30+ hours of gameplay.Good ♥♥♥♥, looking forward to the enhanced edition of SS2.

_childDocuments_.review: I don't get what people like about this game.I haven't played the original System Shocks, so going in as a brand new player of the remake (on default difficulty), this game felt like a chore, start to finish. Once you get past the shiny packaging of learning how the game works, most of the game I ended up doing the ultimate tedium of managing my limited inventory to fit in the things I want to take with me, making space in that limited inventory already filled out with guns and ammo and supplies to make room for random junk I want to recycle for credits, perpetually shooting enemies behind some kind of cover in a mind-numbing "wait for them to shoot, then lean out of cover to shoot back because if you're out in the open they damn near insta-kill you" back and forth, and figuring out where the hell I'm trying to go.Which, by the way, the game doesnt make very clear where you're supposed to go. Despite you getting hints on what's next to be done with the audio logs, data sticks, and incoming messages you get, there are no useful markings on the map. Any undiscovered part of the level you have to hug every wall and corner just to find places that may have doors so whenever you progress a little bit, and you have to go back to another level, you're basically trying every door you haven't already gone through to see if it opens now. Who designed the map, anyway? It sucks! There are so many quality of life changes you can make to it, such as making empty stores not get marked on the map, persisting resources that you scanned in the map so you can come back to them whenever your inventory isn't full (yes, I know I can place markers but they're indistinguishable from one another, so I've used it sparingly), or even just marking points of interest, like the CPU rooms, which you'll inevitably have to come back to once you understand what they're used for. Chances are, you'll end up Googling some of them because you'll simply get very impatient with it.Managing my limited inventory is probably the least favorite part of my game. Even with the 4 box stash that I started using on the Maintenance level, AND the cargo lift, AND throwing stuff I don't think I'll need out, I still didn't have nearly enough inventory space for the things I ultimately wanted to take with me. By near the end of the game, I had no room in my inventory when I went past the point of no return, as I had 4 guns, and the rest of the space being filled with ammo, grenades, and trinkets. Oh, by the way, if you want upgrades or extra stuff like ammo and resources that you're having trouble finding elsewhere because you already scavenged the entire map, you'll have to make a LOT of room for random junk that you can either recycle for credits, or vaporize, for usually a scrap amount equal to roughly half the credit amount of you recycling the item whole. So just to get some upgrades I wanted, I had to walk around empty maps for an hour or so just to collect items, run back to the recycler, recycle them, run around some more to find more items, rinse and repeat. Does that sound fun to you?Story isn't really anything to praise the game for, either. There's sprinkles of story filler in the forms of data sticks (text), and audio logs. They add a bit of info about the life on the Citadel, but the main story isn't much more than "I am a sentient AI, and I'll take over the world to do the things I want to do". Not much about you, the protagonist, not much about the AI (aside from the repetition of how much of a supreme being she is, and how much of a nuisance you are), or the characters that try to talk to you. It was also hard to appreciate the story whenever you start a level and you're immediately ambushed by enemies while the audio plays, or you're focusing on figuring out where the hell you are, much less where you're going.Finally, there's the Cyberspace. ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, what a bore. While I did initially like the navigation controls of being able to rotate yourself however you want in the space, the combat was nothing more than hold down left mouse button, sometimes press right mouse button, and hold one of the direction keys to avoid the bullets. There wasn't really any depth to it, it was just there to pad the gameplay with a whole bunch of nothing. I'd rather do the standard combat than the Cyberspace stuff. Imagine my reaction when the FINAL BOSS FIGHT, BY THE WAY, was a variant of the Cyberspace. One weapon, that didn't even feel good to shoot. Did anyone at Nightdive play it? Did nobody there think that maybe the final boss fight was maybe, just maybe, not fun at all?The puzzles were alright, though.

_childDocuments_.review: Pretty damn good. Although this was one of the first immersive sims ever, I'd still say it's outclassed by later immersive sims like System Shock 2, Deus Ex and Prey, but it feels like this remake is a piece of history that's been polished up and put in a museum so you can go back and see where it all began.System Shock is more or less perfect atmospherically. They preserved the original game's blocky architecture but despite how outdated it appears, it kinda ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ slaps tbh. The game feels extremely "cyber" and like a real kind of auteur work, where although a lot of elements of the game are really weird, it all kind of synergises together.One thing I always enjoy in immersive sim games is that feeling of getting extremely powerful over time. At the start of the game, you're just a dumbass wandering around in the darkness with a wrench and pissed pants, but by the end, you're experienced, brave and loaded with weapons and nobody can ♥♥♥♥ with you. Exploring, dealing with traps and slowly getting new gadgets and weapons tickles my progression itch. System Shock exudes that feeling constantly.There are a few things that I'd class as problems, but nothing major. Perhaps one of the biggest things to complain about is that the game's kind of easy.Granted, I played on normal instead of hard, but it just seems like enemies aren't very intelligent and the tools given to you are really, really strong. I beat every single boss by just taking some drugs that make you take less damage and attack faster and then sprinting at the boss with a laser rapier and slashing till they died. Normally this would take about 5 or 6 slashes, which means basically about 5 seconds at most. The bosses should really be harder.Another thing is that you unlock some boots that let you fly a little bit, just some light propulsion. I'm not sure how it was in the original (because I never played it) but these boots kind of seem to trivialise some things that maybe shouldn't be trivial? There are some areas where it seems like the game has something for you to solve in order to create a path to a location, but most of the time, you can just use your jump boots to fly straight to that location. It feels like there were a couple of times where I shouldn't have been able to skip something so easily, but yet I did. Multiple times.Thirdly, I ran into two softlocks. Both easily fixable softlocks, I imagine. To get around them, I had to reload a save for the first one and spend 30 mins brute forcing a security code for the second one.Last issue, the game lacks scarcity. Immersive sims generally all have a focus on resource management, but then System Shock just ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ showers you in items and you never really have any issue using them. I would use 60 to 70 bullets shooting a bulky security robot only to loot its body and find 50 bullets with another 50 sitting in the room it was guarding. Even with very liberal use of items, I never came close to running out.It's still a really good game, but a little easy and a little barebones at times. And the cyberspace sections are kind of boring.

_childDocuments_.review: For my tastes this updated version of System Shock updates to something more contemporary without going overboard, and was exactly what I was hoping for. But for anyone playing this for the first time should know that this game (along with the Ultima Underworld series, which I didn't come to until much later) was the computer game experience that felt closest to playing a tabletop roleplaying game at the time. Hopefully some of that magic carries through for people playing this game for the first time.

_childDocuments_.review: It's good friends!So, I was a backer of the kickstarter way back then, and I'm an unapologetic fan of the original game. Suffice to say, my trust as to it coming out and being good went downward as time went on.Boy was I wrong.It somehow feels as a remake should: up to modern standards while not being a betrayal of your cherished memories. I instantly recognized Citadel Station, its corridors and gleed as Shodan (still Terri Brosius <3 ) threatened me.Graphics are in the same vein: while the game runs under some version of Unreal Engine, there's a pixelated look to everything which kinda gets you back to 1994.Gameplay lacks a little "umpf" especially kickbacks on weapons, but that doesn't hurt too much the whole experience as System Shock never was only about shooting.I'm only a few hours in as I'm typing this review and might come back later if there are some changes, but so far, I've only one advice: go for it, Hacker!

_childDocuments_.review: I was delighted with the game, but I can't say I can recommend it to everyone. _childDocuments_.review: This remake does a great job bringing System Shock to the modern day by making it much more accessible and easier to control, while upgrading the visuals with a retro cyberpunk style that does a great job retaining the feel of the old simple graphics but making the blocky interior work in a higher fidelity. That must have been a hard balance to find, but it is struck incredibly well.System Shock wrote the dictionary of game design principles that countless later games tapped into. This brings a problem with it: everything that this game does, has been done by games that came after it, and often better. It is not going to break new ground now in 2023 because it built most of that ground in 1994.But this is also its charm. Playing this game feels like going back in time, and seeing the genesis of the immersive sim and survival horror shooter genres. So many modern games can trace their lineage back to System Shock. You are playing 30 year old game design with some modern conveniences introduced to sand off the sharp edges, and this way it holds up surprisingly well.A word of warning: this game does not hold your hand. At all. Even when you flip a switch or solve a puzzle it is often unclear what you have changed. It is up to you to explore the claustrophobic corners of Citadel, listen to and read logs, and pay careful attention to your surroundings to figure out what you need to do and where to go next.But this is part of the challenge. The game expects the player to contribute a lot, and provides just enough tools for them to achieve their goals. Your secondary gameplay loop is to slow down, look over your collected logs, study your map, count your resources, and think about what your next step should be. To me this greatly increases the immersion of the game, because it makes me feel like I'm truly lost and alone with only my wits to save me from SHODAN.
_childDocuments_.name: System Shock

_childDocuments_.review: The original System Shock was one of my favorite games when younger, an interesting take on the fledgling first person shooter/exploration genre that was a bit overdesigned but a very memorable experience.  When a remake hit up Kickstarter, I threw some money at it, and over the years since basically came to accept that it was probably going to be one of those campaigns that didn't amount to anything.  I was pleasantly surprised to find out that not only did the remake actually end up coming out, it was pretty good and worth the wait.System Shock is effectively one of the progenitors of the Immersive Sim genre.  As a formative member, it lacks a lot of the enhancements that came with titles over the years, but it's still a game full of interesting interlocked levels, objectives that span multiple areas and are more complex than "find the key", resource management, environmental and audio storytelling, and puzzle solving.  SS Remake takes the core of what worked, expands on that some, makes some largely sensible redesigns, but still leaves the clunky-but-charming core intact rather than design it as if it was a brand new 2023 title.It's certainly not perfect, and some of that is due to the legacy design inherent in a game almost 30 years old. Some of the design changes don't add to the game in any particular way (especially the overly strict inventory limits), and the periodic boss fights tend to be tuned so high on the default difficulty settings that a deliberate and controlled journey around Citadel Station can suddenly morph into a quickload bonanza due to extreme damage spikes.  Also, unlike a lot of games that came later in the genre, there's not much replayability here as there's no character building to experiment with.If you've enjoyed titles that have come in the years since, like Deus Ex, Dishonored, Prey, or Bioshock, it's worth taking a look at System Shock to see where a lot of the genre originally came from; if you have fond memories of playing it before, then this is as good a way as any to take a trip down memory lane. I'd be happy to see Nightdive give System Shock 2 the same treatment in the future.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a lot of fun. The slightly pixelated aesthetic is very visually pleasing. The combat is fun and the dismemberment is satisfying. Ive never played the original but i am a huge fan of Bioshock. Its been refreshing seeing what inspired those amazing games. _childDocuments_.name: System Shock

_childDocuments_.review: I'm not familiar with the original 1994 release, but this game on its own was torturous to play.  In no particular order:- Dull samey environments to slowly navigate.  Most areas are indistinguishable until you reach the gardens- Limited inventory combined with the huge amount of clutter lying around.  Pick up everything and painstakingly mulch it down to money and scrap, or live with the nagging feeling of missing out on the trickle of loot.- Enemy variety largely boils down to: mutant that runs up to you and clubs you, robot/biomass the hurls projectiles at you or a gun on wheels- Combat is very unsatisfying. There's no meaty contact with anything biological, it's more satisfying to smash glass or walls than an enemy. Gunplay is similarly lacking in delivery.  Most enemies simply slump to the ground unceremoniously when dead, including flying robots which drop like paper plates.- Tiny numbers of enemies at any one time.  Combat is left feeling very orchestrated and in small groups which does not do much to get you excited.- The audio logs are painful to listen to, but you must comb through all their trite cliches to get vital information to progress.- No auto sorting of your inventory, It is a pain to manage. Feels like old clunky western RPG item management.The Descent minigame in cyberspace was cool though.
_childDocuments_.name: System Shock

_childDocuments_.review: I can't recommend this game highly enough. Gorgeous, atmospheric, and accessible while still wearing its old-school design on its sleeve, System Shock feels closer to the dungeon crawlers of the 80s and early 90s than the imsims of now - even System Shock 2's design feels much closer to something like Prey, but if you're willing to meet it on its terms it's extremely rewarding. Absolutely essential game.

_childDocuments_.review: I played this on the default 2,2,2,2 difficulty and a lot of the issues I have with the difficulty of the game can be fixed by playing a lower difficulty. _childDocuments_.review: Decided to finish with the System Shock Remake and uninstall it. A good game and a fantastic remake of a classic game, and should be held high as an excellent example of how these remakes and remasters should be done.However, for me it has been slightly too faithful to the original, missing one key modern touch, which I'm not ashamed to say I needed, and that is a quest log and some kind of waypoint system.Perhaps it's something that could be toggled on, so the purists can have a more classic experience, but for me, I spent a good chunk of the game wondering around, not entirely sure what I was supposed to be doing and where I should go. More than once I had actually unlocked the next part of the game, having completed what I needed to, without actually realising and spent some decent time kind of wondering around.The exploration is pretty fun though, and scoring the map to see if there is a place I haven't explored and then heading there, was engaging.. for a time. However I ended up resorting to guides to understand if I had missed something, or wasn't sure where I needed to be... and I dunno… I just kind of ran out of steam.So.. there we go, an excellent remake that I know is a great game, but... for now I've had my fill. Maybe one day I'll return to it and finish it, who knows.So yeah, recommended for sure, but if you do fancy it, keep in mind you might need a notebook to well... make notes 😃
_childDocuments_.name: System Shock

_childDocuments_.review: System Shock's innovative style, gameplay and story have stood the test of time and the title remains one of *the* best examples of an 'immersive sim'.  Thankfully the remake does everything it can to sand off the rough edges while maintaining the difficult but rewarding gameplay experience. Not only that, but the title is well optimized and runs great on the steam deck right off the bat!The only strange change I've noticed/disagreed with is the lack of any sort of soundtrack. I'm not sure if it was an artistic decision or if there's some day 1 bugginess but there does not really seem to be any ambient soundtracks playing 90% of the time. I would've at least liked an *option* to play the old school Drum n Bass in the background, but I guess I'll have to wait for mods.While I was initially frustrated with the constant delays (well, we all were) the final product proves that it was worth the wait. This title should sit comfortably alongside the other excellent remasters of the year, like Dead Space and RE4Well done, Nightdive.

_childDocuments_.review: I liked it. Not as much as the original (or rather Nightdive's remaster of the original) but nearly as much.Improvements:Story is delivered slightly better; an interactive intro to set the scene, more believable audio log performances.Controls; I love the original but I'll admit it has some wonky movement, the remake is a lot less frictional.Gunplay; feels a lot tighter, grenades behave themselves and are actually usefulProgression; the weapons have been reworked so there are less completely niche options and each non-melee weapon has upgrades to improve performance.Graphics; I'm still fond of the original graphics (which get a cool re-use as hallucinations when using certain stims) but to a newer audience they won't win any contests. Here we get lovely detailed enemies and environments that when paired with the lighting really have a mood.This last section is somewhat more wordy to carry my meaning and may admittedly be pure taste on my part so tldr Nightdive did a good job of updating System Shock, keeping it true to what came before with modern gameplay and I enjoyed it.Drawbacks:Graphics and Music: The original's music can admittedly be a little jarring however it definitely differentiates each level you're in. The remake opts for a more ambient soundscape which isn't bad but it loses a little of the distinct flavour of each area. The graphics of the original are similarly distinct (if cruder) and some areas can feel as though they aren't as thematic as others in their level.Economy; they introduced the recycling mechanic from subsequent ImSim games. You can either scrap items in your inventory or carry them back to a recycler. If you scrap in your inventory, you get an item which occupies 1 slot and stacks up to 100 which can be recycled. I can say as a compulsive recycler, if you carry everything back to the machine you will probably finish the game with much more credits than you can actually spend.The above in itself isn't a universal problem, not everyone is going to play like I did. However they also changed the inventory. Perhaps as part of balancing the economy or balancing the weapons. In the original there were only so many weapons and consumables you could carry by type but you could carry a lot of each's ammo and by the time the enemies stopped dropping a weapon's ammo, you knew to move on from it). Here the inventory space is limited and I only ran out of the first ammo type on the second to last level, meaning I barely needed to touch the fancier weapons obtained later in the game.

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic game with exceptional game play encounters that are diverse and intense thanks to the A.I. I love the atmosphere and feel instantly immersed, the puzzles are ok, but the environment and music perfectly set the tone. Audio logs fill in the gaps and have excellent voice acting. I've never played the OG 1994 SS, so cant speak to keeping to source material however, Its just incredible.
_childDocuments_.name: System Shock

_childDocuments_.review: I never played the Original System Shock, but this remake certainly lives up to its name for sure.  Gonna start by saying this game is hard. From the combat, to the exploration of the space rig, to even doing the main objectives, i was fighting for my life every second trying to get to the end.The space rig is huge, with maze like levels, and a sense of dread around every corner. Also with secret areas to boot. Enemies are plentiful and can be very unforgiving depending on the situation. One second your fighting some basic enemy types, the next your going through a full clip to take down a single enemy. Story was fantastic and that ending was worth all the pain and sweat to defeat a sentient AI. I shall not spoil, but i wish you luck. Also the collectibles shed some more story of whats happened on the station so definitely worth collecting them too.Weapons; limited, ammo; scarce, health; lacking. Playing made me realize that having a strategy when engaging in combat was pivotal in not wasting resources. Sure, later areas could give you a chance at ammo and other items, but if you don't hoard as much as you can, you will notice how quickly everything goes.Conclusion; To some this would be nostalgic if you played the original, to me this was an experience and quite the adventure. If you wanna give this a go and have never played the original, I'd say absolutely give it a try, and also best of luck to you, because it's tough. However, if you have played the original and wanna see what the remake has to offer, i'd also still say jump back in and play it again, you won't be disappointed.
_childDocuments_.name: System Shock

_childDocuments_.review: SHODAN is back! Well... in a retrograde manner of speaking. I've never played the original System Shock but I LOVE LOVE LOVE System Shock 2. I consider it to be the best PC game for a shooter genre ever! Even surpassing Half-Life which has over-shadowed it at that time."Shivers tingling down my spine" is an overly-stated understatement when her digital horrific condescending "Insect" came on, after more than 20 years when I last listened to her. The game kicked me with its graphically-beautiful upgraded boots into the nostalgic realm, and it was a great experience.Any new players can easily tell this is indeed a remake, without prior knowledge that... it is a remake. Because of how faithful it is to the original. They are a few game design choices that seem backward, sort of anti-service to players of this generation. There are no objective prompts to tell you what you should do next. The level design is a maze in the most literal sense ever. There is no indication or feedback if a door can be opened! But I believe the developers have made this intentional.Hey, aren't there comments in many game forums of players complaining of how games are too easy nowadays and serving objectives to you on a golden platter? I feel the System Shock remake is a whole fresh take on today's kind of games, and such indie games of similar style are under-appreciated. While I think this game is not for everybody, this is a must play for those open-minded players who like first person dungeon crawler shooter and are looking for something different.That said, I still feel System Shock 2 is still way superior. After playing this game, you may want to give System Shock 2 a try! ;) I first played this game on 2-2-2-2 configuration and man, it is hard, and I don't mean the Dark Souls kind of hard. I mean it requires some brain power and strategy. For those who have not played at least System Shock 2 before, you may want to set every difficulty option to 1. Setting them to 2 or more MAY repel players from going back to play it after only a few hours in. Also, don't trust reviewers who has played only a few hours of the game. It is also advisable to play this game with a pen and a notebook beside you. You have to listen and read every log carefully and note down details which you think are important, or you will get lost!
_childDocuments_.name: System Shock

_childDocuments_.review: As someone who played System Shock 2 as a young adult it quickly became one of my favourite games way back when I got the big box of it on release, it was also one of the very few games that legitimately scared the hell out of me along with the original Playstation Resident Evils, Silent Hill and the spiders in Thief the Dark Project. It was here that I was introduced to the series titular antagonist Shodan, however I never played the original as it did look incredibly dated. I have a long history with Immersive Sims starting with the original Thiefs and System Shock 2 in the 90's and the original System Shock has not disappointed. The developers have nailed the immersion and environment of Citadel Station. One criticism I do have is I generally don't find this game scary at all and I put that down to the more colourful art style chosen especially for the mutants who in my opinion look slightly cartoony. They also dont seem to speak as much as the mutants in the sequel who you could hear moaning and calling out as Hive Minds of the "Many" which generally scared the hell out of me. One other criticism would be the complete lack of any indicator of where to go or what to do. I get it this is an old game and this is a faithful remake  and the original had nothing like this, but the sequel and the original Thief games at least gave you a rough objective for the level or in this case Deck in a journal and this unfortunately has nothing, you just have to listen to audio logs and notes and kind of guess it. However in conclusion an incredible remake of a cult classic and im eager to continue and finish it for the first ever time, and then we begin the march to System Shock 3!!
_childDocuments_.name: System Shock

_childDocuments_.review: Ladies and gentlemen, the 90's are back. Thank you Nightdive for this awesome remake. The team worked really hard for a risky project, a saga that never made a lot of money in the first place but many players love it and it has been a great inspiration for the gaming industry. This remake makes justice to it. It might not be perfect but I love it, just like the original. There's no "instant gratification" here. the game is not gonna hand hold you like most modern titles do nowadays. You have to think, pay attention to everything, manage your resources, solve puzzles, be tactical about combat (this game REALLY wants to kill you), etc... You have to achieve everything by yourself. Even the plot requires you to listen audio logs and read documents to figure out your objectives. I recommend pen and paper or your phone next to you to take notes. The level desing is amazing. It makes you feel free and trapped at the same time. If you like metroidvania style of progression you're gonna love this. But this goes beyond... sometimes there will be more than one way to approach the same objective, so replayability is guaranteed. Depending on the way you explore you might find certain weapons, abilities, upgrades, etc... in a very different order than other players. There are also shortcuts to connect distant areas and maaany optional zones that reward you with resources and lore. So you can say that the game unfolds in a very organic/diegetic way.Difficulty is very customizable. For example: if you want more challenge on combat and less on puzzles (or viceversa), you can configure it as you want. So even more replayability. I agree with the people saying that melee combat lacks impact sometimes, but I find it satisfactory when I manage to cut an enemy in half or destroy their heads. The gore system has good dismemberment.This is all I have to say by the moment, gotta continue playing. But I recommend this 100%. It really is worth the price and you don't need NASA hardware to run it.
_childDocuments_.name: System Shock

_childDocuments_.review: What a wonderfully crafted experience. Hard as nails, terrifying atmosphere, and a well-observed reverence to the source material. You play as the Hacker, who has just woken up on a space station with a rogue GAI named SHODAN in control. It is up to you to find a way back home to Earth and deal with SHODAN's forces. The game plays a lot like Bioshock meets Rainbow Six: Siege; tons of audio logs to reveal the story of what has happened to the station, along with the slow, methodical corner clearing and quick leaning from R6. There is something of an augmentation system in the game, but expect nothing as deep as a modern game. You can acquire different shields for different damage sources, an upgradable radar, some boost boots, and a headlamp. Most of the weapons you get will have multiple ammo types and upgrades available, but the number of guns you can carry will be limited by an old school inventory system that you will have to manage yourself. There is a customizable difficulty system that allows you to tailor the game to your preferences. That being said the higher up you go, the less the game holds your hand (.) You can adjust the difficulty of the Combat, Mission, Cyber, and Puzzles. I finished the game on 3/2/2/3 a couple days ago and I'm already considering trying a 3/3/3/3. The last time I wanted to do that was when I played DX:HR the first time almost 10 years ago. The only gripe I have with the game has to do with the final section of the game, which I will detail in spoilers for obvious reasons.  Other than those small things mentioned in the spoiler section, this game is an absolute win compared to today's live-service infested, money farming, awfully unfinished AAA games. I went from playing Diablo 4 to this and felt so much more joy in my time playing this game than I did grinding to 100+ content in D4.10/10 Buy now, why are you still reading this? GOTY
_childDocuments_.name: System Shock

_childDocuments_.review: STEAM DECK OWNERS BEWARE - Steam Cloud saves aren't working, so unless you love manually transferring save files from PC to Steam Deck and vice versa, forget taking your PC save file with you on the Deck.This is an advertised feature that isn't working, hopefully the devs will fix it soon.That aside, the game is haunting, atmospheric, and absorbing. I'm engrossed in the story and Shodan is a well-conceived antagonist. As the hacker who essentially caused a catastrophic loss of human life and may be responsible for the destruction of Earth, if saving humanity and redeeming yourself isn't motivation enough to defeat Shodan, your own survival or at least your will to defy her plan to turn you into her slave should be.I can take or leave the throwback pixelated visuals, the gameplay itself is enough of a throwback to the 90's to remind me that I'm playing a remake of a 30-year-old game without making me squint to identify an item before I pick it up. Aside from that, the lighting, animations, sound design, ambient music, level design are all well done. No bugs so far, except for the lack of Steam Cloud saves as I mentioned.Recommended.

_childDocuments_.review: I was definitely going to make a positive review about this game, but what drove me to write it before finishing was one of the NEGATIVE reviews complaining about some of the design aspects. And warning that there are spoilers after this ---Quote from that review:---"System Shock 2 is old, but it holds up. I was expecting this remake--especially one that took eight ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ years to make--to bring System Shock 1 up to at least the standards of the second game. At least. But it doesn't. Instead we get level design from 1994, and gameplay that has only two tactics: murder, and run away.[...]"This is nothing but walking around clicking on everything, hoping it's an audiolog to pick up that'll tell you what to do, or the correct thing that you were supposed to click. Audiologs are the only guidance you receive, by the way, and finding them is your main incentive to explore; unfortunately, almost none of them actually contain important or relevant story information or objectives.[...]What has decidedly killed this game for me is the environmental design. Citadel Station does not look even remotely like a place where real humans once lived. At its best, it's a strange, ugly, confusing labyrinth of corridors, that feels more like a rat lab than a space station.[...]---The first complaint they have is level design from 1994. The game has been accurately remade, and you can almost use an original walkthrough to complete it. The OG game had things you could interact with everywhere; it was part shooter part point-and-click, which is what helped define the genre of 'Immersive Sim'. So many things could be interacted with. It felt like you woke up in a real space station and had to figure out how to do everything, and didn't know what buttons were important or not. This helped people get into games more, but now some people seem frustrated by that - this is probably why there are less people becoming doctors and pilots despite there being more computers in western countries.The enemies are being constantly made by SHODAN and fed into each area, so it's true that you might be walking around a corner and one will literally come out of a delivery lift in the ground then shoved in your face, or slide through a port hole in the wall with zero warning, and it's true that you can really only fight or run away. It is meant to create an atmosphere of danger, that you are always being watched and never safe. You are meant to be always moving - on the highest difficulty level there is even a time limit to complete the game or you will automatically lose regardless of your progress.Next they deride things like audio logs. You are taking the blame for an executive director who is stealing a bio weapon, and he needs access to blocked files. SHODAN, the station AI, goes insane because you turn off the ethical restrictions that secure them, but also prevent her from doing things like killing. No one on the station knows what is going on, so obviously there are audio logs around the place where people are recording messages asking "What is going on? Who is responsible?"If you pay attention to the people who record them and the things they say, there is a narrative to connect where you can figure out the path they've taken, when they realised that things have gone wrong, what they tried to do, and where they eventually died when you discover their body with their name tag (sometimes it even leads you to good pickups, which is exactly what happened in SS2). A lot of people find this stuff really interesting - I personally thought it was one of the most interesting parts of SS2, so it's weird to see someone get annoyed about that detail being lifted from the original game as well.The funniest part for me, is that one piece of information that you can pick up is from a character who discusses how the space station was intentionally designed as an experiment to test people for stress and anxiety - literally treating them like rats in a maze. It is part of the story that the game world has been designed to upset people on purpose - here's that negative review quote again:"What has decidedly killed this game for me is the environmental design. Citadel Station does not look even remotely like a place where real humans once lived. At its best, it's a strange, ugly, confusing labyrinth of corridors, that feels more like a rat lab than a space station." - The game has succeeded by stressing a real person out and creating exactly the kind of atmosphere it wanted to create, but they still gave it a negative review for bad level design and say it shouldn't be like that because we don't make games like that anymore. It wouldn't be the same game if it was any different.This is like one of those things where two people are looking at a canvas - one of them says "I don't like it" and the other fwops their scarf and says "You just don't understand art, darling."

_childDocuments_.review: Updated after patch 1.2.Originally I critizied the game a bit about being placed in a weird spot, where on one hand it does enough changes to annoy the strictest of purist and yet not doing enough to remove the roughest of edges that make it impossible for some gamers to enjoy the original release. Well, after 1.2 and addition of minimal waypoints on the easiest mission difficulty, I think that is no longer a case. There is still a chance to get stuck, you will still get lost here and there - but having some waypoints as a safety net is in my mind a really great way to address that issue and make sure that those, who tried playing the game and ultimately ended up frustrated by being lost and giving up on it have some aid if they are not confident in their abilities to figure everything out - while - at the same time, staying true to the original vision, where you can totally get lost on the citadel station  not knowing what to do, if you dare to start your first playthrough on mission difficulty 2. Other in that - like mentioned before -this is a great (now) significantly more accessible way to experience the 1994 classic. A faithful remake of a truly ground-breaking game that focuses a lot on environmental exploration, filled with environmental storytelling and fantastic audio logs that has since then became a standard in horror games. If anything - just still keep in mind, that even with all the help at lowest difficulty - you will still get lost to an extend and get to know each corner of the station.. so even if objective markers now helping you - you'll need a bit of patience and the right state of mind to get through it.... but it's totally worth it! Even at full price!
_childDocuments_.name: System Shock

_childDocuments_.review: Another fantastic remake of the year, and an even more faithfully-reproduced one at that. Manages to feel fresh, new, and completely reinvigorated in every way. The Cyberspace levels in particular have taken cues from 6DOF games since the 1994 release, namely of which was clearly Forsaken (especially given Nightdive's own work on that game, and its great 2018 rerelease.)I can hardly say anything bad about the game, given its attention to detail, and sheer creativity in some spots to its predecessor- especially since the original was as pixelated and raw as the singular FPS blockbuster that preceded it a year earlier. Nightdive has certainly worked its collective cortex out on this one in all aspects- and it was a treat to unfold its many mysteries as a longtime series fan, and someone often unaccepting of change, and newer design ethos, especially in this industry. On that note, many others have gone in-depth to cover the positives of this game, and I can certainly agree with any and all of them- so instead, I'll cover the few downsides of this game that I can recall: ⁍ The remixed elevator soundtrack is INCREDIBLY  There's a bit more of a tinny-sounding twist on the original's otherwise faithful reproduction on it, and that immediately made it worse than the original's lighter-hearted intermission between The Citadel's sprawling levels. Easily the worst thing about the game by far, hope it becomes swappable by a mod fast. ⁍ There's a few bugs that have the potential to ruin parts of the game; Including, but not limited to:       ◦ Soundtracks disappearing on Quickloads;      ◦ Ambient soundtrack bugging out midway through a track, or not activating properly (delayed, or missing) upon enemy encounter;      ◦ End-game logs becoming bugged in geography, blocking completionist achievements     ◦Game-breaking bug (set to be in the first patch) on Reactor, after       ◦ BIG ONE, at least for me - Left-mouseclicks don't always register as inputs. I don't know how widespread this issue in particular is, because I haven't seen it talked about anywhere else- but one thing I'm certain about is that it is NOT my mouse causing this. The error isn't reproducible in any other game besides this. In spite of this laundry list... It was a long wait, but rest-assured, it wasn't for nothing. I couldn't even imagine attempting to step into the original's antiquated control scheme again after the incredibly job Nightdive has done here.By the way, the  soundtrack is available TLDR: Another fantastic remake of the year, and an even more faithfully-reproduced one at that. Manages to feel fresh, new, and completely reinvigorated in every way, ESPECIALLY within the Cyberspace levels, where most of the combat has taken cues from other 6DOF games since the 1994 original. Hardly any negatives to the game, great release price now. Stop hesitating if you're a fan of narrative-driven, no-handholding game design- this one's made for you.

Really shows its age and not a fan at all.Taking 2 points off for the absolutely pathetic ending. I played through on 3/3/3/3 and died constantly at the end. _childDocuments_.review: Easily the best game I have played in years.  The feeling of isolation, the enemy variety, the weapon variety, the satisfaction of uncovering layer after layer of the enormous space station is something you don't find in much newer games.  I felt like I was in a science fiction novel living it out in real time.The art style is charming and a welcome addition adding to the retro charm that this game has.  I seriously cant say enough good things about this game!I finally beat this game after an entire month and 50+ hours, I savored every moment of it and was bummed out when it finally ended.  I usually get really impatient and look stuff up on google to get though a game but with this one i really just figured everything out on my own and it was so satisfying to progress in a game using your own wits and brain.  This game does not hold your had but the solutions to problems are found in audio logs and its more than fair unlike other old school cryptic games.I also really like the progression of difficulty the game gives you stronger wepons as bigger harder enemies come in the late game and the game is filled with mini bosses and and some pretty hard bosses.  I wish they would make a stand alone game for the cyber space parts of the game, i would buy it in a heartbeat, easily the most tense part of the game IMO.Overall this is a must play for anyone who wants a extremely immersive FPS.  I haven't fallen in love with a game this much since Alien Isolation.  I hope and pray they remake System Shock 2, but they have HUGE shoes to fill, coming after this remake.10/10

_childDocuments_.review: Once More Unto the Breach, Dear Friends, the lone Hacker dives into the empty and lethal halls of Citadel Station.   Why this took over 7 years to update? Don't know, and to be honest I don't care, just being able to once again to take on Shodan is a joy in and of itself.  I still have the original System Shock and System Shock 2 on my computer which I play on a regular basis.  This new and improve version is a blast to play and more or less faithful to the original Origin game.  A few points:1) The graphics are great and the game play is faithful to the original2) If you looking for a game that holds your hand and points you in the right direction, forget it!  Like the original it is up to the player to figure out where you need to be and what you need to do.  The emails and memo's provide information on what tasks should be accomplished but how it gets done is up to you.3) Same with codes.  Hope you have a good memory or at least a notepad to copy to.4) Puzzles and Cyberspace has changed and in my option have gotten more difficult.  Or it could just be the new graphics and format just make it seem so.5) The Station layout has also changed.  Not so much that one does not recognize it from the original.  But some dead ends now provide new paths.  Not an issue, just an interesting side note.All in all it is a great game and one that I am happy to play.  You will not finish this in a couple of hours, even on the easiest setting.  And just like the original I have found myself jumping when surprised by a mutant or cyborg that I was not expecting.  The atmosphere is just as creepy and tense as the original.  Hats off to Nightdive, they did a great job in bringing the Hacker and Shodan back to life.  Now if they start on System Shock 2 and hopefully get it moved over in much less time it will be another win for players who enjoy old school gaming with an updated look.

_childDocuments_.review: As someone who never played the original System Shock, I was baffled to read folks trying to make a thing out of "too faithful to the original."To be honest, some of the weakest parts were actually the parts Nightdive changed significantly.  The cyberspace content was pretty meh.  However, that's not to say they did a poor job.  On the contrary: even with a few flaws, this was one of the most engrossing experiences I've had in a long while.  The core game they were remaking is, quite simply, still a masterpiece head and shoulders above much of the field even today.To Nightdive's credit: if you didn't already know this game was a remake, you wouldn't be able to tell by just playing it.  It, quite seriously, plays like an indie company who played the absolute ♥♥♥♥ out of Prey and the Dishonored series.  And in some ways, the remake still surpasses those (technically more modern) titles.The vibe of being stuck on a space station enduring a horrific catastrophe is absolutely, 100% nailed.  There is no constant narration herding you along, though there's plenty of voice acting in audio logs you can pick up throughout the station.  You, quite literally, bumble around searching the station for anything and everything that can help you counter SHODAN's efforts to stifle the entirety of humanity.  You puzzle together audio logs hinting at what SHODAN is up to (many times from SHODAN herself, who considers the hacker nothing more than a pest in the early portions of the game), how to stop her, as well as where and how to access hidden stashes and other secrets helpful in surviving Citadel Station's many dangers.  It also heavily encourages exploring Citadel Station itself, seeking to manipulate the station's systems to your benefit.  The feeling of piecing something together, reviewing your logs and data files and arriving at an "aha!" moment is exhilarating against the backdrop of an oppressive space station filled with the stuff of robotic nightmares.I can't recommend the game enough.  It's not perfect, but it's still an incredible experience well worth your time and money.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a very faithful remake of the original System Shock released in 1994 by Looking Glass Technologies. In terms of the level lay out, hacking, weapons, and junk items. It's pretty much everything I could have hoped for in a remake of the original. All of the new features they added that were not in the original blend seamlessly, they feel as if they were always there. Like recycling. Or the buy stations. Scavenging the station has never been more fun!There are some things I wish they had left in. The slider on the Sparqbeam and other energy weapons allowed you to scale the damage from anywhere to 1%-100%. It did have generalized settings from low-medium-high. But you could scale it in between that too. Tailoring it to different enemies. Now it's just a switch between low-medium-high. No slider option available. You press T and you can see the Hackers hands turn a dial on the gun. Pretty cool. But not as in depth as the original. My only other complaint are the pixelated graphics mixed with high resolution textures. When I first played the demo it really tripped me up because I was not expecting it at all. I actually thought the game was bugging out so I googled it. Only to find the explanation was that it was an "artistic decision." It is certainly an... interesting feature in some ways. I get why they would do it. For the nostalgia I guess.However, the original developers didn't really have that option. And I doubt they would have even considered it if they had better tools to utilize. Every game was pixelated because those were the hardware limitations of the time. I wanted a high fidelity Citadel Station. Not to be reminded that you're playing a remake of an old game at all times(I already know I am, thanks). It should really be a side option in the graphics. Despite this everything is so well done I've got to recommend the game. I do hope though in the future they release a texture pack so I can see citadel station in the HD textures the way I've always wanted to.

_childDocuments_.review: As someone who was really excited to get into system shock for the first time, I'm pretty disappointed with this remake. I expected a lot more quality of life updates, instead we have a decently good looking game sharing almost every mechanic from its original in the 90's.The gunplay and melee combat is awful. You will use a lot of ammo to kill enemies later in the game, and they constantly respawn as you stumble your way through a very confusing maze on every floor trying to find what your objective is. Constant backtracking with no objective markers or journal entries, combined with an unorganized storage of previously picked up logs you will be forced to read and remember in order to figure out where to go. It does not help at all that most environments use the same color pallets and textures, making it extremely confusing to backtrack without constantly checking the map.Limited items, healing stations, recycle stations and vendors makes the gameplay so much more tedious as you will often need to travel multiple floors to recycle items from your abysmally small inventory space to make room for any new weapons or important items to progress the story. Electricity recharge stations are few and far between, meaning you will rely on guns most of the time to get anything done. Enemies are complete bullet sponges above easy and have pinpoint accuracy, often hitting you behind walls or randomly exploding with no indicator of such.I hate to say it, but this game is so tedious to play and the story is just unrewarding. Can't recommend unless you really enjoyed the original or are a total masochist.

_childDocuments_.review: Despite being old enough to remember the original, this is my first experience of actually playing System Shock. So whilst I can't comment on it's relative strengths and weaknesses as a remake, I can emphatically recommend this as an outstanding game in it's own right. With the greatest of respect to SHODAN, the star of the show here is Citadel Station itself. Exploring the station's deserted corridors, research laboratories and recreational areas whilst trying to piece together a way to stop the malevolent AI is utterly engrossing, and even strangely tranquil. Combat is present, but it's a sideshow to the exploration and broader problem solving aspects, with the station itself presented almost like one giant puzzle cube that needs solving from the inside out. Younger gamers may find it hard going at first, with nothing being overtly sign-posted, but providing you take your time and pour over the audiologs you discover (fear not; they're very brief and this isn't a chore) you'll rarely find yourself truly stuck for where to go next.For those who've played Bioshock and heard of System Shock in the context of of it's spiritual successor, I will say that whilst many similarities are present these are mainly found in the presentation and some environmental detailing. Plot aside, System Shock is a considerably more sophisticated game than Bioshock (I love both, by the way) and scales back considerably from that game's action and set-pieces.Onwards, to System Shock 2!
