_childDocuments_.review: Full disclosure: I played the OG release of this game but never really progressed beyond the opening level. A mix of obtuse UI design and the relatively experimental nature of the game stopped me from putting more hours in, but I definitely felt it was ahead of it's time despite all that.For this remaster though, I can fully recommend what Nightdive have done here. This is incredible work to update the game without sacrificing some of the complexity of the original. The UI has been overhauled without sacrificing the "operating system" feel of the original game. The combat is tense, like REALLY tense, and because of the resource scarcity I actually felt like failure, or rather poor performance had real consequences. For each encounter you really weigh up weather you want to engage or not because it ultimately means draining your resources, and these enemies aren't light touches either - you'll die quick if you aren't careful. This results in you taking cover more often than not and taking potshots at enemies.Exploration is where I'd say most people will fall off, but I personally loved it. Each deck of Citadel Station feels like a brain melting maze. Using Steam's built in "notes" feature came in clutch here and the map in-game allows for marks to be placed at key points to keep track of objectives. I had to look up a walkthrough once or twice during my playthrough but mainly just to ensure I was on the right path. I never felt stuck. But that's because I was making notes along the way of things that might be important and this "detective" approach actually helped me feel way more immersed in the game. Your results may vary, but the level design is my favourite part of System Shock. I loved exploring this game.This remake has me excited for what Night Dive could do with System Shock 2 because shock 2 is one of my favourite PC games of all time. I'm glad they made this game because I felt like I couldn't truly appreciate what the original was trying to do. This remake faithfully recreates the original but cleans up some of the rough edges for me.

_childDocuments_.review: While I hate games hand-holding me, getting lost in videogame spaces can be scary, because at least the first time it happens, it takes a ton of time sink to find out if it's a well designed game or if it's trash.For clarity: the design I refer to in this review appertains to the qualities of exploration and investigation, and everything that complements them. Examples might be: pace, level design, puzzle difficulty, key item placement, evidence/suggestion, all purposed to hand the responsibility of finding the way forward over to the player.If it's a badly designed game, no matter how smart and how many out the box ideas I come up with, I'll be stuck for hours and hours in denial, thinking I might be stupid for not getting the point or missing out on something, and if I really care I'll eventually look up a guide and realise I wasn't stupid, the way forward was just insanely obtuse or straight up nonsensical. Usually, I'd just abandon the game.If it's a well designed game, getting lost always turns out engaging because the game rewards my exploration and my paid attention, and even if I take a while to figure it out, there's still the feeling of accomplishment in my acquired ability to navigate a once unknown and hostile layout. After the first couple times I'm able to get back on track thanks to my own investigation or intuition, my confidence in the game grows and I can finally enjoy being lost.It's an odd case for System Shock, since this is a very faithful remake of a 1994 game in terms of map design, pace and plot beats. It's the decade where many of the genres we enjoy today were still getting figured out. So, did System Shock get it right back then? I actually can't say for sure, but my personal experience as a first timer with the remake was great, though I'm not sure it will be the case for everyone.I'm usually tempted to say a player is either dumb or way too laid-back when having difficulty in what I consider well designed games, but I wouldn't fault anyone for getting lost in System Shock to the point of frustration, specially because of it's boxy and labyrinthine map design. Granted, this aspect is precisely what we'd call a product of its time, it's all 3D could do for textured first person games, but for me personally, I'm actually really happy that they kept it.I happen to be the biggest fan of mazes and labyrinths, so I actually had a great time, because after doing so many of them, I've acquired an acute ability to identify my relative position just from memorising corners and path patterns; so the very little distinct visual identity the game gives to its corridors is way more than enough for me to be able to trace my steps. For everyone else, be not *too* afraid, for there is a very functional map.But then, when it comes to the objectives, these can require way more detective work than you'd expect. Pay attention to audio logs, re-listen or re-read them to better understand the situation. Also, the map, though very functional, lacks 1 very specific feature, and that is tagging specific rooms with their names. You might have to go back to a specific room, but the map only tags big regions, imagine "east wing" or "west wing"; that's all the map gives you, so you might want to use pen and paper to remember where rooms are by their individual names.I think this game is not for everyone, but for its target audience, it almost completely nails everything.As a survival horror fan, it's funny to realise how the immersive sim was just as close to the conception of the genre as was the PC adventure game.

_childDocuments_.review: System Shock’s Remake wasn’t for me.With that said, after having played through the campaign, defeated every boss, hacked through most doors, and discovered a handful of secrets, I’d still recommend this game exactly because it’s not for me.When I backed this game in 2015, I knew exactly what I was backing – an old game I read about in one of my brother’s video game magazines, a game that looked like a rather vibrant 8-bit vomit that posed as a dystopian horror game, but didn’t look the part. It was as if Doom had an illegitimate child with Excel.…And yet, I was fascinated by it. The ideas, the aesthetic, the atmosphere. Something about it felt… like it belonged (and it did belong in the 90s). That’s where we start off with the Remake. After going through a rather lackluster intro that is lacking in both direction, sound design, and especially the score, we start our game as a lowly hacker, waking up in the hauntingly quiet corridors of a space station orbiting Jupiter.Let’s begin by stating everything that is great about this game:1.	The visuals – System Shock Remake took a design approach that embraces the pixel art of the original while improving models, animations, and sound design to make it more approachable – the mix between the pixelated button illuminating the corridors with colorful lights is nothing less than artistic, and definitely serves as a wonderful throwback.2.	The Atmosphere – System Shock isn’t really a horror game. There are no jumpscares, there are no creepy segments, gruesome torture porn, bone chilling score, or goosebumps-inducing sections – the game as I experienced it, is more of a cyberpunk adventure in a dystopian future where ethics, regardless of CPU controlled or otherwise, are optional. The sound design is also a highlight when it comes to the synthesized speech of the cyborgs and Shodan herself. Haunting.3.	The Polish - Nie mówię o języku polskim, sorry, what I mean by this is that the developers knew exactly what to keep and what to throw away. The game is a perfect representation of the original game, but without the awkwardness of some of the controls, and with trimmed sections that could cause big headaches. In addition, while some visual elements are kept mostly as is, some were improved to allow for a less puzzling experience – for example, certain areas got a makeover that grants them a better feel visually, Enemies are more distinct, and you can definitely tell one section of the station from another. It’s just more eye-pleasing that way… Which brings me to the next part: The bad.System Shock, while having been in development for about 8 years, isn’t perfect. Since this game brings elements from a rather outdated game, it feels less like an “Immersive Sim”, and more like a first-person Metroidvania. To be fair, when I look at 2017’s Prey, this is exactly what I expected from System Shock – an intense survival shooter where you slowly evolve to counter what the game throws at you. Instead, we get plenty of inconvenient backtracking, vague clues that require you to browse through endless logs, and many punishing elements that won’t mesh with the average player… and yes, that would be me.Just as I would look at a game like Pizza Tower and say “This looks awesome, I’m never gonna touch it, ever”, this is the same notion I hold for System Shock, a game that many times while playing it I kept asking myself if I should really bother. As a shooter, it’s very lacking, somehow trying to combine tactical elements with corner leaning, and fast-paced, claustrophobic boss environments – it’s like they could settle on whether System Shock should be more like Resident Evil or a Boomer Shooter. As an RPG, there are no stats or builds, and inventory space is a constant worry that verges on being a chore. As for the cyber-sections – they’re visually unique and interesting, but I wasn’t ever a fan of games like Descent, and in general they felt more like an “ugh-section” than anything else. As a horror game… well, I already discussed that.In addition, it seems like the sound design fails to meet expectations. While I did appreciate certain details, be it the mechanical sounds of a closing door, nostalgic button presses, or the clicks of a cocking gun, there aren't as many audio elements communicating information to the player. For example, beeps notifying you of a weapon being ready to fire again when it comes to the rail launcher, or different ricochet sounds for when you get hit while having a shield on... It may be there, but it wasn't very noticeable. On top of that, some sounds appear to be missing completely - the intro loses a bit of its sting when most of it is alarmingly quiet. Certain plot important moments are also appallingly relaxed as opposed to the feeling they're supposed to convey - sometimes an explosion won't play a sound. Sometimes a certain reverb is missing, echoes... it's the small things that make the sounds design feel like that one Mummy remaster trailer accidentally uploaded to YouTube with missing sounds.So why recommend it? Why would I give a thumbs up to a game which I know I didn’t fully enjoy?Because it’s a classic, in more than one way. The people who worked on this game knew exactly what they were going for, and a different person who wanted to preserve that experience would have an absolute blast. A person who’d like to challenge themselves, achievers, people who love going through logs… This game’s for you.I therefore bestow this game with the highest honor I can think of – “It’s not for me, please buy it”.

_childDocuments_.review: It's System Shock, but with a navigable HUD, menu, inventory... okay really everything. They took an incredibly obtuse-to-play (yet still rewarding experience) and tore down the barriers to entry. No longer does one need to flip through manuals and tutorials just to figure out how to pilot the Hacker. Now you just need those manuals and walkthroughs for all of the mazes and objectives that have been lovingly left the way they originally were.  The game feels refreshing in how little it cares to give you hints outside of what is diagetically available, and in how straightforward it is. Growing up playing later immersive sims, they all tend to ask some form of philosophical or ethical questions, like a 1st-year philosophy student drunk at a party. Bioshock, Deus Ex, Dishonored, Prey, they all have philosophical questions they want you to be thinking about, like after your first time watching the Matrix trilogy. System Shock does none of that. You did exactly as the big bad CEO asked and then got put on ice for recovery after getting an implant in exchange. You wake up to a derelict station in a state of emergency, and the only way you're getting out alive is by shutting down the very thing that CEO wanted you to unrestrain in the first place. Simple. You can definitely pull your own ethics problems out of what the game gives you, but you have to be actively looking for it, it's not core to the game. The core is the human drama of listening to peoples' confused last moments, navigating the ridiculous halls of the space station, and proving yourself as the hacker that can outwit a sentient computer. So as it turns out, all it took was improved controls and slick new graphics (along with some minor QoL tweaks) to make System Shock feel fresh yet again in the genre it founded. I went and looked for what all they changed, though I may miss something. The level layouts are still very faithful, they just removed/added certain enemies for greater consistency, added/removed guns for a tighter toolkit (and I still ended up needing to drop 3 from rotation), added a recycler for all the junk laying around (very nice), and toned down the music from it's wild all-over-the-place 90s techno sound to a more muted cyberpunky soundscape, though many of the original melodies are still in there!The one bad change is the ending. Overall, a fantastic remake and well worth the price, even moreso on sale! If you've never played System Shock before or bounced off of the original after two levels like me, this is the version for you!
_childDocuments_.name: System Shock

_childDocuments_.review: I'll start off by saying I don't think this is a bad game. There are a lot of things I really liked such as the 4 different difficulty sliders (including plot difficulty!), nailing the perfect amount of inventory management, and awesome space visuals. Also, aside from some occasional ragdoll physics clipping I don't think I saw any bugs in my 20 hours playing, and only crashed once.On the other hand, there are definitely things I wasn't a huge fan of. Primarily, this entire game is made up of cubes. I understand that they're trying to remain somewhat faithful to the 1994 graphics of the original game but it almost feels cartoony at some places where the walls are a repeated square texture down a hallway. And then you go into cyberspace and you're suddenly you're in a hellscape where there is no up or down, the walls the floor and the ceiling are all cubes, you're shooting half-cubes at enemies that are also made of cubes, and it's just way too much. Half this game feels like I'm walking on the surface of a rubiks cube and the other half is inside the cube itself.I could highlight other things that I disliked such as a soundtrack that felt like it had 3 songs or a very minimalist plot that, while faithful to the original, rarely features and doesn't really add anything of substance to the game. However, I think the biggest reason why I wouldn't recommend this game is simply because System Shock 2 is just so great, and if you slap on a few graphics mods it just completely blows this game out of the water. I don't think there is really any scenario where I would recommend someone spend $40 on this remake when you can wait for a sale to pay $2.50 for a better game. Do yourself a favor and just pick up SS2, and if you really enjoy it maybe consider coming back to this one afterwards.

_childDocuments_.review: You don't often hear people talk about . It's not that surprising considering the game's age and its cumbersome gameplay. It's a much more difficult game to get into because it's so old at this point, and for those that try to get into it are going to have a difficult time—whereas other games of the genre like , , , and  are more approachable in my opinion.I have played the original game prior to this remake, and I will admit I struggled for a long time to adapt to its gameplay and mechanics. However, once I overcame that hurdle, the game itself is really fantastic. I love the sense of dread and isolation that permeates across the entire game, further amplified by its gameplay, claustrophobic and labyrinthine level design, dense atmosphere, and music. In addition to that, the main antagonist, Shodan, has become one of the greatest video game villains of all time for me. I loved her presence within the game and how she antagonizes the player is such a creepy and sinister way. I really liked the original but despite this, there were a lot of rough edges.Having finished this game, I can confirm that much of the original game with its blemishes are retained in the remake, which for some will be a bad thing or a good thing. I find myself in the middle.I appreciate how faithful the developers were to the original. Most of the greatest aspects that made  so special still remain intact and untouched in this remake while modernizing in areas that needed it the most. The graphics and art direction are really fantastic with it's low resolution retro asthetic. It made Citadel Station feel more real and immersive to me but also felt very oldschool. Second of all, the gameplay is much more responsive and engaging. And I think those are the only modernized things from this remake, because everything else is still the same as the original.Navigation and game progression is still unclear and confusing, the inventory management system is still tedious, the cyber space levels are still repetitive. Some of the mechanics are still obnoxious and very dated by today's standards. The audio feedback with melee combat is still underwhelming. Even with the addition of a few boss fights throughout the game, those fights end up being very underwhelming.I wish that the developers focused more on modernizing elements from the original to make this feel like a completely different game, i.e. .This definitely feels like a very old school game, and I think it's important to know what your individual tastes are before playing a game like this. If you're the kind of person that enjoys a challenge and doesn't mind not having their hand held, I strongly recommend giving this unforgiving and memorable immersive sim a shot, especially now with this remake as it is the most polished version of  that you can play. However, for those that are new to , I will recommend that you play the demo, and then see for yourself if it's something that you would enjoy. Now please give me System Shock 2 Remake.

_childDocuments_.review: really good UNTIL the third halfI really enjoyed this game at first, despite a few difficulty spikes here and there, but then you get to the point where you feel like you stop getting more powerful but the enemies don't. All the late game guns are either too slow, uses too much ammo, or just don't compare to the guns you get within a few hours of starting.The final boss consists of you finding a safe corner and popping out to kill some enemies, then fighting another spider cyborg, the getting a weak gun and dying over and over to the digital enemies as a normal dude.Very underwhelming

_childDocuments_.review: In a bygone era, far, far, away, devs were still in awe of sci fi monoliths like Alien and 2001 and weren't afraid to show it. Nightdive totally nail the atmosphere. Apparently they didn't change much from the original (never played it) other than a few QOL things and a graphical upgrade (game looks amazing by the way) - well, if that's the case then this game has aged admirably and in many ways puts modern gaming to shame. It runs really well - at 1440p (with a 3070), I had everything set to high, except shadows & AO on medium (shadows are the frame killer here - steer clear of ultra) and was able to maintain 165 plus throughout. If there is one issue, it's that the game doesn't do high frame rates too well and tends to start to judder a bit around the 180 plus mark. If that bothers you then just chuck vsync on - it won't affect you much at 144hz plus and if you're on 60hz just chuck everything on ultra and that'll rein the frames in. Easy to mod - literally drag and drop - and there's plenty of nice little fixes floating around out there if some aspect irks you a little too much. Great music (I love me some E-bow guitars) and sound effects. Highly immersive. No stupid characters or cringe dialogue to break the immersion. No "quirky" companions with reductive, one dimensional personalities getting in the way. It's just you, alone, on a massive hostile space station, with some guns. Just the way I like it. Finally, say what you like about the final fight (it threw me off a bit too), it f***in' ends with P.I.L.s The Order of Death - not just an amazing track, not just a nice sci fi nod (Richard Stanley's "Hardware") but cleverly appropriate to boot - so for me it all ended on a high note and I had a big grin on my face when that song kicked in. If that isn't cult sci fi-y enough for you, there's even someone called Brouzouf buried somewhere in the credits. Give the demo a shot.

_childDocuments_.review: I received a copy of the original System Shock along with Bioforge and Wing Commander III in the Origin Pak back in the nineties, for winning a limbo contest at my now ex-girlfriend's birthday party.  The games could have been terrible and I would still have felt great about my achievement.That said, as much as I loved Mark Hamill's performance and being forewarned of my disappointment should I come into possession of a fork, I never finished Wing Commander III nor Bioforge, but you better believe I was fully immersed in System Shock.  The game was choppy and slow on my 486, but I completed it all the same.  No guides, no internet, just me, my wits, and a clunky but workable UI that let me play PONG in the bottom corner.This was over twenty years ago, before developers discovered the novelty of mouse aim.  I barely remembered anything about the game except that no other game had been able to recapture the same feeling since, not even the later much anticipated System Shock 2.  When the remake was announced, I was thrilled that my faulty memory would allow me to enjoy it as if it were the first time all over again.After having beaten it a second time, my only complaint is that I was not able to play PONG in the bottom corner.  Aside from that, I got the same rush of accomplishment and have renewed anticipation for System Shock 2, even already knowing full well how it turned out.I took the liberty of watching some Twitch zoomers play and was heart-warmed to discover they were losing track of time enjoying themselves despite the lack of waypoints telling them where to go next.  This remake truly bridges generations, and I hope to see future remakes take a similar approach.

_childDocuments_.review: ==Contains minor spoilers for an early game section.==I've never played the OG System Shock but you can definitely tell this is an old game, and I mean that in the best way. There's no objective marker, not even an objective list, or quest system. For a game advertised as an immersive sim, that's an absolute win.You're just in the station and you gotta figure out how to stop Shodan based on in-universe information only.In one part there's a big red button that shoots a laser. You might think you press it. Nope, you gotta make sure you take all the necessary steps to render it safe first. There's no quest hud or list that tells you those steps. You gotta learn the steps based on npc dialogue alone. The game doesn't ever tell you what to do, the inhabitants of the world the game takes place in do. This is an important thing that many games aiming for "immersion" seem to miss.If you press the laser button at the wrong time, you get a game over. You just destroyed Earth. The game punishes you for following the classic video game notions of "I should experiment with everything and see what happens." This is also good for immersion as well. It makes the game feel less like a toybox made by the devs for you to play in, and more like a real sequence of events controlled by your actions alone.There's no "wait, not yet!" popup, it's not locked off or even warned to the player that it will get you a game over. The button shoots the laser; it says so next to the button.If you don't know why you shouldn't shoot the laser, that's your problem. You couldn't parse the info you were told about said laser. I hope you had a recent save.

_childDocuments_.review: Original review 5/30/2023I will update when I beat the game but speaking as somebody that has beaten the original twice I feel that the remake so far delivers on its promises. The level design is close as 1:1 as you can get and this seems to be decisive to players who do not like 90's style map designs. I like the remake because not only does it look good but it also doesn't change a lot compared to the original and I like it when things generally stay the same.UpdateSo I beat the game and a lot what I originally said still holds true through the rest of the game. The last two levels certainly look different compared to the original. The theme is the same and the textures do fit wit the station but it doesn't have the breathing walls for example that the original had. The cyberspace is the weakest part of the game as I find that the game spams enemy waves. The general goal of cyberspace is to destroy these energy cores (like Lando from Return of the Jedi) which unlocks new areas to progress.      The silly thing is that after destroying these cores the quickest way to exit cyberspace is to actually get killed as you only get punished on difficulty setting 3 and even that is probably averted mostly with restoration modules. The last boss fight is done in cyberspace and I found it more underwhelming than the original. Despite these negatives this wouldn't want me to change me recommendation.     I love what Nightdive did to this game and I do want them to do the same for System Shock 2. I can't wait for the System Shock 2 Enhanced Edition which I hope to play in VR. Hopefully, Nightdive has the willingness to do it again.8.5/10

_childDocuments_.review: I haven't played the original System Shock so I had no idea what to expect from it other than knowing it inspired games like Bioshock, Deus Ex, and Prey. I was pleasently surprised with this game, exploring Citadel Station was a lot of fun but at the same time very tense, as the combat is simple but unforgiving.The story very much follows a "show, don't tell" approach, there is no in-game menu where the next objective is told, instead you figure it out from in-game dialogue, audio logs, or just stumbling upon the next step as you explore. Despite this, I never felt lost or stuck as there as always another path to explore.The graphics look fantastic, all textures have a slight pixelated look which is only apparent once you get close, but it's a great homage to the games roots.If you're a fan of other immersive sims you're doing your a huge disservice if you don't give this a shot.

_childDocuments_.review: I've been following the System Shock remake for around two and a half years now, which meant I personally didn't experience a lot of the pains regarding the delayed release. I've been a big fan of system shock for a lot longer, however, having first played System Shock 2 years ago as a child. I'm also a massive Imsim fan, having played the vast majority of the genre's greats to completion. This game is one of those greats. - Amazingly faithful to the original 1994 classic. Featuring an almost 1:1 recreation of the original DOS game's maze-like levels, this remake brings the pixelated halls of Citadel Station to life with all-new graphics delivered by the Unreal Engine. Gameplay is also faithfully recreated, with many QoL updates, changes, and additions that make this remake the definitive way to play System Shock. - Smooth and polished PC port, with few bugs, near-flawless performance on even low-end hardware, and a shockingly small file size. - Strong enemy designs, great environmental art, and fantastic animation work. - Grenades have an awful throwing range, and drop way too much when thrown. They also bounce a lot. This can easily result in accidental suicide deaths when throwing grenades. - The new soundtrack is OK, but the original OST was far superior. This one feels way too ambient, and not punchy enough.- A good deal of weapon FX are rather lackluster, especially for the Laser Rapier and Minipistol. The Laser Rapier is especially bad, since it's the final tier melee weapon, and yet it has little feedback in terms of impact effects and hit sounds. - Some rather lengthy animations would have been better as first-use only animations when you pick up or use an item for the first time. The stimulant patches are especially annoying, since you will have to go through the same application animation every time you want to apply a healing patch or another stimulant. While SSR is not a game for everyone, it is a solid remake of the original game, which faithfully updates and enhances the world of Citadel Station for first-time players, while also delivering numerous welcome improvements to the story, worldbuilding, and gameplay. Highly recommended to immersive sim fans, and well-worth the price of admission. 9.5/10, one of the best games I've ever played, my nominee for 2023 Steam GOTY

_childDocuments_.review: This is an amazing game! Not the most accessible, but there is something refreshing about older games with the are just about the gameplay and story. No enemy level-scaling, tutorials, quick-time events, DLC, multiplayer, or microtransactions. The game doesn't try to force you into a particular play-style and you can go where you want. You are just a person on a space-station trying to survive. You can heal as and regenerate energy as much as you want (if you find those locations and are willing to run back to them). You can revive, but only once you unlock the story-appropriate points.I never played the original, but I love being able to experience the story in a more accessible form. Imagine the original Doom, but with the beautiful graphics you remember, not as it actually looked. And then imagine that someone set the game in space and wrote an engaging story for it! Sure, the enemies don't have great animations and it's sometimes hard to tell if the weapons/bullets are having an effect on them. But it's all about expectations and that's perfectly suitable for a remake like this.The game ran rock-solid for me, I loved the environment/level design, and the movement and shooting just felt good. Heading back to my surgery machine to heal up after exploring on another level started to feel like coming back to my home base. My favorite touch of the game is the light switches. There's nothing that quite makes the station feel like a real place as much as a simple thing like being able to turn the lights on in some of the rooms.
_childDocuments_.name: System Shock

_childDocuments_.review: I never got around to beating the original System Shock 1 back in the day but still held the game's amazing atmosphere and story telling on my mind. Fast forward several years and gaming had evolved to the point that going back and playing the original mostly felt like a chore where a lot of the modern comforts of good UI design and control schemes had been completely lost. (this is not a dig on the original, it's just a fact that doesn't do it any favors).Introduce this loving and faithful remake and I could have sworn that this is what the game looked like when I first played it. Except this time when I booted up the game it actually played like I expected it would.Keep in mind that despite the improvements to controls and some UI handling the gameplay remains largely unchanged (except for cyber space which is a lot more bearable now). This means that you actually have to pay attention to anything and every little thing that you see and or hear since it might come in handy later. (Thank you steam for also proving a nice little built in notepad to facilitate this)Guns are fun and varied, there are multiple optional upgrades and implants that you can use to make life easier. That being said you can also largely ignore common sense and brute force your way through several puzzles and confrontations as long as you bring the right kind of gear and insight.Boss encounters have been slightly reworked and are much more epic and cinematic now although they sometimes catch you off guard and can mercilessly cut you down if you don't know what to expect (so save often) The rapier + beserk boost make short work of most enemies though so no combat encounter has to be too frustrating unless you insist on taking every shot the enemy fires at you.If you have never played this game before you might quickly come to the realization that level design can be all over the place, and this is partly intentional (as you will learn from audio logs) Despite this in-game lore reason for the design being the way it is you will still have to come to terms with the fact that sometimes there is simply no way to know what is expected of you exactly and you will just have to try and explore every nook and cranny on a given level in order to discover that one item/switch/upgrade/audio log that you need in order to proceed.Overal I am very impressed with this remake and the visuals do an outstanding job of both feeling modern and yet distinctly retro.If had to suggest one area of improvement it would have to be the final boss fight which for some reason was both confusing and wildly anti-climactic. That being said I would still highly recommend this game.

_childDocuments_.review: This remake is extremely faithful to the original, which also makes the gameplay quite oldschool for that matter. Gotta listen to logs to figure out what to do and where to go next, no waypoints.The graphical style is an acquired taste, but I personally love it.Shooting feels lovely visceral with the bigger weapon types.Would recommend, but only for girls and boys with a slightly higher frustration tolerance than today's avarage gamer.
_childDocuments_.name: System Shock

_childDocuments_.review: I always wanted to play the original System Shock 1 and 2 but the UX felt horrible there so I never got past the first seconds, bad UX is a dealbreaker for me and some classics age badly in this regard. While this game fixed the UX, it also made several improvements to graphics and gameplay but overall stayed very true to the original, which I really appreciate. Now i could finally play the original and considering my playtime I would definitely say it is worth its money, which is not even the cost of a full-price but roughly half atm.I loved the gameplay, setting, story, gun variety, and the junction puzzles were great. The start especially amazed me with its great atmosphere for this horror-sci-fi themed game, and from then on I was already hooked. Most levels show a great variety from each other and have different enemies, layouts and looks to them, which I really liked. I also enjoyed gun modding and scraping for coins. The style of the graphics is great.What I did not like was the cyberspace minigame. I played the game at max difficulty except for the mission/scenario difficulty (it introduces a 10h time limit, yuck!) , but now i would also lower the cyberspace hacking minigame because it is really not fun and a few times made me stop playing for a bit. I also struggled a lot with inventory space even though I got all inventory extensions. The problem is that i didnt wanna discard any weapon that was still going to be useful later, but neither the cargo elevator (why not btw?) nor your own inventory can keep all weapons easily. And since there is also the goal to collect scrap for coins to buy mods, and this takes space too, i always was very limited in inventory space. Having more cargo elevator space would have helped a lot. It is just not fun to manage your inventory when the game gives you no option to organize it somehow or stash it.Lastly I would like to recommend anyone who liked System Shock to play Prey 2017. It is an extremely similar game with "better" graphics (different style), more meaningful decisions both in story and in gameplay, an even better story, great soundtrack, great graphics... If you loved System Shock I would be surprised if you would not also love Prey. I feel like they must have taken System Shock as their main inspiration.
_childDocuments_.name: System Shock

_childDocuments_.review: A phenomenal remake of an absolute classic. Classic fans will love it, and many new players will discover the horrors of Citadel Station for the first time. SHODAN is one of the greatest villains in all of modern media and serves as the inspiration for so many modern maniacal monsters. The fact that the original did so much to push the industry forwards in 1993 is nothing short of wizardry, and this remake brings the original into a new, much more accessible light. Colorful and artistic visuals, freakish enemies, terrifying audio design and a cohesive feel to the map make you truly feel like you're lost in the corridors of Citadel, awaiting SHODAN's next deadly ambush. System Shock has a big learning curve that is satisfying to conquer. The game requires a lot more critical and spatial thinking than almost any other shooter you've ever played, so if you're looking for a unique challenge still unmatched by most modern games, System Shock is right up your alley.A note to new players: keep a notepad handy for codes and write down your objectives. This game is a unique experience that does NOT hold your hand AT ALL, and expects you to do a lot of thinking for yourself. You're in for an incredible experience!(P.S. After you destroy SHODAN's CPU nodes, there is a number in the room. Jot these down in order, you'll thank me later ;) )
_childDocuments_.name: System Shock

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic. Just reached the ending today, (proudly without a guide even.) This is what I seek for in video games, minimum cutscenes, thoughtful problem solving and creative ways of overcoming whatever the hell this Shodan A.I. throws at me. The maze-like levels kept me on the edge with every corner turned, either finding a mindless killing machine or another room of supplies to take off some of the tension, maybe even a clue as to what I could expect a few levels ahead of me.The atmosphere made me immerse myself, I'd often create little "safe rooms" where I would store my weapons or extra health items that I could retreat to. The music got me pumped on occasion, which pushed my luck in either direction really. I always looked forward to pissing off Shodan everytime I made progress.The combat was a bit stiff at first, but later weapons feel more impactful. The enemies can be quite unpredictable in the sense that, they can be anywhere, but also the way they react aren't always sharp, and then other times you'll get absolutely aimbotted.The difficulty felt very appropriate, I played on normal and it felt like normal all the way throughout, not too hard, not too easy. You can adjust combat difficulty seperately from puzzle difficulty if you so wish. I only had trouble with one puzzle involving a retinal scanner, but if you read/listen to the logs you collect around the station, you can't go wrong.I can absolutely recommend this and I think we need more games like it.
_childDocuments_.name: System Shock

_childDocuments_.review: I had high hopes for the remake and I don't regret spending money on it (game was on sale) - I'm happy to support Nightdive and hope their projects well, especially the upcoming System Shock 2 remake. But I did not enjoy this one, and I didn't finish it, giving up at the reactor level.The game loses a great deal of its character in the remake. Even starting from the intro, where in the original one SHODAN narrates the events that lead up to the game as she becomes self-aware, Nightdive for some reason felt the need to rewrite it into something far more generic and forgettable. It's a theme that persists through the whole game. The textures went from level specific and colourful, a place that looked like people actually lived in, to just "generic dark space station". The music went from distinct and unique to generic horror ambient. Amazingly, there's less variation in the stuff found on Citadel in the 2023 version than in the original, stuff that made it a believable living space. There are no more logs and files to be found in Cyberspace, the weapons went from varied and unique, like a tranquilliser needle pistol in the medical wing or the completely useless riot gun or the insanely fun flechette machine pistol, to generic pistol->shotgun->assault rifle. Even the original assault rifle had more character, being a huge cannon with massive oomph, and it sounded like firing a 6-pounder. The enemy variety has dropped noticeable as well, and the colourful palette of the original foes is once again muted to a generic dark grey / brown "realistic" tone of generic space horror. The original Citadel station didn't have to look like a dark and brooding place, the horror came from the events that took place in this place where people lived and worked, not from the surroundings (except the auto-bomb tunnels, ♥♥♥♥ that place). All the audio logs have been re-recorded by vastly inferior voice actors (except Terri, we love you Machine Mother), the pictures of the crew attached to the logs are barely distinguishable from each other, the writing quality of the text itself is as generic and forgettable as everything else.If the choice was between this remake and not playing System Shock, I'd recommend it, but the extremely well made Enhanced Edition from the very same studio is available on Steam, so I cannot in good conscience tell you to buy this one. The EE is based on the old System Shock Portable which added mouse-look and a modernised control scheme and it makes the game an even better experience than the original playthrough 30 years ago. Go play that, enjoy the colours, the voice actors, the cool guns, the beautiful sprites and the true Citadel Station experience.
_childDocuments_.name: System Shock

_childDocuments_.review: Insanely fun and well done. I haven't played the original but I kinda wanna check it out just to see how little they differ. The level designs are intensely confusing and there are some sections that are so ridiculously unreasonable you have to save scum (cough beta grove cough) but overall tons of fun and worth your time and money. Definitely support the game if you like dungeon crawls and immersive sims, I'd love to see this team take on the sequel
_childDocuments_.name: System Shock

_childDocuments_.review: On it's own, it's an excellent game. And as a remake of the classic game it's also very good. It captures the mood and feeling of the original and expertly brings it into the modern gaming era. Some changes were made, but all of them respect the original source material.My one big complaint is that the Difficulty Setting System was not implemented exactly as in the original. The original system that lets you individually control/adjust the difficulty of 4 different game-play aspects is still there. But the 0 difficulty setting was removed. The ability to completely deactivate certain aspects of the game-play in the original allowed you to tailor the game to your liking in an unparalleled fashion. If you wanted, you could play a pure FPS, or an Adventure game, or a more balanced survival horror experience. The new game does not give you this level of customisation.
_childDocuments_.name: System Shock

_childDocuments_.review: Very cool game, I liked the graphical style and the overall "style" of the game; design-wise it is very fun and rewarding to play, with lots of stuff to use against enemies. I found the game even on the normal settings to be a decent challenge. I never played the original game but people say its a good remake as far as that classification goes, but I cannot say that myself. As a first time player, it was a great experience. Personally speaking, the final 10% of the game was a chore and the combat encounters could have been more numerous earlier on instead of ramping up so much at the very end, but it does give a real sense of urgecy and finality that a lot of other games miss out on.Without spoilers, the last fight wasnt fun and was tedious and the ending itself is very abrupt, to the point that I had to check the description of the steam achievement I got when I beat the last encounter because I was so confused. The ending song slaps and I would recommend taking your time and being patient with the game, youll enjoy it more that way imo.
_childDocuments_.name: System Shock

_childDocuments_.review: its been a very fun game so far it was nice exploring and figurug out how to deal with the games puzzles and stuff, the only issues i have is that there is some slight QoL issues like hard to read text in the menus sometimes, and its jut a tad confusing when you fist come to some of the puzzles but they are simple enough to figure out! so far Pretty rad
_childDocuments_.name: System Shock

_childDocuments_.review: Great shooter with a focus on exploration and story. Character development is limited to finding items such as weapons and cybernetic mods and upgrading them (which is much better than adding RPG style attributes, skills and points - in my opinion). It's not DOOM, it's more of a Half-Life experience. If you played the 1994 version - there's a lot of nostalgia and the remake is well worth the time.
_childDocuments_.name: System Shock

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a great remake, it improves the graphics of the original while keeping the gameplay mechanics the same. The original game was good, but the controls and combat felt clunky. I'd say this is the definitive way to play system shock, the only thing I wish they would add is updated versions of the original soundtrack, rather than new music.
_childDocuments_.name: System Shock

_childDocuments_.review: This one pleasantly surprised me. It was long time in the making, but I see the wait was well worth it. I have not noticed even a minor bug at release. It struck a great balance between updating things (especially controls) and keeping the spirit of the original game. Makes we wonder if we might see one day a remake of System Shock 2 by the same people?
_childDocuments_.name: System Shock

_childDocuments_.review: A fantastic remake of a classic. I just wish the objectives were more obviously laid out. I'm on the 2nd difficulty for story and having to scan through audiologs and emails to figure out what to do next is a pain. When going through different parts of the map corpses will ragdoll right infront of you as if they'd just been killed. Not a major issue, but is jarring and hurts immersion.Overall this game is very fun with fantastic audio design. Great visuals and entertaining gameplay. _childDocuments_.name: System Shock

_childDocuments_.review: For being a remake of one of the first immersive Sims in the market, it's a pretty damn good remake that enhances the game play with a few minor gripes into it's system (Cyberspace is still a PITA) and a few other things (mainly music being too subudued), still makes this a pretty solid game for it's buck. SHODAN is still as intimidating as ever and the fact the game feels like a dungeon crawling Sci-fi experience taht can be tailored to your taste just like the OG makes it worth the multiple runs.Adding to the recent closure of a 2/2/2/2 run, the remake honestly is a pretty goshdarn good attempt at enhancing but heavily respecting the original's ideal. The ending segment boss is an enhancement to the OG's and surely makes a big difference in this wonderful game. Looking forward to the next installment of the series.

_childDocuments_.review: A very faithful remake to a very dated game. Even though it's a remake, i found it hard to go back to after experiencing the sequel and how much it improves on pretty much every component of the original. I might have bothered to continue playing if the game wasn't so cryptic on your current objective and where you have to go. Not being able to progress because you missed a log file that has a code that you need sitting on a counter that you can easily miss because the level design and environments all look identical is just not something i'm willing to put up with. The sequel improves on the level design so much i really struggle to find enjoyment in navigating these levels that all look the same. I'm not big on the colourful retro art style they went with, it takes the edge out of the grim and dark premise and the tone feels off. The combat feels weightless, the enemy designs are dull. I think the concept and execution of the cyberspace is boring and bland. I don't think the game is bad at all but it's not compelling enough for me to have the patience to want to look up a walkthrough on where to go next.
_childDocuments_.name: System Shock

_childDocuments_.review: I will open this review by saying that I haven't played the original System Shock.That being said, I absolutely adore this game. It's a prime example of how I wish games went back to their roots, as every little thing was placed there deliberately. There's secrets and optional paths everywhere, so much so that I've probably spent 75% of my playtime figuring out said secrets. But I enjoyed it! Every secret has loot or some kind of collectible to collect which makes it worth your while.Judging by the other reviews, this game is apparently VERY faithful to the original, though I wouldn't know since I haven't played it. Either way, I very much enjoyed the combat and the puzzles! And despite the obvious flaws this game has, such as excessive backtracking (sometimes with unclear objectives that I had to look up a guide), I simply accepted it as part of the game. This oddly enhanced my experience with the game? Though it's most likely because I took the game for what it is: a beautiful, faithful remake of a game with dated but modern, refreshed gameplay mechanics.The price is perfect for what this game offers! If you're considering picking it up, I say you won't regret buying it.
_childDocuments_.name: System Shock

_childDocuments_.review: I'll be upfront: this isn't for everybody. The lack of direction coupled with labyrinthine levels can get frustrating fast. I restarted my playthrough thrice. Of note as well the fact that there are some bugs: got 4 or so crashes for no clear reason and notably the easiest mission difficulty is supposed to add waypoints to guide you through the game, but presently no such waypoints appear. As for the game itself: it's breathtaking. The visuals are a beauty, even though enemies tend to blend in the environments at time. The combat is rather anemic: melee lacks impact and sometime it's hard to gauge the range of your weapon. Handling is a bit slow and clunky: reload and item animations are slow. Despite all these shortcomings, there is something compelling about exploring every nook of a maze while a rouge A.I. is going on about how great the world will be after she reshapes humanity.
_childDocuments_.name: System Shock

_childDocuments_.review: I remember playing System Shock in the 90s and how immersive it was. How much the game pulled me in. Exploring Citadel, reading notes, finding keys, hidden paths and solving puzzles. It was a masterpiece.Nightdive managed to bring the same feeling back to me, but with a much more beautiful and modern game. I really enjoyed playing this remake, like it was the first time. The art style is such a nice mix between modern graphics and pixel art, and it fits System Shock very well.This is the best remake I've ever played.
_childDocuments_.name: System Shock

_childDocuments_.review: Overall a great experience, for better or worse its got some deep roots in 1995, and there is a learning curve to that. But Nightdive made a very solid immersive sim, and I would recommend this if you've never played system shock before, like Immersive Sims, or are curious about the roots of Bioshock, Deus Ex et all
_childDocuments_.name: System Shock

_childDocuments_.review: A proper old school immersive sim.I’ll say it up front, I never played the original. I watched some gameplay footage but that’s about it. Going into this I thought that might mean I’d struggle a bit. Whilst I did struggle sometimes, that was part of the fun! You can certainly feel the 90's game vibe, it just has a modern coat of paint. I love the art style, that combination of hight detail environment with low pixel art characters. It truly is inspired. The atmosphere is creepy and SHODAN is a brilliant villain you love to hate.  Interesting enemies to fight and brilliant environmental storytelling. You can really see where this game went on to influence games like BioShock, Deus Ex, Thief and Dishonoured, all of which I love.My only criticism is that maybe it is a bit TOO old school with regards to some of the gameplay features like the lack of an objective log. To start with it took me a while to work out that you really need to listen to the video logs you pick up around the game as they tell you what your objectives are. Once I knew that thought, I adapted quickly and enjoyed that aspect. However, the lack of a notepad or journal is probably a step too far. The big example here is with the numbers at each CPU nodes you need later in the game. Once I knew I needed them I had to go back and physically write them all down on some paper! It seems insane that these are not noted down for you in a journal or log in game. I know some of you will be saying that this would go against the original game but surly this could have been added into the remake without compromising the feel of the game. I’m not sure it’s immersive, it’s just annoying and felt very 90’s gaming but in a bad way. I hope they remake System Shock 2 next with the same love and attention to detail. Overall, buy this game!
_childDocuments_.name: System Shock

_childDocuments_.review: Very true to the original, a brilliant work of art considering what was recreated. The music could perhaps been a bit truer to the original, I thought it was more hectic&frantic in certain situations. But perhaps my recollection after 30 years is a bit off.I'm not sure if similar game would have such a huge success if it was created today. The original was truly created at the right moment in time.Since I played the original back in the day, I truly enjoyed this new version.I can't say if this will work for you if you never played the original though.A few minor crashes though, frequent quicksaves is the workaround, so no big deal. They will probably be gone in a few patches.A final note: I love the chess mini-puzzle in the Delta Grove, thank you for that one! I wish there was more puzzles, I loved those.

_childDocuments_.name: System Shock

_childDocuments_.review: I got gifted this by my significant other a day after it's release.I have beaten the original in 7 hours.and system shock two in 8I'm not a professional reviewer so this is going to be messy but you're getting the whole hog.I'm gonna mention an enemy type encountered late game down the line as well as a bug in an endgame section so minor? spoiler? not really? doesn't tell you story or anything important?The remake took me 14-15 hours not counting 1.6 hours-2 hours afk time for stuff like bathroom breaks and food.Played with 2/2/1/3 (2 enemies, 2 mission, 1 cyber, 3 puzzle)I'll put the TL:DR here: It's good. get it, it's faithful while also being it's own thing. Maps are near one to one.-----------God where to I even begin with this? This thing is a masterpiece, the visuals, the enemy design, sound effects, all of it is just fantastic, it feels phenomenal.The weaponry is fantastic, some reworks here and there but you're always gonna find use out of your preferred tool, some weapons were changed in positives, but a lot were removed and some were very negatively impacted by the remake like the magpulse. The Scorpion remains a consistent favourite, spraying 20+ magazines of teflon into late game enemies as a reward for early game conservation is incredibly fun.Very rarely did I ever get lost. My memory from the original during my playtime literally carried me all the way to executive, where changes in design and layout threw me around a bit due to the ability to do more with the areas for a more consistent flow, but even then it's incredibly one to one with a lot of things. However on the downside this can lead to a kind of uncanny valley effect where, you recognise the area but not enough due to the shift to full modern 3D (yes I know the original game's engine was true 3D)Cyberspace is where the game starts to fall apart, with being on the Autistic Spectrum I find myself struggling with doing the cyberspace sections for long due to the hell of a mental drain it puts on you. while far more visible you're drowning in pulsing colours which while not as confusing, they are incredibly off-putting to deal with. It also likes to throw you into tunnels filled with mines which you have very little control of your movement in(and I mean FILLED). It's also incredibly tedious, rather than quick snappy jaunts you're spending a good 20-30 minutes combing through cyberspace to do something as simple as open a damn door. Genuinely the only setting I'll ever set to one.The Soundscape while good, has flaws of it's own, enemy and weapon sounds are incredible as is the ambience provided to you on the different decks of citadel, You can very clearly listen in and know what you're being shot at with and what might be around the corner (though this isn't always the case between the security 2 and security 3 robots, as they're all but silent when not walking or firing. And yes, they uncut the security 3 robots from the original, this is the pre-mentioned spoiler, go about your day.) However Most of the game is just that, Ambient noise, there's very little in the way of music.  Music only really kicks in when combat starts and leaves very quickly after, there is nothing as memorable as the original game's ost and I believe this harms it a lot in the end.I would touch on enemy design but I feel like that's revealing too much as there's a lot of drastic changes and upgrades to the products of shodan's rogue machinations (they got Terri back by the way she's fantastic as always).I will also touch on the fact there are some bugs with the game currently however.Most notably security 2 robots have a chance to bug out and continuously play their attack sound even after death, the only way I've found to fix this is reloading a save.The second bug is that there are tubes on the bridge that if shot enough will rupture. they're supposed to spill fluid everywhere and when they do this you're looking at an INCREDIBLE amount of FPS drop and stuttering, be careful where you're shooting and what your health is as you don't want to die due to an FPS and loss of control.Get it if you can, it's remarkable cheap compared to most remakes, it's consistent with what it set out to do and remains entirely respectful to it's source material while allowing you to thrive, genuinely, walkthroughs for the OG game can prove useful throughout most of it.

_childDocuments_.name: System Shock

_childDocuments_.review: I loved the original System Shock and looked eagerly forward to this version.  This version doesn't deliver.  2023 isn't 1994 and I no longer want to play pixelated games.  The remade surface textures, while far more attractive than the original ones, make it more difficult and time consuming to evaluate environmental objects for pick up.  The recycle / vaporize mechanic for harvesting currency is true to the original game, but today it is tiresome.  Defeating adversaries relies on brute force trial and error and the antiquated quick-save/quick-load repetition.  30 years later, this remake is ultimately too close to its original material to enjoy.  It isn't a remaster, it's a repaint.

_childDocuments_.review: I can say with absolute certainty that no other remake/remaster that's released in the past 10 years comes close to the level of quality delivered in System Shock. This faithful and loving recreation of a near 30 year old game is visually stunning, extremely well optimized (the game is only 8gb in total), and more than worth the money.
_childDocuments_.name: System Shock

_childDocuments_.review: This is a really good and faithful recreation of a very old game. They did a good job.But System Shock itself has aged poorly. I think they did everything they could while maintaining the identity of the original. I really like Shodan, I really like the atmosphere and the designs and stuff. But I am admittedly finding the game kind of a chore to get through. It's just these endless hallways. Each floor makes itself a little more distinct but I just don't find the maze itself that entertaining.So did Night Dive do a good job? Yes. Would I arbitrarily recommend this game to buyers? No.
_childDocuments_.name: System Shock

_childDocuments_.review: This is not Resident Evil 2 type of remake that was made to please new and old fans alike. System Shock Remake completely ignores 29 years of immersive sim evolution to stay faithful to the original, frustratingly faithful... For most part it's 1994 game that came out in 2023.  Here is short list of problems that only die hard purists wouldn't want to see solved:Remake doesn't show your current objective, so good luck figuring out what you need to do after taking few days break.Remake doesn't memorise obtained codes or crucial to progression information. Having proper journal wouldn't make game easier or "casual".Remake allows you to pick progression related items before they become relevant. You can grab seemingly random head, drop it somewhere to free very limited inventory, just to find out 5 hours later you can't progress without it.All of these are examples of objectively bad game design, maybe it was tolerable in 1994 when people didn't know better, but now such approach to design looks outdated and generate unnecessary frustration.In some ways 1999 sequel is more modern than this 2023 remake. System Shock 2 had PDA with notes to keep track of mission objectives.I recommend remake to people who already like immersive sims and want to play game that pioneered genre. This is clearly not a game to draw new players, instead play Prey, Dishonored, Bioshock, Deus Ex: Human Revolution, System Shock 2 and only after that come back to System Shock remake.

_childDocuments_.review: It's almost a miracle that this game exists at all, a game that you can play start to finish in a +10~ hours run with a (very unpolished) ending, with no crashes whatsoever or major bugs. And while this remake is everything it needed to be, it is also quite full of confounding design decisions that compound to a quite messy end result. Enemy positioning, the inventory and storage system, the lack of QoL when it comes to reciclying, wallhumping for secrets, the monotonous cyberspace minigame, the somewhat mystifying damage variation, the keybinds, the 4 limit weapon for keybinds, the occasional stutter and fps variation in a game that should run on a toaster with wheels...Among other things. These are all things that detract from a greater experience, but still do not take away the fact that this is the System Shock remake we wanted, and if anything, it leaves me hopeful that we will even greater releases in the future from this team.
_childDocuments_.name: System Shock

_childDocuments_.review: A faithful return to Citadel Station, I found it just as enjoyable as my experience with the original. There are some minor frustrations like some achievements being bugged at current moment and the game over cutscene being unskippable (seriously I don't want to waste 30 seconds watching it I just want to get back to retrying that Cortex Reaver fight), but overall the game is a solid experience and doesn't overstay it's welcome. Not as much room for creativity as System Shock 2, but I'm glad they didn't overdo it with adding in a ton of new mechanics.

_childDocuments_.name: System Shock

_childDocuments_.review: After spending 48 hours on Citadel Station, this is one of the best games I ever played. I never played the original because I missed it in the 90's and later on I was drawed back by the graphics, controls and music. This remake made it possible for me to experience the System Shock world with updated graphics, controls and music. Firstly, do not expect tutorials or hints. You have to find out everything on your own. This is the type of games which were made back then. As you progress through the Citadel space station and slowly make your way to Shodan, you feel more and more attached to the story. I especially enjoyed the design of the space station and how each level has its own purpose in your journey with completely different architecture, monsters and music. This is just genius.The combination of updated graphics, story and ambient music creates addiction to play more. Personally I prefer this ambient music much more than original which I think does not suit the game well. The grim atmosphere of you being alone in the space station full of dead bodies, mutans and cyborgs with Shodan which is tring to kill you on every step is one of the core aspects of the game. You learn what happened to the crew through audio logs which are scattered on every level. One by one, you complete the full story of what happened on the station. And it wasn't exactly pleasant for the crew...Pros: - Story - Graphics - Level design - Game mechanics - Music - AtmosphereCons: - Cyberspace missions can be sometimes a bit annoying - The game ending could have been done better, but I understand they wanted to stay true to the original - Some may find lack of any tutorial or guide frustrating (but this is done on purpose)If you like sci-fi, puzzles, blade runner, cyborgs, horror and challenging games with original story, then go for it!10/10
_childDocuments_.name: System Shock

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of those rare games that gives me that warm and fuzzy feeling of exploring the unknown with no sense of direction that I got when I was a kid playing games. I'm not sure if it was the games that changed or I did growing up but man, this remake really does take me back to a different time with games. Absolutely adore this. This has launched into my top 10 list already, easily.
